sections.heading: Introduction: The End-Times Call — Are You Ready?
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning.

In the small hours of 15 April 1912, on the surface of the North Atlantic, a great liner they called “unsinkable” was going down. On her maiden voyage the Titanic struck an iceberg, and two hours and forty minutes later she sank to the bottom of the sea; more than fifteen hundred people died. The most heartbreaking detail is not the iceberg but the reaction on board. After the alarm had sounded, the band in the lounge played on and the first-class cabins stayed brilliantly lit. Some passengers, when they were asked to go up on deck and put on life jackets, were still grumbling, sure it was nothing but a tiresome drill. It was not that they never heard the warning. They heard it, and they did not believe it. And the most luxurious ship in the world carried lifeboats for only half the people on board.

Brothers and sisters, doesn’t today’s world look a lot like that ship?

The footsteps of Jesus’ return are drawing near. The exact day and hour we cannot know; the Lord himself said so very plainly: “But no one knows of that day and hour, not even the angels of heaven, but my Father only.” (Matthew 24:36) Yet the Lord also rebuked those who could read the sky but could not read the times. Looking at the turmoil among the nations, the collapse of moral standards and the constant run of disasters, natural and man-made, all of us share the same sense in our hearts — he is right at the door.

In Matthew 25 the Lord Jesus told a parable. Ten virgins took their lamps and went out to meet the bridegroom. Five were wise and five were foolish. The foolish took their lamps but brought no oil; the wise took their lamps and also took oil in their jars. While the bridegroom was delayed, they all grew drowsy and slept. At midnight there was a cry: “Behold! The bridegroom is coming! Come out to meet him!” Then Scripture goes on: “Those who were ready went in with him to the wedding feast, and the door was shut.” (Matthew 25:10)

Notice the details of this parable. All ten were virgins, all ten carried lamps, all ten were waiting, and all ten fell asleep. The difference between them came down to one thing — whether or not they were ready. At the end of the parable the Lord said, “Watch therefore, for you don’t know the day nor the hour in which the Son of Man is coming.” (Matthew 25:13)

So revival is not an emotional meeting, not a moving sermon, not a lively conference. Revival is a life of reverence and readiness.

And in these last days God has issued his people a call that could not be clearer or more urgent:

“Come out of her, my people, that you have no participation in her sins, and that you don’t receive of her plagues,” (Revelation 18:4)

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully to whom these words are spoken. They are not shouted to the Gentiles, not to people who do not know God. They are called out to “my people” — to God’s own people, to you and to me.

God is calling us to come out of “that city”. And who is that city? That city is Babylon.

Today we will look at four things together. What exactly is Babylon? Where did it come from? Where is it today? And how are we to come out of it?

sections.heading: Scripture Background: The Setting of Revelation 18
sections.html:
To understand the call of Revelation 18:4, we first need to stand beside the man who wrote the book.

First, the author and the date. Revelation was written by John, the disciple whom the Lord Jesus loved. The earliest witnesses of church history, such as the second-century church father Irenaeus, place John’s writing of Revelation around AD 95, towards the end of the reign of the Roman emperor Domitian. By then John was an old man, exiled on the island of Patmos for preaching God’s word and bearing witness to Jesus (Revelation 1:9).

Second, the readers and their situation. Revelation was written to seven churches in Asia Minor — Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia and Laodicea. These seven churches lived under the shadow of the Roman Empire. Rome required its people to burn incense before the emperor’s image and to call Caesar lord. Those who refused might, at best, lose their business or their job, and at worst be thrown into prison or martyred. At the same time Rome used its other hand to seduce the church — the glitter of trade, the banquets of the trade guilds, meat sacrificed in idol temples, a climate of moral licence. So the seven churches faced persecution with one hand and assimilation with the other: a lion on one side, honey on the other.

Third, the context. Revelation 17 and 18 belong together. Chapter 17 uses the vision of “the great prostitute” to describe the nature of this system; chapter 18 announces its end. The angel said to John, “Come here. I will show you the judgment of the great prostitute who sits on many waters, with whom the kings of the earth committed sexual immorality. Those who dwell in the earth were made drunken with the wine of her sexual immorality.” (Revelation 17:1–2) Then in chapter 18 another angel with great authority comes down from heaven, the earth is lit up with his glory, and he cries out with a mighty voice: “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great, and she has become a habitation of demons, a prison of every unclean spirit, and a prison of every unclean and hateful bird!” (Revelation 18:2)

Right after that, verse 3 explains why she fell: “For all the nations have drunk of the wine of the wrath of her sexual immorality, the kings of the earth committed sexual immorality with her, and the merchants of the earth grew rich from the abundance of her luxury.” (Revelation 18:3) Notice the three groups of people here: nations, kings and merchants — politics, power and the economy, all of them swept up in it. Then verse 5 adds: “For her sins have reached to the sky, and God has remembered her iniquities.” (Revelation 18:5)

And verse 4 is driven like a blade between the sentence and the lament: “Come out of her, my people.” Before God’s judgment falls, God first gives his people a way out. This is how God has always worked. Noah’s ark was prepared before the flood; the Passover blood was put on the doorposts before the destroying angel passed through; Lot was taken by the hand by the angels before the fire and brimstone fell. Before judgment, grace sends out the call.

Fourth, the Babylon of history. The “Babylon” John writes about was not a living city in his day. The historical city of Babylon reached its height under Nebuchadnezzar II (who reigned 605–562 BC). Its walls were massive and its palaces magnificent; tradition even placed the Hanging Gardens, one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world, within it. The Greek historian Herodotus, in his Histories, describes Babylon’s walls as wide enough for chariots to run side by side along the top. Later scholars think his figures are exaggerated, but they show at least one thing: in the minds of the ancient world, Babylon was a byword for splendour and might. Yet in 539 BC Cyrus, king of Persia, took the city in a single night. By John’s day Babylon had long lain desolate.

So when John wrote “Babylon the great”, his first-century readers understood at once: he meant Rome. But the inspiration of the Holy Spirit reaches far beyond Rome. Rome would pass away; the spirit of Babylon would not. From Babel to Babylon, from Babylon to Rome, from Rome to today, the system that says “let’s make a name for ourselves” and breaks free of God’s rule has kept changing its clothes, but never once changed its nature.

That is why Revelation 18:4 still speaks to us today. Brothers and sisters, this word has not yet expired.

sections.heading: Key Point 1: Babylon Is Not a City but a System
sections.html:
“He cried with a mighty voice, saying, ‘Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great, and she has become a habitation of demons, a prison of every unclean spirit, and a prison of every unclean and hateful bird!’” (Revelation 18:2)

Brothers and sisters, if Babylon were only a city, this verse would have been completely fulfilled back in 539 BC, and reading it today would be nothing more than reading a piece of history. But Revelation tells us this city is a mystery. Scripture itself says: “And on her forehead a name was written, ‘MYSTERY, BABYLON THE GREAT, THE MOTHER OF THE PROSTITUTES AND OF THE ABOMINATIONS OF THE EARTH.’” (Revelation 17:5)

The Greek word for “mystery” is mystērion: something once hidden and now revealed. In other words, the Holy Spirit is telling us plainly here: don’t stop at the literal city walls; see the spiritual reality behind them. Babylon is not an address; Babylon is a system. It is not a pile of bricks but a logic; not a dot on the map but the core program on which the world runs.

This system bears three clear marks.

The first mark is seduction. “With whom the kings of the earth committed sexual immorality. Those who dwell in the earth were made drunken with the wine of her sexual immorality.” (Revelation 17:2) Notice that word — “drunken”. Babylon doesn’t force you at sword point; it invites you with a wine cup. A sword puts people on their guard; wine puts them in a good mood. The chief mark of a drunk person is not that he can’t stand straight but that he doesn’t know he’s drunk. Brothers and sisters, this is the most frightening thing about Babylon: it doesn’t kidnap you; it buys you a drink.

The second mark is trade. “The merchants of the earth grew rich from the abundance of her luxury.” (Revelation 18:3) Babylon is a gigantic marketplace that puts a price tag on everything.

The third mark is the most chilling of all. Revelation 18 sets out Babylon’s cargo list: “merchandise of gold, silver, precious stones, pearls … and cinnamon, incense, perfume, frankincense, wine, olive oil, fine flour, wheat, sheep, horses, chariots, and people’s bodies and souls.” (Revelation 18:12–13) Listen to the last item on that list: people’s bodies and souls. In Babylon’s ledger, human beings are listed after the horses. That is the nature of this system — it turns people, created by God and bearing God’s image, into goods to be bought and sold. Wherever people are treated as a means to an end, wherever things are counted as more important than people, there you will catch the smell of Babylon.

I often use a picture to describe this system. Brothers and sisters, have you ever looked up at the night sky in a big city? You can hardly see a single star. Have the stars disappeared? No. Not one star is missing; the city lights are simply too bright. Astronomers call this “light pollution” — artificial light from the ground scatters through the atmosphere and drowns out the faint light of the stars. But drive two hours out of the city, up into the mountains, switch off your headlights and look up, and the whole sky is full of stars. They are there. They were always there.

The Babylonian system is light pollution in the spiritual world. It doesn’t need to deny God. All it has to do is turn the lights on earth up bright enough, and you can no longer see the God of heaven. It doesn’t need to argue with you about the Bible. All it has to do is keep you too busy, too tired, with too much information and too many choices, and your heart will never again be still.

Psychology also confirms the power such a system has to assimilate people. In 1951 the social psychologist Solomon Asch carried out his famous conformity experiment at Swarthmore College. He asked participants to compare the lengths of several lines — an answer so easy it was almost impossible to get wrong. But he planted several fake participants who gave obviously wrong answers first. The result: about three-quarters of the real participants, at least once, went along with the group and gave an answer they could plainly see was wrong. Brothers and sisters, remember that figure: not one in four, but three in four. A system doesn’t need to persuade you. It only needs to leave you standing alone, and you will change your answer by yourself.

As early as the fifth century, the church father Augustine, in The City of God, saw the whole of human history as the story of two cities. Two cities, he said, have been built by two loves: the earthly city by the love of self, even to the contempt of God; the heavenly city by the love of God, even to the contempt of self. Sixteen hundred years have passed, and humanity still has only these two choices.

This is the very heart of the 321 vision: Babylon is a system, so God’s answer must also be a system. You can’t fight a complete system with scattered resolutions. God’s intention is not that we live by Babylon’s logic while squeezing out a little time to worship. God’s intention is to establish God’s system on earth — with Jesus as our role model, the Bible as our standard and the Holy Spirit as our guide, letting Jesus be King and letting Jesus receive all the glory. A system can only be replaced by another system.

sections.heading: Key Point 2: The Tower of Babel — the Source of the Babylonian System
sections.html:
To understand Babylon, we have to go back to where it was born. The first time Scripture mentions this name is in Genesis 11.

“The whole earth was of one language and of one speech. As they traveled from the east, they found a plain in the land of Shinar, and they lived there. They said to one another, ‘Come, let’s make bricks, and burn them thoroughly.’ They had brick for stone, and they used tar for mortar. They said, ‘Come, let’s build ourselves a city, and a tower whose top reaches to the sky, and let’s make a name for ourselves, lest we be scattered abroad on the surface of the whole earth.’” (Genesis 11:1–4)

Brothers and sisters, look carefully at the four “us” and “we” phrases in this passage: let’s make bricks, let’s build ourselves, let’s make a name for ourselves, lest we be scattered. This is the first humanist manifesto in human history. In the whole speech God is not mentioned once.

Their problem was not their building technique but their attitude. In Genesis 1:28 God had commanded humankind: “Be fruitful, multiply, fill the earth, and subdue it.” (Genesis 1:28) God said, “Fill the earth”; people said, “Lest we be scattered abroad on the surface of the whole earth.” God said go; people said we won’t. God said spread out; people said gather together. This was no misunderstanding. This was open defiance.

There is another detail well worth noticing: “They had brick for stone, and they used tar for mortar.” (Genesis 11:3) Stones are made by God, and no two are alike; bricks are made by people, and every one is identical. From its very first day the Babylonian system has been doing the same thing — taking people whom God made one of a kind and firing them into uniform bricks that can be stacked high. How many people today live like bricks: the same definition of success, the same ways of comparing, the same anxiety, the same emptiness — and then they are stacked into a tower they never wanted to build.

And the outcome? “Therefore its name was called Babel, because there Yahweh confused the language of all the earth. From there, Yahweh scattered them abroad on the surface of all the earth.” (Genesis 11:9)

There is a beautiful play on words here. The Hebrew for “Babel” is Bābel, and the verb “to confuse” is bālal. The two words sound alike. More interesting still, in the local Akkadian language, Bāb-ili means “the gate of god”. Do you see it? People named their city “the gate of god”, and God’s verdict on it was “confusion”. People thought they were building a gate to heaven; God said, what you are building is chaos.

From Babel to Babylon, the nature of this system has never changed: it wants people to break free of God’s sovereignty and live under their own control.

This proud heart is laid bare in Isaiah 14. The chapter begins, “You will take up this parable against the king of Babylon, and say …” (Isaiah 14:4) And then come these words: “You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! I will sit on the mountain of assembly, in the far north! I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!’” (Isaiah 14:13–14)

Five times, “I will”. Brothers and sisters, this is the anatomy of pride. Pride is not merely feeling good about yourself. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place. Its core sentence is always “I will”.

History gives us a living example. The book of Daniel records how King Nebuchadnezzar, walking on the roof of his royal palace, said these words: “Is not this great Babylon, which I have built for the royal dwelling place, by the might of my power and for the glory of my majesty?” (Daniel 4:30) The words were still in his mouth when God’s judgment fell. He was driven away from people and ate grass like an ox until seven times had passed over him. When at last he lifted his eyes to heaven and his understanding returned, the first thing he said was: “Now I, Nebuchadnezzar, praise and extol and honor the King of heaven; for all his works are truth, and his ways justice; and those who walk in pride he is able to abase.” (Daniel 4:37)

C. S. Lewis says in Mere Christianity that pride leads to every other vice; it is the complete anti-God state of mind. He reminds us that what makes pride so terrible is this: the prouder a person is, the less he can see his own pride.

Brothers and sisters, the 321 vision puts it plainly: the problem of the old self is the self-centred life; the self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of every problem. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.

So dealing with Babylon is not about changing your surroundings; it is about changing your heart. Because the Tower of Babel was not built in the land of Shinar. The Tower of Babel is built in the human heart.

sections.heading: Key Point 3: Today’s Babylon — a World System Full of Temptation
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, we no longer fire bricks or build towers today. But please don’t imagine that work on the Tower of Babel has stopped.

Today we build brands, build personas, build communities, build platforms, build data. The tools have all changed; the motive hasn’t changed by a single word — “let’s make a name for ourselves” (Genesis 11:4). The ancient tower was stacked high with bricks; today’s tower is stacked high with followers, likes and click-through rates. People back then were afraid of being “scattered abroad on the surface of the whole earth”; people today are afraid of being forgotten by the algorithm. This is the modern version of the Babylonian system.

According to the Digital 2024 report published by DataReportal, there are now more than five billion social media user identities worldwide. Never before in human history have so many people stood at the same time on one invisible tower, straining to be seen.

The question is, has this tower made people any happier? In 2012 Hui-Tzu Grace Chou and Nicholas Edge published a study in the journal Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social Networking. They found that the longer people used Facebook, the more inclined they were to believe that “others are doing better than I am, and are happier than I am”. That is Babylon’s wine. You raise your glass to celebrate, but what you swallow is comparison. You step onto the stage to be seen, and you step off feeling even more that you are not enough.

Let’s look at another study. In 2010 the Nobel laureate Daniel Kahneman and Angus Deaton published a Princeton analysis in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. They found that rising income does raise people’s overall evaluation of their lives, but emotional well-being stops rising with income beyond a certain threshold. Money can buy a taller tower; it cannot buy a deeper peace.

So what is Babylon? Let’s honestly translate it into today’s language:

When we compromise our values for the sake of clicks, that is Babylon.

When the church abandons truth for the sake of growth, that is Babylon.

When the focus of our faith shifts from God to ourselves, that is Babylon.

Brothers and sisters, the most sobering of these is the second. The Babylonian system is not just the world’s problem; it has quietly slipped into the church. Without realising it, we treat ministry success as glorifying God, numbers and influence as signs of blessing, applause on the platform as approval from heaven — and in the process we lose our simple reverence for the Lord.

The Lord Jesus said something to the church in Laodicea that sends a chill down the spine: “Because you say, ‘I am rich, and have gotten riches, and have need of nothing;’ and don’t know that you are the wretched one, miserable, poor, blind, and naked.” (Revelation 3:17) Notice that these words were not spoken to the world; they were spoken to a church. Their self-assessment was “need of nothing”; the Lord’s assessment was “wretched, miserable, poor, blind, and naked”. Two reports — how could they be further apart?

Then the Lord said the words we all know so well: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, then I will come in to him, and will dine with him, and he with me.” (Revelation 3:20) Brothers and sisters, the most heartbreaking thing about this verse is not the “knock” but where he is standing — outside. The meetings go on as usual, the offerings are still collected, the worship songs are still sung, but the Lord is outside the door. That is what it looks like when Babylon has got into the church.

The apostle John drew the anatomy of this system very clearly: “Don’t love the world or the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the Father’s love isn’t in him. For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, isn’t the Father’s, but is the world’s. The world is passing away with its lusts, but he who does God’s will remains forever.” (1 John 2:15–17)

The lust of the flesh — I want it. The lust of the eyes — I see that others have it. The pride of life — I must be better than others. Brothers and sisters, aren’t these the very three cups of wine Babylon hands us to drink?

Here the 321 vision gives us a very practical measuring rod: a shift of perspective — from the human perspective to God’s perspective, from the earthly perspective to the heavenly, from the temporary perspective to the eternal, from the worldly perspective to the godly. Paul says, “Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth.” (Colossians 3:2) And again: “while we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.” (2 Corinthians 4:18)

So every day we need to ask ourselves one question: this thing I’m pursuing right now — is it to make my name great, or his? Brothers and sisters, the question is simple, but it cuts to the bone. For Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not others, not our circumstances. The moment the focus shifts, the system changes.

sections.heading: Key Point 4: Coming Out of Babylon Is Where Revival Begins
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, as you listen to this, some of you may be getting anxious. Does this mean I should quit my job? Delete all my social media accounts? Move up into the mountains?

No. God is not telling us to run away from the world. God is calling us to come out of this system — to be in the world but not of the world.

On the night he was betrayed, the Lord Jesus prayed for his disciples: “I pray not that you would take them from the world, but that you would keep them from the evil one. They are not of the world even as I am not of the world.” (John 17:15–16) Look at those two sentences. He does not ask that they be taken “from the world”, only that they be “not of the world”. A boat can be in the water, but the water must not be in the boat. A boat in the water is just doing what boats do; once the water gets into the boat, it sinks.

The call to “come out” is a scarlet thread running through the whole of Scripture. God said to Abram: “Leave your country, and your relatives, and your father’s house, and go to the land that I will show you.” (Genesis 12:1) Through Isaiah God said: “Leave Babylon! Flee from the Chaldeans! With a voice of singing announce this, tell it even to the end of the earth: say, ‘Yahweh has redeemed his servant Jacob!’” (Isaiah 48:20) Through Jeremiah God said: “Flee out of the middle of Babylon! Everyone save his own life! Don’t be cut off in her iniquity.” (Jeremiah 51:6) And Paul quotes it too: “‘Come out from among them, and be separate,’ says the Lord. ‘Touch no unclean thing. I will receive you.’” (2 Corinthians 6:17)

From Genesis to Revelation, God’s call has always been the same word: come out.

So what does “come out” actually mean?

Brothers and sisters, it is not a change of location; it is a transfer of sovereignty over your life. It is turning from “I want, I can, I like” back to “Lord, your will be done.”

Our Lord walked this road himself. In Gethsemane, “He went forward a little, fell on his face, and prayed, saying, ‘My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass away from me; nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire.’” (Matthew 26:39) Brothers and sisters, notice the turning word — “nevertheless”. The whole door of salvation swung open on that one word. In the heart of the king of Babylon were five “I will”s; in the Garden of Gethsemane there was only “not what I desire”.

Paul speaks of this as an accomplished fact: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20)

The 321 vision calls this selflessness. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the boundless and living out the boundless — “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. Humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan.

The finest example in Scripture is Daniel. Brothers and sisters, have you ever considered that Daniel really did live in Babylon? He was taken captive as a youth, given a new name, sent into the palace and taught the language and literature of the Chaldeans. He spent his whole life as an official at the Babylonian court, serving Nebuchadnezzar, Belshazzar, Darius and Cyrus in turn. His body never left Babylon, yet his heart never belonged to Babylon for a single day. Where was the turning point? At a meal: “But Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the king’s dainties, nor with the wine which he drank.” (Daniel 1:8)

Coming out of Babylon often begins with a single meal, a single decision, a single word you refuse to say.

His three friends were the same. Facing the blazing furnace, they said: “But if not, let it be known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods or worship the golden image which you have set up.” (Daniel 3:18) “But if not” — if God saves me, I will worship him; if God does not save me, I will still worship him. Brothers and sisters, those three words are the proof that a person has already come out of Babylon. For every good thing Babylon offers comes as a deal with conditions attached, and faith is not a deal.

The German pastor and martyr Dietrich Bonhoeffer wrote a famous line in The Cost of Discipleship: when Christ calls a man, he bids him come and die. It sounds severe, but it is in fact the greatest grace — what dies is the old self that Babylon had kidnapped, and what lives is the new self, free in Christ.

That is why the 321 vision says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. The order of change is fivefold — a change of mindset brings a change of life; a change of life brings a change of daily living; a change of daily living brings a change of relationships; and only when relationships change is there genuine ministry. Babylon’s way is exactly the reverse: it starts with ministry and uses results to prove life. No wonder so many who serve are worn out and dried up.

Brothers and sisters, coming out of Babylon is the first step of every spiritual revival. Not the second step, not the third step — the first. Because to let Jesus be King, we must first step down from the throne ourselves.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, when we set this lesson within the 321 framework, we see a complete picture.

Babylon is a system, and God’s answer is also a system. This is the “1” of 321 — the Goal: establish God’s system.

This system has the Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. Babylon’s three foundations are exactly the opposite: I am my own role model, the trend is my standard, my feelings are my guide. Brothers and sisters, see this clearly — the difference between the two systems is not in their outward form but in their foundations underneath.

This system has the Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. The core of the Tower of Babel was “let’s make a name for ourselves”; the core of God’s system is “may your name be kept holy” (Matthew 6:9). Babylon wants human beings to be king; God’s system lets Jesus be King. One day “the kingdom of the world has become the Kingdom of our Lord, and of his Christ. He will reign forever and ever!” (Revelation 11:15) All we are doing today is handing the throne back to him ahead of time.

Now look at the most crucial line of all: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of every problem. The Tower of Babel is a monument to the self-centred life; the cross is the sign of selflessness. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. Humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan.

Next, look at the order of change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. That is why today’s lesson started with mindset — if you don’t first see that Babylon is a system, all you will ever do is patch up your behaviour. Life first, then relationships, then ministry; people matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things. The priority of relationships must not be turned upside down either: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things. Babylon turns this order completely on its head — get the job done first, worry about relationships later, and remember God last of all. That is why the more successful people in Babylon become, the lonelier they are.

Then look at the shift of perspective: from the human to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. These four shifts are four doors out of Babylon.

In practical terms, this lesson is especially suited to “920”. The 9 is the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23) The 2 is every person I am in relationship with; the 0 is selflessness. Every day, towards the “2” right beside me, I live out the life of the “0” and bear the fruit of the “9” — that is how, in the most ordinary places, we walk out of Babylon one step at a time.

And when we no longer walk alone, we enter into “235” relationships: becoming a “2” with someone selfless, spiritual companions to one another; building the “3”, the heritage of spiritual parents and spiritual children; and finally becoming the “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades working hand in hand. Brothers and sisters, one person can escape Babylon, but only a system can replace Babylon.

Finally there is the Path of Serving: Spirit → Understanding → Life → Service → God. The Holy Spirit is my guide — that is Spirit. The Bible is my standard — that is Understanding. Jesus is my role model — that is Life. Let Jesus be King — that is Service. Let Jesus receive all the glory — that is God. When we have walked these five steps, we have walked into the longing of the Lord’s Prayer: “Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.” (Matthew 6:10)

And one more very practical reminder: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’re glad, rely on the brain and you worry. For “out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23). What Babylon does best is move our faith from the heart to the head, turning it into knowledge, into argument, into performance. Coming out of Babylon means moving our faith back into the heart.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Three Daily Steps Out of Babylon
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, truth that never touches the ground remains just a feeling. Here are three practices you can do every single day.

Practice 1: Hand Back Sovereignty Every Day

In your early-morning prayer, say to the Lord: “Lord, I hand you the right to make today’s decisions. Not according to my will, but according to your heart.”

An illustration: it’s like handing over the steering wheel. So often we invite Jesus into the car but sit him in the passenger seat. We drive; he navigates. And when he points the way, we even say, “I know this road better.” Handing back sovereignty means getting out, changing seats and letting Jesus truly take the wheel.

The scriptural ground for this is the Lord’s own prayer: “nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire.” (Matthew 26:39) And the psalmist’s reminder: “Unless Yahweh builds the house, they who build it labor in vain.” (Psalm 127:1) Brothers and sisters, we would rather build a small house that God has built than a tall tower raised in vain labour.

Practice 2: Recognise Babylon’s Voice Every Day

Watch the information you take in each day — social media, news, your WeChat Moments, advertising — and ask yourself: Is this message exalting self? Is it stirring up comparison? Is it encouraging showing off and pleasure-seeking? Then, with courage, let God’s word redefine what “good” means, what “success” means, and what is “worth it”.

An illustration: it’s like picking out the Lord’s voice in the middle of noise. We need to learn to put this world’s channel on “mute” and tune our frequency to “Kingdom Radio”. The Lord says: “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.” (John 10:27) Elijah learned the same lesson at Horeb. A great wind blew, but Yahweh was not in the wind; after the wind an earthquake, but Yahweh was not in the earthquake; after the earthquake a fire, but Yahweh was not in the fire; “after the fire, there was a still small voice” (1 Kings 19:12). Brothers and sisters, Babylon is always the loudest voice; God’s voice is often the quietest. That is why we need stillness every day.

Practice 3: Choose One Selfless Step Every Day

In one small matter, deliberately lay down self-centredness and choose to serve, to obey or to forgive. Give up a seat; pray for a colleague; forgive a family member for a hurtful remark; admit one of your own mistakes.

An illustration: every act of denying ourselves is one step back from the Babylonian system and one step forward into the territory of God’s kingdom. The Lord said, “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.” (Luke 9:23) The Chinese Union Version here reads “take up his cross daily” — notice that word: daily.

Taking the Practices Deeper with the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset

The 321 vision teaches us that a change of mindset passes through eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Let’s use these eight stages to turn the three practices above into a lifelong discipline.

1. Information: You have already received it today. You now know that Babylon is a system, not a city.

2. Revelation: Ask the Holy Spirit to turn this information into revelation for you. Pray: Lord, show me where Babylon is in my life. Information goes into the head; revelation goes into the heart.

3. Conviction: Be truly persuaded in your heart, and willing to obey. Conviction is not just saying, “What a great sermon.” It is saying, “Lord, I yield.”

4. Implementation: Starting tomorrow morning, put the three practices into action. Don’t wait until you understand it all before you begin; understand it as you act.

5. Evaluation: Every evening, be still for three minutes and ask yourself: At what moment today did I live by Babylon’s logic? At what moment did I let Jesus be King?

6. Correction: Don’t condemn yourself; adjust yourself. Failure is not the end; failure is data.

7. Repetition: This is the most crucial stage. A research team led by Phillippa Lally at University College London published a study in 2010 showing that it takes, on average, sixty-six days for a person to form a new automatic habit, with wide variation between individuals. Neuroscience also tells us that the brain has neuroplasticity — neurons that fire together wire together. Brothers and sisters, this is the scientific basis for Repetition: every time you choose selflessness, you lay down another inch of new road in your life.

8. Multiplication: Pass on what you have received to the next person. Find a spiritual companion and practise together; then take on a spiritual child and teach them what you have learned. When one person comes out of Babylon, we call it salvation; when a whole community comes out of Babylon, we call it revival.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: Starting with Me, Starting Today
sections.html:
Dear family, coming out of Babylon doesn’t mean waiting for the world to get better before we act. It begins with a heart — yours and mine — that is willing to turn back.

This age is pressing us to take sides. Will we choose worldly glory, or God’s kingdom? Revival is not some future wave; revival is the choice you make today.

The Lord Jesus told the church in Laodicea that he stands at the door and knocks. Brothers and sisters, the handle is on the inside. God will not kick your door in. He only knocks, and then he waits.

Let us answer this call together: “Come out of her, my people.” (Revelation 18:4)

Come out in your heart — no longer letting yourself sit on the throne of your heart.

Come out in your daily living — no longer letting your calendar decide your priorities.

Come out in your values — no longer measuring yourself with Babylon’s ruler, nor measuring others with it either.

Brothers and sisters, Babylon will fall; that is the ending Scripture has already declared. That being so, why stake your whole life’s savings on a city that is doomed to fall? The Lord Jesus said: “For what will it profit a man, if he gains the whole world, and forfeits his life? Or what will a man give in exchange for his life?” (Matthew 16:26)

Today, beginning this very morning: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory.

keyVerses: “I heard another voice from heaven, saying, ‘Come out of her, my people, that you have no participation in her sins, and that you don’t receive of her plagues.’” (Revelation 18:4)
practices: Hand back sovereignty every day
Recognise Babylon’s voice every day
Choose one selfless step every day
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,
We thank you that before judgment is pronounced, you first open a door for your people. You say, “Come out of her, my people.”

Lord, we confess that Babylon is not only in the world but in our hearts. We too have laboured to make a name for ourselves; we too have drunk the wine of comparison and showing off; we too have invited you into the car but not let you take the wheel. Forgive us, we pray.

Holy Spirit, shine your light on us and show us the piece of ground in our lives we have not yet handed over. Give us Daniel’s resolve, to purpose in our hearts, even in the king’s palace, not to defile ourselves; give us the faith of his three friends, to say “But if not” and still worship you.
Lord, exchange the “I will” inside us for your “not what I desire, but what you desire”. Let it be no longer we who live, but Christ who lives in us.
Use us, together with our brothers and sisters, to establish God’s system. Reign as King in our homes, reign as King in our workplaces, reign as King in our church, until you come again.
May all the glory be yours. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Revelation 18:4 says: “Come out of her, my people, that you have no participation in her sins, and that you don’t receive of her plagues.” In your life right now, what most represents “Babylon’s voice” (for example, a particular platform, a particular kind of comparison, a particular standard of success)? From what specific thing is God calling you to “come out” today?

Matthew 26:39 says: “nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire.” Is there a decision this week that you have been wanting to make your own way? If you handed the steering wheel to Jesus now, what would you do? Name one concrete action, and ask the brothers and sisters in your small group to pray for you and hold you accountable this week.
