sections.heading: Introduction: A Battlefield on a Spreadsheet
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Let me begin with a kind of morning many of us have lived through.

A sister works as an accountant at her company. The day before the quarter closes, her manager slides the report back across her desk and says, in the most relaxed of tones, “Just nudge this column up a little. We’ll make it up next quarter anyway. Everybody does it.” He doesn’t pound the table. He doesn’t threaten her. He even smiles and makes her a cup of coffee. In that moment she notices her heart racing and her palms going damp. And suddenly she understands something: this is not an argument about numbers. This is a war over “who is King in my life.”

Brothers and sisters, Babylon is not some ancient city far away, not a heap of broken walls in a museum. Babylon is a system that is still running. It has its values: success ranks above faithfulness. It has its rewards and punishments: those who play along get promoted, those who don’t get pushed out. It has its worship: the worship of money, of power, of reputation, of self. And its greatest skill is not forcing you at sword-point. It is convenience, fitting in, the warmth of a cup of coffee — slowly assimilating you.

In our last lesson we heard together the call from heaven: “Come out of her, my people, that you have no participation in her sins, and that you don’t receive of her plagues” (Revelation 18:4). We said “Amen,” and we decided to come out of Babylon. But the moment we step out the front door, we still ride the same metro, walk into the same office and face the same manager. And so a very practical question rises in our hearts —

Once I’ve come out, then what? I still live in this world. How am I supposed to live?

That is exactly the question today’s lesson answers: how to overcome the Babylonian system.

Notice that the Bible does not tell us to “flee” the world. When the Lord Jesus prayed for his disciples before going to Gethsemane, he said it plainly: “I pray not that you would take them from the world, but that you would keep them from the evil one” (John 17:15). God does not intend to move us out of Babylon. God intends, right inside Babylon, to form a people who do not belong to Babylon.

Scripture already has a ready-made model of such a person. His name is Daniel.

In 605 BC, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon besieged Jerusalem for the first time. The Bible records: “In the third year of the reign of Jehoiakim king of Judah Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came to Jerusalem and besieged it” (Daniel 1:1). That year a teenage boy was marched more than a thousand kilometres to the most splendid and the proudest city in the world of his day. They changed his name, changed his textbooks, assigned him food from the king’s table and trained him as a civil servant of the empire. Babylon gave itself three years to turn a Hebrew boy into a Babylonian.

And the result? Babylon did not change Daniel; Daniel changed Babylon. He lived through four reigns — Nebuchadnezzar, Belshazzar, Darius and Cyrus — from boyhood to white hair, serving for nearly seventy years. He lived in Babylon, yet he did not belong to Babylon. He lived inside a pagan system, yet that system never absorbed him. He was no deserter; he was the light and salt of his generation.

Brothers and sisters, can we be like Daniel?

Yes, we can. And the Bible has distilled the secret of victory into a single verse — just three phrases, yet three keys. That is our theme verse today, Revelation 12:11.

sections.heading: 1. Scripture Background: A Letter to Churches Under Pressure
sections.html:
Before we open the three keys, let’s first stand where this verse originally stood and see the circumstances in which it was written. For a verse only gives off its original light when it is put back into its context.

1. Author, date and recipients

The author of Revelation is the apostle John. He says of himself: “I John, your brother and partner with you in the oppression, Kingdom, and perseverance in Christ Jesus, was on the isle that is called Patmos because of God’s Word and the testimony of Jesus Christ” (Revelation 1:9). Patmos was a bleak little island in the Aegean Sea, a place where the Roman Empire banished political prisoners. Church tradition and most evangelical scholars generally hold that Revelation was written around AD 95, near the end of the reign of the emperor Domitian.

The letter was addressed to seven churches in Asia Minor — Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia and Laodicea (Revelation 1:11). These were not seven churches theorising on paper. These were seven churches living under real pressure.

2. The historical and cultural setting: trade, guilds and emperor worship

First, there was religious pressure. Rome promoted emperor worship. Citizens had to offer a pinch of incense before the emperor’s image and declare, “Caesar is Lord.” To Romans this was merely a patriotic ritual. For Christians it was a life-or-death choice — because we acknowledge only one Lord.

Second, there was economic pressure. Every trade in Asia Minor had its guild, every guild had its patron god, and joining meant taking part in sacrificial banquets. If you didn’t join, you didn’t get the business. Revelation 13 captures this pressure vividly: “He causes all, the small and the great, the rich and the poor, and the free and the slave, to be given marks on their right hands, or on their foreheads; and that no one would be able to buy or to sell, unless he has that mark, which is the name of the beast or the number of his name” (Revelation 13:16–17).

Brothers and sisters, did you hear it? “No one would be able to buy or to sell” — that is not a knife at your throat; that is your livelihood taken away. The Babylonian system’s favourite weapon has never been the execution ground. It is “you’ll lose your opportunity.”

Third, there was social pressure. Those who held to their faith were seen as antisocial, tactless, killjoys, trouble.

So when John cried out “Babylon the great,” first-century readers understood at once: “Another, a second angel, followed, saying, ‘Babylon the great has fallen, which has made all the nations to drink of the wine of the wrath of her sexual immorality’” (Revelation 14:8). In Revelation, “Babylon” is not a geographical term. It is the code name for every Worldly system that opposes God, puts man at the centre and makes self into god.

And the source of that code name goes back to Genesis 11. The people of Shinar said: “Come, let’s build ourselves a city, and a tower whose top reaches to the sky, and let’s make a name for ourselves, lest we be scattered abroad on the surface of the whole earth” (Genesis 11:4). Notice those words — “let’s make a name for ourselves.” The original name of Babylon, “Babel” (בָּבֶל, Bavel), meant to the locals “the gate of god,” but the Bible says: “Therefore its name was called Babel, because there Yahweh confused the language of all the earth. From there, Yahweh scattered them abroad on the surface of all the earth” (Genesis 11:9). The Hebrew word for “confused” is בָּלַל (balal), a sound-play on “Babel.” Man wanted to build a gate to heaven; God turned it into turmoil.

This is the DNA of the Babylonian system: leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights, making a name for ourselves, wanting to replace God. In the language of 321, this is “the self-centred life.” From the moment the serpent in Eden said, “you will be like God, knowing good and evil” (Genesis 3:5), down to today’s workplaces, homes and churches, the root of the problem has never changed: pride.

3. The context: a war already fought

Now let’s zoom in on Revelation 12.

Three figures appear in this chapter: a woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet; a great red dragon with seven heads and ten horns; and a male child who is to rule all the nations with a rod of iron. The dragon waits to devour the woman’s child, but the child is caught up to God’s throne. Then war breaks out in heaven: Michael and his angels fight against the dragon, and the dragon is thrown down to the earth. The Bible plainly identifies who this dragon is: “The great dragon was thrown down, the old serpent, he who is called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world” (Revelation 12:9).

Then comes verse 10: “I heard a loud voice in heaven, saying, ‘Now the salvation, the power, and the Kingdom of our God, and the authority of his Christ has come; for the accuser of our brothers has been thrown down, who accuses them before our God day and night’” (Revelation 12:10).

Satan’s title is “the accuser.” He accuses us before God day and night, and he accuses us inside our own hearts day and night. He tells you: you’re not worthy, you’re not qualified, didn’t you compromise last time too, this is all you’ll ever be.

Right after that comes verse 11: “They overcame him because of the Lamb’s blood, and because of the word of their testimony. They didn’t love their life, even to death.”

Brothers and sisters, please notice two things.

First, the Greek word for “overcame” is νικάω (nikaō) — to win, to conquer. This word appears again and again at the close of the seven letters in Revelation: “To him who overcomes I will give to eat from the tree of life, which is in the Paradise of my God” (Revelation 2:7). To overcome is the Lord’s common call to every church and every believer.

Second, the verbs in this verse are completed, accomplished. The war in heaven is not still being fought; it is already over. The dragon has already been thrown down. Our battle today is not “fighting to win” but “standing in a victory already won.” The difference between the two is big enough to change your whole mood for the day.

So by what did they overcome him? Three things: the blood of the Lamb, the word of their testimony, and not loving their lives even to death.

One is what God has accomplished for us (the foundation of grace); one is what we live out (a genuine life); one is what we lay down (a heart unafraid of death). None of the three can be missing, and the order cannot be reversed. Now let’s take them one at a time.

sections.heading: 2. The Blood of the Lamb — the Foundation of Grace
sections.html:
“They overcame him because of the Lamb’s blood …” (Revelation 12:11)

1. Why we cannot rely on ourselves

Let’s first admit a very uncomfortable fact: we cannot overcome the Worldly system by our own willpower or strength.

The reason lies not in our circumstances but in our bloodline. Paul says: “Therefore as sin entered into the world through one man, and death through sin; so death passed to all men, because all sinned” (Romans 5:12). Within us we carry the fallen life inherited from Adam. That is not a behaviour problem; it is a life problem. You can break a bad habit by willpower, but you cannot exchange your heart by willpower.

It’s like a computer infected with a virus. You can delete a few files and close a few windows, but as long as the virus is still in the system, in a few days it grows back. What you need is not a clean-up but a complete reinstall.

To go deeper still: the problem between us and Babylon is not an “outside” problem but an “inside” one. The world can hook us only because there is a hook inside us. John puts it precisely: “For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, isn’t the Father’s, but is the world’s” (1 John 2:16). Babylon doesn’t need to kidnap you. It only needs to press the right three buttons inside you.

So the first step in overcoming Babylon is not trying harder but admitting that we can’t. This is exactly what 321 says: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem. And the first move against pride is to kneel.

2. The blood of the Lamb: the only way out

Our only way out is the precious blood of Jesus.

The Greek word for “Lamb” is ἀρνίον (arnion), originally meaning “little lamb.” It is Revelation’s favourite title for Jesus, used nearly thirty times in the book. And here is the wonder: in chapter 5, when John is weeping because no one is worthy to open the scroll, the elder tells him, “the Lion who is of the tribe of Judah … has overcome.” But when John turns to look, “I saw in the middle of the throne and of the four living creatures, and in the middle of the elders, a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain” (Revelation 5:6). The Lion overcomes by becoming the slain Lamb. That one sentence overturns the whole logic of Babylon. The world says: the strong win. The kingdom of heaven says: the one who lays down his life wins.

What has this blood accomplished?

First, a ransom. “Knowing that you were redeemed, not with corruptible things, with silver or gold, from the useless way of life handed down from your fathers, but with precious blood, as of a lamb without blemish or spot, the blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:18–19). Notice “the useless way of life handed down from your fathers” — that is exactly what the system passes down. The precious blood doesn’t only forgive your sins; it cuts the umbilical cord between you and that system.

Second, forgiveness. “According to the law, nearly everything is cleansed with blood, and apart from shedding of blood there is no remission” (Hebrews 9:22).

Third, cleansing. “But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus Christ, his Son, cleanses us from all sin” (1 John 1:7).

Fourth, a new identity. The song of the Lamb goes like this: “for you were killed, and bought us for God with your blood out of every tribe, language, people, and nation, and made us kings and priests to our God, and we will reign on the earth” (Revelation 5:9–10). You have been bought back. You are no longer Babylon’s property; you are God’s own possession.

Brothers and sisters, this point is crucial: when Satan the accuser comes to you, you don’t need to argue with him about how good you are — you can’t win that argument, because most of what he says is true. You only need to point to the cross and say: this debt has already been paid.

3. A scientific side-light: what blood does

God did not choose “blood” as the sign of salvation at random. “For the life of the flesh is in the blood” (Leviticus 17:11).

Physiologically, this sentence, written more than three thousand years ago, is astonishingly accurate. An adult carries about five litres of blood, and the heart beats about a hundred thousand times a day. The blood at once delivers oxygen and nutrients, carries away waste and mobilises white blood cells against invaders. Any cell cut off from the bloodstream soon dies.

The precious blood does these same three things: it carries the life of Christ into us, it carries away sin and filth, and it resists the evil one. And blood is only useful when it “circulates” — the precious blood is not a picture hanging on the wall; it is living water that must reach my heart every day.

4. A reminder from psychology: what people do worst is admit they’re wrong

To receive this grace, the first move is humble repentance. And that is exactly what human beings are worst at.

In 1957 the social psychologist Leon Festinger proposed the theory of “cognitive dissonance”: when a person’s actions clash with his view of himself, he feels discomfort, and the least effortful way to relieve it is often not to change the behaviour but to change the story — to find himself a reason. In their 2007 book “Mistakes Were Made (But Not by Me),” the social psychologists Carol Tavris & Elliot Aronson called this mechanism “self-justification”: almost automatically, before we are even aware of it, we have already acquitted ourselves.

Brothers and sisters, this is why confession is so hard. It isn’t that we don’t know we’re wrong; it’s that we explain ourselves too quickly. “Everybody does it.” “I had no choice.” “Compared with others, I’m not too bad.” Those few sentences are the passes Babylon issues us.

The remedy the Bible gives is startlingly simple: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9). The Greek word for “confess” is ὁμολογέω (homologeō), which literally means “to say the same thing” — no explanations, no discounts. Whatever God says, I say the same.

5. Three concrete actions

The lesson gives us three actions for receiving this grace, and each one is worth stopping to practise.

First, humble repentance: confess before God your pride and your self-centredness. Not in vague terms — “Lord, I’m a sinner” — but concretely: Lord, at ten o’clock this morning, in that meeting, to protect my own face, I pushed the blame onto a colleague.

Second, believe in the power of the precious blood: believe that the blood of Jesus has already overcome sin and death. Faith is not a feeling; it is a position. You don’t believe you’ve been washed because you feel clean. You believe you’ve been washed, and slowly you come to feel clean.

Third, depend on the Holy Spirit for renewal: day by day let the new life of Jesus replace the life of the old self. “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20).

The German theologian Dietrich Bonhoeffer (1906–1945), in “The Cost of Discipleship,” warns us to distinguish “cheap grace” from “costly grace.” Cheap grace is forgiveness that requires no repentance; costly grace is precious because it cost the life of God’s Son. Costly grace is what we want.

6. Applying the 321 vision: humility overcomes pride, selflessness overcomes Satan

The blood of the Lamb corresponds precisely to the very heart of the 321 message.

Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights, wanting to replace God. Humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God. The whole driving force of the Babylonian system is pride: let’s make a name for ourselves. The whole driving force of the cross is humility: though he existed in the form of God, he emptied himself and took the form of a servant (see Philippians 2:6–7).

The Bible says: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6). The very next verse says: “Be subject therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you” (James 4:7). Notice the order: first submit to God, and only then can you resist the devil. Resistance without submission is mere bravado; resistance with submission is victory.

Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. In the Babylonian system, if you answer pride with pride and hardness with hardness, you’ve already lost — because you’re already playing its game by its rules.

7. Suggested practice

Every day, declare in prayer: “I am cleansed by the precious blood of Jesus. I do not belong to Babylon; I belong to the Kingdom of God!”

Don’t just recite this declaration like a slogan. Try saying it at three moments: when you open your eyes in the morning (to take your bearings), before you face people (to put on your armour), and at night when accusation and shame close in (to stand firm against them).

sections.heading: 3. The Word of Our Testimony — a Genuine Life
sections.html:
“… and because of the word of their testimony.” (Revelation 12:11)

1. Witness and martyrdom were once the same word

The Greek word for “testimony” is μαρτυρία (martyria), and the English word “martyr” comes from it. The word’s history is a sermon in itself: in the early church, bearing witness and paying the price were one and the same thing.

The Greek word for “word” is λόγος (logos). This is not a slogan; it is speech with content, with weight, with truth. So “the word of their testimony” does not mean “I speak well.” It means “what I believe has come true in me.”

James puts it bluntly: “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves” (James 1:22). Notice those last words — deluding your own selves. When we only hear and don’t do, the first person deceived is not someone else; it is ourselves.

2. Daniel: a young man who resolved in his heart

Daniel and his three friends could stand firm in Babylon because they lived out a genuine faith. They didn’t only “believe”; they “lived out” what they believed.

The Bible records the decisive moment: “But Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the king’s dainties, nor with the wine which he drank. Therefore he requested of the prince of the eunuchs that he might not defile himself” (Daniel 1:8).

The Hebrew phrase for “purposed” is שִׂים עַל־לֵב (sim al-lev), literally “to set upon the heart.” It is a decision made before the event. Brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: Daniel didn’t begin to struggle the moment the royal food was set in front of him. Before he ever saw the food, he had already drawn the line in his heart.

What a vital lesson this is. Most people don’t fail when temptation arrives; they fail because they didn’t prepare before it arrived. If you only start thinking when the manager pushes the report back across your desk, it’s usually too late. Victory is decided in the prayer closet, not on the battlefield.

Now look at Daniel more than sixty years later, his hair white. King Darius has issued a decree: for thirty days no one may petition any god or man except the king. The Bible says: “When Daniel knew that the writing was signed, he went into his house (now his windows were open in his room toward Jerusalem) and he kneeled on his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did before” (Daniel 6:10).

“As he did before” — these four words are the most powerful words in the whole book of Daniel. He didn’t pray one extra time as a show of defiance, nor one time fewer to protect himself. He simply kept doing what he had always done. Brothers and sisters, true testimony is not a performance under the spotlight. It is consistency, day after day, when no one is watching.

A window open toward Jerusalem was the direction Solomon asked God to hear when he dedicated the temple (see 1 Kings 8:48). All his life Daniel kept his windows open in that direction. Which way are your windows and mine open?

3. The faith we profess and the faith we live

In 1974 the organisational psychologists Chris Argyris & Donald Schön drew a very useful distinction: everyone has an “espoused theory” — what we say we believe — and a “theory-in-use” — the rules we actually follow when we act. The two are often out of step, and when they are, we ourselves are usually the last to know.

Put this distinction next to our faith, and it cuts to the heart. Our “espoused theory” is: Jesus is Lord. What is our “theory-in-use”? “Don’t offend the boss”? “Look after yourself first”? “Everybody does it”?

The world doesn’t read what we espouse; the world reads what we use. The Lord Jesus said: “You are the salt of the earth” (Matthew 5:13). And again: “Even so, let your light shine before men; that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:16). Notice that the Lord did not say “that they may hear your good doctrine” but “that they may see your good works.”

Paul said to the church at Philippi: “that you may become blameless and harmless, children of God without defect in the middle of a crooked and perverse generation, among whom you are seen as lights in the world” (Philippians 2:15). “A crooked and perverse generation” is Babylon; “seen as lights” is testimony. Light doesn’t need to argue with the darkness. Light only needs to stay lit.

4. The pressure to conform, and the power of one companion

In 1951 the social psychologist Solomon Asch ran a famous experiment at Swarthmore College in the United States. He showed participants a line on one card and asked them to pick the line of equal length from three lines on another card — an answer so easy it was almost impossible to get wrong. But everyone else in the room was a research assistant, and they would say, in unison, an obviously wrong answer. The result was shocking: about three-quarters of the participants, at least once, went along with an answer they knew to be wrong.

But Asch’s follow-up experiments brought hope. He found that if just one person in the group gave the right answer — just one — the rate of conformity dropped sharply.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly the power of what 321 calls your “2.” The first step in 235 relationships is to become a “2” with one selfless person, being spiritual companions to each other. At the office you don’t need an army; you need one person. In your extended family you don’t need everyone to believe; you need one person who can pray with you in one accord. The first person to speak the truth has the hardest time; the second finds it far easier. And your presence may be exactly someone else’s “one.”

5. Not arguing with the world, but living an uncompromising life

We overcome Babylon not by arguing with the world but by living out the testimony of an uncompromising life. The world watches to see whether we really believe what we say we believe.

Here I want to stress two things in particular.

First, uncompromising does not mean ungracious. When Daniel approached the chief of the eunuchs, he used a request, not a shout. He proposed an alternative — “Test your servants, I beg you, ten days” (Daniel 1:12) — leaving the other man a way to save face. The Bible says: “Now God made Daniel find kindness and compassion in the sight of the prince of the eunuchs” (Daniel 1:9). A firm stand can go together with a gentle manner. This is just what 321 says: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances.

Second, testimony is the whole of life, not a slice of it. How you drive, how you queue, how you treat the waiter — all of it is the word of your testimony.

6. Applying the 321 vision: life first, then relationships, then ministry

In 321 we say: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

Many people are in a hurry to “do things” for the Lord without first letting the Lord gain their “life.” The result is that the bigger the ministry grows, the bigger the breach becomes. Daniel’s order was right: first he had the life that “purposed not to defile himself” (Daniel 1), and only then came the ministry of interpreting dreams and governing the nation (Daniel 2 onward). If the life isn’t ready, ministry will only magnify the cracks inside.

Then there is the fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change your daily living; change your daily living and you change your relationships; change your relationships and you change your ministry. So everything has to start with “mindset” — from “I have to win” to “let Jesus be King”; from “what will people think of me?” to “what does my Lord think of me?”

We can also practise 920 here: everyone we are in a relationship with is our “2.” Facing that difficult manager, that critical mother-in-law, that child who talks back, practise living out a selfless life (0), and bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions — “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23). Brothers and sisters, the hardest person in your office is not your obstacle; they are your training ground.

7. Suggested practice

Each week, set yourself one “act of faithful testimony,” for example: refusing to lie, holding to integrity, staying out of office politics, openly acknowledging your faith, forgiving someone, helping someone weak. Live out your “word.”

I suggest you write it down, and the more specific the better. Don’t write “I want to be more loving.” Write “This Wednesday afternoon I’ll buy a cup of coffee for the colleague who criticised me last time.” Vague resolutions change no one; concrete actions do.

sections.heading: 4. Not Loving Our Own Lives — a Heart Unafraid of Death
sections.html:
“They didn’t love their life, even to death.” (Revelation 12:11)

1. This is the decisive key

Brothers and sisters, this is the decisive key to overcoming Babylon.

Most people are willing to accept the first two keys. The precious blood — yes, I want it. Testimony — yes, I’ll try. But at the third key, most people stop. Because the name of this key is “death.”

The Greek for “didn’t love” is οὐκ ἠγάπησαν — simply “did not love” (the negative of ἀγαπάω, agapaō). The Greek word for “life” is ψυχή (psychē), which can be translated life, soul or self. Put together, the meaning is: they did not treat “self” as the most precious thing they had — not even to the point of death.

Note that the verse does not say they “hated life”; Christianity has never taught anyone to treat their life cheaply. The verse says: in their hearts there was a Lord more precious than their own lives, and when the two collided, they knew which one to let go.

2. “But if not”: the summit of faith

The Bible gives us a magnificent demonstration.

King Nebuchadnezzar made an image of gold, “whose height was sixty cubits, and its width six cubits. He set it up in the plain of Dura, in the province of Babylon” (Daniel 3:1). Taking a cubit as about forty-five centimetres, the statue stood some twenty-seven metres high — the height of a nine-storey building. All the officials of the realm were summoned; the horn sounded, and everyone fell prostrate. This was the Babylonian system at its most naked: one music, one posture, one worship — and whoever refused would be thrown into the burning fiery furnace.

Three young men of Judah stayed on their feet. The king gave them one last chance. Their reply is one of the most resounding declarations in all of Scripture:

“Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego answered the king, ‘Nebuchadnezzar, we have no need to answer you in this matter. If it happens, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace; and he will deliver us out of your hand, O king. But if not, let it be known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods or worship the golden image which you have set up’” (Daniel 3:16–18).

The whole passage rests on three words: But if not.

Brothers and sisters, chew slowly on these three words. They were not saying, “God will certainly save us, so we’re not afraid.” That would be a transaction, treating God as an insurance policy. They were saying: God is able to save; we also believe he will save; but even if he doesn’t — we still won’t bow.

This is “faith unafraid of death.” Faith like this does not make the outcome a condition. It doesn’t say, “Lord, as long as you heal me, I’ll follow you.” It says, “Lord, but if not, you are still my Lord.”

What they gave up was not only their physical lives but their attachment to fame and gain, status and security. They were senior officials over the province of Babylon (see Daniel 2:49). One bow, and their careers, their salaries and their lives would all have been safe. They chose to obey God rather than please the world.

We all know how it ended: the fire had no power over them; not a hair was singed, their clothes were unchanged, and there was not even the smell of fire on them (see Daniel 3:27). The king saw a fourth man in the fire: “The appearance of the fourth is like a son of the gods” (Daniel 3:25). Notice that God did not stop them from going into the furnace; God was with them in the furnace. So often God does not move us out of Babylon; God is with us inside Babylon.

3. True denying of self: not giving up behaviours, but laying down the self

Coming out of the Worldly system is not only about giving up certain behaviours. It means laying down a “self-centred” life.

The Lord Jesus said: “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me. For whoever desires to save his life will lose it, and whoever will lose his life for my sake will find it” (Matthew 16:24–25). When Luke’s Gospel records the same saying, it adds one word: “daily.” As the Chinese Union Version reads it: “let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me” (Luke 9:23).

Denying of self is not a one-time heroic gesture. It is a choice every morning.

Paul describes this experience most fully: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me” (Galatians 2:20). And again: “He died for all, that those who live should no longer live to themselves, but to him who for their sakes died and rose again” (2 Corinthians 5:15).

This is what 321 means: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless.

Please hear this clearly: selflessness is not having nothing. It is not annihilating the self, not becoming a person with no thoughts and no feelings. Selflessness is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living it out — because when my limited self steps aside, the limitless Christ lives himself out in me. “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. This is not a loss; it is an exchange. We are not emptied out; we are filled.

4. Psychology: the fear of death is the system’s biggest bargaining chip

Why is “not loving our own lives” so crucial? Because the fear of death is the biggest bargaining chip in Babylon’s hand.

In 1986 three American social psychologists, Jeff Greenberg, Tom Pyszczynski and Sheldon Solomon, building on the work of the anthropologist Ernest Becker, proposed “terror management theory.” Their argument runs like this: human beings are the only creatures clearly aware that they will one day die, and that awareness brings a deep anxiety. To manage it, people cling tightly to two things — a worldview that makes the world feel meaningful, and the self-esteem that proves their own worth within that worldview. In their experiments, participants who had been reminded of death tended to defend the values of their own group more fiercely.

Brothers and sisters, this explains exactly why the Babylonian system is so powerful. It supplies a worldview (success is meaning), it supplies self-esteem (titles, salaries, likes), and then it uses “you’ll lose all of this” to buy your compliance.

And the gospel has done something earth-shaking: it has snatched that bargaining chip out of Satan’s hand. Hebrews says that Christ partook of flesh and blood “that through death he might bring to nothing him who had the power of death, that is, the devil, and might deliver all of them who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage” (Hebrews 2:14–15). “Through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage” — that one line lays bare the secret of the entire system.

What can you still threaten a person with who has already died once in Christ? Paul says: “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Philippians 1:21). A person like that is free.

5. Courage born of conviction

In 1988 the sociologists Samuel P. Oliner & Pearl M. Oliner published “The Altruistic Personality,” based on interviews with more than seven hundred people, including over four hundred non-Jews who risked their lives to rescue Jews under the Nazis. The study found that these rescuers were not unusually brave by temperament. What they most consistently shared was that from childhood they had been taught a moral code that applied to “everyone,” and they regarded helping others as simply the natural thing to do — many said in the interviews that at the time they didn’t feel they were making any great decision at all.

Brothers and sisters, isn’t that exactly “as he did before”? Real courage is mostly not a rush of blood in the moment but long-term consistency.

On 28 October 1949 the missionary Jim Elliot (1927–1956) wrote in his journal: “He is no fool who gives what he cannot keep to gain what he cannot lose.” Seven years later he was martyred in Ecuador while taking the gospel to the Auca people, at just twenty-eight years old. He gave what he could not keep, and gained what he could not lose.

The early church father Tertullian (c. 155–c. 240) left us a saying usually rendered, “The blood of the martyrs is the seed of the church.” Church history has proved it again and again: Babylon can kill Christians, but it has never once killed the church.

6. Applying the 321 vision: let Jesus be King

Not loving our own lives, put another way in the language of 321, means this: let Jesus be King.

On the plain of Dura there was, in the end, only one question: who is King? Nebuchadnezzar wanted to be king, so he set up an image. The three young men let Yahweh be King, so they did not kneel. Every compromise you and I face today is, at bottom, the same question: in this matter, who is King?

To let Jesus reign as King means that I am not king. I step down from that position of “leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to replace God,” and return to my originally intended position as a creature — letting man be man and letting God be God.

And our perspective has to shift with it: from man’s viewpoint to God’s viewpoint; from the earthly to the heavenly; from the temporary to the eternal; from the Worldly to the godly. Paul says: “Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth” (Colossians 3:2). A person who sees only thirty years on earth will never be willing to let go; a person who sees eternity in heaven can let go.

7. Suggested practice

Every day, ask yourself one question: “What am I willing to lose for God today?” Then bravely carry out one choice that will make you “lose yourself,” for example: humbling yourself, apologising first, willingly taking the loss, giving up an unjust gain, courageously acknowledging your faith.

Notice that the point of this question is not “suffering” but “making room.” Every time you choose to lose a little of yourself, you clear a little more space for Christ to live in you.

sections.heading: 5. Integrating the 321 Vision: Three Keys and the Three Foundations
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s set today’s three keys side by side with the framework of 321, and you will see a beautiful picture.

1. The Three Foundations

The first key, the blood of the Lamb, corresponds to the first foundation: Jesus is my role model. He is the slain Lamb; his victory came through denying himself. Our victory, too, can only come through his blood and by walking his way.

The second key, the word of our testimony, corresponds to the second foundation: the Bible is my standard. Daniel purposed not to defile himself because God’s word was the standard in his heart. People with no standard can testify to nothing; people with a blurry standard will certainly be absorbed by the system.

The third key, not loving our own lives, corresponds to the third foundation: the Holy Spirit is my guide. Flesh and blood cannot produce this kind of courage by itself. The Lord said: “But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you. You will be witnesses to me in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the uttermost parts of the earth” (Acts 1:8). Both the power and the witness are given by the Holy Spirit.

Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves. Rely on the heart and you’ll be glad; rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled. Facing Babylon, the more you scheme with your brain, the more troubled you become; the more you trust with your heart, the more peace you have.

2. The Two Core Values

The first core value: let Jesus be King. The golden image on the plain of Dura fell, not on the day it was pushed over, but long before — when the three young men had already enthroned another King in their hearts.

The second core value: let Jesus receive all the glory. The most moving thing in the book of Daniel is not that the young men were saved but that pagan kings opened their mouths to praise God. Nebuchadnezzar said: “Now I, Nebuchadnezzar, praise and extol and honor the King of heaven; for all his works are truth, and his ways justice; and those who walk in pride he is able to abase” (Daniel 4:37). King Darius too issued a decree: “for he is the living God, and steadfast forever. His kingdom is that which will not be destroyed. His dominion will be even to the end” (Daniel 6:26).

Brothers and sisters, this is the fruit of victory: the kings of Babylon opening their mouths to glorify God. Your victory in the workplace is ultimately not about proving you were right. It’s so that people who don’t know God will one day also open their mouths and say: your God really is God.

3. The Goal

The Goal: establish God’s system.

Notice that overcoming the Babylonian system is not only the defence of “not being absorbed”; it is the offence of “establishing another system.” Daniel didn’t hide in a corner guarding his own holiness. He served as a chief administrator in the government of Babylon, and he brought God’s wisdom, justice and mercy into that system. God’s strategy has never been simply to keep his children safe, but through them, at the very heart of Babylon, to establish God’s system.

The final outcome has already been written: “The kingdom of the world has become the Kingdom of our Lord, and of his Christ. He will reign forever and ever!” (Revelation 11:15).

4. Life first, then relationships, then ministry

The order of the three keys is the very order of 321. The blood of the Lamb is “life” — it settles first the question of who I am. The word of our testimony is “daily living and relationships” — lived out before others. Not loving our own lives is “ministry and self-offering” — what we lay down for the Lord.

Never reverse this. People who have ministry without life collapse under pressure. The priority of relationships is the same: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. Daniel knelt before God three times a day (with God); he knew who he was (with himself); he found favour with the chief of the eunuchs (with others); and only then came the affairs of state (with things).

5. 920 and 235

The 920 practice: everyone we are in a relationship with is our “2.” In the Babylonian system, the hardest person to practise on is often the one who is pushing you down. Right there, practise selflessness (0) and bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions.

235 relationships: first become a “2” with one selfless person, supporting each other; then build a “3,” with spiritual parents and spiritual children; and finally become a “5,” a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. Asch’s experiment has already shown us that a person fighting alone gives in far too easily; with one companion, you can stand. Don’t face Babylon alone.

sections.heading: 6. Putting It into Practice: Going Deeper with the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset
sections.html:
The lesson gave us three practices. Now let’s set them inside “the eight stages of changing our mindset” — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — so that they become not just three good suggestions but something that truly grows into our life.

Three practices

Practice 1 (the blood of the Lamb): every day, declare in prayer — “I am cleansed by the precious blood of Jesus. I do not belong to Babylon; I belong to the Kingdom of God!”

Practice 2 (the word of testimony): each week, set one “act of faithful testimony,” such as refusing to lie, holding to integrity, staying out of office politics, openly acknowledging your faith, forgiving someone, helping someone weak.

Practice 3 (not loving our own lives): every day, ask yourself — “What am I willing to lose for God today?” Then carry out one choice that will make you “lose yourself.”

Stage 1: Information

First let the right information in. This week, please memorise Revelation 12:11 and read through Daniel chapters 1, 3 and 6. If information doesn’t come in, the mindset won’t move. Many people aren’t unwilling to change; they have simply never heard of another way to live.

Stage 2: Revelation

Information is knowing; revelation is seeing. Ask the Holy Spirit to let you “see” — to see that the precious blood is real in your life, to see the true face of the thing you’ve been compromising on. You might pray like this: Lord, what is my Babylon? Is it face? Money? Other people’s opinions?

Stage 3: Conviction

Once you’ve seen, you still need to accept it wholeheartedly. Conviction isn’t a nod; it is truly believing in your heart, “this is right, and it is good for me.” Most people get stuck here: they know full well they should be honest, yet inside they feel honesty will cost them. Ask the Lord to renew your sense of value until you believe that nothing lost for the Lord is really lost.

Stage 4: Implementation

Put the three practices into your calendar. The declaration goes in the morning; the act of testimony goes into your plan every Monday, with a name and a time attached; “What am I willing to lose for God today?” goes just before evening prayer. A resolution that doesn’t make it into the calendar usually vanishes by the third day.

Stage 5: Evaluation

Each week, set aside ten minutes for an honest review: Where did I compromise this week? What was the pressure? What excuse did I use? Remember what Festinger reminds us — what people are best at is finding reasons for themselves. So when you evaluate, don’t defend yourself. Just “say the same thing” as God.

Stage 6: Correction

Evaluation isn’t self-reproach; it’s correction. Find the one key breach and make one concrete adjustment. For example, if you notice that in meetings you always go along just to fit in, decide that next time you will stay quiet for three seconds before you speak. A small correction beats a great regret.

Stage 7: Repetition

Victory isn’t a one-off; it is “as he did before.” Daniel prayed for decades, three times a day. Habits are formed by repetition, and so is spiritual life. Don’t stop because you fell; begin again because you fell.

Stage 8: Multiplication

The last stage, and the one most easily skipped: pass on what you have received to one person. Find a brother or sister, share these three practices with them, and check in with each other once a week. Then you go from one person to a “2,” from a “2” towards a “3,” and from a “3” towards a “5.” This is how God’s system is truly established.

sections.heading: 7. Closing and Call: We Can Come Out of Babylon Because of Jesus’ Grace
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s go back to where we started today.

What became of that sister sitting at her desk with sweaty palms? She took a deep breath, carried the report back to her manager and said, “I can’t do it this way. But I can help you lay out the real figures more clearly, and we can work out a solution together.” She didn’t know how it would turn out. But she knew one thing — today she had not bowed down.

Don’t be afraid of Babylon, and don’t lose heart.

Don’t be afraid, because the outcome of the battle was settled long ago. In the vision John saw, the dragon has already been thrown down. The Lord Jesus said: “In the world you have trouble; but cheer up! I have overcome the world” (John 16:33). Paul said: “No, in all these things, we are more than conquerors through him who loved us” (Romans 8:37). We are not “fighting for” victory; we are “carrying out” a battle that has already been won.

Don’t lose heart, because what we overcome by does not rest in us. It is the blood of the Lamb, not my good character; the word of testimony, not my eloquence; a heart that does not love its own life, not my courage. Not one of these three did I produce myself. All of it is grace.

So this morning I want to give you three calls:

First, come to the cross, confess specifically, and draw afresh on the cleansing of the precious blood. To Satan’s accusations, give only one answer: the Lamb has already paid this debt.

Second, choose one thing and live it out this week. Don’t wait until you feel good enough before you start to testify. The world doesn’t need to see a perfect Christian; the world needs to see a genuine one.

Third, say “but if not” to the Lord in your heart once. But if not, you are still my God; but if not, I still will not kneel.

The Lord Jesus is already waiting for us in the furnace. He may not put out the fire, but he will surely walk with us in it.

May we spend this life living in Babylon yet not belonging to Babylon. Wherever we go, may people see not how strong we are but how glorious our King is. Let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory.

keyVerses: “They overcame him because of the Lamb’s blood, and because of the word of their testimony. They didn’t love their life, even to death.” (Revelation 12:11)
practices: Every day, declare in prayer — “I am cleansed by the precious blood of Jesus. I do not belong to Babylon; I belong to the Kingdom of God!”

Each week, set one “act of faithful testimony,” such as refusing to lie, holding to integrity, staying out of office politics, openly acknowledging your faith, forgiving someone, helping someone weak.
Every day, ask yourself — “What am I willing to lose for God today?” Then carry out one choice that will make you “lose yourself.”
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,

We confess that we cannot overcome this world by ourselves. There is too much of the self-centred life in us, too much pride, too much attachment to fame and gain, status and security. Please forgive us.

Thank you that you are the Lamb who was slain. Your precious blood washes away all my sins and cuts the chains between me and Babylon. Today I declare: I am cleansed by the precious blood of Jesus. I do not belong to Babylon; I belong to the Kingdom of God.

Lord, fill me with the Holy Spirit, so that I not only believe but am able to live out what I believe. Let me be like Daniel, purposing in my heart before temptation ever comes; and let me be like him, too, in the places no one sees — just as I did before.

Lord, give me “but if not” faith. But if not, you are still my Lord; but if not, I still will not bow to the golden image of this age. Take away my fear of loss, for I have been crucified with you, and it is no longer I who live, but you who live in me.
Use me to establish God’s system in my family, my workplace, my school and my community. Let my colleagues and my family one day open their mouths to praise you too.
May all glory be yours. In the victorious name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Revelation 12:11: “They overcame him because of the Lamb’s blood, and because of the word of their testimony. They didn’t love their life, even to death.” In your life right now, what is the most concrete shape the “Babylonian system” takes? What does it most often use to buy your compliance — your income, your relationships, your face, or your sense of security? Please share one specific recent incident.

Daniel 3:17–18: “If it happens, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace; and he will deliver us out of your hand, O king. But if not, let it be known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods or worship the golden image which you have set up.” Is there something in your heart about which you need to say to the Lord, “But if not”? This week, which concrete choice that will make you “lose yourself” are you willing to carry out? Pray for one another, and agree to come back next week and review it together.

l002.subtitle: In Babylon, but Not of Babylon
