sections.heading: Introduction: A Generation Standing on the Dividing Line
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning I’d like to begin by asking you to picture something in your mind.

In Italy there is a world-famous building called the Leaning Tower of Pisa. Construction began in AD 1173; it was built as a bell tower to glorify a great cathedral. The craftsmanship was first-class, the marble carving fine and graceful, the arcades on every storey precisely symmetrical. Yet by the time the tower had risen only to its third storey, it had begun to lean. The cause was not the tower itself but what lay beneath it — the ground was soft alluvial soil, a mix of clay and fine sand, and the foundation laid at the time is generally thought to have been only about three metres deep. For more than eight hundred years people have tried everything to save it: adding counterweights, pumping out groundwater, drilling out soil. In 1990 it even had to be closed, for eleven full years of repairs. It still stands today, but it can never be set upright again.

Brothers and sisters, this tower reminds us of one thing: however exquisite the superstructure, it cannot rescue a mistake in the foundation beneath it.

We are living in a generation full of tension. The Worldly system is expanding fast, while God’s people often lose their way. What does today’s world promote? Self-actualisation, individual rights, instant gratification, humanity above all. These values aren’t pressed on us in a single lecture. They seep, drop by drop, into our thinking and our choices through our phones, advertising, films and shows, and algorithms.

Have you noticed how easily we are assimilated without even realising it? We still pray, we still gather, we still read the Bible; but the ruler we measure things by has quietly been swapped for the world’s ruler. We ask, “Is this good for me?” rather than “Is this God’s will?” Even as Christians, if we lack clear discernment and a solid foundation, we too will be swallowed bit by bit by the Babylonian system, drifting out of focus and into compromise.

In 1951 the American social psychologist Solomon Asch carried out a famous conformity experiment. He asked participants to compare the lengths of lines — a question even a child would get right. But when everyone else in the room declared, in unison, an obviously wrong answer, about one third of the responses went along with the error; across the whole experiment, about three-quarters of the participants conformed to the mistaken majority at least once. Brothers and sisters, the eyes can see perfectly clearly, and yet the mouth finds it very hard not to follow the crowd.

So in an age like this, if we are to stand firm, we must take hold once again of the true foundation and the central goal of our faith. That is the purpose of this lesson: to help us recognise the deceptions and illusions that come from the Worldly system, to examine ourselves afresh, to return to God’s heart, to live out God’s system, and to let God receive all the glory.

Today’s message comes down to one sentence: hold fast to the foundation, come out of the Worldly, and establish God’s system.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: A Foundation Already Laid, a People Called Out
sections.html:
Our theme verse today comes from 1 Corinthians 3.

The author of 1 Corinthians is the apostle Paul. He wrote this letter from Ephesus around AD 55, and it was addressed to the church in Corinth. Corinth was then the capital of the province of Achaia. It sat on an isthmus, and its two ports, east and west, made it a trading hub of the Mediterranean. Wealth, shipping, athletic games, philosophy and a multitude of religions all converged in this city, and its moral corruption was such that “to Corinthianise” had almost become a term of contempt.

In other words, the Corinthian church did not come to faith in a vacuum. They came to faith inside a Babylonian system that gloried in wealth, treated eloquence as authority and put self at the centre.

So it is not hard to see why this letter opens by dealing with factions. 1 Corinthians 1:12 says: “Now I mean this, that each one of you says, ‘I follow Paul,’ ‘I follow Apollos,’ ‘I follow Cephas,’ and, ‘I follow Christ.’” They had carried the world’s celebrity culture into the church and turned servants into brand names. Paul’s answer was: “I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase” (1 Corinthians 3:6).

Then Paul changed his metaphor, from a field to a building. He called himself “a wise master builder” who “laid a foundation.” The Greek word behind “master builder” is architektōn, the root of our word “architect,” meaning “chief builder.” Paul’s point was: what I have done is lay the foundation; as for how the building goes up on it, let each one be careful.

Then comes that stunning declaration: “For no one can lay any other foundation than that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 3:11). Notice that Paul did not say “the best foundation is Jesus,” as if there were a second-best option. He said “no one can lay any other foundation.” The foundation is not a multiple-choice question. The foundation is the only one.

The second passage, Revelation 18:4, says the same thing from the other end. Its author is the apostle John, who wrote the book on the island of Patmos around AD 95, addressed to the seven churches of Asia Minor. Believers at the time faced emperor worship and economic exclusion: if you didn’t worship Caesar, you couldn’t do business. John uses “Babylon the great city” to describe this Worldly system, at once prosperous and immoral.

And then a voice from heaven says: “Come out of her, my people, that you have no participation in her sins, and that you don’t receive of her plagues” (Revelation 18:4).

Brothers and sisters, please look at these two verses together. One side is “come out,” the other is “build”; one side tears down, the other sets up. God never simply calls us away from something; even more, he calls us into something. He calls us out of the Babylonian system so that, on the one foundation of Jesus Christ, we might establish God’s system.

This is the road we are going to walk today.

sections.heading: Key Point 1: The Blueprint of God’s System — the “3-2-1” Structure
sections.html:
The message of this entire course can be expressed simply in a “3-2-1” framework:

The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide.

The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory.

The Goal: establish God’s system.

This is not a set of slogans; it is a real spiritual blueprint. Only when we live on these three solid foundations and hold fast to these two core convictions can we keep from straying from the true purpose for which we were created and called.

sections.heading: 1. The Three Foundations: Not Three Tasks, but the Threefold Provision of One Lord
sections.html:
The first foundation: Jesus is my role model. After the Lord Jesus washed the disciples’ feet at the Last Supper, he said: “For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you” (John 13:15). The Greek word for “example” is hypodeigma, literally “a sample placed underneath for people to see.” The Lord did not stand up high shouting slogans; he stooped down and set the sample at our feet. Philippians 2:5–7 says: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men.” That phrase “emptied himself” is ekenōsen in Greek, meaning “to pour oneself out.” This is exactly what 321 calls “selflessness.”

The second foundation: the Bible is my standard. 2 Timothy 3:16–17 says: “Every Scripture is God-breathed and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for instruction in righteousness, that each person who belongs to God may be complete, thoroughly equipped for every good work.” The Greek word for “God-breathed” is theopneustos — literally “breathed out by God.” The Bible is not man’s impressions of God; it is the breath God breathes out to man.

The third foundation: the Holy Spirit is my guide. The Lord Jesus said: “However when he, the Spirit of truth, has come, he will guide you into all truth, for he will not speak from himself; but whatever he hears, he will speak. He will declare to you things that are coming” (John 16:13). Notice that the Spirit “will not speak from himself” — even the Holy Spirit is selfless. The triune God himself lives out the role model of selflessness.

Brothers and sisters, these Three Foundations are not three things to do but a threefold provision from one and the same Lord: the role model leads the way in front, the standard draws the line beneath our feet, and the guide moves us from within. Lose any one of them and we fall out of balance. A role model without a standard becomes imitation by feeling. A standard without a guide becomes cold legalism. A guide without a standard becomes do-as-you-please charismatic subjectivism.

sections.heading: 2. The Two Core Values: Let Jesus Be King, Let Jesus Receive All the Glory
sections.html:
“Let Jesus be King” is a question of sovereignty. Revelation 11:15 says: “The kingdom of the world has become the Kingdom of our Lord, and of his Christ. He will reign forever and ever!” To let Jesus be King is to ask the self that sits so comfortably on the throne of our life to step down.

“Let Jesus receive all the glory” is a question of ownership. Revelation 4:11 says: “Worthy are you, our Lord and God, the Holy One, to receive the glory, the honor, and the power, for you created all things, and because of your desire they existed, and were created!” Glory is not something we “give” God; glory was his all along — we simply must not steal it. 1 Corinthians 10:31 puts it very practically: “Whether therefore you eat, or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.”

These Two Core Values are really two sides of one coin. Whoever is King receives the glory. If self is king, the glory flows to self; if Jesus is King, the glory goes to Jesus.

sections.heading: 3. The Goal: Establish God’s System
sections.html:
What is a “system”? A system is a whole set of values, ideas, relationships and institutions that are linked to one another and run on their own. Babylon is a system, and it began as far back as Genesis 11: “They said, ‘Come, let’s build ourselves a city, and a tower whose top reaches to the sky, and let’s make a name for ourselves, lest we be scattered abroad on the surface of the whole earth’” (Genesis 11:4). Look at the key phrase — “let’s make a name for ourselves.” At the core of the Babylonian system is “my” name.

God’s system is the exact opposite: at its core is “his” name. The Lord’s Prayer says: “Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy. Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven” (Matthew 6:9–10).

Ephesians 2:20–22 paints a picture of what this system looks like: “being built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the chief cornerstone; in whom the whole building, fitted together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord; in whom you also are built together for a habitation of God in the Spirit.” Notice those words, “fitted together”: God’s system is never a matter of a single brick; it is a matter of many living stones interlocking with one another.

Let me use a modern illustration. Taipei 101 stands 508 metres tall in an earthquake zone, and one key to its standing firm is its foundation engineering: 380 piles driven deep into the hard bedrock below. Above ground is the splendour of glass and steel; below ground, where no one sees, is the reason it stands.

Brothers and sisters, the 321 blueprint is exactly this kind of “invisible foundation engineering.” The Three Foundations are the piles, the Two Core Values are the pillars, and the Goal is the reason the building exists.

Applying the 321 vision: here we need to see an order — life first, then relationships, then ministry. Many people, as soon as they believe, rush to ask, “What ministry can I do?” without first asking, “What is my life built on?” The order of change is: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. These five changes cannot skip a step. Skipping life and charging straight into ministry is like skipping the foundation and going straight to building the tower — the higher you build, the worse it falls.

sections.heading: Key Point 2: A Wrong Foundation Brings the Collapse of Faith
sections.html:
The foundation of our faith must be unchanging and non-negotiable. Yet today, many buildings of faith stand on unstable ground.

Psalm 11:3 asks a piercing question: “If the foundations are destroyed, what can the righteous do?” David is not asking “Can the righteous still pray?” He is asking: when the whole foundation has been hollowed out, however hard a person tries, what can he still hold up?

At the end of the Sermon on the Mount, the Lord Jesus used an illustration everyone can understand. Matthew 7:24–27 says: “Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine, and does them, I will liken him to a wise man, who built his house on a rock. The rain came down, the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat on that house; and it didn’t fall, for it was founded on the rock. Everyone who hears these words of mine, and doesn’t do them will be like a foolish man, who built his house on the sand. The rain came down, the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat on that house; and it fell — and great was its fall.”

Notice something that is often overlooked: both men heard the same sermon and met the same rain, the same floods, the same wind. The difference was not the weather; the difference was the foundation. The storm was never the enemy. The storm is simply the inspector who exposes the foundation.

Luke 6:48 adds a detail: “He is like a man building a house, who dug and went deep, and laid a foundation on the rock.” “Dug and went deep” — this is the least romantic, least visible and most time-consuming work of all. Brothers and sisters, the most vital work in the spiritual life is often exactly this kind of deep digging that no one applauds.

sections.heading: 1. Building Faith on Our Own or Others’ Experience
sections.html:
Some people build their faith on their own experience or on other people’s. Experience in itself is not a bad thing; the Bible is full of experiences of signs and wonders. The problem is that experience is subjective and limited, and it cannot apply to everyone.

You have one special healing, and you conclude that God must deal with everyone in that same way; when others haven’t had the same experience, you doubt their faith. Experience is like the waves of the sea, sometimes high, sometimes low. Build your house on a wave, and when the wave goes out, the house is gone.

The apostle Peter was the person most qualified to speak of experience: he saw with his own eyes the Lord transfigured on the mountain. Yet he said: “We have the more sure word of prophecy … as to a lamp shining in a dark place” (2 Peter 1:19). Even Peter said that the prophetic word was “more sure” than his experience.

The psychologist and Nobel laureate in economics Daniel Kahneman, in his 2011 book “Thinking, Fast and Slow,” distinguished between “System 1” and “System 2”: System 1 is fast, intuitive and effortless; System 2 is slow, effortful and requires reasoning. He pointed out that people naturally prefer System 1, but precisely because it is effortless, it is the most easily misled by vivid images and strong emotions. Experience moves us precisely because it appeals to System 1; God’s word is reliable precisely because it stands up to repeated examination.

Please hear this clearly: we are not against experience. We are against putting experience in the place of the standard. Experience should be tested by Scripture, not Scripture revised by experience.

sections.heading: 2. Building Faith on Denominational Tradition
sections.html:
Some people lean on denominational tradition. Tradition is not a sin; healthy tradition is wisdom built up by those before us through blood and tears. But tradition does not necessarily agree with the Bible, and sometimes it actually blurs God’s truth and heart.

The Pharisees are the clearest cautionary example. They were the most devout, most earnest people of their day; they tithed even their mint and dill. But what did the Lord Jesus say of them? Mark 7:8–9: “For you set aside the commandment of God, and hold tightly to the tradition of men”; “Full well do you reject the commandment of God, that you may keep your tradition.” By 7:13 the Lord’s words are heavier still: “making void the word of God by your tradition, which you have handed down.”

Brothers and sisters, notice the terrifying logic: they did not miss Jesus through self-indulgence; they missed Jesus by holding tightly to tradition. The most devout gatekeepers can sometimes shut the Lord himself outside the door.

Paul gives the same warning in Colossians 2:8: “Be careful that you don’t let anyone rob you through his philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the elements of the world, and not after Christ.” The key phrase here is “not after Christ.” Any tradition whose centre is no longer Christ becomes a rope that takes people captive.

The way to test a tradition is simple. Ask: “Does this draw people closer to Jesus, or closer to us?”

sections.heading: 3. Building Faith on Modern Currents of Thought
sections.html:
And quite a few people, influenced by modern theology and cultural currents of thought, begin to question the authority of the Bible and the uniqueness of Jesus. The result is a shaken foundation of faith, even the collapse of faith altogether.

The most popular saying of our age is: “That’s your truth, not my truth.” It sounds very tolerant, but in fact it is very cruel — because if everyone sets their own truth, then the victim has no ground to say the abuser was wrong. When truth is broken up into one portion per person, justice has nowhere to stand.

But the Lord Jesus said: “I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father, except through me” (John 14:6). This saying is either the most arrogant lie in the universe or the most solid foundation in the universe. There is no middle ground.

Let me use another picture, from the natural sciences. In the great Niigata earthquake in Japan in 1964, the most shocking photographs were not of collapsed houses but of an entire four-storey apartment block “lying down” intact. The cause was soil liquefaction: during the quake, water-saturated sandy soil instantly lost its bearing capacity and behaved like a liquid. Nothing was wrong with the building; the ground had turned to water.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly the faith of many people today. Nothing is wrong with their devotion, nothing is wrong with their zeal; the problem is that the ground beneath their feet has liquefied under the shaking of the currents of thought.

Just as you must first lay a firm foundation before building a high-rise, if we are to stand firm in the shaking of the last days, we must make sure that the foundation of our faith is built on Jesus Christ and his word. Hebrews 12:27–28 says: “This phrase, ‘Yet once more’ signifies the removing of those things that are shaken, as of things that have been made, that those things which are not shaken may remain. Therefore, receiving a Kingdom that can’t be shaken, let’s have grace, through which we serve God acceptably, with reverence and awe.”

The shaking will come. But God permits the shaking so that what cannot be shaken may be revealed.

Applying the 321 vision: these three wrong foundations look different on the surface, but at the core they are one and the same problem — “the self-centred life.” Build on experience, and my feelings set the standard. Build on tradition, and the way our group does things sets the standard. Build on currents of thought, and the “me” of this age sets the standard. Whichever it is, the one sitting on the throne is still “me.” And 321 has only one remedy: selflessness. Not I setting the standard, but Jesus as King; not my opinions, but the Bible as my standard; not my impulses, but the Holy Spirit as my guide.

sections.heading: Key Point 3: Come Out of the Worldly, Return to God’s Blueprint
sections.html:
Today God is calling his people. Revelation 18:4 says: “I heard another voice from heaven, saying, ‘Come out of her, my people, that you have no participation in her sins, and that you don’t receive of her plagues.’”

Notice that this is not about leaving a geographical Babylon. When John wrote this book, the historical city of Babylon had already lain in ruins for several hundred years. So the “come out” of this verse is not telling us to move house; it is telling us to come out of the thinking, culture, habits and values of the Worldly system.

The Greek for “come out” is exelthate, an aorist imperative, meaning “come out now, decisively.” What God gives is not a suggestion but a command; not a gradual option but a decision made here and now.

sections.heading: 1. Coming Out Means Coming Out of the Mould That Shaped Us
sections.html:
He wants us to break free from the pattern this world has shaped in us and enter the pattern of his Kingdom. Romans 12:2 says: “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.”

The Greek for “be conformed” is syschēmatizesthe, whose root is related to “schema” (an outward shape or style). It means changing your outward form to follow a mould outside you, like pressing dough into a biscuit mould. The Greek for “be transformed” is metamorphousthe, the root of our word “metamorphosis.” It means a change of nature from the inside, like a caterpillar becoming a butterfly.

Brothers and sisters, these two words describe two completely different kinds of change. The world’s change is pressing into a mould: from the outside in, changing the outward shape. God’s change is new creation: from the inside out, changing the very nature. And where does this new creation begin? The verse says it plainly: “be transformed by the renewing of your mind.” Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change your daily living. This is the very starting point of what 321 calls the fivefold change.

In biology, the process by which a caterpillar becomes a butterfly is called complete metamorphosis. Inside the chrysalis, the caterpillar’s tissues are broken down into an almost liquid state, then reorganised into wings and compound eyes by “imaginal discs” that were there all along. It looks like destruction, but in fact it is reconstruction. Brothers and sisters, if right now you are going through a season when “everything has been torn down,” please don’t panic — God may be remaking you from a caterpillar into a butterfly.

sections.heading: 2. Coming Out Is Not Escape, but Active Building
sections.html:
We are not passively escaping the world; we are actively building a system distinct from the world — God’s system. A system not centred on self, but with Jesus as King; not living by our own will, but living according to God’s heart.

The Lord Jesus prayed for his disciples: “I pray not that you would take them from the world, but that you would keep them from the evil one” (John 17:15). Not of the world, yet sent into the world; not stained by it, yet not fleeing it. This is the Christian’s tension.

Daniel is the best role model. He was carried off to Babylon, renamed Belteshazzar, enrolled in the palace education system and taught the language and literature of the Chaldeans; his situation was entirely inside Babylon. Yet Daniel 1:8 says: “But Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the king’s dainties, nor with the wine which he drank.”

Notice that he did not run away from the palace, nor did he refuse to learn the learning of the Chaldeans. The line he drew was at the point of “defiling himself.” And he did not protest in fury: he “requested of the prince of the eunuchs that he might not defile himself” (Daniel 1:8). Gentle firmness is more powerful than fierce confrontation. And through several reigns he was never assimilated.

Brothers and sisters, to be in Babylon in body but not in Babylon in heart — that is “coming out.”

sections.heading: 3. Coming Out Requires a Visible Decision
sections.html:
At the end of his life Joshua said to the Israelites: “But as for me and my house, we will serve Yahweh” (Joshua 24:15). This was a public, concrete, line-drawing decision.

1 John 2:15–17 draws this line even more clearly: “Don’t love the world or the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the Father’s love isn’t in him. For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, isn’t the Father’s, but is the world’s. The world is passing away with its lusts, but he who does God’s will remains forever.”

The lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, the pride of life — these three are the three pillars of the Babylonian system, and they are exactly the three baits the serpent used in Eden: “the tree was good for food” (the lust of the flesh), “it was a delight to the eyes” (the lust of the eyes), and “the tree was to be desired to make one wise” (the pride of life) (Genesis 3:6). From Eden to Babylon, Satan has never come up with a new trick.

Applying the 321 vision: coming out of the Worldly is essentially a shift of perspective — from man’s perspective to God’s perspective; from an earthly perspective to a heavenly perspective; from a temporary perspective to an eternal perspective; from a Worldly perspective to a godly perspective. Paul says: “while we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal” (2 Corinthians 4:18). And again: “Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth” (Colossians 3:2). Brothers and sisters, what are you anxious about today? Measure it against the ruler of eternity, and you’ll know how big it really is.

sections.heading: Key Point 4: How to Put It into Practice — Three Ways of Daily Living That Establish God’s System
sections.html:
So that “3-2-1” becomes something you practise in your life and not just something you know, please begin with the following three simple, concrete practices.

Before we go into them, let me say something honest: knowledge does not automatically turn into life; only repeated practice does. In a study published in 2010 in the “European Journal of Social Psychology,” Phillippa Lally and her colleagues at University College London found that it takes an average of sixty-six days for a behaviour to become automatic, with individual differences ranging from eighteen to two hundred and fifty-four days. Brothers and sisters, don’t imagine that you’ve changed just because you heard one lesson, and don’t give up because you failed on day three. A foundation is dug deeper one day at a time.

Practice 1: Meditate on 321 every day, and adjust your heart and your focus

How: every morning, or during your prayer time, take three minutes to ask yourself five questions:

sections.heading: 1. Am I taking Jesus as my role model today?
2. Are my decisions taking the Bible as my standard?
3. Am I seeking the guidance of the Holy Spirit?
4. Is what I’m doing letting Jesus be King, or am I making myself master?
5. Is my goal to let the Lord receive glory, or to make a name for myself?
sections.html:
This is a way of spiritual refocusing. It helps you, every day, to pull your heart’s navigation out of the Worldly system and reset it on the course of heaven.

Why the “heart”? Proverbs 4:23 says: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” The Hebrew word for “keep” is natsar, which carries a military sense of “guarding, standing watch,” like a sentry guarding a city gate. The fruit of a whole life does not flow from ability, nor from opportunity; it flows from the heart.

Let me use a sailing illustration. When a ship leaves port, if its heading is off by one degree, you can hardly tell at the quayside. But after sailing a hundred nautical miles, you will be nearly two nautical miles off your destination. Drift doesn’t happen all at once; drift accumulates. So correction can’t be once a year either. It has to happen every day.

Applying the 321 vision: this is exactly “rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves.” Rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad. These three minutes are not about thinking more; they are about bringing things into focus — Jesus is the focal point, not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. When the focus is right, many things that were crushing the breath out of you will settle back into their proper place on their own.

Practice 2: Each week, take one deliberate action that tears down the Worldly system

How: each week, challenge yourself to make one choice that reflects “God’s values” and differs from the way the world does things:

Refuse to show off and compare; choose humility and authenticity.

Lay down emotional retaliation; choose forgiveness and love.

Don’t fight for your own advantage; choose to suffer loss for the Lord.

Don’t try to please the crowd; choose to please God.

This is a kind of spiritual resistance training. It helps you, in the concrete details of daily living, break free from Babylon’s control over your thinking.

Notice the shared structure of these four choices: the first half is always “lay down,” and the second half is always “choose.” This is the practice of selflessness. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living it out. “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. Galatians 2:20 says: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.”

The first: refuse to show off and compare. 2 Corinthians 10:12 says: “But they themselves, measuring themselves by themselves, and comparing themselves with themselves, are without understanding.” Comparison is a race with no finish line. The second: lay down emotional retaliation. Romans 12:21 says: “Don’t be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.” When people repay evil for evil, both of them lose. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.

The third: don’t fight for your own advantage. 1 Corinthians 6:7 says: “Why not rather be wronged? Why not rather be defrauded?” In today’s workplace that sounds almost absurd, yet it is precisely the logic of the cross. The fourth: don’t try to please the crowd. Galatians 1:10 says: “For am I now seeking the favor of men, or of God? Or am I striving to please men? For if I were still pleasing men, I wouldn’t be a servant of Christ.”

Let me give a historical example. In 1521 Martin Luther stood before the Diet of Worms, facing the Holy Roman Emperor and the assembled bishops, and was ordered to recant his writings. His reply, in substance, was that unless he was convinced by the testimony of Scripture or by clear reason, he could not and would not retract a single word. (The best-known line, “Here I stand,” is generally thought to have been added later.) Brothers and sisters, that day he had no army and no powerful backer — only one foundation: the Bible is my standard.

Applying the 321 vision: this one action a week is the 920 practice. Everyone we are in a relationship with is our “2”; live out the selfless “0” before them, and you will bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions. Galatians 5:22–23 says: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.” Notice that in the original, “fruit” is singular: the nine are nine facets of one fruit. You can’t pick patience and leave out gentleness.

Practice 3: Each week, remind and share with a spiritual companion

How: find a spiritual companion, and each week briefly share the following:

This week, in what things did I let Jesus be King?

In what things am I still relying on myself and haven’t yet handed over sovereignty?

Is there anything for which I should step out of Babylon for the Lord?

This is a way of walking together in spiritual building. Ecclesiastes 4:9–10 says: “Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor. For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him who is alone when he falls, and doesn’t have another to lift him up.” A following verse says it even more powerfully: “If a man prevails against one who is alone, two shall withstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken” (Ecclesiastes 4:12).

Look at the picture: one strand breaks easily, two are a little better, and three are very hard to break. And many interpreters point out that this third strand is the Lord himself, who is with us.

Nature gives us a picture too. The redwoods of North America are the tallest trees in the world; they can grow to more than 110 metres, yet their roots are surprisingly shallow. Why don’t they fall? Because redwoods grow in groves, and their roots are tightly interwoven underground, joined into one. One redwood holds up another, and the whole forest stands.

The Harvard Study of Adult Development began in 1938 and has spanned more than eighty years. Its current director, Robert Waldinger, has said publicly many times that the study’s clearest conclusion is this: what makes people happier and healthier throughout life is not wealth, not fame, but good relationships. Brothers and sisters, what science took eighty years to prove, the Bible wrote down three thousand years ago.

Applying the 321 vision: this is exactly 235 relationships. Become a “2” with one selfless person, spiritual companions supporting each other; go on to build a “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children; and finally become a “5,” a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. And the priority of relationships cannot be reversed: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

Let me add an honest word as a pastor: many brothers and sisters fall not because they lack gifts but because they lack a companion. This morning, if you don’t yet have a companion like this, please make finding one the most important assignment of this lesson.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: One Blueprint, a Fivefold Change
sections.html:
Let’s gather what we have seen today into the 321 blueprint.

The Three Foundations, the Two Core Values, the Goal

The Three Foundations answer “What do I stand on?”: Jesus is my role model, so I know which way to go; the Bible is my standard, so I know where the boundaries are; the Holy Spirit is my guide, so I have the strength to keep going.

The Two Core Values answer “Who is at the centre?”: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory.

The Goal answers “What am I living for?”: to establish God’s system, to see the Lord’s Prayer fulfilled, to press on into the end time revival, and to walk alongside every person until they become an overcomer.

The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless

The root of humanity’s fall is “the self-centred life,” and the root of the problem is pride. Isaiah 14:13–14 records five “I will”s: “You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! I will sit on the mountain of assembly, in the far north! I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!’” Five “I will”s — a complete anatomy of pride.

Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights, wanting to replace God. Humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God. James 4:6–7 says: “But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’ Be subject therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.” Notice the order: first submit to God, and only then can you resist the devil. Submission comes first; resistance follows.

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Satan’s favourite weapon is pride, because that was the cause of his own fall; and what he is least able to deal with is a truly selfless person — because a selfless person gives him nothing to grab hold of.

The fivefold change and the Path of Serving

The fivefold change is: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change your daily living. What today’s lesson does is precisely the first step — changing the mindset: exchanging the three rulers of “my experience, my tradition, my age” for the Three Foundations of “Jesus, the Bible, the Holy Spirit.”

The Path of Serving is: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God. First let the Holy Spirit guide (Spirit), then let the Bible open our understanding (Understanding), then live out the pattern of Jesus’ life (Life); only then do we enter the service that lets Jesus be King (Service), and finally give the glory to God (God). Many people today fail because they start from “Service” instead of from “Spirit.”

A shift of perspective

From man’s perspective to God’s perspective, from an earthly perspective to a heavenly perspective, from a temporary perspective to an eternal perspective, from a Worldly perspective to a godly perspective.

Paul gives the most thorough demonstration in Philippians 3:7–8: “However, I consider those things that were gain to me as a loss for Christ. Yes most certainly, and I count all things to be a loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus, my Lord, for whom I suffered the loss of all things, and count them nothing but refuse, that I may gain Christ.” He didn’t lose those things; he redid the accounts. When Christ goes to the top of the assets column, all the other figures change places on their own.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Deepening the Three Practices with the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset
sections.html:
The lesson has given us three practices: meditate on 321 every day, take one action each week that tears down the Worldly system, and share each week with a spiritual companion. Now let’s use “the eight stages of changing our mindset” to drive them deep. The eight stages are: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Stage 1: Information

First get hold of the knowledge. This week, please copy out the theme verses and put them somewhere you are sure to see every day — your desk, your mirror, your phone wallpaper. I suggest you first get to know four passages well: 1 Corinthians 3:11, Revelation 18:4, Romans 12:2 and Matthew 7:24–25.

Stage 2: Revelation

Ask the Holy Spirit to turn information into revelation. Knowledge is “I know”; revelation is “I see.” Pray like this: “Lord, shine your light on me. What is my faith really built on?” Then be still and wait for three minutes. Revelation seldom comes in the noise; it comes in the stillness.

Stage 3: Conviction

Seeing is not enough; you must be wholeheartedly persuaded. The mark of conviction is “I no longer defend it.” If God points out one of your Worldly values — comparison, competitiveness, face, control — please don’t rush to find excuses for it. Admitting it is where conviction begins.

Stage 4: Implementation

Start with the smallest, most concrete, most achievable step. Don’t resolve, “I will never compare again” — that is a goal with no edges. Change it to: “This week, when I see a colleague being praised, I will go over and offer a sincere word of congratulations.” Small enough that you will certainly do it, specific enough that you know whether you did. This is how Practice 2 touches the ground.

Stage 5: Evaluation

Set a fixed time each week to look back honestly: this week, in what things did I let Jesus be King? In what things did I still make myself master? This is exactly the content of Practice 3. Evaluation is not condemnation; evaluation is measuring the depth of the foundation. 1 John 1:9 says: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”

Stage 6: Correction

After evaluating, adjust the method — don’t pile on self-blame. If you keep failing at the three-minute morning meditation, don’t condemn yourself as unspiritual. First ask: Is it at the wrong time? Should it move to my commute, or to bedtime? Correction is an engineer’s attitude; self-blame is a loser’s emotion.

Stage 7: Repetition

Repeat, repeat and repeat again, until it becomes automatic. Remember that number? Sixty-six days on average. Brothers and sisters, give yourself sixty-six days, not six. Digging deep is slow work.

Stage 8: Multiplication

Once you have tasted it, go and bring someone else along. This is where the heartbeat of 321 lies. You begin with a “2” — find a companion; then become a spiritual parent and build a “3”; and finally work together with others as a “5” team. 2 Timothy 2:2 says: “The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.” A change that doesn’t multiply is just one person’s good habit; only a change that multiplies becomes a system.

Please write these eight stages in your notebook, and at your next gathering tell your companion which stage you’ve reached.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: Starting Today, Build a System That Cannot Be Shaken
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters, the system of this world is decaying ever faster, but God is looking for a people — not more capable, but better grounded; not more up on the trends, but more like Jesus; not just shouting for revival, but first establishing the system of God’s Kingdom.

Are you willing to be such a person?

Let me show you the picture of the Leaning Tower of Pisa once more. That tower had the finest craftsmen, the most beautiful marble, the most precise arcades — it lacked only a deep enough foundation, and so for eight hundred years it has been leaning. Brothers and sisters, let’s not be a beautiful leaning tower. Let’s be the man in Luke 6:48 who “dug and went deep.”

The Lord Jesus said: “I also tell you that you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my assembly, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it” (Matthew 16:18). The builder is the Lord himself, the rock is the Lord himself, and the guarantee of victory is the Lord himself. All we have to do is place ourselves on the right foundation.

Starting today, let’s return to the essentials of our faith and hold fast to the foundation that cannot be shaken —

taking Jesus as our role model,

taking the Bible as our standard,

taking the Holy Spirit as our guide,

letting Jesus be King,

letting Jesus receive all the glory,

establishing God’s system until the Lord returns.

May all glory be to him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb, forever and ever. Amen.

keyVerses: 1 Corinthians 3:10–11

“According to the grace of God which was given to me, as a wise master builder I laid a foundation, and another builds on it. But let each man be careful how he builds on it. For no one can lay any other foundation than that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ.”
Revelation 18:4
“I heard another voice from heaven, saying, ‘Come out of her, my people, that you have no participation in her sins, and that you don’t receive of her plagues.’”
practices: Meditate on 321 every day, and adjust your heart and your focus
Each week, take one deliberate action that tears down the Worldly system
Each week, remind and share with a spiritual companion
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, we bow down before you.

Lord, we confess that, often without realising it, we have let the world’s ruler measure our lives. We have built our faith on our own experiences, on familiar traditions, on the currents of our age. Have mercy on us, and forgive us.

Today we return once more to the foundation already laid — Jesus Christ. Help us to take Jesus as our role model, the Bible as our standard and the Holy Spirit as our guide. Bring down the self that sits on the throne of our hearts; let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory.

Lord, give us courage to come out of the Babylonian system, and give us perseverance to dig deep, day by day. Provide us with spiritual companions, so that we may support one another and stand together.
Establish God’s system among us, and let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Question 1: Matthew 7:24–25 says: “Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine, and does them, I will liken him to a wise man, who built his house on a rock. The rain came down, the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat on that house; and it didn’t fall, for it was founded on the rock.” Think back to the biggest “storm” since you came to faith. What did that experience reveal about what your foundation is built on — experience, tradition, currents of thought, or Christ and his word? Please share one specific incident.

Question 2: Ecclesiastes 4:9–10 says: “Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor. For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him who is alone when he falls, and doesn’t have another to lift him up.” Do you have a spiritual companion right now with whom you can honestly share “the things in which I haven’t yet let Jesus be King”? If so, tell us how you build each other up; if not, whom are you going to approach this week?
