sections.heading: Introduction: A Foundation That Stands Firm — Back to Jesus
sections.html:
In August 1173, the Italian city of Pisa broke ground on a bell tower for its cathedral. The design was exquisite, the marble gleaming white, and the whole city was proud of it. But by the time the builders reached the third storey, the tower had begun to lean to the south. The cause was not the carving, not the marble, not the skill of the masons. It was underground. The foundation had been dug only about three metres deep, and beneath it lay soft clay, fine sand and marl.

For more than eight hundred years people have tried everything to save that tower: halting construction to let the ground settle, correcting the angle of the upper storeys, pumping in grout, hanging lead counterweights on the north side, slowly drawing out soil through boreholes. In 1990 it was even closed to the public over safety concerns, and it did not reopen until 2001. All that engineering, all that money, all that ingenuity — and every bit of it spent on one thing: a foundation that was not properly laid in the first place.

Brothers and sisters, that is a picture of many Christian lives today. Above ground the building is tall and handsome: we can sing, we can pray, we can serve, we can give our testimony. But look underneath, and the foundation is three metres deep with soft sand below. So a gust of wind comes, a storm breaks, a blow lands, and the whole person begins to lean. And the lean never happens in a day — it started back when the third storey was going up.

At the close of the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus told a parable about foundations. He said:

“Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine, and does them, I will liken him to a wise man, who built his house on a rock. The rain came down, the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat on that house; and it didn’t fall, for it was founded on the rock. Everyone who hears these words of mine, and doesn’t do them will be like a foolish man, who built his house on the sand. The rain came down, the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat on that house; and it fell—and great was its fall.” (Matthew 7:24–27)

Notice the details of this parable. Both men heard the same words; both met the same storm. The difference was not in the hearing but in the doing. The rock is not “how many sermons I have heard”; the rock is “how much of these words I have actually lived out.” And what are these words about? They are about the very pattern of Jesus himself. To hear his words and to live after his pattern — that is building your house on the rock.

The Three Foundations of Kingdom 321 are: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. This morning we look at the first. Why does “Jesus is my role model” come first? Because in building any system, the first thing you need is to see the pattern. When God told Moses to make the tabernacle, he said, “See that you make them after their pattern, which has been shown to you on the mountain” (Exodus 25:40). The golden lampstand followed the pattern, the ark followed the pattern, even the colours of the curtains followed the pattern. To establish God’s system, we too must follow the pattern God has shown — and that pattern is not a rulebook. It is a person. It is Jesus.

Facing a world so full of temptation and twisted values, if we want to stand firm in our faith, we have to go back to the true foundation of faith. Not emotions, not experiences, not tradition — back to Jesus. He is not merely the starting point of our faith; he is the role model and the direction for our life every single day. Too many Christians today believe with great fervour but have no foundation; their faith is like a house built on sand, shaken by every wind and rain. May the Lord help us this morning to dig the foundation deep again, all the way down to the rock that cannot be moved.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: A Towel, a Basin of Water, and a Pattern for All Time
sections.html:
The first theme passage of this lesson comes from John chapter 13. The author of John’s Gospel is generally held to be John the son of Zebedee, the disciple whom the Lord Jesus loved. It was written around AD 80–90, most likely in Ephesus, for the churches scattered across Asia Minor — believers of Jewish background, and second-generation Christians from a Greek cultural background. They had never seen Jesus with their own eyes, yet they had to hold on to their faith under the pressure of the Roman Empire. John’s purpose in writing is perfectly clear: “but these are written, that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name” (John 20:31).

Structurally, John chapters 1 to 12 are often called “the Book of Signs,” recording how Jesus revealed himself to the world; chapters 13 to 21 are called “the Book of Glory,” where Jesus turns to face his disciples and, on the last night before his suffering, leaves his deepest words with those closest to him. Chapter 13 is exactly where that turn begins.

“Now before the feast of the Passover, Jesus, knowing that his time had come that he would depart from this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end.” (John 13:1) What follows is one of the most staggering scenes in the whole Gospel:

“Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he came from God, and was going to God, arose from supper, and laid aside his outer garments. He took a towel and wrapped a towel around his waist. Then he poured water into the basin, and began to wash the disciples’ feet and to wipe them with the towel that was wrapped around him.” (John 13:3–5)

To grasp how shocking this was, you need to know the culture of the day. The roads of Palestine were thick with dust, people wore sandals, and washing your feet before entering a house was the most basic of courtesies. But foot-washing was a slave’s job, and in Jewish society it was regarded as one of the lowliest jobs of all; rabbinic tradition even ruled that a Jewish servant need not wash his master’s feet — that was a task for Gentile slaves. That night the disciples had just been arguing over “which of them was considered to be greatest” (Luke 22:24). Twelve men sat there, and not one of them would pick up the basin.

So the Lord, who knew “that the Father had given all things into his hands,” stood up, took off his outer garment and wrapped a towel around his waist — the very dress of a slave. He held all things in his hands, yet with those hands he washed twelve pairs of dusty feet, including the feet of the man who would betray him. He did not use his authority to press people down; he used his authority to serve them. When he had finished, he put his clothes back on, sat down, and spoke the theme verses of this lesson:

“So when he had washed their feet, put his outer garment back on, and sat down again, he said to them, ‘Do you know what I have done to you? You call me, “Teacher” and “Lord.” You say so correctly, for so I am. If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet. For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you.’” (John 13:12–15)

The Greek word for “example” here is ὑπόδειγμα (hypodeigma), meaning “a demonstration set before your eyes, a model, a sample.” Jesus did not begin with a theory of ethics; he first gave a demonstration on the spot, and then said: do the same. The teaching method of God’s system has never been “Did you understand?” but “Did you see? Now follow.”

Another New Testament passage on example uses a different word: “For you were called to this, because Christ also suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow his steps” (1 Peter 2:21). Here “example” is ὑπογραμμός (hypogrammos), literally “writing underneath.” When children in the ancient world learned to write, the teacher first wrote a line of model letters on a wax tablet or on paper, and the pupil traced over them stroke by stroke — exactly what Chinese children call miaohong, tracing over red model characters. Brothers and sisters, the Christian life is taking up Jesus as our copybook and tracing him stroke by stroke. It doesn’t matter if the strokes aren’t pretty at first; as long as the direction is right, in time the writing begins to look like his.

The second theme verse, Philippians 2:5, was written by Paul around AD 60–62 while he was imprisoned in Rome, to the church at Philippi. Philippi was a Roman colony in Macedonia; its citizens were proud of their Roman citizenship and set great store by status and rank. A crisis had arisen in the church too: some were acting out of rivalry, some were chasing empty glory, and two sisters, Euodia and Syntyche, were at odds with each other (Philippians 2:3; 4:2). Paul’s prescription was not management technique, not a mediation meeting, but to set the pattern of Christ before their eyes again: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 2:5).

As for Matthew 7:24, it comes from the close of the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew chapters 5 to 7). Matthew wrote mainly for believers of Jewish background, to show that Jesus is the Messiah promised in the Old Testament, a Teacher greater than Moses. Having laid out the pattern of the people of the kingdom of heaven, Jesus sums up the Sermon with “two foundations,” and hands the question back to every listener: you have heard — now, will you do it?

sections.heading: 1. The Foundation of Faith Is Not Human Experience, Nor Denominational Tradition
sections.html:
“Everyone who hears these words of mine, and doesn’t do them will be like a foolish man, who built his house on the sand.” (Matthew 7:26)

Sand has one peculiar quality: it looks like ground, but it moves. The crescent dunes of the Sahara, pushed along by the wind, can travel anywhere from a few metres to several dozen metres a year. Plant a post on one today, come back a few years later, and the post is still there but the landscape has changed. Experience and tradition are the sand dunes of the life of faith: they really exist, and they really have carried us for a season, but they cannot carry us for a lifetime.

First, experience is precious, but it is subjective.

The experiences God gives us are grace; they are signs and milestones. But experience cannot be a foundation. The reason is simple: experiences pass, and our memory of them is not reliable. In a famous 1974 study by the cognitive psychologist Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer, participants watched film of a car accident and were then asked questions with slightly different wording. Asked “How fast were the cars going when they hit each other?” or “How fast were the cars going when they smashed into each other?”, people gave noticeably different estimates of speed. Asked again a week later, more of those in the “smashed” group even “remembered” seeing broken glass — when in fact there was none in the film. Human memory is not a video recording; it is a fabric rewoven every time we recall it. To build an eternal faith on “that time I remember being so moved” is to build your house on sand that moves.

Look at Elijah. On Mount Carmel he challenged four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal; he prayed once, fire fell from heaven, and all Israel fell on their faces crying, “Yahweh, he is God!” (1 Kings 18:39). What a summit of spiritual experience that was. Yet not long after, one threatening message from Jezebel reached him, and this great prophet fled into the wilderness, “sat down under a juniper tree” and asked to die, saying, “It is enough. Now, O Yahweh, take away my life” (1 Kings 19:4). Yesterday’s fire could not burn up today’s fear. The experience was real, but experience is not a foundation.

The lesson puts it precisely: some people’s faith is shaken because they meet a kind of suffering they have never been through before. Their faith had always been propped up by “how God treated me in the past”; when a new suffering goes beyond the range of their old experience, that pillar snaps.

Second, tradition has value, but it is not always right.

Tradition itself is not the enemy. Paul says, “So then, brothers, stand firm and hold the traditions which you were taught by us, whether by word or by letter” (2 Thessalonians 2:15). The creeds, hymns, orders of worship and missionary experience the church has gathered over two thousand years are the fruit of the Holy Spirit’s work through every generation, and we should treasure them.

So where does the problem lie? In putting tradition where Jesus belongs. Jesus said to the Pharisees, “For you set aside the commandment of God, and hold tightly to the tradition of men” (Mark 7:8); and again, “making void the word of God by your tradition, which you have handed down” (Mark 7:13). The Pharisees were not bad people; they were the most earnest, most devout, most rule-keeping people around. Their error was to hold the traditions of their forefathers above the word of God, so that when the Son of God stood in front of them, they did not recognise him. The lesson reminds us that some churches are so bound by tradition that they miss God’s fresh leading. “We’ve always done it this way” — those words are often the death certificate of a spiritual life that has stopped growing.

Third, Jesus alone is the foundation that never changes.

“For no one can lay any other foundation than that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ.” (1 Corinthians 3:11)

“Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever.” (Hebrews 13:8)

He is the Word that was in the beginning — “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1). He is the rock that cannot be moved — “For they drank of a spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4). He is the author and perfecter of our faith — “looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising its shame, and has sat down at the right hand of the throne of God” (Hebrews 12:2).

The Greek pair behind “author and perfecter” is beautiful. “Author” is ἀρχηγός (archēgos): the pioneer, the commander, the one who leads out in front. “Perfecter” is τελειωτής (teleiōtēs): the one who brings a thing to completion. He is not a referee waiting for us at the finish line; he is the commander marching ahead. He did not merely hand us a map; he walked the whole route himself, the cross included. That is why he can be our foundation — he has already walked every road we will ever have to walk.

From the 321 angle, this is “a shift of perspective”: from man’s perspective to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. Experience is temporary, tradition is earthly, feelings are human; only Jesus is eternal, heavenly and of God. When our foundation is moved from the temporary to the eternal, the storms will still come — but the house no longer leans.

Brothers and sisters, this morning you can ask yourself one honest question: if every beautiful spiritual experience of my past were taken away, if the meeting format, the style of worship, the denominational habits I know so well were all taken away, what would I have left? If the answer is “I would still have Jesus,” then your house is built on the rock. If the answer is “then I’d have nothing at all,” then today is the day to dig the foundation again.

sections.heading: 2. Jesus Is the Role Model We Follow All Our Lives
sections.html:
If the foundation is Jesus, the next question is very practical: how is he our foundation? The answer is — he is our role model. God did not toss us a rulebook and leave us to work it out; he sent his Son, who became a man, walked ahead of us, and said: follow. The lesson unfolds this main point in three layers.

1. The Life of Jesus — the Pattern of Our New Self

“But you didn’t learn Christ that way, if indeed you heard him, and were taught in him, even as truth is in Jesus: that you put away, as concerning your former way of life, the old man that grows corrupt after the lusts of deceit, and that you be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who in the likeness of God has been created in righteousness and holiness of truth.” (Ephesians 4:20–24)

Paul uses two verbs here: “put away” (ἀποτίθημι, apotithēmi) and “put on” (ἐνδύω, endyō). These are the movements of changing clothes. The old self is like a garment worn far too long, already “growing corrupt” through its lusts — the original carries the sense of rotting step by step, getting worse and worse. You cannot keep wearing it and hope to smell like new. But notice the phrase in the middle: “and that you be renewed in the spirit of your mind.” Between taking off and putting on there is a crucial process — the renewal of the mind. The 321 vision puts it plainly: change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. Trying to change behaviour without first changing the mindset is called suppression, not renewal.

So what does this garment of the “new self” look like? Paul says it is created “in the likeness of God.” Where can we see the likeness of God? In Jesus. “He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation” (Colossians 1:15). “His Son is the radiance of his glory, the very image of his substance, and upholding all things by the word of his power” (Hebrews 1:3).

Jesus became flesh — “The Word became flesh, and lived among us … full of grace and truth” (John 1:14) — and one of the most important purposes of that was to let us see with our own eyes: this is what a human being was always meant to look like. After Adam fell, humanity lost the beauty of God’s image; we no longer knew how a “human” ought to live. Jesus came and lived that pattern out again before our eyes. That is why Paul says, “As we have borne the image of those made of dust, let’s also bear the image of the heavenly” (1 Corinthians 15:49). And God’s intent is clearer still: “For whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brothers” (Romans 8:29). Brothers and sisters, God saves us not only to forgive us, but to shape us into the likeness of his Son.

The lesson offers a fine illustration. If a painter wants to learn from a masterpiece, the best way is not to imagine it but to copy the master’s original. Since the late eighteenth century the Louvre in Paris has run a copyists’ programme: painters can apply to set up their easels in front of the real works and paint, day after day. They are not trying to forge; they are teaching their hands to move like the master’s hand. To become a new creation, we too must “copy Jesus” day after day — setting our easel up in front of him, not glancing at a catalogue from a distance, but facing the original every day.

Scientifically speaking, imitation is the deepest learning mechanism God has built into us. In his famous 1961 “Bobo doll experiment,” the Stanford psychologist Albert Bandura (1925–2021) found that children who had merely watched an adult beat a doll would repeat those actions without being told to; in Social Learning Theory, published in 1977, he argued that most human behaviour is learned by observing models. Also in 1977, Andrew Meltzoff and M. Keith Moore published a study in Science showing that infants only twelve to twenty-one days old could imitate an adult sticking out the tongue or opening the mouth. In the early 1990s, Giacomo Rizzolatti’s team at the University of Parma in Italy discovered “mirror neurons” in the premotor cortex of macaque monkeys — the same group of neurons fired when a monkey performed an action and when it watched another perform the same action.

In other words, when God made us, he wired “see it and learn it” right into us. That is exactly why he did not only give the Law; he gave his Son. The Law tells us what we ought to be; a role model shows us what we can be. Whatever you look at every day, you gradually become — that is not only a spiritual principle, it is the design of how God made us.

2. The Teaching of Jesus — Inviting His Disciples to Follow Him

Jesus did not only say “Believe in me”; he also said “Follow me.” The religious teachers of the world say, “Listen to my teaching.” Jesus said, “Come after me” (Mark 1:17). That is the fundamental difference.

“Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.” (Matthew 11:28–30)

“Learn from me” is μάθετε ἀπ᾿ ἐμοῦ in Greek — literally “learn from me.” The noun formed from this verb μανθάνω (manthanō, to learn) is μαθητής (mathētēs) — disciple. A disciple is not “someone who has taken the course”; a disciple is “someone who is still learning from him.” In first-century Jewish society, following a rabbi did not mean enrolling in a class; it meant moving in to live with him — watching how he ate, how he prayed, how he treated people, how he faced opposition. The Sayings of the Fathers (Pirkei Avot) urges a man to “sit in the dust of the feet of the wise and drink in their words with thirst.” A disciple should be covered in the dust of his teacher’s feet — what a fitting picture.

In rabbinic language, “yoke” already meant “the yoke of the Law.” When Jesus says “Take my yoke,” he is saying: stop carrying the heavy yoke the Pharisees have laid on you, and carry mine. Some pastors explain it with the picture of two oxen under one yoke: a young ox yoked with a seasoned one doesn’t have to work out the direction and pace by itself; it simply follows along. Jesus did not say “my yoke weighs nothing”; he said “my yoke is easy” — because he shares the yoke with us, and up front he carries most of the weight.

After washing their feet he said, “For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you” (John 13:15). Then straight away he gave a new commandment: “A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another. Just as I have loved you, you also love one another. By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:34–35). Notice the standard — not merely “love one another,” but “just as I have loved you.” The standard is Jesus himself.

So what Jesus taught was never abstract theory, but love, forgiveness, humility, obedience, patience and mercy in real life. These qualities are the DNA of God’s system. DNA has one particular trait: it isn’t on the surface, yet it decides what every cell grows into. You can copy a church’s programme sheet, but you can’t copy its DNA; God’s system is not established by replicating forms but by replicating life.

And Paul long ago spelled out what that life looks like: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law” (Galatians 5:22–23). This is exactly the content of the 321 “920 practice”: every person we are in a relationship with is our “2”; before every “2” we practise living out the selfless (0) life, so that the nine (9) graces of the fruit of the Spirit grow one by one. The hardest person to live with in your home today is the examination hall God has given you; the patience you bear before that person looks more like Jesus than ten sermons you might preach from a pulpit.

3. The New Testament Teaching — Have the Mind of Christ

“Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross. Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, those on earth, and those under the earth, and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.” (Philippians 2:5–11)

“Have this in your mind” translates the Greek φρονεῖτε (phroneite). The verb φρονέω refers not just to feelings but to the orientation of one’s thinking, the setting of the mind, the direction of one’s value judgements. Paul is not telling us to imitate Jesus’ emotions; he is telling us to change the coordinate system of our minds. This is the first of the five changes: the change of mindset.

So what is “the mind of Christ”? Paul goes on to explain it in a passage widely recognised as an early Christian hymn. Look at this staircase going down: he existed in the form of God; he did not consider equality with God a thing to be grasped (ἁρπαγμός, a prize or privilege to be clutched and held on to); he emptied himself (ἐκένωσεν); he took the form of a servant; he was made in the likeness of men; he humbled himself; he became obedient to the point of death — and death on a cross, the most shameful death of all, which the Romans reserved for slaves and rebels. Step by step down, all the way to the very bottom.

Let me be clear: “emptied himself” does not mean he emptied out his deity. On earth Jesus was still fully God. “Emptied himself” means that he did not treat “equality with God” as a privilege to cling to and enjoy for himself; instead he willingly took the form of a servant, veiled his glory, and obeyed to the point of death. He did not become less; he simply stopped living for himself.

Now set this picture side by side with another passage. Isaiah records the inner voice of the one who exalted himself: “You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! I will sit on the mountain of assembly, in the far north! I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!’” (Isaiah 14:13–14). Five “I will”s, climbing all the way up, ending in “I will make myself like the Most High.”

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? Satan’s road is “I will make myself like the Most High”; Jesus’ road is “didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped.” One grabs desperately upward; the other walks willingly downward. One is the self-centred life; the other is selflessness. This is the heart of what the 321 vision teaches: pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. That is why humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan. You don’t have to wrestle pride head-on; you only have to walk Jesus’ downward road, and pride has nowhere left to stand.

And look at how it ends. Jesus went all the way to the bottom — “Therefore God also highly exalted him.” The one who grabbed upward was thrown down; the one who walked downward was lifted up. This is the law of physics in God’s system, the exact opposite of the world’s law. The world says: climb up and you will have glory. God says: go down and you will have glory — and in the end that glory goes “to the glory of God the Father.”

A line generally attributed to the German theologian Dietrich Bonhoeffer (1906–1945), from The Cost of Discipleship, says: “When Christ calls a man, he bids him come and die.” It sounds harsh, but it is in fact the greatest grace. For what dies is the old self’s “self,” and what comes alive is Christ’s fullness. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into fullness and living it out — “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. Denying of self, humility, obedience — this is the mind of Jesus, and it is the role model we are to learn from every day.

sections.heading: 3. Do Not Let People, Systems or Experiences Replace Jesus
sections.html:
Here the lesson sounds a very timely warning: people today are quick to chase celebrities, chase speakers, chase miracles. None of these can replace Jesus as our role model.

Don’t let a successful ministry model replace the pattern of Jesus; don’t let the style of a spiritual leader hide the face of Jesus; don’t let your own wonderful spiritual experiences replace the words of Jesus.

Scripture’s warning about this is sterner than we imagine. In the wilderness, when the Israelites were bitten by venomous snakes, God told Moses to make a bronze serpent and set it on a pole, and whoever looked at it lived (Numbers 21:8–9). That was an object God himself had commanded, carrying real healing. Yet more than seven hundred years later, Scripture records the reforms of King Hezekiah: “He removed the high places, and broke the pillars, and cut down the Asherah. He also broke in pieces the bronze serpent that Moses had made, because in those days the children of Israel burned incense to it” (2 Kings 18:4). Brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: the bronze serpent itself had not changed; the human heart had. An object God once used, once it is put in God’s place, becomes an idol that has to be smashed.

The same danger came to the apostles. When Paul healed a lame man at Lystra, the crowd shouted, “The gods have come down to us in the likeness of men!” and wanted to offer sacrifices to them. What did Paul and Barnabas do? “But when the apostles, Barnabas and Paul, heard of it, they tore their clothes, and sprang into the multitude, crying out, ‘Men, why are you doing these things? We also are men of like passions with you’” (Acts 14:14–15). They did not enjoy that glory; they tore their clothes. Even an angel did the same: when John fell down to worship the angel who had appeared to him, the angel said, “Look! Don’t do it! I am a fellow bondservant with you and with your brothers who hold the testimony of Jesus. Worship God” (Revelation 19:10).

As for chasing miracles, Jesus himself said, “Most certainly I tell you, you seek me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate of the loaves, and were filled” (John 6:26). It is so easy to fall in love with the bread in God’s hand rather than with God himself — to fall in love with the thrill of the miracle rather than with the Lord who works it.

The most beautiful picture of all is on the Mount of Transfiguration. Peter saw Jesus appear together with Moses and Elijah, and proposed to build three tents — one for Jesus, one for Moses, one for Elijah. On the surface it was devotion; in reality it put the representative of the Law and the representative of the prophets on a level with the Son of God. Then “a voice came out of the cloud, saying, ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to him’” (Matthew 17:5). The disciples fell on their faces, terrified; Jesus came, touched them, and told them to get up. And then comes one of the quietest and most powerful sentences in the whole Bible: “Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone” (Matthew 17:8).

Brothers and sisters, the mark of spiritual maturity is not how many spiritual giants you know, but that when the cloud lifts, you look up and “see no one else but Jesus.”

Why are we so easily led along by people? Psychology holds up an honest mirror. In the early 1950s, in the social psychologist Solomon Asch’s conformity experiments at Swarthmore College, participants had to judge which line matched a standard line in length — the answer was obvious. But when everyone else in the room (all of them research assistants) gave the same wrong answer in unison, a sizeable proportion of participants went along at least once with an answer they knew was wrong. Stanley Milgram’s obedience-to-authority experiments at Yale in the early 1960s were even more chilling: under continued instruction from a researcher in a white coat, most participants were willing to give another person what they believed were dangerous electric shocks. There is a switch inside us: given enough voices, or an image of enough authority, we hand over our judgement.

This is not to say we should trust no one; it is to say we reserve “absolute trust” for One alone. That is exactly how the Corinthian church split: “each one of you says, ‘I follow Paul,’ ‘I follow Apollos,’ ‘I follow Cephas,’ and, ‘I follow Christ.’” Paul immediately fires back: “Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you?” (1 Corinthians 1:12–13).

The 321 vision says: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. So the One we look to is not a person, not a feeling, but Jesus himself. Pastors are to be honoured, spiritual elders are to be thanked, miracles are to be remembered; but the easel always stands in front of the original, never in front of someone else’s copy.

sections.heading: 4. Integrating the 321 Vision
sections.html:
The framework of Kingdom 321 is simple: the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values, the Goal. The Three Foundations are: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. The Two Core Values are: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. The Goal is: establish God’s system.

Why is “Jesus is my role model” the first foundation? Because building any system always starts with the pattern. Speaking of the tabernacle, the writer of Hebrews says that the priests “serve a copy and shadow of the heavenly things, even as Moses was warned by God when he was about to make the tabernacle, for he said, ‘See, you shall make everything according to the pattern that was shown to you on the mountain’” (Hebrews 8:5). Moses could not build the tabernacle by his own sense of beauty; he had to follow the pattern shown on the mountain. If we are to establish God’s system today, we cannot go by our own imagination, by success stories or by fashionable models either; we must follow the pattern revealed on the mountain — Jesus Christ.

First, from the old self’s self-centred life to the new self’s selflessness.

The root of humanity’s fall is the self-centred life; the root of the problem is pride. The serpent’s words to Eve — “you will be like God” (Genesis 3:5) — moved human eyes off God and onto ourselves. From that moment people began to put themselves at the centre, to be their own king, to define good and evil for themselves. Jesus came and walked the exact opposite road: he did not consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself. His whole life was a demonstration of selflessness. So the heart of following Jesus is not mimicking his words and mannerisms, but entering into his life of “not for himself.” Selflessness is not becoming nothing; it is entering into fullness and living it out — “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me.

Second, humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan.

Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. That night the disciples were arguing about who was greatest — pride against pride, and left to run its course it would have ended with everyone hurt. Jesus picked up the basin, and one act of humility changed the air in the whole room. Brothers and sisters, the stalemate in your home, your workplace or your small group often doesn’t need a debate; it just needs one person to pick up the basin first.

Third, the fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry.

Following Jesus does not start with imitating behaviour; it starts with mindset. When Paul says, “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus,” he is talking precisely about a reorientation of the mind. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living; change daily living and you change relationships; and only changed relationships bring forth ministry that truly has life. Never reverse the order: life first, then relationships, then ministry. How many people put ministry first, only to find that the bigger the ministry grows, the drier their life becomes and the more broken their relationships? People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

Fourth, the priority of relationships: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things.

Before Jesus washed their feet, the text makes a point of saying that he knew “that he came from God, and was going to God” (John 13:3). He was first secure in his relationship with the Father and clear about his own identity; only then could he lay aside his honour to serve people, and only last did he deal with the business of that night. Someone who doesn’t know who they are cannot be humble — they have to keep proving themselves. Only someone at rest before the Father can bend down.

Fifth, the shift of perspective: from man’s to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly.

In the world’s eyes, washing feet is losing face; in God’s eyes it is the highest glory. Through earthly eyes the cross is defeat; through heavenly eyes it is the throne of victory. Following Jesus really means changing your glasses. Once the glasses change, the same event takes on an entirely different meaning.

Sixth, the 920 practice and 235 relationships.

The 920 practice: every person we are in a relationship with is our “2”; before every “2” we practise living out the selfless (0) life, so that the nine (9) graces of the fruit of the Spirit — love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control — grow one by one (Galatians 5:22–23). That night Jesus washed not only Peter’s feet but Judas’s too. His “2” included the man who was about to betray him.

235 relationships: becoming a “2” with someone who lives selflessly means having a spiritual companion with whom you can be honest and whom you can remind; building a “3” means spiritual parents and spiritual children, the passing on of life; and going on to become a “5” means a team of spiritual comrades, a fivefold-ministry team. The third practice in this lesson is about exactly this: following Jesus is not homework you do alone in your room; it is holding up a mirror to one another within the relationship of your “2.”

Finally, the Path of Serving is: Spirit (the Holy Spirit is my guide), Understanding (the Bible is my standard), Life (Jesus is my role model), Service (let Jesus be King), God (let Jesus receive all the glory). When we have followed Jesus to the point where what others see in us is no longer our style, our gifts or our name, but Jesus, then the Two Core Values are fulfilled: Jesus truly reigns as King, and Jesus receives all the glory. And that is precisely the Goal: to establish God’s system.

sections.heading: 5. Putting It into Practice: Three Daily Actions for Learning from Jesus
sections.html:
Practice 1: Read a passage from the Gospels every day and watch what Jesus does

Don’t only read “what Jesus said”; look at “how Jesus acted.” Take to heart the tone in which he spoke to people, his attitude towards sinners, his response to persecution. How did he look at the woman surrounded by the crowd? How did he treat the disciple who denied him three times? When people spat on him, what did he say? What did he not say?

Suggestion: read Matthew, Mark, Luke and John in turn, and each day write down one aspect of Jesus’ pattern you want to learn. Don’t try to take in too much — one action, one look, one sentence a day is enough. You can write three lines in your notebook: Today I saw Jesus ______; I usually ______; today I will ______.

The four Gospels have only eighty-nine chapters in all. Read one chapter a day and in three months you will have walked through the whole life of Jesus once; in a year you can walk through it four times. Ten years from now you will find your reactions have changed — not because you worked hard at suppressing them, but because you have looked at him long enough.

Practice 2: In conflict, ask, “If Jesus were here, what would he do?”

When you meet unfairness or discomfort at home, at work or in ministry, stop and ask this one question. Don’t let your instinctive reaction control you; let the role model of Jesus guide you.

This question has an honourable history. In 1896 the American minister Charles M. Sheldon published the novel In His Steps, in which members of a church resolve that for one year they will first ask, in everything, “What would Jesus do?” — and the whole city is turned upside down. The book went on to become a phenomenal bestseller, and the WWJD wristbands popular among American teenagers in the 1990s took their inspiration from it.

A word of caution: this question is not asking us to guess at Jesus’ mind from our imagination, but to call up the real Jesus of the Gospels and compare. The more you read, the more accurate your answer to this question becomes. That is exactly why Practice 1 and Practice 2 must go together — without Practice 1, Practice 2 becomes going by feeling; with Practice 1, Practice 2 is putting what you have read to use.

Every time you choose to be like Jesus, a little more of God’s system is built. A system isn’t put up overnight; it is laid brick by brick. And every conflict is a brick God places in your hand.

Practice 3: Remind one another with a spiritual companion that Jesus is our role model

Build a 321 companionship and remind each other: we do not live for ourselves; we are to live like Jesus. Not just studying the Bible together, but examining one another — are we really following Jesus?

Why must there be a companion? Because the thing the “self” does best is defend itself. I can’t see my own blind spots, any more than I can see the back of my own head. Paul could say, “Be imitators of me, even as I also am of Christ” (1 Corinthians 11:1). He was not boasting; he was putting himself where he could be examined. Disciples are not accumulators of knowledge; they are people who follow Jesus.

In practice: find a “2,” and once a week ask each other three questions — this week, in what was I like Jesus? In what was I not? Next week, in which specific relationship will I practise? No judging, no lecturing — only companionship, reminding and prayer.

Deepening these three practices with the eight stages of changing our mindset

1. Information: start with the right data. Reading the Gospels every day is a steady input of first-hand information about Jesus. Without information, every practice is empty talk.

2. Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to turn information into seeing. You read the same passage ten times, and one day it suddenly “lights up” — that is revelation. You can pray like this: Lord, don’t let me merely read it; let me see it.

3. Conviction: from “I know” to “I’m persuaded.” After seeing the pattern of Jesus, your heart needs to say, “Lord, you are right, and I was wrong.” Without conviction, behaviour will never truly change.

4. Implementation: use what you saw today. Read about Jesus’ mercy today, and find someone to show mercy to today. Don’t wait until you feel ready — you will never feel ready.

5. Evaluation: spend three minutes each evening looking back. At what moment today was I like Jesus? At what moment did the old self’s instinct jump out? Evaluation isn’t condemnation; it is honesty.

6. Correction: make a concrete adjustment at the point where you failed. Not a vague “I’ll be more humble,” but “when I see him tomorrow morning, I’ll be the first to say good morning.”

7. Repetition: once doesn’t count; keep doing it. A study by Phillippa Lally’s team at University College London, published in 2010 in the European Journal of Social Psychology, found that forming a new daily habit takes sixty-six days on average, ranging from eighteen to two hundred and fifty-four days for different people. So, brothers and sisters, don’t declare yourself a failure on day five. Repeat, repeat and repeat again — the pattern of Jesus is traced, not dreamed up.

8. Multiplication: pass on what you have learned to the next person. “The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also” (2 Timothy 2:2). When you start helping someone else follow Jesus, you learn faster and stand firmer yourself. This is moving from “2” to “3,” and from “3” to “5.”

sections.heading: Closing Word: Let Jesus Be Not Only Saviour but Role Model
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, we often say, “Jesus is my Saviour.” That is absolutely true, and it is the foundation of all our hope. But today the lesson asks us to take one step further: Jesus not only saves us from sin; he calls us to live out a godly pattern. He is not only the starting point of our faith; he is the model for our whole life.

If we take Jesus only as Saviour, we will live as a “forgiven old self” — sins forgiven, pattern unchanged, still centred on ourselves, just holding a ticket to heaven. Only when we take Jesus as our role model will we live as a “renewed new self” — putting off the old self, being renewed in the spirit of our mind, putting on the new self created in the likeness of God.

Back to the Leaning Tower of Pisa. People spent eight hundred years trying to save that tower, because its foundation could not be laid again. Thank God, our lives can. This morning the Lord Jesus stands before us; he has taken off his outer garment, wrapped a towel around his waist, and holds a basin of water, and he says to us: “For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you” (John 13:15).

To establish God’s system, the first step is to set our hearts: Jesus is the role model I will follow all my life. Not for one season, not in one kind of situation — for life. When I am at home, he is my role model; when I am at the office, he is my role model; when I am misunderstood, wronged or ignored, he is still my role model.

As day by day we trace over his copybook, one day people will look at us and see that familiar handwriting; it won’t be us they recognise, but Jesus. Then Jesus will truly reign as King; then all the glory will go to him.

As we leave this morning’s devotion, may we lift up our eyes and, in our hearts, see no one else but Jesus. Amen.

keyVerses: “For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you.” (John 13:15)
“Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus.” (Philippians 2:5)
“Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine, and does them, I will liken him to a wise man, who built his house on a rock.” (Matthew 7:24)
practices: Read a Gospel passage daily and watch what Jesus does
Remind each other with a spiritual companion that Jesus is our role model
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you. You existed in the form of God, yet you did not consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied yourself and took the form of a servant. You bent down and washed our dusty feet; you went to the cross and laid down your life for us. Lord, you are not only our Saviour; you are our role model.

Lord, forgive us. So often we build our house on sand — on past experiences, on familiar traditions, on the influence of some person, on our own feelings. Help us today to dig the foundation deep again, all the way down to you, our rock.

Lord, give us a heart that is willing to learn. As we open the Gospels each day, let us see not only what you said but how you acted. In every conflict, every hurt, every time we are misunderstood, let us stop and ask: Lord, if you were here, what would you do?

Holy Spirit, be our guide; make your word our standard, and trace the pattern of the Lord Jesus into our lives stroke by stroke. Take away our self-centred life and bring us into your fullness; take away our pride and teach us your gentleness and humility.

Lord, today we set our hearts: Jesus is the role model we will follow all our lives. May our homes be changed by you, our relationships reconciled by you, and our service filled with life by you. Reign as King among us, and let all the glory be yours. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine, and does them, I will liken him to a wise man, who built his house on a rock.” (Matthew 7:24) Think honestly: over this past season, what has mainly been holding up my faith — a past experience, a spiritual leader, a familiar style of meeting, or Jesus himself? If all of those were taken away, what would I have left?

“For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you.” (John 13:15) Name specifically the one relationship or situation in your life this week where you most need to “be like Jesus.” In that situation, what would Jesus do? What is the first concrete step you are willing to take? Agree with your spiritual companion to review it together next week.
