sections.heading: Introduction: This Age Has No Shortage of Voices — What It Lacks Is a Standard
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning, let’s grow quiet together and reflect on the second of the Three Foundations of 321 — the Bible is my standard.

Let me begin with a true story about “standards.” At Sèvres, just outside Paris, in a vault beneath the International Bureau of Weights and Measures, there sits a small cylinder cast from platinum-iridium, less than four centimetres in both diameter and height. It has a grand name: the International Prototype of the Kilogram. From 1889 onward, every kilogram in the world was defined by it. The bathroom scales in your home, the scales at the market, the balances in a pharmaceutical lab — trace them all back, and they point to that one little cylinder.

But scientists later discovered something awkward: this “standard” was itself changing. Over a hundred-odd years, a discrepancy of about fifty micrograms had opened up between it and the copies kept by countries around the world. Fifty micrograms is tiny, too small for the naked eye to see. But here is the problem — when the standard itself drifts, the whole world loses its reliable point of reference. So on 20 May 2019, the international metrology community formally retired that lump of metal and redefined the kilogram using a physical constant that never changes — the Planck constant.

Brothers and sisters, it took humanity a hundred and thirty years to learn one lesson: a standard must be unchanging, or it is no standard at all.

That is exactly what today’s lesson is about. In this age of information overload and confused values, what we need most is not more voices but one clear standard; not more choices but one right road.

Have you noticed that our problem today is not too little information but too much? Open your phone, and within thirty seconds ten people are telling you how to live. This one says, “Loving yourself is what matters most”; that one says, “Make your money first, then worry about the rest.” This one says, “If it feels right, do it”; that one says, “Don’t take things so seriously — good enough is good enough.” The more voices there are, the more lost people become.

A famous study by Sheena Iyengar of Columbia University and Mark Lepper of Stanford, published in 2000 in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, put numbers on this. They set up a jam-tasting stand in a supermarket: sometimes with twenty-four flavours, sometimes with only six. Twenty-four flavours drew sixty per cent of passers-by to stop; six drew only forty per cent. But — among those who stopped, only three per cent of those facing twenty-four flavours actually bought a jar, whereas thirty per cent of those facing six flavours did. Four times the choice, and the purchase rate fell to a tenth. Psychologists call this “choice overload.”

Too many choices, and people freeze. That is the spiritual portrait of our age. It isn’t that there is no road; there are too many roads. It isn’t that there is no voice; the voices are too jumbled. People stand at life’s crossroads holding a hundred maps and have no idea which one is real.

And God’s answer is very simple: he has given us one book. Not a hundred maps, but one; not a hundred standards, but one.

“Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path.” (Psalm 119:105)

The Bible is not one religious classic among many, nor a reference book for faith. It is the standard God has given for our lives, the sole authority for our faith and our daily living.

Brothers and sisters, the Three Foundations of 321 are: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. These three are not three parallel things; they are one chain of life. In the last lesson we saw that Jesus is my role model — he lived out the pattern God desires. But how do I know how Jesus lived? The answer is today’s lesson: through the Bible. Without the Bible, the role model becomes imagination; without the Bible, guidance becomes mere feeling. The Bible is the ruler that measures the truth of the role model and tests whether the guidance is genuine.

Today we will look together at four things: first, the Bible is the plumb line of our life; second, the Bible is the only standard for knowing Jesus; third, God’s word is absolute; fourth, the Bible is complete and cannot be altered. Then we will learn three concrete practices for making God’s word truly our standard every day.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Psalm 119 and 2 Timothy
sections.html:
Before we come to the main points, let’s understand the background of our theme passages. It will help us read them more accurately and apply them more rightly.

Psalm 119 is the longest chapter in the whole Bible, with 176 verses. It is a carefully crafted acrostic: the psalm is divided into twenty-two stanzas, matching the twenty-two letters of the Hebrew alphabet; each stanza has eight verses, and every verse in a stanza begins with that stanza’s letter. In other words, the writer used the Hebrew “A to Z” to compose a hymn to God’s word from beginning to end. The structure itself declares something: God’s word covers the whole of life, from A to Z; there is no corner his word does not reach.

The psalm is unsigned. From its content, the writer was a godly man in trouble, mocked by others and persecuted by the powerful. He says, “They had almost wiped me from the earth, but I didn’t forsake your precepts” (Psalm 119:87), and, “Princes have persecuted me without a cause” (verse 161). Many commentators suppose it was written in the period after the return from exile — just when the Israelites had come back from Babylon to a Jerusalem in ruins, the temple broken, the nation shattered, the future bleak. In such circumstances, what this poet held on to was not politics, not military strength, not connections, but the word of God.

Brothers and sisters, notice this: Psalm 119:105 was not written on a sunny day; it was written in the night. “Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path” — only someone walking a road at night treasures a lamp like that.

The “lamp” here is the Hebrew ner, the small oil lamp people in ancient times carried in the hand or hung from the belt. It doesn’t shine far; it lights only the one small step in front of your feet. This is a vital spiritual principle: God’s word often isn’t a searchlight showing you the whole road, but a lamp for your next step. He doesn’t let us see the whole journey; he makes us depend on him at every step. And “light” is the Hebrew or, a broader light, the light of dawn. He lights the near step, and he also sets the far direction.

Now look at 2 Timothy 3:16. This is the apostle Paul’s deathbed letter, written around AD 66–67, during his second imprisonment in Rome as he awaited execution. He wrote to his spiritual son Timothy, who was then pastoring in Ephesus. It was a time when heresies were springing up everywhere and false teachers were running rampant. In verse 13 of the same chapter Paul says, “But evil men and impostors will grow worse and worse, deceiving and being deceived.”

In that darkness, an old apostle about to be martyred handed his final charge to a young pastor. What did he say? He said, “Every Scripture is God-breathed.”

“God-breathed” is the Greek theopneustos, formed from theos (God) and pneō (to breathe) — literally, “breathed out by God.” This word appears only this once in the entire New Testament. Paul is saying that Scripture is not a human work that God has blessed; it is the breath God himself breathed out, written down through human hands. 2 Peter 1:21 says it even more clearly: “For no prophecy ever came by the will of man: but holy men of God spoke, being moved by the Holy Spirit.”

Brothers and sisters, this is the foundation we must stand firm on today: the Bible is the word God breathed out. Because God breathed it out, it carries God’s authority, God’s power, and God’s unchangingness.

sections.heading: 1. The Bible Is the Plumb Line of Our Life
sections.html:
The first point: the Bible is not a reference; it is a plumb line.

What is a plumb line? When builders in the ancient world put up a house, they held a cord with a lead weight tied to it; let it hang, and you have an absolutely vertical line. Whether the wall is straight is not decided by the builder’s eye, nor by how it looks to anyone else, but by that line. The line doesn’t bend to the wall; the wall must conform to the line.

That is the place the Bible holds in our lives.

Psalm 19:7–8 says: “Yahweh’s law is perfect, restoring the soul. Yahweh’s covenant is sure, making wise the simple. Yahweh’s precepts are right, rejoicing the heart. Yahweh’s commandment is pure, enlightening the eyes.”

Notice the four adjectives here: perfect, sure, right, pure. Perfect, so it needs no supplement; sure, so it will not waver; right, so it will not go astray; pure, so it will not be contaminated. Those four words are the very definition of a plumb line.

How did Jesus himself treat the word of God? In Matthew chapter 4, Jesus was tempted in the wilderness. Satan came at him three times, and three times Jesus answered on the strength of the same words: “It is written.”

The first time, Satan said, “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become bread.” Jesus answered, “It is written, ‘Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds out of God’s mouth’” (Matthew 4:4).

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? At the moment when the Son of God was at his hungriest, his weakest, and had every reason to bend the rules, he did not use a miracle, he did not use feelings, he did not use argument. What he used was — it is written.

The Lord Jesus is our role model. If he took Scripture as his standard, how can we not take Scripture as ours?

Let me ask you a very honest question, brothers and sisters: in your life, is the Bible really a “plumb line,” or is it “decoration”?

There is a test that cuts to the heart. When the words of the Bible clash with your own ideas, who gives way?

If the Bible gives way — if you say, “That verse was just the cultural background of the time,” or “That principle doesn’t apply today,” or “God will surely understand my situation” — then the Bible is not a plumb line in your life; it is an ornament. Because you are using your wall to correct the line.

If you give way — if you say, “Lord, I don’t understand, but what you say is right, and I will obey” — then the Bible truly is your plumb line.

In Memory, published in 1885, the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus used rigorous experiments on himself to draw his famous “forgetting curve.” He found that, without review, people forget about forty per cent of newly learned material within twenty minutes, and after one day only about a third remains. What does this remind us of? That if God’s word is only “heard,” it won’t survive in you for twenty-four hours.

That is why the psalmist says, “I have hidden your word in my heart, that I might not sin against you” (Psalm 119:11). Not “put it on the bookshelf,” but “hidden it in my heart.” The Hebrew word for “hidden,” tsaphan, carries the sense of treasuring, storing away, burying a treasure. People hide what is most precious to them. When you hide God’s word in your heart like treasure, then at the moment temptation comes it will leap out from within you and rescue you.

From the 321 angle, this is the first link in the five changes: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. All change begins with mindset. And what is mindset? Mindset is the plumb line in your heart. Romans 12:2 says, “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.”

“Be transformed by the renewing of your mind” — the original means to have your thinking thoroughly remade. Remade by what? By God’s word. When your plumb line changes, the results of your measuring change; when the results change, your choices change; when your choices change, your life changes.

Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. This is not a slogan; it is spiritual cause and effect.

sections.heading: 2. The Only Standard for Knowing Jesus
sections.html:
The second point: without the Bible, no one can truly know Jesus.

Some people say, “I don’t need to read the Bible; it’s enough to have Jesus in my heart.” Brothers and sisters, that sounds very spiritual, but it is actually very dangerous. Because — who told you about the Jesus in your heart?

If it wasn’t the Bible, that “Jesus” may well be one you made up yourself — the way you wish he were, not the way he really is.

John 1:1 says, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” Verse 14 says, “The Word became flesh, and lived among us. We saw his glory, such glory as of the one and only Son of the Father, full of grace and truth.”

“Word” in Greek is logos. To Jewish ears, logos echoed the creative word of Genesis — “God said … and there was”; to Greek ears, logos was the reason and order behind the universe. With this single word John told both kinds of people: the “Word” who created all things and runs through all things has become a man and lived among us.

So Jesus is the personal embodiment of God’s word. He is the fulfilment of Old Testament prophecy and the completion of New Testament truth.

What did Jesus himself say? John 5:39: “You search the Scriptures, because you think that in them you have eternal life; and these are they which testify about me.” (Or: “Search the Scriptures.”)

To the Pharisees, the people who knew the Scriptures best by heart, he said: you search the Scriptures, yet you have not seen that this whole book bears witness to me.

On the day of the resurrection, on the road to Emmaus, what did Jesus do for two discouraged disciples? Luke 24:27: “Beginning from Moses and from all the prophets, he explained to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself.”

Brothers and sisters, picture that scene. The risen Lord could have simply shown his glory, could have worked a great miracle, could have proved himself any way he liked. But what did he choose? He opened the Scriptures and, from Genesis to Malachi, went through every word of the Old Testament that pointed to himself, verse by verse.

This tells us something: Jesus himself held that the right way to know him is through the Scriptures.

So we do not believe in Jesus by feeling, nor love Jesus by experience; we follow him through the revelation of Scripture.

Feelings change. Today you are moved to tears; tomorrow your heart is hard as iron. Experiences get interpreted. The same event you could call God’s discipline, or you could call bad luck. Only God’s word is an unchanging point of reference.

Let me put it more clearly: feelings and experiences are not bad, and God often speaks to us through being moved and through experiences. The issue is the order. The Bible is the standard; feelings and experiences must be brought before the Bible to be tested, not the other way round, using feelings to test the Bible. Acts 17:11 commends the Bereans: “Now these were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, examining the Scriptures daily to see whether these things were so.”

Even what Paul preached, they checked against the Scriptures. That is not irreverence; it is the highest reverence.

Here is a vivid illustration. In 1947 a Bedouin boy searching for a stray goat in the caves at Qumran, on the north-west shore of the Dead Sea, idly tossed a stone into a cave and heard the sound of pottery breaking. What he had found were the Dead Sea Scrolls, which astonished the world. The most complete of them is an entire scroll of Isaiah, copied around the second century BC. Before it came to light, the earliest Hebrew manuscripts of Isaiah that scholars had were from the tenth century AD. More than a thousand years lay between them.

What would a thousand years of copying do to a text? The result astonished the world: the two are remarkably consistent; the vast majority of differences are only details of spelling and letter forms, and not one of them changes any doctrine.

Brothers and sisters, God himself has preserved his word. He did not leave his revelation to human memory; he had it written down, and he has kept it unchanged for a thousand years, two thousand years.

From the 321 angle, this is where Foundation One and Foundation Two join: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard. If you want to learn from a role model, you need a clear photograph. The Bible is that photograph. Apart from the Bible, our knowledge of Jesus gets distorted; hold fast to the Bible, and our faith stays true.

And the 321 vision says: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. How do we bring Jesus into focus? Open the Bible. When you read it each day, don’t just ask, “What benefit does this passage have for me?” Ask, “What kind of Jesus does this passage let me see?” See him, and you will be changed by him.

sections.heading: 3. God’s Word Is Absolute
sections.html:
The third point: God’s word is absolute; it has no grey areas and no room for compromise.

Jesus said, “But let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes’ and your ‘No’ be ‘No.’ Whatever is more than these is of the evil one” (Matthew 5:37).

Notice the second half of what the Lord Jesus said — “Whatever is more than these is of the evil one.” Pile up vague, evasive, leave-yourself-a-way-out words between “yes” and “no,” and their source is the evil one.

The evil one’s name is Satan. His scheme, from the beginning until now, has had only one move: to make people feel “uncertain” about God’s word.

Let’s go back to the Garden of Eden. What did God say? Genesis 2:16–17: “Yahweh God commanded the man, saying, ‘You may freely eat of every tree of the garden; but you shall not eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; for in the day that you eat of it, you will surely die.’”

God’s word contains two absolutes: “you may freely eat” is absolute grace; “you will surely die” is absolute warning. Crystal clear, not the least bit ambiguous.

What was Satan’s first line? Genesis 3:1: “He said to the woman, ‘Has God really said, “You shall not eat of any tree of the garden”?’”

He didn’t deny God; he just asked a question. “Has God really said …?” — he put a question mark on God’s word.

Then came the second step. Genesis 3:4: “The serpent said to the woman, ‘You won’t really die.’” The Chinese Union Version renders it, “You will not necessarily die.”

Brothers and sisters, look at those two words: “not necessarily.”

He didn’t say, “You will certainly not die”; he said, “You won’t necessarily die.” He didn’t overturn God’s word outright; he turned an “absolutely” into a “probably.” God said “surely”; he said “not necessarily.” The difference of a word or two — and the whole human race fell.

This is exactly what the 321 vision teaches: pride is the root of the problem; the self-centred life is where the fall begins. The real damage done by Satan’s words was to turn “what God says goes” into “let me weigh it up.” The moment people start deciding for themselves whether God’s word applies, they have already sat down on God’s seat. That is leaving our originally intended position and wanting to take God’s place.

Satan has been using this move for six thousand years, and he has never changed it.

Today he is still saying to you: it won’t necessarily go wrong — one more try won’t hurt; it isn’t necessarily wrong — everyone does much the same; you don’t necessarily have to be so serious — God will forgive, surely.

“Not necessarily” — those words are the smoothest road to sin. Because it never forces you; it just lets you “keep a little room.”

Doubt is where the collapse of faith begins.

The work of one psychologist sheds light on this. In 1957 the American social psychologist Leon Festinger put forward the theory of “cognitive dissonance”: when a person’s beliefs and behaviour don’t match, an uncomfortable tension arises inside; to relieve that tension, people usually don’t change their behaviour — they change their belief, finding a new way to explain what they’re doing.

Brothers and sisters, that is exactly where “not necessarily” goes to work. I want to do that thing, but God’s word forbids it. The least effort way to relieve the tension is not to stop, but to change God’s word into “not necessarily.” People don’t sin first and then doubt; very often they doubt first, and then sin.

So what is the antidote? The antidote is to return to the “absolute” of God’s word.

2 Corinthians 1:20: “For however many are the promises of God, in him is the ‘Yes.’ Therefore also through him is the ‘Amen’, to the glory of God through us.”

In Christ, every one of God’s promises is “Yes,” is “Amen.” God never says “not necessarily.”

History records a famous scene. In April 1521, at the Imperial Diet of Worms in Germany, the young monk Martin Luther was ordered to recant what he had written. Facing the pressure of the emperor, the bishops and the whole empire, his final words were in essence: unless I am convinced by the testimony of Scripture or by clear reason, I cannot and will not recant anything, for my conscience is captive to the word of God.

“My conscience is captive to the word of God” — brothers and sisters, that is what a person looks like who takes the Bible as the absolute standard. It is not the Bible held captive by my circumstances; it is my conscience held captive by God’s word.

From the 321 perspective, this is “let Jesus be King.” What does it mean for him to be King? It means what he says goes. If I keep a patch of “not necessarily” on God’s word, then the one reigning on that patch isn’t Jesus; it’s me. Selflessness overcomes Satan — when I no longer have any “but” toward God’s word, Satan no longer has any foothold.

sections.heading: 4. The Bible Is Complete and Cannot Be Altered
sections.html:
The fourth point: the Bible is complete, authoritative and secure.

Revelation 22:18–19 is the last warning in the whole Bible: “I testify to everyone who hears the words of the prophecy of this book, if anyone adds to them, may God add to him the plagues which are written in this book. If anyone takes away from the words of the book of this prophecy, may God take away his part from the tree of life, and out of the holy city, which are written in this book.”

This principle is not new with the New Testament. Moses said long before in Deuteronomy 4:2: “You shall not add to the word which I command you, neither shall you take away from it, that you may keep the commandments of Yahweh your God which I command you.”

Proverbs 30:5–6 says too: “Every word of God is flawless. He is a shield to those who take refuge in him. Don’t you add to his words, lest he reprove you, and you be found a liar.”

From the law of Moses, to the wisdom of Proverbs, to the last book written by the apostle John on the island of Patmos — from beginning to end the Bible speaks with one voice: do not add, do not take away.

This means three things.

First, the Bible is complete; it needs no supplement of secret knowledge. Today some people say, “Besides the Bible, there is another, higher revelation.” Brothers and sisters, be extremely careful of anything that makes “the Bible plus something else” a requirement for salvation or holiness. 2 Peter 1:3 says that his divine power has granted to us all things that pertain to life and godliness. Already granted — nothing lacking.

Second, the Bible is authoritative; it does not allow human opinion to override it. “Taking away” doesn’t necessarily mean cutting with scissors; far more often it means — skipping. The verses that make me uncomfortable, I just don’t preach, don’t read, don’t think about. That is the most genteel way of taking away.

Third, the Bible is secure; it does not change with culture or era. Isaiah 40:8: “The grass withers, the flower fades; but the word of our God stands forever.” The Lord Jesus said, “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Matthew 24:35).

Here we return to the story of the kilogram prototype we began with. Human standards drift, so they have to be replaced; God’s word never drifts, so it never needs replacing. The greatest mistake of our generation is often to do it backwards: treating the unchangeable as changeable and the changeable as unchangeable. We work hard at revising the Bible to suit the times, while working just as hard to protect our face and our habits from any change.

But the lesson reminds us here of something very serious: many people own a Bible, yet do not necessarily truly know Jesus.

Why? Because they treat the Bible only as a book of knowledge, not as the standard for life.

Here is a comparison that stings. A man falls ill, and the doctor prescribes medicine. He takes it home, puts it on the table, reads the leaflet three times a day, learns it by heart, and can explain to anyone the ingredients, the dosage and the side effects — but he has never swallowed a single pill. Tell me, will he get better?

James 1:22 puts it bluntly: “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.”

“Deluding your own selves” — the original, paralogizomai, means “misleading yourself by false reasoning.” A person hears a great many sermons, feels deeply moved, and so mistakenly believes he has already changed. This is the most common self-deception in the spiritual life.

Hebrews 4:12 says, “For the word of God is living and active, and sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing even to the dividing of soul and spirit, of both joints and marrow, and is able to discern the thoughts and intentions of the heart.”

A two-edged sword left in its sheath, however sharp, saves no one. God’s word has to come out of the sheath, pierce us and lay us open; only then do we truly change. The nineteenth-century English “Prince of Preachers,” Charles Spurgeon, is generally credited with saying that the Bible is like a lion: it doesn’t need anyone to defend it; just let it loose.

Brothers and sisters, the purpose of the Bible is not to make us know more, but to make us repent, change, be renewed, and live more like Christ.

This is the shift of perspective the 321 vision speaks of: from man’s perspective to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. Every time you open the Bible, you are undergoing surgery on your perspective. You are not going to find answers that support what you already thought; you are going to let God’s thoughts replace yours.

sections.heading: 5. Building a Way of Life with the Bible as Our Standard
sections.html:
If we truly believe the Bible is God’s word, we cannot stop at “reading”; we must go on to “believing,” “doing” and “living it out.”

In Joshua 1:8, God said to Joshua, who had just taken up the baton from Moses: “This book of the law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night, that you may observe to do according to all that is written in it; for then you shall make your way prosperous, and then you shall have good success.”

Notice the order: not departing from your mouth — meditating day and night — carefully observing to do it — a prosperous way. Three actions come first; the blessing comes after.

The following three practices help us turn God’s word into the standard of our lives.

Practice 1: Affirm one word of God each day to break the voice of doubt

Each morning, choose one verse, declare it out loud, and say firmly: “Lord, I believe your word is truth; this word is spoken to me, and I am willing to do what it says.”

Why “declare it out loud”? Because Satan’s attacks come through words. He says “not necessarily,” so you must answer with God’s “surely.” Ephesians 6:17 says, “And take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.” In the whole armour Paul lists, the only offensive weapon is the word of God.

Here are three examples:

When the doubt rises up — “I’ll fail, I’ll go without” — declare Psalm 23:1: “Yahweh is my shepherd: I shall lack nothing.”

When the pride rises up — “I can handle this on my own” — declare John 15:5: “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.”

When the emotional lie rises up — “I have no reason to rejoice” — declare 1 Thessalonians 5:16–18: “Always rejoice. Pray without ceasing. In everything give thanks, for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus toward you.”

This is a form of spiritual counter-attack: replacing lies with God’s word and building faith. Brothers and sisters, remember: you cannot “chase away” a lie; you can only “replace” it with the truth. The darkness in a room isn’t swept out with a broom; it is driven out by light.

Practice 2: Choose one verse each week and live it out in action

Each week, meditate on and choose one verse, and think: “How can I put this verse into practice in daily life?”

For example:

John 13:34: “A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another. Just as I have loved you, you also love one another.” — This week, take the initiative to care for a struggling member of the body.

Romans 12:21: “Don’t be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.” — Choose not to retaliate, but to bless the person who attacks you.

Matthew 18:22, where the Lord Jesus answers Peter’s question, “How often shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him?”: “I don’t tell you until seven times, but, until seventy times seven.” — Decide not to bring up the other person’s wrong again; choose to let it go.

This is a kind of hands-on training in truth, so that the Bible lives not only in our heads but in our actions.

In a study published in 1993 in Psychological Review, the psychologist K. Anders Ericsson and his colleagues showed that outstanding performance comes not from talent alone but from long-term, goal-directed “deliberate practice” with feedback. Brothers and sisters, the spiritual life is the same. Nobody “understands it” first and then loves people; we all “go and love” and gradually come to understand. Actually doing a verse once beats reading it a hundred times.

Practice 3: Each week, discuss with a spiritual companion how the Bible guides your decisions

Find a spiritual companion, study a passage together each week, and share with each other: “How was (or wasn’t) a recent decision of mine guided by the Bible?”

Such discussion can cover: choices and ethics at work; roles and responsibilities at home; values and priorities in daily living.

This is a Bible-led approach that trains you to judge everything by God’s word — not by feelings, not by trends, not by the crowd.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly the 321 “235 relationships.” The “2” is walking with a selfless spiritual companion; the “3” is building the legacy of spiritual parents and spiritual children; the “5” is entering a team of spiritual comrades, a fivefold-ministry team. God’s word grows strong only within relationships. Read the Bible alone, and it’s easy to read into it what you want to hear; read it together, and there is someone who can ask you, “Are you sure?”

2 Timothy 2:2: “The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.”

sections.heading: 6. Integrating the 321 Vision
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s set today’s message within the whole picture of the 321 vision.

The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. Today we have spoken about the second foundation, but the three are one lifeline. Jesus is the pattern, the Bible is the blueprint, the Holy Spirit is the master builder at work. Without the blueprint, the builder has nothing to build from; without the builder, the blueprint is only paper. That is why the Lord Jesus said, “However when he, the Spirit of truth, has come, he will guide you into all truth” (John 16:13). The Holy Spirit and the Bible never conflict, because the Bible was written by people moved by the Holy Spirit.

The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. Taking the Bible as our standard is, at heart, letting Jesus be King. Because “standard” means “what he says goes.” When I read a verse I don’t like and still obey, at that moment Jesus is enthroned in my heart.

The Goal: establish God’s system. The most fundamental difference between God’s system and the Babylonian system lies in “whose standard is used.” Babylon’s standard is human, earthly, temporary and worldly; the standard of God’s system is God’s, heavenly, eternal and godly. Whatever standard you measure things by, that is the system you are building.

The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred person reads the Bible to support himself; the selfless person reads the Bible to replace himself. Galatians 2:20: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into fullness and living it out. When my own standard is gone, God’s standard becomes my standard; when my thoughts make way, the mind of Christ is at work in me.

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; when it comes to reading the Bible, pride is “I decide whether this passage counts.” Humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. Letting God’s word be God’s word — that is returning to our originally intended position. Philippians 2:5–8 says: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.”

Life first, then relationships, then ministry. Many people read the Bible to prepare a sermon, to lead a Bible study, to meet the needs of ministry. Brothers and sisters, if that order is reversed, God’s word becomes a tool and no longer a plumb line. First let God’s word feed your life, then let it heal your relationships, and only then let it bear the fruit of ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

The 920 practice: every person we have a relationship with is our “2.” As we practise living out the selfless “0,” the nine graces of the fruit of the Spirit grow in those very relationships. Galatians 5:22–23: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.” Notice: the Bible is a standard, but it is not a ruler for measuring other people; it is a ruler for measuring ourselves. Measure yourself once a day, and the people around you will be that much more blessed.

Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves. Read the Bible with the brain, and what you get is knowledge and comparison; read it with the heart, and what you get is illumination and life. Psalm 119:130 says, “The entrance of your words gives light. It gives understanding to the simple.” Rely on the brain and you worry; rely on the heart and you rejoice. The outcomes of a whole life flow from the heart.

sections.heading: 7. Putting It into Practice: Going Deeper with the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset
sections.html:
The 321 vision tells us that changing our mindset has eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Let’s walk today’s three practices through these eight stages.

Information: first take God’s word in. Open the Bible at a set time, on a set reading plan, every day. Without information, nothing that follows can happen. This step is very basic, yet it is the one most people skip.

Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to turn words into light. When you finish reading, don’t rush to close the book; be still for a minute and ask the Lord, “Lord, which sentence are you speaking to me today?” Information enters the head; revelation enters the heart.

Conviction: say “yes” to that sentence. Not “I understand,” but “I am convinced.” Conviction is bowing your heart to that word and admitting it is more right than your own ideas. The declaration in Practice 1 is how conviction finds its voice.

Implementation: live that sentence out once this week. Practice 2 is this step. Don’t choose five verses; choose one. Don’t set a big goal; set one action you can do today.

Evaluation: look back at the end of the week. In what this week did I do as it said? In what did I fall back on “not necessarily”? Write it down honestly.

Correction: not self-blame, but adjustment. When you find the point of failure, ask the Lord’s forgiveness, then make the method smaller and more concrete. When a goal can’t be reached, it’s usually not that you’re hopeless; it’s that the goal was too vague.

Repetition: if one week with the same verse isn’t enough, do it for a month. Spiritual habits are not built on resolve but on repetition. Ebbinghaus’s forgetting curve tells us that the only way to beat forgetting is spaced repetition. God’s word is the same — meditating day and night is God’s version of spaced repetition.

Multiplication: share the change this verse has brought with your “2.” Practice 3 is this step. When you can pass on to another person a change you received from God’s word, only then has that mindset truly taken root in you. What you have taught is what you have learned.

Brothers and sisters, these eight stages are not walked once and finished; they are walked round and round. Each time round, your plumb line becomes a little straighter, and your house stands a little truer.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: Let God’s Word Be Your Daily GPS
sections.html:
Today nearly all of us use satellite navigation. The Global Positioning System was built by the US Department of Defense and became fully operational in 1995; it needs signals from at least four satellites at once to fix a position. What makes it remarkable is not that it knows the way, but that — when you take a wrong turn, it recalculates; and when you insist on carrying on the wrong way, it still keeps steering you back to the right road.

But there is one condition: you have to switch it on and follow it.

A GPS left in your pocket will never get you home.

The Bible is the same. In this bewildered and chaotic age, the one choice that can never be wrong is to make the Bible our standard. Not an occasional reference, but something we lean on continually; not kept on a bookshelf, but hidden in our hearts; not interpreted to suit ourselves, but obediently put into practice.

As the Lord Jesus said: “Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine, and does them, I will liken him to a wise man, who built his house on a rock.” (Matthew 7:24)

He went on: “Everyone who hears these words of mine, and doesn’t do them will be like a foolish man, who built his house on the sand. The rain came down, the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat on that house; and it fell—and great was its fall.” (Matthew 7:26–27)

Brothers and sisters, notice: both men heard. The difference was not in hearing; the difference was in doing. And — both men met the rain, the floods and the wind. God has not promised that those who trust him will never meet a storm; what he has promised is that the house will not fall.

Your choices every day are deciding whether your life is built on sand or on rock.

This morning I invite every brother and sister to make a decision before the Lord. Not a decision to “read the Bible more from now on,” but a decision that “from today, what God’s word says goes.”

Let Jesus be King over your judgements. Let Jesus be King over your choices. Let Jesus be King over your family, your work, your money and your tongue. Let God’s word no longer be an advisory opinion, but the highest court.

May we resolve to say: the Bible is my standard; I will live by God’s word, no longer wavering, no longer compromising.

May all the glory go to Jesus Christ — the Word made flesh, who laid down his life for us and lives for ever.

keyVerses: Psalm 119:105: “Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path.”

2 Timothy 3:16–17: “Every Scripture is God-breathed and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for instruction in righteousness, that each person who belongs to God may be complete, thoroughly equipped for every good work.”
practices: Affirm one word of God daily to break the voice of doubt
Choose one verse each week and live it out
Discuss weekly with a spiritual companion how the Bible guides your decisions
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you that you have not left us groping in the dark; you have given us your word as a lamp to our feet and a light for our path.
Lord, forgive us. So often we own a Bible yet do not know you; so often we hear many sermons yet do not act; so often we add our own “not necessarily” to your clear words.

Lord, today we choose to repent. Sanctify us in your truth, for your word is truth. Holy Spirit, open the eyes of our hearts, so that your word enters not only our heads but pierces our hearts, laying bare our thoughts and intentions.
Lord, we hand over our own standards; measure us by yours. In every choice, let us let you be King; let our lives become vessels for your glory.
Help us, from today, to affirm one word of yours every day, to live out one verse of yours every week, and every week to support one another with our companions in your word.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
Yahweh bless you, and keep you. Yahweh make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.
discussion: Matthew 5:37: “But let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes’ and your ‘No’ be ‘No.’ Whatever is more than these is of the evil one.” In what matter recently have you added a “not necessarily” to God’s clear word? What is the real reason behind that “not necessarily”?

James 1:22: “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.” Name one verse you know well but have not yet lived out. This week, what concrete action are you willing to take to put it into practice? Whom will you invite to be your spiritual companion so you can review it together?
