sections.heading: Introduction: Who Is Navigating Your Life?
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning I’d like to begin by asking you to picture a scene.

You get into a car, ready to set off for a place you have never been before. What do you do? Today most of us would give the same answer: open the phone, type in the address and let the satnav lead the way. We keep the steering wheel in our own hands, yet we hand the question of “which way do I go?” over to a system we cannot see. That system depends on satellites in the sky. The Global Positioning System (GPS), maintained by the United States government, has a baseline constellation of at least twenty-four satellites orbiting some twenty thousand kilometres above the earth, and your phone has to pick up signals from at least four of them at once to work out where you are. You cannot see those satellites, and you could not understand the signals they send, yet every day you trust them.

We obey an invisible satellite system so readily, yet we are so often strangers to the true and living Holy Spirit who dwells within us. Isn’t that strange?

We live in an age that leans on reason, prizes efficiency and worships technology. We are used to analysing first, assessing first, running the cost-benefit numbers first — and only at the very end do we think of praying. Sometimes we even treat prayer as a kind of “blessing on top”: the plan is already settled, and we simply ask God to bless the decision we have made ourselves. And so, for many believers, “the invisible Holy Spirit” has been quietly moved out to the edges of their faith, as though he were an optional extra — nice to have, but you can still drive without him.

But that is not what the Bible says. In Galatians 5:25 Paul says plainly, “If we live by the Spirit, let’s also walk by the Spirit.” Brothers and sisters, listen to the logic of that sentence. It does not say, “If you’re interested, you could try relying on the Spirit.” It says: since the beginning of your life was given by the Spirit, the walking out of your life ought to be led by the Spirit as well. If we receive life by the Spirit, how can we walk by our own strength? If someone’s life has been reborn by the Holy Spirit, yet they go about their days by the methods of the old self, it is like starting a car with the most advanced engine in the world and then getting out to push it along by hand.

The most powerful testimony of all comes from the Lord Jesus himself. The Lord Jesus is the Son of God, and all power is his, yet in his thirty-three years on earth he did not act on his own. At his baptism, “He saw the Spirit of God descending as a dove, and coming on him” (Matthew 3:16). Before he began his ministry, he “was led up by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil” (Matthew 4:1). When he declared his calling in the synagogue at Nazareth, the first words out of his mouth were, “The Spirit of the Lord is on me, because he has anointed me” (Luke 4:18). When he cast out demons he said, “But if I by the Spirit of God cast out demons, then God’s Kingdom has come upon you” (Matthew 12:28).

Brothers and sisters, think about it: if even Jesus relied on the Holy Spirit, who are we to dare to rely on ourselves?

So it was with the writers of Scripture, so it was with the first disciples, so it has been with the saints of every generation. And today we need it even more. The leading of the Holy Spirit is not a luxury, not the privilege of a spiritual elite, not an optional extra; he is a daily necessity in the life of every Christian. That is the lesson we are going to receive together today.

Of the Three Foundations of Kingdom 321, we have already looked at two: Jesus is my role model, and the Bible is my standard. Today we come to the third — the one that “plugs in” the other two: the Holy Spirit is my guide. The role model gives us direction, the standard gives us a measure, and the guide gives us leading for every day and every step. Not one of the three can be missing.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Three Passages, Three Eras, One Voice
sections.html:
Today’s three key passages come from three different writers in three different eras, yet they all point to the same truth. If we first set each of them back in its own setting, the message will stand out in full relief.

The first is Galatians 5:25, written by the apostle Paul. Galatians is generally regarded as one of Paul’s earliest letters, written somewhere between AD 48 and 55 to the churches of the region of Galatia. A group had arisen in the church, known as the “Judaizers”, who were telling Gentile believers: believing in Jesus is not enough — you must also be circumcised and keep the law of Moses before you are truly saved. Paul was furious. In Galatians 3:3 he fires back: “Having begun in the Spirit, are you now completed in the flesh?” That is the central issue of Galatians — beginning by the Spirit, then carrying on by the flesh. By chapter 5, Paul sums up his answer in one sentence: “If we live by the Spirit, let’s also walk by the Spirit.”

The word “walk” here is the Greek stoicheō, which originally means “to walk in line”, “to advance in order” — like soldiers marching in formation, keeping step, one stride at a time, with the command given from the front. Paul is not using the picture of a stroll; he is using the picture of keeping in step. Walking by the Spirit is not being moved now and then; it is keeping pace with the Holy Spirit day after day, falling into step with him. Brothers and sisters, this word reminds us: the spiritual life is not an improvised performance but an ongoing following.

The second is Romans 8:14. Paul wrote Romans from Corinth to the church in Rome around AD 56–57, and it is the fullest statement of his theology. Chapter 7 describes a person struggling under the law — “For the good which I desire, I don’t do; but the evil which I don’t desire, that I practice” (Romans 7:19). Then chapter 8 turns, and the air is entirely new: the chapter mentions the Spirit some twenty times, making it the most concentrated teaching on the Holy Spirit anywhere in the New Testament. Here Paul declares that the way to overcome the flesh is not to try harder at keeping the law, but to be led by the Spirit of God. So he says, “For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are children of God.” The next two verses are warmer still: “For you didn’t receive the spirit of bondage again to fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, ‘Abba! Father!’ The Spirit himself testifies with our spirit that we are children of God” (Romans 8:15–16).

The third is Proverbs 3:5–6. The main author of Proverbs is King Solomon, and the book took shape around the tenth century BC; later, in the time of King Hezekiah (around the eighth century BC), his officials collected and added to it (Proverbs 25:1). Proverbs is wisdom literature, addressed to “my son” — a father patiently and lovingly guiding his child. And here is the striking thing: Solomon is the man the Bible calls the wisest of all, and yet this cleverest of men wrote, “Don’t lean on your own understanding.” Coming from his lips, those words carry exceptional weight.

The Hebrew behind “trust” is bāṭaḥ, which originally means “to lean back and rest on”, “to hand over your whole weight” — like a child flopping, whole body, into his father’s arms. The word “acknowledge” is the Hebrew yādaʿ, which means “to know” or “to recognise”, and points to recognising his sovereignty in all that we do. And the word translated “make straight” carries in the original the sense of “to straighten” or “to make level” — God does not merely tell you which way to turn at the fork in the road; he himself straightens your path.

Brothers and sisters, three passages, three eras, but one voice: do not rely on yourself; rely on him.

sections.heading: Key Point 1: The Holy Spirit Is Not an Optional Extra but a Necessity
sections.html:
Let’s look at the first key point.

“If we live by the Spirit, let’s also walk by the Spirit.” (Galatians 5:25)

In this age that leans on reason and prizes efficiency and technology, “the invisible Holy Spirit” is often overlooked by believers. We would never deny that the Holy Spirit exists — we confess him in the creeds, we sing his praise in our hymns, we are baptised in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. But in the office at nine o’clock on a Monday morning, on the night when one of the children is in trouble, at the crossroads of whether or not to change jobs — how many times have we actually stopped and said, “Holy Spirit, how do you see this?”

The Holy Spirit has been treated as an “optional extra”. When you buy a car, the sunroof is optional, leather seats are optional — nice if you add them, but the car still runs without them. That is exactly where many people have placed the Holy Spirit in their hearts: nice to have, but life goes on without him. Yet the Bible has never put the Holy Spirit in the options column. He is the engine, not the sunroof.

Look at how the Lord Jesus himself lived. While he was on earth, the Lord Jesus did not act on his own; he depended entirely on the leading and power of the Holy Spirit. At his baptism the Spirit came down on him; he was led by the Spirit into the wilderness; by the Spirit he cast out demons, healed the sick and preached. John 5:19 records his own words: “The Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing. For whatever things he does, these the Son also does likewise.”

Brothers and sisters, what an astonishing statement that is. The Son of God, the Word made flesh, stood on this earth and said: I can do nothing of myself. Then what about us? In John 15:5 the Lord Jesus says it even more directly: “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.”

Notice the two ends of that sentence. At one end is “bears much fruit”; at the other is “can do nothing”. There is no third option in between. There is no “apart from me you can do a little bit”. In spiritual things there is no bare pass mark — only connected or cut off.

I often think of the appliances at home. Take the finest air conditioner — however well designed, however energy-efficient — if it isn’t plugged in, it is just a very expensive metal box. It isn’t broken; it simply isn’t connected to the power. That is the condition of many Christians: not that they aren’t earnest enough, not that they aren’t gifted enough, but that they aren’t plugged in. We use our own willpower to love the person who is so hard to love, our own grit to break the habit we have failed to break time and again, our own cleverness to plan a road God never asked us to take. And the result is exhaustion.

Zechariah 4:6 could not be clearer: “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit,’ says Yahweh of Armies.” Those words were spoken to Zerubbabel. Zerubbabel was to rebuild the temple on a heap of ruins, facing too few workers, too few resources and opposition from the surrounding nations. God did not first give him more people and more money; God first gave him a word: by my Spirit.

In the natural world, too, we see the mystery of “guidance”. The European robin migrates thousands of kilometres each year and can find its way accurately in the pitch dark of night. Research by Wolfgang and Roswitha Wiltschko, published in the journal Science in 1972, showed that the robin has a “magnetic compass” that senses the earth’s magnetic field to find its bearings. That little bird cannot see the magnetic field and knows nothing of physics, but it yields to that invisible guidance and reaches its destination. Brothers and sisters, if God has built a navigator even into a small bird, would he leave the children he bought back with his precious blood to lose their way in the wilderness of life?

Seen through the 321 lens, this key point presses right on our deepest sickness: the self-centred life. The core of the old self is self-centredness — my views, my plans, my abilities, my face. A self-centred person will inevitably rely on himself; and whoever relies on himself will inevitably crowd out the Holy Spirit. For two kings cannot sit on the same throne at the same time. When I climb onto it, the Holy Spirit steps aside as a guest; when I step down, the Holy Spirit becomes Lord within me.

So the foundation “the Holy Spirit is my guide” is not a doctrinal topic; it is a throne question. It forces us to answer: today, this day, who is King?

Humility is returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. Relying on the Holy Spirit is humility at its most concrete; relying on ourselves is pride at its most everyday. And we know: humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan.

sections.heading: Key Point 2: Living by the Spirit Is the Mark of God’s Children
sections.html:
In the second key point we look at what this means for our identity.

“For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are children of God.” (Romans 8:14)

The true children of God will always be learning to let the Holy Spirit lead them, and no longer act on their own will. Notice that this is not merely a spiritual experience; it is the display of an identity. Paul does not say, “As many as are led by the Spirit of God are rather more spiritual”; he says, “these are children of God.” Being led is the mark of a son or daughter.

This mark matters, because it carries both a comfort and a reminder.

The comfort is this: you are led not because you are good enough, but because you are a child of God. In the very next verse Paul says, “For you didn’t receive the spirit of bondage again to fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, ‘Abba! Father!’” (Romans 8:15). “Abba” is Aramaic, the most intimate word a little child in a Jewish home of that time would use for his father — much like a child today calling out “Daddy”. Paul took that household baby-word and set it in the most rigorous theological letter he ever wrote. What he wants to say is this: your relationship with God is not that of a slave and a master, but of a child and a father. A slave listens for orders; a child listens for the father’s heart. A slave is afraid of doing wrong; a child loves to be close.

The reminder is this: since you are a child of God, you ought to live in a way that is different from the world. In verse 16 of the same chapter Paul says, “The Spirit himself testifies with our spirit that we are children of God.” It is a double witness — the Spirit testifies, and our own spirit testifies too. When, in a moment where you would normally lose your temper, you suddenly grow quiet; when, at a moment where you could take advantage, you choose to take the loss; when, in a situation where everyone says “just let it go”, you still choose to forgive — in that moment the Holy Spirit is setting his seal upon you.

Ezekiel 36:27 is the Old Testament’s most beautiful prophecy of this: “I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes. You will keep my ordinances and do them.” Look at the order: first the Spirit is put within, and only then comes obedience. It is not that you obey first and then God gives you his Spirit; it is that God first gives you his Spirit, and only then are you able to obey. The law of the Old Covenant was written on tablets of stone; the law of the New Covenant is written on the tablets of the heart — and the pen is the Holy Spirit.

A picture from everyday life comes to mind. A child is playing outside; it is getting dark, and his mother calls his name from the front door. Dozens of children are running about up and down the street, but only one lifts his head. Why? Because it is his mother’s voice. He needed no training; he simply grew up hearing it. Brothers and sisters, knowing the voice of the Holy Spirit is just the same — it comes not from a set of techniques but from a relationship; not from one special conference but from being with him every day.

Psychology offers an interesting piece of supporting evidence here. When people face too many choices, they often become not freer but more paralysed. In a well-known study published in 2000 in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, Sheena Iyengar of Columbia University and Mark Lepper of Stanford University set up jam-tasting stalls in a supermarket: one display offered twenty-four kinds of jam, the other only six. The display with twenty-four drew more people to stop, but only about three per cent of them actually bought; at the display with just six, the purchase rate was as high as about thirty per cent. With too many choices, people simply freeze.

Brothers and sisters, that is exactly where many people are today. We have more information and more options than ever before, and we are more lost than ever before. What we need is not more options but a Guide. The privilege of God’s children is that we do not have to grope our way alone through endless possibilities, because we have a navigator living within us.

The Holy Spirit is able to lead us at any time and in any place. He is the indwelling Teacher, the Counsellor, the Guide. In John 14:26 the Lord Jesus promises, “But the Counselor, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things, and will remind you of all that I said to you.” And in 16:13 he says, “However when he, the Spirit of truth, has come, he will guide you into all truth.”

“Counselor” is the Greek paraklētos, which literally means “the one called alongside”, and can be rendered comforter, advocate or helper. The word tells us that the Holy Spirit does not shout at us from a distance; he is the one sent to our side, the one who lives within us.

So he leads us not only in the broad direction of our lives but also in the details and choices of daily living. He helps us understand God’s word, and he also reminds us of the words we ought to speak and the road we ought to take. Some think the Holy Spirit only handles the big things — “calling”, “vision” — while the daily trivia is up to us. But a real father doesn’t turn up only when his child sits university entrance exams, and then go missing when the child falls over.

The 321 vision says: the priority of relationships is first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things. A life led by the Holy Spirit is a life that gets that order right. When we are connected with God every day, we come to know who we truly are; when we know who we are, our relationships with others become healthy; and when our relationships are healthy, ministry stops being a burden. Life first, then relationships, then ministry — this is not a slogan; it is an order. And the Holy Spirit is the guardian of that order.

sections.heading: Key Point 3: How to Actually Experience the Holy Spirit’s Leading
sections.html:
The third key point is the question everyone most wants to ask.

We often ask, “The Holy Spirit can’t be seen or touched — so how can I be led by him?” It is an honest question, and a good one.

Proverbs 3:5–6 gives us a key answer: “Trust in Yahweh with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight.”

Notice that the emphasis of this passage is not on technique but on attitude. It does not teach us a method for discerning voices; it speaks of only three things: trust with all your heart, don’t lean on your own understanding, and acknowledge him in all your ways. Only then comes the promise: he will make your paths straight.

The key to the Holy Spirit’s leading is not whether we hear a voice, but whether we are willing to lay ourselves down and rely on him wholeheartedly. Many people strain desperately to “hear”, yet refuse first to “let go”. It is like turning the stereo up to full volume and then complaining that you can’t make out what someone is saying. The problem isn’t that the volume is too low; it’s that there’s too much noise. And the loudest noise inside us is our own voice.

Put simply: rely on the heart and not the brain.

Please don’t misunderstand: this is not a call to abolish reason. God gave us minds to use. The Bereans were “examining the Scriptures daily” (Acts 17:11) — that is using the mind — and Scripture commends them as “more noble than those in Thessalonica”. When 321 says “rely on the heart and not the brain”, it means an order of surrender: let the heart surrender before the head does. Not first analysing whether it’s feasible, but first seeking his will; not first calculating whether it’s worth it, but first asking whether this is God’s way.

Proverbs 4:23 says, “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” The wellspring of life flows not from the brain but from the heart. Rely on the heart and you’ll be glad; rely on the brain and you’ll be sad — that familiar saying actually holds a deep truth: the head is good at calculating risk, so when the head speaks first, fear is usually the loudest voice.

The Bible gives us a painful example. Joshua chapter 9 records how the Gibeonites disguised themselves as envoys from a distant land and came to sue for peace, carrying mouldy bread and split wineskins. The leaders of Israel looked, touched and smelled, and everything seemed to add up, so they made a covenant with them. Scripture pinpoints the whole problem in a single sentence: “The men sampled their provisions, and didn’t ask counsel from Yahweh’s mouth” (Joshua 9:14). Brothers and sisters, it wasn’t that they weren’t clever enough; it was that they didn’t ask. And so many of our mistakes today come not from being foolish but from not asking.

By contrast, Acts 16 gives us a beautiful picture. Paul and his companions wanted to preach in Asia, but “they were forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia”, so they went through the region of Phrygia and Galatia. “When they had come opposite Mysia, they tried to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit didn’t allow them” (Acts 16:6–7). Look — this was a good plan; they were going to preach the gospel, not to do something wrong. But the Holy Spirit said “no”. So Paul changed course, and then in Troas he saw the vision of the man from Macedonia, and through that the gospel set foot in Europe for the first time.

Brothers and sisters, had Paul insisted on his own good plan that day, the history of the church in Europe might have been written differently. Sometimes the Holy Spirit’s “no” is more precious than his “yes”.

When we first begin to practise this, it may feel unfamiliar. That is perfectly normal. Research by Phillippa Lally’s team at University College London, published in 2010 in the European Journal of Social Psychology, found that forming a new daily habit takes on average about sixty-six days, with wide individual variation — anywhere from eighteen to two hundred and fifty-four days. Brothers and sisters, if even small habits like brushing your teeth or drinking water take two months, how much more a habit like “ask the Holy Spirit first in everything”, which has to overturn the instincts of the old self?

So don’t give up just because the first few times you felt unsure or couldn’t discern clearly. As long as we learn each day to rely on the Holy Spirit and to acknowledge the Lord’s sovereignty, he will make our paths straight. We will grow more and more sensitive to the Spirit’s promptings, and more and more used to following his leading in matters great and small. Spiritual sensitivity, like an athlete’s muscle memory, is built by training, not by thinking.

Seen through 321’s fivefold change, this is a complete process: change the mindset (I don’t have to rely on myself after all), and you change the life (I begin to rely on the Holy Spirit); change the life, and you change daily living (the way I make decisions is different); change daily living, and you change relationships (the way I respond to people is different); change relationships, and you change ministry (my service no longer flows from my own will but from his sending). The starting point of it all is a change of mindset.

sections.heading: Key Point 4: How the Holy Spirit Leads in Our Lives
sections.html: In the fourth key point, we look at the four main channels through which the Holy Spirit leads. God is a God of order; his leading, though mysterious, is never chaotic.

sections.heading: 1. Through God’s Word
sections.html:
The Holy Spirit makes the words of Scripture a living reminder and illumination in our hearts.

This is the most basic, the safest, and also the most neglected channel of the Spirit’s leading. For Scripture is inspired by the Holy Spirit: “Every Scripture is God-breathed and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for instruction in righteousness” (2 Timothy 3:16). Since he wrote this book, of course he knows best how to use it to speak to us.

Psalm 119:105 says, “Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path.” Notice how precise that picture is. An ancient lamp was a small oil lamp carried in the hand or hung near the feet, and the circle it lit was about the size of the next step. God’s word is mostly not a searchlight that lights up the next ten years of your future in one sweep; it is a lamp to your feet, lighting the one step you should take today. That is exactly why we need to read Scripture every day — the lamp has to stay in our hand for the path to stay lit.

Hebrews 4:12 says, “For the word of God is living and active, and sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing even to the dividing of soul and spirit, of both joints and marrow, and is able to discern the thoughts and intentions of the heart.” Have you ever had this experience: a passage you have read dozens of times suddenly, one morning, reads as though for the first time, and every word lands on your heart? That is no coincidence; that is the Holy Spirit picking up the book he himself wrote and speaking to you.

There is an important principle here: the Holy Spirit will never lead us to do anything that contradicts Scripture. The Holy Spirit does not contradict himself. Any “prompting” that runs against the plain teaching of Scripture does not come from the Holy Spirit — without exception. Among 321’s Three Foundations, the Bible is my standard — and a standard is a ruler to measure by; the Spirit’s leading must stand up to being measured against that ruler.

So morning devotion is not a religious habit; it is keeping an appointment. You open your Bible not to tick off your reading plan but to keep a date with the Holy Spirit.

sections.heading: 2. Through Inner Promptings and Peace
sections.html:
When we obey the Holy Spirit, a heavenly steadiness and peace follow.

Colossians 3:15 says, “And let the peace of God rule in your hearts.” The word “rule” here is the Greek brabeuō, which originally means “to act as umpire”, “to arbitrate” — like the referee on the sports field who makes the final call. Paul means: let Christ’s peace be the referee in your heart. When two roads lie before you and your heart argues back and forth without end, that referee will blow the whistle.

Philippians 4:6–7 has been the experience of countless saints: “In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.” Notice the words “surpasses all understanding”. It is a peace that defies logic — the circumstances haven’t changed, the difficulty hasn’t been removed, and yet you suddenly find yourself settled. That peace is not something you manufacture; it is something he gives.

We must also be honest: feelings can deceive, and emotions rise and fall. That is why the Bible never asks us to act on feelings alone. This channel must always be used together with the first one (God’s word). A prompting that truly comes from the Holy Spirit has several marks: it agrees with Scripture; it makes us humble rather than boastful; it brings peace rather than panic; it stands the test of time, rather than being strong today and gone tomorrow; and it makes us love God more and love people more.

From a scientific angle, “stopping to be still” is itself beneficial. In his 1975 book The Relaxation Response, Dr Herbert Benson of Harvard Medical School proposed that when people become still, breathe slowly and focus on a repeated word or phrase, the body enters a physiological state that is the opposite of the “fight or flight” response: the heart rate slows, blood pressure falls and oxygen consumption drops. Brothers and sisters, this of course is not the same thing as spiritual peace — heavenly peace comes from the Holy Spirit, not from a breathing technique. But it does show one thing: when God made us, he built into our very bodies the principle that “you only hear when you are still”. Isaiah 30:15 says, “You will be saved in returning and rest. Your strength will be in quietness and in confidence.”

sections.heading: 3. Through Circumstances and Confirmation
sections.html:
God uses people, events and things to confirm his leading, but our spirit must first be aligned with the Lord before we can read them correctly.

This channel is very important, and very easily misused. God really does arrange circumstances: he had Rebekah drawing water at the well for Abraham’s servant (Genesis 24), and in Philippi he opened Lydia’s home to Paul (Acts 16:14–15). But circumstances are not a self-translating dictionary. Faced with the very same circumstances, a person whose heart is aligned with God reads “God is opening a door”, while a person whose heart wants a detour reads “God is letting me run away”. When Jonah wanted to flee to Tarshish, there just happened to be a ship in port bound for Tarshish (Jonah 1:3). An open door does not necessarily mean God wants you to walk through it.

So the order must not be reversed: first align, then interpret. First align with God’s will, and only then use circumstances as confirmation — not decide first and then go looking for circumstances to endorse the decision.

Isaiah 30:21 holds a beautiful promise: “When you turn to the right hand, and when you turn to the left, your ears will hear a voice behind you, saying, ‘This is the way. Walk in it.’” Notice the word “behind”. A shepherd sometimes walks behind his flock, and his voice comes from the rear. That means sometimes you have to take a step forward before you will hear the voice. God’s leading is often made clear only in the act of obeying — we don’t see clearly and then walk; we walk, and then we see clearly.

In terms of 321’s shift of perspective, what this channel most needs us to practise is turning from man’s perspective to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. Take the same job offer: from an earthly perspective it is salary and job title; from a heavenly perspective it is whether I can be light and salt there. From a temporary perspective it is about the next five years; from an eternal perspective it is about to whom I must give account on that day. Change the perspective, and the answer often changes too.

sections.heading: 4. Through the Reminders and Prayers of Spiritual Companions
sections.html:
The Holy Spirit often speaks to us through the words, teaching and intercession of members of the church.

God never intended us to listen for his voice alone. The most important decision of the early church was made at the Council of Jerusalem, and their conclusion reads: “For it seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us, to lay no greater burden on you than these necessary things” (Acts 15:28). Look at that wonderful combination — “the Holy Spirit, and us”. The Holy Spirit speaks through a group of people who are seeking together.

So it was in the church at Antioch: “As they served the Lord and fasted, the Holy Spirit said, ‘Separate Barnabas and Saul for me, for the work to which I have called them’” (Acts 13:2). The most important sending of Paul’s life did not happen in his private prayer closet; it happened among a group of companions.

Ecclesiastes 4:9–12 says, “Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor. For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him who is alone when he falls, and doesn’t have another to lift him up … a threefold cord is not quickly broken.”

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly what 321 calls “235 relationships”. Become a “2” with someone selfless — a spiritual companion who can steady you when you’ve heard wrong; build a “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children, so that life is passed on from one generation to the next; become a “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades who take up God’s charge together. One person listening for the Holy Spirit alone can easily mistake his own voice for God’s; a group of humble people listening together has protection.

Note this, though: a spiritual companion is not a rubber stamp. A true companion will tell you the truth when you’ve gone off course. Proverbs 27:6 says, “The wounds of a friend are faithful, although the kisses of an enemy are profuse.” It isn’t hard to find someone who only ever says “Amen”; to find someone who dares to say “I think you need to pray about this some more” — that is grace.

Seen through the 920 practice: every person we are in relationship with is our “2”. As we practise living out a selfless (0) life in these relationships, the nine (9) graces of the fruit of the Spirit will grow — “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23). Notice that it says “fruit”, not “product”. A product is manufactured; fruit is grown. You cannot grit your teeth and “manufacture” patience; you can only stay joined to the vine and let it grow. That is the greatest difference between relying on the Holy Spirit and relying on ourselves.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: Letting the Holy Spirit Plug In the Three Foundations
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s set today’s message back into the whole picture of 321.

The Three Foundations are: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. These three are not three options but one whole. Jesus is my role model — he shows us what the destination looks like. The Bible is my standard — it gives us a ruler that never warps. The Holy Spirit is my guide — he turns the first two into what I actually do at eight o’clock this morning.

Without the Holy Spirit, the role model of Jesus is just an impossibly high standard that leaves us feeling inferior; without the Holy Spirit, the standard of Scripture is just a strict set of rules that leaves us worn out. When the Holy Spirit comes, the role model becomes hope, and the standard becomes living water. He is the one who turns knowledge into life.

The Two Core Values are: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. And being led by the Holy Spirit is the most everyday, most real form of letting Jesus reign as King. Being King is not a slogan; it is ownership of one decision after another. Today, in this decision, who has the final say? Am I King, or is he? Speaking of the Holy Spirit in John 16:14, the Lord Jesus said, “He will glorify me, for he will take from what is mine, and will declare it to you.” See — the very centre of the Holy Spirit’s own work is to glorify Jesus. So any “leading” that shifts the focus onto people, gives the glory to some great spiritual figure, or causes us to exalt ourselves, does not come from the Holy Spirit, who glorifies Christ alone.

The Goal is: establish God’s system. God’s system is not piled up by human organisational skill; it is built by the Holy Spirit, brick by brick. The essence of the Babylonian system is the self-centred life — man wants to make a name for himself, to seize power, to take God’s place. The essence of God’s system is selflessness — let man be man and let God be God.

So today’s lesson strikes at the very deepest point of 321: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred person’s first reaction is “I’ll find a way”; the selfless person’s first reaction is “Lord, what do you want me to do?” The self-centred life is not merely an expression of pride; it is pride itself — leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place. And humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position.

Relying on the Holy Spirit is selflessness at its most practical. Galatians 2:20 sums it all up: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.”

Please note: selflessness is not having nothing; it is not erasing yourself into a hollow shell. Selflessness is entering into the limitless and living out the limitless. When the limited “I” steps aside, the limitless Lord lives himself out within me. A cup is emptied not so that it can stay empty, but so that it can be filled.

And remember this too: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. At home, at work, at church, when we rely on ourselves and fight in the flesh over who is right, the result is usually that both sides lose; when we first grow still and ask, “Holy Spirit, how do you see this?”, we often find that the road he gives is one on which both sides can stand.

Finally, the order: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. What the Holy Spirit’s leading first sets out to change is not our schedule but our life; not what we have done, but what kind of people we have become. The Path of Serving runs like this: Spirit (the Holy Spirit is my guide), Understanding (the Bible is my standard), Life (Jesus is my role model), Service (let Jesus be King), God (let Jesus receive all the glory). Every day begins with “Spirit”.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Practising a Rhythm of Life Led by the Holy Spirit
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, hearing the word isn’t hard; doing the word is what discipleship is. Here are three practices simple enough for anyone to do, yet deep enough to change a whole life.

Practice 1: Pray every day, “Holy Spirit, I am willing to be led by you today.”

When you get up each morning, before you plan your schedule, quiet your heart and pray this one sentence: “Holy Spirit, I am willing to let you lead me today; I won’t rely on my own plans — may you reign.”

Notice the word “before”. Most people’s first move on opening their eyes is to reach for the phone, and their first thought is how many things need doing today. Our day is often already crammed full of appointments before we have even met with God. What this practice does is slip one sentence of surrender in at the very front of the day.

The point of this practice is not some special experience but forming a habit of dependence, bringing the heart back to relying on the Lord. Don’t expect a wonderful prompting every morning. The precious thing about a habit is that it keeps working on the days when you feel nothing.

Psalm 143:8 is a fine model for a morning prayer: “Cause me to hear your loving kindness in the morning, for I trust in you. Cause me to know the way in which I should walk, for I lift up my soul to you.”

Practice 2: Before you decide, pause and ask, “Holy Spirit, how do you see this?”

When you face a choice or a judgement, first stop in your tracks, keep your mouth shut for one minute, and ask the Holy Spirit in your heart: “Lord, which way do you want me to choose?”

That one-minute pause gives the Holy Spirit a chance to speak. Perhaps he will remind you through a verse you know by heart; perhaps he will give you a peace and certainty that surpass understanding.

Brothers and sisters, most of life’s regrets happen in those minutes when we “had no time to think”. A word blurted out, an email sent, a promise made on the spot. James 1:19 says, “Let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger.” That one minute is what “slow” looks like in practice.

James 1:5 also gives us assurance: “But if any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives to all liberally and without reproach, and it will be given to him.” Notice “without reproach” — God won’t find you a nuisance because you’ve come asking again. He gives generously, and he does not reproach.

Practice 3: Each evening, quietly look back: did I obey the Holy Spirit today?

Before bed each night, be still for a while and ask yourself three questions: Was there one thing today that I did in obedience to the Holy Spirit’s prompting? Was there a prompting today that I ignored? In what area tomorrow am I willing to be more sensitive to the Holy Spirit’s leading?

This kind of review helps us get to know the Holy Spirit’s voice and rhythm better, and build a more real walk together with him.

The value of review has evidence behind it. In a 2014 research paper, “Learning by Thinking”, Harvard Business School scholars including Francesca Gino, Gary Pisano and Bradley Staats found that trainees who spent about fifteen minutes each day after training writing down reflections went on to perform significantly better than a comparison group who spent the same time on extra practice. Brothers and sisters, the same amount of time spent on review is more effective than spending it on one more lap.

Psalm 139:23–24 is the best bedtime prayer: “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way.”

Deepening the three practices with the eight stages of changing our mindset

Brothers and sisters, if practice stops at “knowing”, it will never change a life. 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset can turn these three practices from a passing stirring into a lifelong habit.

Stage 1: Information. Today you have heard that the Holy Spirit is not an optional extra but a necessity, and that living by the Spirit is the mark of God’s children. This is information — knowledge coming in from outside.

Stage 2: Revelation. For information to become revelation, it needs the Holy Spirit’s illumination. Ask the Lord to let you suddenly see, at some moment: “So that’s why I’ve been so tired all these years — I’ve been relying on myself the whole time.” At that moment, the knowledge becomes yours.

Stage 3: Conviction. For revelation to become conviction, the heart must surrender. Conviction says: I believe that relying on the Holy Spirit really is better than relying on myself, even though I can’t yet see the results.

Stage 4: Implementation. Starting tomorrow morning, do Practice 1: pray first, then plan your schedule. Starting this afternoon, do Practice 2: pause for a minute before you reply. Tonight, do Practice 3: the three bedtime questions.

Stage 5: Evaluation. After a week, take an honest look: how many days did I manage? On which day did it break down? Why? Evaluation is not condemnation; it is seeing the truth.

Stage 6: Correction. If mornings are always too rushed, set your alarm ten minutes earlier, or keep your phone somewhere other than beside the bed. If a minute is too long, start with ten seconds. The point of correction is to keep the practice alive.

Stage 7: Repetition. Lally’s research reminds us that it takes on average about sixty-six days. So give yourself at least two or three months, coming back to the same practice again and again. There is no shortcut to spiritual maturity, only repetition.

Stage 8: Multiplication. When this practice has become your life, bring someone along to do it with you. Find your “2” and agree to ask each other one question every week: “This week, what is one thing you did in step with the Holy Spirit’s prompting?” That is where 235 relationships begin, and it is how God’s system is established.

Brothers and sisters, the eight stages are not eight steps you finish and then graduate from; they are a spiral, rising round after round. Each time you come back round to “Information”, you are standing on higher ground.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: May the Holy Spirit Navigate Your Whole Life
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, everything we have received today is built on the Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. Not one of the three can be missing.

Jesus gives us direction, the Bible gives us the standard, and the Holy Spirit is our navigator every day.

All of this is not just about passing on knowledge; it is about practice and revelation under the Holy Spirit’s leading. You could memorise the notes from the whole course and still live a life that relies on yourself; or you could remember just one sentence — “Holy Spirit, how do you see this?” — and from then on walk a completely different road.

When we are willing to let Jesus be King and let him receive the glory, the Holy Spirit will lead us step by step along the road he has prepared for us.

Come back to the picture we began with this morning. We are willing to hand an unfamiliar journey over to satellites we cannot see, yet unwilling to hand our whole life over to the Holy Spirit who lives within us. This morning, let’s put that order right.

Hand over the steering wheel. Not to fate, not to feelings, but to the true and living Counsellor who has been sent to our side.

May we practise every day: laying down our own cleverness, choosing to rely on the Holy Spirit’s leading, and walking a road that truly belongs to God.

May all the glory go to Jesus. He is King, and he is worthy.

keyVerses: “If we live by the Spirit, let’s also walk by the Spirit.” (Galatians 5:25)
“For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are children of God.” (Romans 8:14)
“Trust in Yahweh with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight.” (Proverbs 3:5–6)
practices: Pray every day: “Holy Spirit, I am willing to be led by you today.”
Before deciding, pause and ask: “Holy Spirit, how do you see this?”
Each evening, quietly look back: did I obey the Holy Spirit today?
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, we thank you.

Thank you that you not only sent your Son to die for us, but also sent your Holy Spirit to live within us. Thank you that you did not leave us to grope our way alone in the wilderness, but gave us the Counsellor to be our guide for life.

Lord, we confess that we have often treated you as an optional extra. We plan first and pray afterwards; we decide first and then ask you to bless it. By our own cleverness we have taken many needless detours and caused much needless hurt. Please forgive us.
Holy Spirit, I am willing to let you lead me today. Not relying on my plans, not relying on my cleverness, not relying on my experience. May you reign within me.
Make me willing to pause before every decision; let me hear you as I read your word; make me ever more sensitive to your promptings, and ever more watchful over my own voice.
Give me spiritual companions to steady me when I go my own way; and make me a companion to others, so that this road of relying on you is passed on.
May it no longer be we who live, but Christ who lives in us. May Jesus be King in our lives, and may all the glory go to him.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “Trust in Yahweh with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight.” (Proverbs 3:5–6) Think back over the last three months: what is one decision you made “without asking”? How did it turn out? If you could do it again, at what point would you stop first?

“For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are children of God.” (Romans 8:14) Of the four channels of the Holy Spirit’s leading (God’s word, inner promptings and peace, circumstances and confirmation, the reminders and prayers of spiritual companions), which is most familiar to you? Which is least familiar? This week, in which channel are you willing to take a step?
