sections.heading: Introduction: Whose Hands Are on the Wheel?
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Please picture a scene with me first.

A husband and wife set out in the car. He is driving; she is in the passenger seat. The junction ahead is jammed, and she says, “You should have taken that side street back there.” He says nothing and turns the music up a little. Two junctions later she says, “See? I told you so.” He turns the music up a little more. A bit further on, the satnav says, “Make a U-turn ahead,” and she reaches across and gives the steering wheel a nudge to the right.

The car doesn’t overturn, but for the rest of that day the two of them don’t say another word to each other.

Brothers and sisters, a car can only have one steering wheel. When the hand from the passenger seat reaches across, it isn’t helping; it’s grabbing. We all laugh at this scene, because we are all in it. That hand is in our marriages, that hand is in our workplaces, that hand is in our church service, and that hand is in our prayers too — even as we say, “Lord, your will be done,” we quietly nudge the wheel towards the direction we want.

Today we enter the second part of Kingdom 321. In the last five lessons we looked together at the Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. With the foundations laid, next come the Two Core Values. The first of these core values is today’s theme — let Jesus be King.

“Let Jesus be King” is not a slogan, not the chorus of a worship song, not a rousing line we shout at the end of a meeting. It is the centre of the whole system of our faith. It is a decision — a decision that has to be made afresh every morning: today, whose hands are on the wheel?

Let me begin with something that may sting a little: a person can love Jesus very much, serve Jesus very zealously, and yet never have let Jesus be King. Because loving him and serving him can still mean “I am King, and he is helping me.” Letting Jesus be King is the opposite order — he is King, and I am following.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: The King and the Kingdom in the Sermon on the Mount
sections.html:
Our key passage comes from Matthew chapter 7.

The author of Matthew’s Gospel is the apostle Matthew, formerly a tax collector in Capernaum, who was called by the Lord to become one of the twelve apostles. Most evangelical scholars hold that this Gospel was written somewhere between AD 50 and 70, chiefly for communities of Jewish believers. That is why Matthew opens his very first verse with: “The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham” (Matthew 1:1). “Son of David” is a royal title. From beginning to end, Matthew sets out to prove one thing: this Jesus of Nazareth is the King the Jewish people had been waiting for through hundreds of years.

That is why the phrase “Kingdom of Heaven” appears more than thirty times in Matthew. The first thing the wise men from the east asked when they arrived was, “Where is he who is born King of the Jews?” (Matthew 2:2). The first message the Lord Jesus preached when he began his ministry was, “Repent! For the Kingdom of Heaven is at hand” (Matthew 4:17). When he was crucified, the sign on the cross read, “THIS IS JESUS, THE KING OF THE JEWS” (Matthew 27:37). And the first thing he said to his disciples after his resurrection was, “All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth” (Matthew 28:18).

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? The whole of Matthew’s Gospel is the record of a coronation.

And the Sermon on the Mount, in chapters 5 to 7, is the charter of the kingdom proclaimed by this King. He is not teaching a somewhat higher grade of morality; he is declaring: in my kingdom, this is how things work. So he says blessed are the poor in spirit, he says love your enemies, he says don’t be anxious about tomorrow, he says seek first his Kingdom and his righteousness. If these words did not come from the mouth of a true King, they would all be empty words.

Chapter 7 is the conclusion, and the Lord Jesus sums up with four contrasts in a row: two roads, two kinds of tree, two kinds of people, two foundations. Our key verse falls in the third — two kinds of people.

“Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter into the Kingdom of Heaven; but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven.” (Matthew 7:21)

Notice the title “Lord”. In Greek it is κύριε (kyrie), from κύριος (kyrios), meaning master, owner, the one with absolute right to dispose of what is his. In the Roman world it was what a slave called his master, and what a subject called Caesar. When someone calls Jesus “Lord”, the very grammar of it already concedes: all that I have is his, and he may dispose of it entirely as he wishes.

The Lord Jesus says: saying it is not enough.

Luke’s Gospel records the same teaching in even more direct terms: “Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and don’t do the things which I say?” (Luke 6:46). The Lord Jesus is exposing a spiritual contradiction: with our lips we set him on the throne, while in our living we ask him to step down from it.

That is the question we must face today.

sections.heading: 1. Only Jesus Is Worthy to Be King
sections.html:
The lesson begins by setting the most important reason right in front of us: because only Jesus died for our sins, only he rose from the dead and overcame the power of Satan and of Hades, he alone is worthy to reign and to sit upon the throne.

That word “worthy” is the bedrock of this lesson.

Revelation chapter 5 shows us the most solemn scene in heaven. In God’s right hand is a scroll, sealed tight with seven seals. A mighty angel proclaims with a loud voice, “Who is worthy to open the book, and to break its seals?” (Revelation 5:2). And no one in heaven, on earth or under the earth was worthy to open the scroll or to look into it. So John wept bitterly. Then one of the elders said to him, “Don’t weep. Behold, the Lion who is of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has overcome: he who opens the book and its seven seals” (Revelation 5:5).

The word “worthy” is the Greek ἄξιος (axios). It was originally a word from trade and measurement, meaning “of equal weight” — placed on one side of the scales, it exactly balances what is on the other side, no more and no less. So “worthy” is not a polite compliment, and not a matter of our voting for him; it is a fact that has been weighed: only his weight matches that throne.

So on what grounds is he worthy? The Bible gives three answers.

First, because he died for our sins.

The new song in heaven goes like this: “You are worthy to take the book and to open its seals: for you were killed, and bought us for God with your blood out of every tribe, language, people, and nation” (Revelation 5:9). Notice that word “for”. The reason he is worthy is not his almighty power — he was almighty all along; the reason is “you were killed”. In heaven, the one on the throne does not appear in the form of a lion; what John saw was “a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain” (Revelation 5:6).

Brothers and sisters, what a wonderful thing this is. Every throne in this world was won with other people’s blood; only this one throne was won with the King’s own blood.

Second, because he rose from the dead and overcame the power of Satan and of Hades.

“who was declared to be the Son of God with power, according to the Spirit of holiness, by the resurrection from the dead” (Romans 1:4). The resurrection is God’s most public coronation of this King.

Paul describes it more concretely: “Having stripped the principalities and the powers, he made a show of them openly, triumphing over them in it” (Colossians 2:15). Hebrews puts it in words that come even closer to our hearts: “Since then the children have shared in flesh and blood, he also himself in the same way partook of the same, that through death he might bring to nothing him who had the power of death, that is, the devil, and might deliver all of them who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage” (Hebrews 2:14–15).

Third, because God the Father has exalted him to the highest place.

“Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, those on earth, and those under the earth, and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.” (Philippians 2:9–11)

“He has on his garment and on his thigh a name written, ‘KING OF KINGS, AND LORD OF LORDS.’” (Revelation 19:16)

So letting Jesus be King is not us doing him a favour, not us generously giving up our seat for him. He has always been on the throne. What we call “letting” is really acknowledging the facts — coming back to the truth.

Let me use an illustration. While the grown-ups are out, a little boy climbs into his father’s office chair, picks up the company seal and stamps away happily. He’s having a wonderful time, and he feels very important. But that chair has never for one second belonged to him. When his father comes in and he climbs down from the chair, he hasn’t “lost” anything; he has gone back to where he belongs — back to the place of a son, which is a better place than the boss’s.

Brothers and sisters, letting Jesus be King means climbing down from a chair that was never ours.

In 1880, in his address at the founding of the Free University of Amsterdam, the Dutch theologian and statesman Abraham Kuyper said words that are still quoted today: there is not a square inch in the whole domain of our human existence over which Christ, who is sovereign over all, does not cry, “Mine!”

Not a square inch. Not ninety per cent, not the two hours on Sunday — every square inch.

Seen through 321, this is the first of the Two Core Values. The Three Foundations are the root: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. When the root is firmly planted, it must bear the fruit of the core values: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. And the purpose of it all is to establish God’s system.

Brothers and sisters, remember this order: first we see that he is worthy; only then are we glad to let him be King. If we don’t first see that he is worthy, “let Jesus be King” turns into a religious burden instead of a response of love.

sections.heading: 2. Everyone Is Born Wanting to Be King
sections.html:
The lesson says: every one of us is born wanting to “be king ourselves” — wanting to control our lives, call the shots, even manipulate others. And it is precisely this “I’ll be king” attitude that becomes the root of every quarrel, every confusion and everything that destroys unity.

The Bible’s very first tragedy was a struggle for the throne. The serpent said to the woman, “For God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil” (Genesis 3:5). “Like God” — that was the first advertising slogan in human history, and the most successful one ever. What it was selling was not fruit; it was a throne.

This temptation appeared even earlier, in the fall of the angels. Isaiah records the monologue: “You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! I will sit on the mountain of assembly, in the far north! I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!’” (Isaiah 14:13–14). In just two verses, five times: “I will”.

Brothers and sisters, the grammar of pride is the first person.

321 says: “self” is the root of our fall; pride is the root of the problem. What is pride? Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights that are not ours, wanting to take God’s place. What is humility? Humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

The book of Judges sums up the chaos of a whole era in a single sentence: “In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did that which was right in his own eyes” (Judges 21:25). Notice the cause and effect between those two sentences: because there was no king, everyone did what was right in his own eyes. If a family has no king, everyone does as they please; if a church has no king, everyone does as they please too. The chaos isn’t because people are so very wicked; the chaos is because the throne is empty.

Later, when the Israelites demanded a king, God said to Samuel: “Listen to the voice of the people in all that they tell you; for they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me as the king over them” (1 Samuel 8:7). It wasn’t that they didn’t want a king; they didn’t want this King. They wanted a king they could see, who would listen to them and do things their way.

In the New Testament, the Lord Jesus says in a parable: “But his citizens hated him, and sent an envoy after him, saying, ‘We don’t want this man to reign over us’” (Luke 19:14).

From Eden to the cross, humanity’s problem has always been the same sentence: we don’t want this man to reign over us.

Here I want to mention a psychological study that helps us see ourselves. In 1975 the psychologist Ellen Langer published a famous paper in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology entitled “The Illusion of Control”. She ran a series of experiments, one of which went like this: two groups of people bought identical lottery tickets; one group could choose their own numbers, while the other group were handed tickets at random. The odds of winning were exactly the same. But when the researchers later tried to buy the tickets back, the group who had picked their own numbers asked for a markedly higher price.

Langer named this phenomenon “the illusion of control” — people systematically overestimate how much control they have over outcomes.

Brothers and sisters, this study says nothing about faith, yet it describes our condition precisely. We grip the steering wheel tightly not because we can really control things, but because holding on to something makes us feel secure inside. What we are clutching is often nothing more than a lottery ticket whose odds haven’t changed at all.

That is why the Lord Jesus spoke our key verse: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter into the Kingdom of Heaven; but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 7:21).

Brothers and sisters, the title is a matter for the mouth; doing his will is a matter of kingship. I can call him Lord in the most devout tone of voice and at the same time be king myself in every decision. What the Lord Jesus looks at is not our volume but our steering wheel.

Then he says, “Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine, and does them, I will liken him to a wise man, who built his house on a rock” (Matthew 7:24). He didn’t say, “Everyone who hears these words of mine and is moved”; he said, “and does them”.

321’s fivefold change says it clearly: change of mindset, change of life, change of daily living, change of relationships, change of ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. A faith that stops at the “title” has stopped at the Information stage and has not yet entered into life. Today’s lesson wants to take us one step further: from a title on our lips to a handing-back in our daily living.

sections.heading: 3. Wherever Jesus Is King, There Is Victory
sections.html:
The lesson says: Jesus is the victorious King; he has already overcome every power of darkness. When we are willing to let Jesus be King in every area of our lives, that area will experience victory.

The reverse is also true: wherever we don’t let Jesus be King, we go on losing battles.

It isn’t that God refuses to help us; it’s that we haven’t invited the King in. If the city gates aren’t opened, the King’s army won’t force its way in. The psalm cries out: “Lift up your heads, you gates! Be lifted up, you everlasting doors, and the King of glory will come in” (Psalm 24:7).

(1) Let Jesus Be King over Our Emotions

The lesson says: if we let Jesus be King over our emotions, we will no longer be ruled by anger, fear and anxiety.

The Bible saw long ago that emotions are a battlefield: “One who is slow to anger is better than the mighty; one who rules his spirit, than he who takes a city” (Proverbs 16:32). And again: “Like a city that is broken down and without walls is a man whose spirit is without restraint” (Proverbs 25:28).

For an ancient city, its walls were its life. Once the walls were breached, no enemy army needed to attack — anyone could just walk in. Brothers and sisters, a person whose emotions have no King over them is a city without walls — a colleague’s remark can walk in, a family member’s expression can walk in, a comment online can walk in, and once inside it settles down in your heart and stays for days.

Paul says, “‘Be angry, and don’t sin.’ Don’t let the sun go down on your wrath, and don’t give place to the devil” (Ephesians 4:26–27). Notice the words “give place”. Nursing anger until sunset is setting aside a plot of ground in your heart for the enemy to build a house on.

There is a fascinating finding from psychology here. In 2007 a team led by the psychologist Matthew Lieberman at the University of California, Los Angeles, published a study in the journal Psychological Science. They showed participants pictures of disturbing faces while observing their brains with functional magnetic resonance imaging. They found that when participants simply “felt” the emotion, the amygdala was highly active; but when they put the emotion into words and labelled it — for example, “this is anger”, “this is fear” — activity in the amygdala dropped markedly, and the regulating regions of the prefrontal cortex became active. The researchers call this phenomenon “affect labelling”.

Brothers and sisters, hear me clearly: this study cannot save us; only Scripture can save us. But from one angle it confirms a spiritual fact — bring an emotion into the light, say it out loud, hand it over, and the emotion loses its violence.

And Christians have something better than naming, and it’s called prayer: “In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 4:6–7). The Greek verb for “guard”, φρουρέω (phroureō), is a military term meaning to post soldiers to garrison the city gates. When you hand over your anxiety, the King sends his peace to stand sentry.

321 says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the brain and you’ll be sad, rely on the heart and you’ll be glad. Out of the heart flows the wellspring of life (see Proverbs 4:23). Emotions are not managed by suppression; they are governed by a change of King.

(2) Let Jesus Be King in Our Families

The lesson says: if we let Jesus be King in our families, our families can experience reconciliation and healing.

When Joshua was old, he gathered all the people at Shechem and said to them, “As for me and my house, we will serve Yahweh” (Joshua 24:15). Notice that he didn’t say, “As for me”; he said, “me and my house”. A family needs someone to stand up first and decide, on the family’s behalf, who the King is.

Brothers and sisters, nine times out of ten, quarrels at home are not about right and wrong; they are about the throne. Who has the final say? Who has to apologise? Who backs down first? As long as there are two kings under one roof, the home is a battlefield. 321 puts it exactly: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win.

Paul’s prescription is simple, yet hard: “bearing with one another, and forgiving each other, if any man has a complaint against any; even as Christ forgave you, so you also do” (Colossians 3:13).

The psychologist John Gottman of the University of Washington in the United States has studied marital interaction for many years. He identified four patterns of communication that do the most damage to a relationship and called them “the Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse”: criticism, contempt, defensiveness and stonewalling.

Brothers and sisters, have you noticed that every one of these four is an expression of “I want to be king”? Criticism is me sitting in the judge’s seat; contempt is me placing myself above the other person; defensiveness is me guarding my borders to the death; stonewalling is me declaring by my silence: on this, my word is final.

If there is a King in the home, these four horsemen cannot get in. Because once the King is seated on the throne, I have stepped down from the judge’s seat.

(3) Let Jesus Be King over Our Money

The lesson says: if we let Jesus be King over our money, we will be set free from greed and enter into trust and abundance.

When the Lord Jesus spoke about money, he used the language of kingship: “No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other; or else he will be devoted to one and despise the other. You can’t serve both God and Mammon” (Matthew 6:24).

He didn’t say “you shouldn’t”; he said “you can’t”. This is a statement about what is possible, not a piece of moral advice. Money is not a neutral tool; money will try to be king. The Lord Jesus personifies it and calls it “Mammon”.

The Lord Jesus also said, “For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (Matthew 6:21). Brothers and sisters, you can use that sentence as a mirror. Do you want to know where your heart is? Look at your bank statements. Do you want to know who you’ve given the throne to? Look at the sum you would find hardest to part with.

In 2008 Elizabeth Dunn, Lara Aknin and Michael Norton published a study in the journal Science. They gave participants a sum of money and randomly assigned one group to spend it on themselves and the other to spend it on others. When their happiness was measured that evening, the group who had spent the money on others were noticeably happier.

The Lord Jesus said this long ago: “It is more blessed to give than to receive” (Acts 20:35).

Seeking God’s kingdom first is not a financial strategy; it is the order of kingship: “But seek first God’s Kingdom, and his righteousness; and all these things will be given to you as well” (Matthew 6:33). In Malachi, God even makes an exceptional invitation to put him to the test: “Bring the whole tithe into the storehouse, that there may be food in my house, and test me now in this,” says Yahweh of Armies, “if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there will not be room enough for” (Malachi 3:10).

321’s shift of perspective is at its most practical here: from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal. The money is the same money, but when the King is on the throne, money goes from being master to being servant.

(4) Let Jesus Be King in Our Relationships

The lesson says: if we let Jesus be King in our relationships, conflicts can be resolved and we can be one with each other.

In his high-priestly prayer before his suffering, this is what the Lord Jesus asked for us: “that they may all be one; even as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be one in us; that the world may believe that you sent me” (John 17:21).

Paul says, “being eager to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Ephesians 4:3). “Eager to keep” means that unity does not happen by itself; unity has to be guarded.

Brothers and sisters, why won’t a conflict resolve? Because at the scene of a conflict there are usually two kings, and no King. When two kings are present, all you can do is decide a winner and a loser; only when one King is present can there be reconciliation.

Picture an orchestra. Twenty-odd people, each with a different instrument in hand, each with a different part on the music stand. Without a conductor, each would play to his own beat, and the harder they tried, the worse the noise. But the moment the conductor raises the baton, the very same twenty-odd people with the very same different parts become a symphony. The conductor hasn’t replaced anyone; he has simply given them one beat.

Jesus being King is that baton. Unity has never meant making everyone the same; unity means everyone looking to the same King.

321’s 920 practice says: every person we are in relationship with is our “2”. As we practise living a selfless (0) life, the nine (9) graces of the fruit of the Spirit grow in these relationships — “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23). Brothers and sisters, fruit is not something we manufacture; fruit is the result of the King’s reign. Whichever relationship lets Jesus be King is the relationship that begins to bear fruit.

The lesson sums up this section in one sentence that I love: whichever part of our life hands over its sovereignty will move from chaos into order, from a breach into blessing.

sections.heading: 4. Letting Jesus Be King Means Handing Back Sovereignty
sections.html:
The lesson says: at the moment we came to faith, we said, “I receive Jesus as my Saviour and the Lord of my life.” That was not just the beginning of faith; it was a transfer of sovereignty — I no longer live for myself, but let Jesus be Lord and reign in my life.

In history, when a city changed hands, there was a ceremony of handover: the old governor of the city would lay the keys of the city gates on a tray and present them with both hands to the new king. From that moment on, the city’s taxes, laws, defences and comings and goings all came under the new king. When the keys were handed over, it wasn’t a piece of iron that changed hands; it was a whole city.

Paul turns this into the most personal of testimonies: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me” (Galatians 2:20).

This is what 321 means: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. Selflessness is not having nothing, not wiping ourselves out; selflessness is no longer being confined by that small “self”, but entering into the limitless and living out the limitless. “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me.

The lesson lists four areas in which sovereignty must be handed back. Let’s look at them one by one.

(1) Personal Life: No Longer Deciding Life’s Direction by Ourselves

The lesson says: no longer deciding the direction of our lives by ourselves, but seeking God’s will and obeying his leading.

In the Garden of Gethsemane the Lord Jesus himself set the example for us: “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42).

Notice the structure of this verse. The first half is honesty: he does not pretend it doesn’t hurt. The second half is handing back: nevertheless, not my will. Brothers and sisters, handing back sovereignty doesn’t mean feeling nothing; it means feeling everything and still saying “nevertheless”.

Every day we meet that “nevertheless”. A child’s ambitions, whether to stay in a job or leave, a health report, a relationship we have waited on for a long time without any answer. We can all say the first half; the second half takes grace.

Paul urges us like this: “Therefore I urge you, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service” (Romans 12:1). The sacrifices of the Old Testament were dead; the sacrifice of the New Testament is living. The biggest problem with a living sacrifice is that it keeps crawling off the altar. So handing back sovereignty is not a one-off ceremony; it is a decision, every morning, to climb back onto the altar.

321 says: the priority of relationships is first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things. If the direction of our life is not first set true with God, every decision that follows will drift.

(2) Relationships: No Longer Reacting from Our Emotions

The lesson says: no longer reacting from our emotions, but letting Jesus be King in our relationships and living out forgiveness, forbearance and unity.

“Reacting” and “responding” sound almost alike, yet a whole throne lies between them. Reacting is when someone presses my button and I leap up — the button is in their hand, which means the throne is in their hand. Responding is when I first bring the matter before the King, and then decide how to speak.

Peter says, “Yes, all of you clothe yourselves with humility, to subject yourselves to one another; for ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble’” (1 Peter 5:5). The word behind “clothe yourselves” pictures tying on an apron — what a servant does before starting work, the very thing the Lord Jesus did at the Last Supper when he took a towel, tied it around himself and washed the disciples’ feet (see John 13:4–5).

Brothers and sisters, humility is not thinking badly of yourself; humility is returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. Only when I no longer need to win every conversation am I truly free.

(3) Resources and Finances: No Longer Storing Up Wealth Just for Ourselves

The lesson says: no longer storing up wealth just for ourselves, but letting Jesus direct how our money is used, to the glory of his kingdom.

The Lord Jesus told a parable about a rich man. His land produced a bumper harvest, so he planned to pull down his barns and build bigger ones. There is a jarring detail in what he says: “What will I do, because I don’t have room to store my crops? … This is what I will do. I will pull down my barns, build bigger ones, and there I will store all my grain and my goods” (Luke 12:17–18). In just two verses, “I” five times and “my” four times — and the next verse has still more. But God said to him: “You foolish one, tonight your soul is required of you. The things which you have prepared — whose will they be?” (Luke 12:20).

Brothers and sisters, this rich man was not a villain; he was simply his own king. And the end of being your own king is that not one of his plans had God written into it, and not one had other people written into it.

As David prepared the offerings for the temple, he prayed: “I know also, my God, that you try the heart, and have pleasure in uprightness. As for me, in the uprightness of my heart I have willingly offered all these things” (1 Chronicles 29:17). And he said: “For all things come from you, and we have given you of your own” (1 Chronicles 29:14).

That is handing back sovereignty in our finances: I am not giving to God; I am giving back to God.

(4) Choices of Time: No Longer Arranging Everything for Ourselves

The lesson says: no longer arranging everything for ourselves, but being willing to set time apart for the Lord, seeking first his kingdom and his righteousness.

David says, “My times are in your hand” (Psalm 31:15). Moses says, “So teach us to count our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom” (Psalm 90:12). Paul says, “Therefore watch carefully how you walk, not as unwise, but as wise, redeeming the time, because the days are evil” (Ephesians 5:15–16).

“Redeeming the time” in the original means “buying up the opportunity” — like snapping up goods in the marketplace, buying back the opportunities that are slipping away.

Brothers and sisters, our diaries are our most honest confession of theology. They don’t lie. There are a hundred and sixty-eight hours in a week; whoever we give our time to is the one who is king.

We often say, “I don’t have time,” but what we really mean is, “This isn’t one of my priorities.” The Lord Jesus said, “seek first his Kingdom and his righteousness” — and that word “first” is sovereignty over our time. This is exactly what makes 321 Morning Devotion so precious: the clearest-headed, most precious part of the day, we give first to the King.

Hand Over Sovereignty, Receive Authority

The lesson ends this section very powerfully: letting Jesus be King looks like “losing control”, but in fact it is returning to the order of creation and receiving true freedom and glory. When we hand over our sovereignty, he gives us authority to rule that comes from heaven, so that we overcome on earth and will one day reign with him in heaven.

Let’s feel the force of that through a fact of astronomy. Right now the earth is orbiting the sun at about 29.8 kilometres per second — that’s the figure published by NASA. The speed is astonishing, yet here on the ground we feel not the slightest wobble, because the earth is held firmly in its orbit.

Brothers and sisters, think about it: if the earth were “set free”, broke loose from the sun’s gravity and was no longer held — what would happen? It wouldn’t become freer; it would drift in the dark, grow cold and die. The earth’s freedom comes precisely from being in its orbit; the earth’s stability comes precisely from having a centre.

Being held by gravity is not losing freedom; it is gaining an orbit.

Letting Jesus be King is just the same. Giving up the throne is not a loss; it is coming back into orbit.

What is more, those who hand over receive authority. The Lord Jesus says, “He who overcomes, I will give to him to sit down with me on my throne, as I also overcame, and sat down with my Father on his throne” (Revelation 3:21). Paul says, “If we endure, we will also reign with him” (2 Timothy 2:12). And the ending John saw in the New Jerusalem is: “They will reign forever and ever” (Revelation 22:5).

Brothers and sisters, this is God’s economy: those who fight for the throne on earth lose everything; those who let the King be King on earth will one day sit with the King on his throne.

sections.heading: 5. Integrating the 321 Vision: When the King Is on the Throne, Everything Falls into Place
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s set what we have seen today back into the whole picture of 321.

The Three Foundations are three paths by which we come to know this King. Jesus is my role model — he himself first lived out “not my will, but yours”, and so he has every right to ask us to hand over the throne. The Bible is my standard — the King’s will is not something we guess at by feeling; it is written in Scripture, and someone who doesn’t read the Bible has no way to truly obey the King. The Holy Spirit is my guide — without the Holy Spirit we could not even call Jesus Lord: “No one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ but by the Holy Spirit” (1 Corinthians 12:3).

Of the Two Core Values, the first is today’s theme: let Jesus be King; the second is the theme of the next lesson: let Jesus receive all the glory. These two core values are bound together — if the King is not on the throne, the glory will certainly go to someone else, and most likely to ourselves.

The Goal: establish God’s system. Brothers and sisters, what is God’s system? God’s system is an operating system with Jesus as King. The Babylonian system is “everyone is their own king”, so the harder people try, the greater the chaos; God’s system is “one King, many children”, so the more united we are, the stronger we become. This is the longing of the Lord’s Prayer: “Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven” (Matthew 6:10).

From the self-centred life to selflessness. The old self is self-centred, so it fights for the throne; the new self is selfless, so it can let the King be King. Selflessness is not the low self-esteem of self-rejection; selflessness is “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). A selfless person doesn’t need to win, because he is already in the Overcomer.

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Satan’s favourite line of attack is to stir up our pride and get us to grab a seat that isn’t ours. He used this move on Eve, and he used it on the Lord Jesus in the wilderness — “I will give you all of these things, if you will fall down and worship me” (Matthew 4:9). The Lord Jesus’ answer was simple: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and you shall serve him only” (Matthew 4:10). James says, “Be subject therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you” (James 4:7). Notice the order: first submit to God, and only then can you resist the devil. Someone who has not let the King be King cannot stand against the enemy.

The fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Today we are not here to learn one more doctrine; we are here to change a mindset — from “my life is mine to run” to “my life is his to rule”. Once the mindset changes, the life changes; once the life changes, daily living changes; when daily living has changed, relationships can change; and when relationships have changed, ministry has a foundation.

Life first, then relationships, then ministry. Many people burn out in their service because the order is upside down — they charge into ministry first, then struggle to keep their relationships going, and only at the end discover that their life dried up long ago. Brothers and sisters, people matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. If the King reigns in our life, ministry is no longer my stage but his kingdom.

The shift of perspective: from man’s to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. The very same difficult situation, seen from my throne, is a loss; seen from before his throne, it is a trust.

The 920 practice and 235 relationships. 920: every person we are in relationship with is our “2”; in every “2” relationship we practise selflessness (0), and the nine (9) graces of the fruit of the Spirit grow. 235: become a “2”, a spiritual companion, with someone selfless; build a “3”, the legacy of spiritual parents and spiritual children; and go on to become a “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. Brothers and sisters, this is exactly the “King-reminder companion” in the lesson’s third practice — that is your “2”.

The Path of Serving: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God. The Holy Spirit is my guide (Spirit), the Bible is my standard (Understanding), Jesus is my role model (Life), let Jesus be King (Service), let Jesus receive all the glory (God). Today we are standing at the “Service” station.

sections.heading: 6. Putting It into Practice: Learning Every Day to Let Jesus Be King
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. I want to set these three practices within 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — so that they become not just three things to do but a road we can keep walking.

Practice 1: Say one sentence every morning — “Lord Jesus, today I let you be King”

The lesson says: early each morning, say to the Lord, “Lord Jesus, today I am not in charge; you are King. Please lead my thoughts, my words, my decisions and my actions.” This is a kind of spiritual refocusing that helps us hand our sovereignty to him right from the start.

Stage 1, Information: today’s lesson is the information. You now know that “only Jesus is worthy to be King”, and you have heard the Lord himself say that only “he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven” will enter (Matthew 7:21).

Stage 2, Revelation: for information to become revelation, we need the Holy Spirit. In prayer, ask the Lord to shine his light: Lord, in what matter am I still being king myself? Don’t rush to answer; let the Holy Spirit point out that one thing. Revelation is often very specific — a face, a number, a date will come to mind.

Stage 3, Conviction: conviction is the heart nodding yes. You don’t just agree with the teaching; you are persuaded — you really believe that his being King is better than my being king. Implementation without conviction won’t last three days.

Stage 4, Implementation: build this sentence into your morning. I suggest a method proposed by the psychologist Peter Gollwitzer in 1999 and shown to be effective by a great deal of research since, called “implementation intentions”: don’t just resolve “I will pray every day”, but say specifically, “When I have done X, I will do Y.” For example: “When I switch off my alarm in the morning, before I sit up I will say: Lord Jesus, today I let you be King.” Hang a new behaviour on a fixed old action, and the success rate rises markedly.

Stage 5, Evaluation: take a minute in the evening to look back. Was there a moment today when I grabbed the steering wheel back? Not to condemn myself, but to see the truth.

Stage 6, Correction: for that moment, prepare a different response for tomorrow. For example: “Tomorrow, when my colleague speaks to me like that again, I’ll first take a deep breath and say in my heart: Lord, you are King here.”

Stage 7, Repetition: this is the most important stage. Research published in 2010 by a team led by the psychologist Phillippa Lally at University College London found that it takes on average about sixty-six days for a new habit to become automatic, with wide individual differences — some take a little over ten days, others more than two hundred. Brothers and sisters, give yourself time. Change of life is not a sprint; it is a journey walked together.

Stage 8, Multiplication: when this sentence has become your life, pass it on to one person — your child, your colleague, someone in your small group. Once a habit can be passed on, it is no longer just a habit; it is a legacy.

Practice 2: Each week, choose one area and specifically let Jesus be King there

The lesson says: choose one area of your life (for example, your attitude at work, conflict with others, how you use your time, how you plan your money) and ask the Lord, “Am I still being king myself in this area? How do you want me to obey you?” Then make one concrete response, an action that hands sovereignty back to him.

Brothers and sisters, notice the lesson’s two key phrases: one area, one action.

Why one area? Because total surrender sounds very spiritual but can be very hollow in practice. God has never asked us to change everything at once. When Israel entered Canaan, God said, “Little by little I will drive them out from before you” (Exodus 23:30). Spiritual ground is taken one piece at a time.

Why must there be an action? Because the Lord Jesus spoke of “everyone … who hears these words of mine, and does them” (Matthew 7:24). A stirring without an action evaporates by the next day.

What does this look like in practice? Here are a few examples.

Letting him be King over my attitude at work: this week I will no longer stay late just to prove myself; I’ll finish my work on time, and give the credit for the results to the team first.

Letting him be King in conflict with others: this week I will make that phone call I’ve put off for so long — not to explain myself, but to make peace.

Letting him be King over how I use my time: this week I will set apart a fixed block of time for the Lord, and even if that day is busy, I won’t borrow from it.

Then write it down. Once it’s written down, it goes from a wish to a commitment.

Practice 3: Remind one another each week with a spiritual companion

The lesson says: find a “King-reminder companion” and each week briefly share three questions: In what area did I learn this week to let Jesus be King? Where have I still not handed over sovereignty? Where am I willing to let the Lord reign next week?

This is exactly 321’s “2”.

Ecclesiastes says, “If a man prevails against one who is alone, two shall withstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken” (Ecclesiastes 4:12). Hebrews says, “Let’s consider how to provoke one another to love and good works … exhorting one another, and so much the more as you see the Day approaching” (Hebrews 10:24–25).

Brothers and sisters, what someone who is his own king fears most is being asked questions. Because a king doesn’t have to give account. So being willing to let someone ask me these three questions every week is already, in itself, handing over the throne.

Please note that this companion is not there to supervise you but to walk with you. When they ask, they bring no judgement; when you answer, you needn’t dress it up. Three questions, ten minutes, once a week. A year from now you’ll see a different you.

These three practices begin with one sentence, move to one area, then to one companion — which is exactly the movement from “me and God”, to “me and myself”, to “me and others”. 321 says: the priority of relationships is first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things. The lesson’s three practices walk precisely in that order.

sections.heading: 7. Closing and Call: Only When the King Is on the Throne Is There True Peace
sections.html:
The lesson’s closing word says: when we no longer fight for the throne ourselves, but gladly let Jesus be King, our lives will enter into true peace and order. Darkness must retreat, and Satan has no power to harm, because the King is reigning.

Brothers and sisters, notice that the two words “peace” and “order” belong together.

We often understand peace to mean “nothing happening”. Biblical peace isn’t like that. Biblical peace is shalom (שָׁלוֹם), which means wholeness, nothing missing, everything in its place. When every part of a machine is running in the right place, that is shalom; when every member of a family is in the right place, loving one another, that is shalom too. So peace is not the storm stopping; peace is the King being in the boat.

More than seven hundred years beforehand, Isaiah prophesied of this King: “For a child is born to us. A son is given to us; and the government will be on his shoulders. His name will be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace. Of the increase of his government and of peace there shall be no end, on David’s throne, and on his kingdom, to establish it, and to uphold it with justice and with righteousness from that time on, even forever. The zeal of Yahweh of Armies will perform this” (Isaiah 9:6–7).

See the cause and effect clearly: “the government will be on his shoulders” comes first; “of the increase of his government and of peace there shall be no end” comes after. Only when the government rests on his shoulders does peace increase. Brothers and sisters, we keep wanting peace, yet we refuse to hand over the government. We ask him to give us peace, yet we won’t let him be King. It doesn’t work.

Paul says, “And let the peace of God rule in your hearts” (Colossians 3:15). The Greek verb for “rule”, βραβεύω (brabeuō), originally meant “to act as umpire” — the one who makes the call on the field of play. Brothers and sisters, when your heart is in uproar, who is the umpire? If your emotions are the umpire, you will end up with regrets; if other people’s opinions are the umpire, you will end up exhausted; only when you let the peace of Christ be the umpire will you be at rest.

The lesson puts it beautifully: letting Jesus be King does not restrict us; it restores us — it restores our identity, restores our authority, and restores our glorious destiny in Christ.

It restores our identity: we are no longer people who must survive on performance, on winning, on other people’s approval. “But as many as received him, to them he gave the right to become God’s children, to those who believe in his name” (John 1:12). Our identity as children is not something we fight for; it is something given.

It restores our authority: “Behold, I give you authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy. Nothing will in any way hurt you” (Luke 10:19). Notice that this authority is “given”, not “grabbed”. What is grabbed is usurpation; only what is given is authority.

It restores our glorious destiny: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God’s own possession” (1 Peter 2:9). “A royal priesthood” — brothers and sisters, royalty was ours from the start. We don’t need to grab that seat; we only need to return to it.

At the end, the lesson asks us a question, and I now hand that question to you: today, in which area are you willing to let Jesus truly be King?

Don’t answer “everything”. Please answer with one. The one that came to mind just now, the one you’re a little reluctant to hand over — that’s the one.

Let us resolve every day and say: Jesus is King; he reigns within me, he reigns in my home, he reigns in every area of my life.

Let Jesus be King on earth, and one day we will reign with him in heaven, for ever.

Brothers and sisters, the heart of this lesson is a single sentence: only Jesus is worthy to be King. When we climb down from that chair that was never ours, the Lamb who was slain takes his seat on the throne, and we return to our place as children — the safest place in the whole universe.

May all the glory go to this King.

keyVerses: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter into the Kingdom of Heaven; but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven.” (Matthew 7:21)
practices: Say one sentence every morning: “Lord Jesus, today I let you be King”
Each week, choose one area and specifically let Jesus be King there
Remind one another each week with a spiritual companion
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we worship you.

You are the Lamb who was slain; with your own blood you bought us back out of every tribe, language, people and nation. You rose from the dead and overcame the power of Satan and of Hades. You are King of kings and Lord of lords. Lord, you alone are worthy.

Lord, we confess that we often call you Lord with our lips while being king ourselves in our hearts. We pray in the most devout words, yet quietly nudge the steering wheel towards the direction we want. Please forgive us.

Lord Jesus, today I am not in charge; you are King. Be King in my thoughts, be King in my words, be King over my emotions, be King in my home, be King over my money, be King over my time, be King in every one of my relationships.

Lord, I especially place (name that one area silently in your heart) into your hands. In this area I will no longer be my own master. Holy Spirit, remind me: when I reach out again to grab the steering wheel, let me hear your gentle voice.
Lord, give me an obedient heart, and give me spiritual companions to walk with, so that we may remind one another, support one another, and walk together on the road of letting you be King.
Let your Kingdom come; let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter into the Kingdom of Heaven; but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven.” (Matthew 7:21) Share: is there an area of your life where you already call Jesus Lord with your lips, but in reality you are still king yourself? What makes it hard for you to hand over that steering wheel?

“I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20) Share: in what situation have you experienced “handing over sovereignty, and finding freedom instead”? This week, in which specific area are you willing to let Jesus be King? How would you like your spiritual companion to remind you?
