sections.heading: Introduction: The Last Three Letters on the Score
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Before we open this morning’s reading, I want to ask you to picture a scene in your mind.

Germany, the eighteenth century. A church organist sits at his desk, dips his quill, and finishes off a stack of freshly written music. His name is Bach (Johann Sebastian Bach, 1685–1750). Music history has kept a well-known detail about him: at the top of his manuscripts Bach habitually wrote two letters, “J. J.” — short for the Latin Jesu Juva, “Jesus, help me.” And at the end of a manuscript he would write three letters, “S. D. G.” — short for Soli Deo Gloria, “To God alone be the glory.”

At the beginning, he asked Jesus for help; at the end, he gave the glory to God. The hundreds of pages of notes in between are among the greatest works in the history of human music. And yet the man who wrote them knew perfectly well: this is not my monument; this is a gift offered to God.

Brothers and sisters, let me ask you: if everything you did today — every report you write, every meal you cook, every Bible study you lead, every sermon you preach, every message you type in the group chat — had to be signed at the end with a set of initials, what would you sign?

Some would sign “S. D. G.”: to God alone be the glory. Some would sign their own name. And more often than not, what we sign is a set of invisible letters: “Please notice me,” “Please affirm me,” “Please remember it was me who did this.”

In the last lesson we looked together at the first of the 321 vision’s Two Core Values: let Jesus be King. Today we come to the second: let Jesus receive all the glory. These two core values are two sides of one coin. If “let Jesus be King” is a choice about sovereignty, then “let Jesus receive the glory” is about the direction and the goal of our lives. Sovereignty answers the question, “Who rules?” The goal answers the question, “Who am I living for?” And both questions have only one answer — Jesus.

Why does this lesson matter? Because the question of glory is the deepest, most hidden and most stubborn battlefield in the human heart. The battle over sovereignty is usually fought over big things: whether to obey, whether to give, whether to let go. The battle over glory is fought over small things: a word of thanks that was overlooked, a programme with my name left off, an occasion when someone else was praised and I wasn’t mentioned. The battle over sovereignty you can hand over once, in prayer; the battle over glory you must hand over daily, hourly, again and again.

Psychology holds up a very honest mirror here. In a classic study published in 1981 in the journal Acta Psychologica, the Swedish psychologist Ola Svenson found that among the American drivers he tested, around 93 per cent believed their driving skill was better than the median. Statistically, that is impossible — 93 per cent of people cannot all be in the top 50 per cent. The phenomenon came to be called the “better-than-average effect.” It tells us one thing: overrating ourselves and shifting the halo onto our own heads is not the flaw of a few bad people; it is the default setting of the whole human race.

So today’s lesson isn’t for “those people who love the limelight.” It’s for you and me. Let’s face the theme together: the focus of glory can have no one else in it.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: The Summit of a Hymn of Praise
sections.html:
Our key passage is Romans 11:36. To receive it rightly, we first need to know the situation in which it was written.

First, the author and the date. The author of Romans is the apostle Paul. It is generally held that the letter was written around AD 56–57, in Corinth in Greece, towards the end of Paul’s third missionary journey. The text itself leaves clues: Romans 16:1 says, “I commend to you Phoebe, our sister, who is a servant of the assembly that is at Cenchreae,” and Cenchreae was the port of Corinth; Romans 15:25 says, “But now, I say, I am going to Jerusalem, serving the saints,” referring to Paul’s journey to take the gift from the churches of Macedonia and Achaia to Jerusalem.

Second, the readers and their situation. The church in Rome was not founded by Paul, and at that point he had never been to Rome. The church was a mixture of Jewish and Gentile believers, and there was real tension between the two groups. Acts 18:2 records: “He found a certain Jew named Aquila, a man of Pontus by race, who had recently come from Italy, with his wife Priscilla, because Claudius had commanded all the Jews to depart from Rome.” Around AD 49 the emperor Claudius expelled the Jews from Rome, and for a time the church became a largely Gentile community; later, as Jewish believers gradually returned, the question arose: “Who matters more?” Gentile believers were inclined to look down on the Jews; Jewish believers were inclined to boast of their bloodline.

Third, the surrounding context. Romans 9–11 is the very heart of Paul’s response to that tension. He works his way through God’s choosing of Israel, Israel’s stumbling, the Gentiles’ receiving of mercy, and finally the mystery that “all Israel will be saved” (Romans 11:26). When he has laid out the whole sweep of salvation history, he does not hand out a league table of “who is superior.” He does something far better — he worships.

Romans 11:33–36 says: “Oh the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and the knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past tracing out! ‘For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor?’ ‘Or who has first given to him, and it will be repaid to him again?’ For of him, and through him, and to him are all things. To him be the glory for ever! Amen.”

Brothers and sisters, notice what this passage does: it is a doxology. At the summit of his argument, Paul pours out in one go all the heat of the debate, all the comparing, all the pride of “I’m the more spiritual one,” and then he lifts up God. This is the final full stop of the long argument of Romans 9 to 11 — not “So I am right,” but “To him be the glory.”

Fourth, the key words in the original. Romans 11:36 uses three extremely compact prepositional phrases. “Of him” is ἐξ αὐτοῦ, meaning “out of him, coming from him” — the source of all things. “Through him” is δι᾽ αὐτοῦ, meaning “by means of him” — the means and the channel by which all things exist. “To him” is εἰς αὐτόν, meaning “towards him, with him as the end point” — the purpose and destination of all things. Source, channel, goal: all of it is him. You and I are not at either end of that line; we are created things held within it.

As for the word “glory,” the Greek is δόξα (doxa), which corresponds to the Hebrew כָּבוֹד (kabod). The root meaning of kabod is “weight, heaviness.” So in the Bible’s way of thinking, to give glory to someone is to acknowledge who truly carries weight; to seize glory is to pile onto yourself a weight that doesn’t belong to you — and that does not lift you up; it crushes you.

With this background in view, let’s go step by step into the five key points of this lesson.

sections.heading: Key Point 1: The Focus of Glory Can Have No One Else in It
sections.html:
“For of him, and through him, and to him are all things. To him be the glory for ever! Amen.” (Romans 11:36)

This verse makes it clear that everything we have comes from him, depends on him, and ought to return to him. We are not the centre of the universe; Jesus is the purpose for which all things exist.

Letting Scripture interpret Scripture, we can set this truth among three other passages and see it more clearly.

The first is Isaiah 42:8: “I am Yahweh. That is my name. I will not give my glory to another, nor my praise to engraved images.” God is not being petty here; he is being truthful. If a god were to share his glory with false gods, that god would be lying, because he would be conceding that false gods also deserve worship. God cannot lie, so God cannot share his glory.

The second is Colossians 1:16–17: “For by him all things were created in the heavens and on the earth, visible things and invisible things, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers. All things have been created through him and for him. He is before all things, and in him all things are held together.” Note the words “and for him.” You were not created to fulfil your dreams, but to fulfil his purposes.

The third is Revelation 4:11: “Worthy are you, our Lord and God, the Holy One, to receive the glory, the honor, and the power, for you created all things, and because of your desire they existed, and were created!” The worship of heaven has no second focus.

Let me use an illustration. Have you ever looked up at the moon at night? The moon is beautiful and bright; countless poems down the ages and across the world have praised it. But here is a fact about the moon: it does not give off a single ray of its own light. According to NASA, the moon’s surface has an albedo of only about 12 per cent — that is, only about a tenth of the sunlight striking the moon is reflected back. All the moonlight we admire is the sun’s light. The moon has never felt inferior about this, and it has never claimed the credit either. It simply stands quietly in the right place and reflects the light to people in the dark.

Brothers and sisters, a Christian’s glory is the moon’s glory. 2 Corinthians 3:18 says: “But we all, with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, even as from the Lord, the Spirit.” “As in a mirror” — we are reflectors, not light sources. The greatest failure of a mirror is when it begins to think the light is its own.

Scientifically, humanity took a long time to learn this lesson. In 1543 Copernicus (Nicolaus Copernicus) published On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres, arguing that the earth is not the centre of the universe but revolves around the sun. The shift was hard not only because of the limits of observation but because of human psychology — we instinctively want to believe we are at the centre. Today astronomy tells us that the observable universe alone contains galaxies numbering in the hundreds of billions, perhaps trillions. How tiny we are on that scale — and yet the Lord who made it all was willing to die on a cross for you and me. That is the glory that truly takes our breath away.

Applying the 321 vision: the first of the Three Foundations is “Jesus is my role model.” And where was the focus of Jesus’ whole life? John 8:50 records his words: “But I don’t seek my own glory. There is one who seeks and judges.” The Son of God, on earth, did not seek his own glory. What about us? The 321 vision says: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. Today’s lesson is about recalibrating our focus — in the lens of glory there can be only one leading role. The focus of glory can have no one else in it.

sections.heading: Key Point 2: Serving Is Not About People Seeing Us, but About Them Seeing Jesus
sections.html:
Everything Jesus did on earth — preaching, healing, casting out demons, even being nailed to the cross — was so that people would see the Father’s glory. He said, “He who has seen me has seen the Father.” (John 14:9)

Reading the verse in its context brings it home even more. John 14:8–9: “Philip said to him, ‘Lord, show us the Father, and that will be enough for us.’ Jesus said to him, ‘Have I been with you such a long time, and do you not know me, Philip? He who has seen me has seen the Father. How do you say, “Show us the Father?”’”

Jesus is fully God; glory was rightly his. But look at how he prays — John 17:4: “I glorified you on the earth. I have accomplished the work which you have given me to do.” His summary of his own life was not “Look how much ministry I’ve accomplished,” but “I glorified you.”

In the same way, the apostles of the early church understood this principle. Paul said, “So then neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase.” (1 Corinthians 3:7)

The setting of that sentence is crucial. The Corinthian church was splitting into factions. 1 Corinthians 1:12 records: “Now I mean this, that each one of you says, ‘I follow Paul,’ ‘I follow Apollos,’ ‘I follow Cephas,’ and, ‘I follow Christ.’” Believers were dividing according to which preacher they liked. How did Paul deal with it? He didn’t say, “You should choose me.” He said: the one who plants and the one who waters are nothing. He took his own name down off the signboard. The apostles knew deeply: serving is not about making people admire our talents, but about leading people to worship the greatness of Jesus.

1 Corinthians 4:7 lands an even heavier blow: “For who makes you different? And what do you have that you didn’t receive? But if you did receive it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?” Brothers and sisters, your gifts were received; your opportunities were received; your health, your intelligence, your eloquence, your time — all received. Nothing received can ever be grounds for boasting.

An everyday illustration. I once heard a saying that captures this well: a good servant is like a window. A window does not exist to be looked at, but to let the light in. If someone walks into a room and the first thing they say is, “What a beautiful window,” it usually means the window is blocking the view. If someone walks in and says, “What a beautiful view outside,” the window has succeeded. Brothers and sisters, our service is the window, not the view.

Management research also bears out this spiritual principle. In his 2001 book Good to Great, the American business writer Jim Collins analysed eleven companies that went from mediocre to excellent and stayed there, and found that their leaders shared one trait, which he called “Level 5 Leadership”: deep personal humility combined with intense professional will. Collins described in particular a phenomenon he called “the window and the mirror”: when things go well, these leaders look out of the window and give the credit to other people and outside factors; when things go badly, they look in the mirror and take responsibility. Less successful leaders do exactly the opposite: when things succeed they look in the mirror, and when things fail they look out of the window.

Brothers and sisters, even the world’s research can see it: those who give the glory away end up achieving the most. How much more should we, who live for Jesus?

Our serving, leading, preaching, praying, worship and talents today — if they are not for Jesus’ glory, they easily turn into paving the road for ourselves. This is no scaremongering; it’s a temptation every person who serves has to face every day. The same sermon can be a sacrifice or a performance; the same time of leading worship can usher people into God’s presence or become a personal concert; the same post can share the gospel or collect likes. The dividing line is not in the action; it’s in the motive.

Applying the 321 vision: 321 says “life first, then relationships, then ministry.” Why must life come before ministry? Because if our life has not first been dealt with, ministry becomes a granary that feeds the ego. When a self-centred life does ministry, the bigger the ministry grows, the bigger the self becomes; when a selfless life does ministry, the bigger the ministry grows, the bigger Jesus becomes. 321 also says: “rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves.” Ministry that relies on the brain and on ourselves keeps calculating, “What do people think of me?” Ministry that relies on the heart and the Holy Spirit simply asks, “Lord, are you pleased?” Rely on the heart and you’re glad; rely on the brain and you fret — and nowhere is that truer than in serving.

sections.heading: Key Point 3: Stealing Glory Is a Grave Spiritual Offence
sections.html:
The Old Testament warns us again and again: “You shall not bow yourself down to them, nor serve them, for I, Yahweh your God, am a jealous God.” (Exodus 20:5)

The Hebrew word here is קַנָּא (qanna), which English Bibles mostly render “jealous.” Read only at the surface level — in Chinese it can sound like plain envy — it might lead us to think God is petty. In fact, in the Bible this word belongs to the language of covenant love, of marriage: a husband’s exclusive love for his wife will, by its very nature, not tolerate a third party. God has made a covenant with his people, like a marriage covenant; he is jealous because he loves exclusively and loves in earnest. He will not give his glory to idols, nor will he allow Satan to seize the worship of human beings.

Satan fell precisely because he wanted to seize God’s glory; he wanted to be exalted, and as a result he fell from heaven and will suffer eternal punishment in the lake of fire.

Isaiah 14:13–14 describes it like this: “You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! I will sit on the mountain of assembly, in the far north! I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!’” Count how many times “I will” appears in these verses — five times. Ezekiel 28:17 also says: “Your heart was lifted up because of your beauty. You have corrupted your wisdom by reason of your splendor. I have cast you to the ground.”

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully: Satan’s sin was not murder, not adultery, not stealing money. His sin was wanting a “weight that didn’t belong to him.” The 321 vision puts it with great precision: pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take the place of God. Satan left his originally intended position as a creature and tried to sit on the Creator’s throne.

So if we, by grace, are used by God, but then turn to exalting ourselves, showing ourselves off and harvesting the glory, could we fall into the same danger?

The Bible gives us two fearful examples. The first is Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. Daniel 4:30 records: “The king spoke and said, ‘Is not this great Babylon, which I have built for the royal dwelling place, by the might of my power and for the glory of my majesty?’” And the text says that while the words were still in the king’s mouth, a voice came down from heaven; he was driven away from people and ate grass like an ox until seven times had passed over him. The second is King Herod. Acts 12:23 says: “Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him, because he didn’t give God the glory. Then he was eaten by worms and died.” The Jewish historian Josephus, in his Antiquities of the Jews, also records how this Herod Agrippa I was acclaimed by the crowd in the theatre at Caesarea and immediately fell gravely ill and died, around AD 44.

When people do not give glory to God, they become foolish and corrupt. As Romans 1:21 says: “Because knowing God, they didn’t glorify him as God, and didn’t give thanks, but became vain in their reasoning, and their senseless heart was darkened.”

Notice the chain of cause and effect in this verse: failing to glorify God and failing to thank him is the cause; futile reasoning and a darkened heart are the effect. In other words, the first punishment for stealing glory is not a bolt from the blue, but a mind that begins to grow muddled. A person who keeps gathering glory to himself will see himself less and less clearly, and see God less and less clearly too.

Psychology offers valuable corroboration here. The American psychologists Jennifer Crocker and Lora Park, in their 2004 paper “The Costly Pursuit of Self-Esteem” in Psychological Bulletin, showed that when people build their self-worth on outside approval, they may enjoy short-term emotional highs, but over the long run they pay a price — their motivation to learn declines, their relationships suffer, and their autonomy and health are affected. Why? Because they have to keep winning, keep being seen; the moment the applause stops, they collapse. Brothers and sisters, this is exactly what makes the self-centred life so exhausting: you have to carry your own glory yourself — and you can’t carry it.

If we do not glorify Jesus, we may make a name for ourselves on earth, yet have our name struck off in heaven. “Nameless on earth, named in heaven; famous on earth, struck off in heaven.” Every one of us who serves the Lord should ponder that saying deeply. In Luke 10:20 Jesus said to the seventy disciples: “Nevertheless, don’t rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.” If even authority over demons is not worth rejoicing in, how much less the applause of people?

Applying the 321 vision: 321 says, “humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.” Why can selflessness overcome Satan? Because Satan’s very nature is the self-centred life, and he can find no foothold in a person who has already emptied out the “self.” Satan cannot tempt someone who doesn’t want the glory, just as a thief cannot steal from an empty house what isn’t there. On the other hand, 321 also says, “pride provokes pride and both sides lose; humility inspires humility and both sides win.” When we grab the glory in a team, others start grabbing too; when we are willing to give the glory away, others breathe a sigh of relief and begin to learn to give way as well. That is the spiritual chain reaction.

sections.heading: Key Point 4: Earthly Glory Is Temporary; Only Heavenly Glory Is Eternal
sections.html:
We have to decide: do we want brief applause or eternal commendation? Do we want people’s approval or the Lord’s reward?

Jesus put it very bluntly. Matthew 6:2: “Therefore when you do merciful deeds, don’t sound a trumpet before yourself, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets, that they may get glory from men. Most certainly I tell you, they have received their reward.” Matthew 6:5 on prayer and 6:16 on fasting both end with the same conclusion: “Most certainly I tell you, they have received their reward.”

“They have received their reward” — the Greek uses the verb ἀπέχω (apecho). In the commercial documents of the day this was a technical term meaning “paid in full,” like the “PAID” we stamp on a receipt today. Jesus’ meaning is: you wanted people’s applause? Fine — you’ve received it. Please sign here. The account is settled, and heaven owes you nothing more.

Brothers and sisters, what a sobering sentence that is. If we collect all the glory here on earth, we will not be able to receive the true reward in heaven. God will not share his glory with anyone, and he will not let those who covet glory take first place in his kingdom.

Jesus gave a grievous diagnosis of this mindset — loving human glory more than God’s glory. John 12:42–43: “Nevertheless even many of the rulers believed in him, but because of the Pharisees they didn’t confess it, so that they wouldn’t be put out of the synagogue, for they loved men’s praise more than God’s praise.” They believed in their hearts but did not dare to confess it — not because they didn’t believe, but because they couldn’t bear to give up the glory that comes from people.

Let me give an everyday illustration. We’ve all seen fireworks. A rocket shoots up and bursts across the night sky, dazzling, and the whole crowd gasps. And then? Three seconds later there is nothing left but a wisp of smoke and paper scattered on the ground. Earthly glory is like fireworks: extremely bright, extremely beautiful, extremely short. And what is heavenly glory like? Like starlight. Starlight doesn’t dazzle; you even have to be somewhere very dark to see it. But it has already been shining for millions of years, and it will keep on shining. Daniel 12:3 says: “Those who are wise will shine as the brightness of the expanse. Those who turn many to righteousness will shine as the stars forever and ever.” Brothers and sisters, do you want to be a three-second firework, or a star forever and ever?

History records a group of people who made their choice. In the eighteenth century the Moravian Brethren, led by Count Nikolaus von Zinzendorf (1700–1760), launched the earliest large-scale missionary movement of modern Protestantism. Some of them sold themselves into slavery simply to be able to live among slaves and preach the gospel. The words generally said to have spurred them on were: “May the Lamb that was slain receive the reward of his suffering.” Notice the direction of that sentence — not “May I receive the reward of my labour,” but “May the Lamb receive his reward.” Most of their names are remembered by no one, yet the missionary fire they lit has burned for three hundred years.

People with a true kingdom-of-God perspective don’t care whether their own name is remembered; they care only that the name of Jesus is lifted high.

Applying the 321 vision: this is exactly what 321 calls “a shift in perspective” — from man’s perspective to God’s, from an earthly perspective to a heavenly one, from a temporary perspective to an eternal one, from a worldly perspective to a godly one. Brothers and sisters, when you measure something with the ruler of “temporary,” you will care a great deal whether your name was mentioned this time; when you measure the same thing with the ruler of “eternal,” you’ll find it isn’t worth losing a night’s sleep over. Change your perspective and your emotions change; change your perspective and your choices change. This is the starting point of what 321 calls the fivefold change: change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living.

sections.heading: Key Point 5: Selflessness, Hiddenness, the Kingdom — All So That the Glory Goes to Jesus
sections.html:
Many of the core ideas the 321 vision emphasises — such as “selflessness,” “hiddenness,” “the kingdom” and “see no one else but Jesus” — all serve to accomplish one thing: to let Jesus receive all the glory.

First, selflessness means letting the “self” step down so that Jesus is glorified. Galatians 2:20 says: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” Note what the 321 vision stresses again and again: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living it out; “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. A cup full of itself has no room for anything else; a life emptied of “self” gives God room to fill it.

Second, hiddenness means being willing not to be seen, so that Jesus is made great. Colossians 3:3 says: “For you died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.” John the Baptist is the model of hiddenness. John 3:30 records his words: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” When his disciples came to tell him that everyone was going to Jesus, he did not defend his ministry territory; instead he said this was the fulfilment of his joy. To be able to say “I must decrease” without bitterness in your heart is enormous freedom.

Third, the kingdom means not building a kingdom for our own ministry but establishing the kingdom of Christ. This is exactly the 321 vision’s Goal: establish God’s system. Brothers and sisters, a ministry empire and the kingdom of God can look very much alike, but there is a touchstone: when another group does better than us and more people are saved, a ministry empire grows anxious, while the kingdom of God rejoices. The Lord’s Prayer teaches us to pray “Let your Kingdom come” (Matthew 6:10), not “Let my kingdom expand.”

“See no one else but Jesus” comes from the Transfiguration. Matthew 17:8 says: “Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone.” Just before that, Peter said something very human: “Lord, it is good for us to be here. If you want, let’s make three tents here: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.” (Matthew 17:4) Peter wanted to put Jesus on a level with Moses and Elijah. Then a cloud overshadowed them, and a voice said: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to him.” When the cloud lifted, Moses was gone, Elijah was gone; only Jesus remained. Brothers and sisters, God himself removed every supporting actor, because the focus of glory can have no one else in it.

So are we never to be seen at all? No. Jesus said: “Even so, let your light shine before men; that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven.” (Matthew 5:16)

Look carefully at the logic of this verse: the light is to shine before people, and the good works are to be seen — but the end point is “glorify your Father who is in heaven.” So hiddenness does not mean passivity, it does not mean doing nothing, and it does not mean pretending to be terrible. True hiddenness is this: I give it everything, I do it beautifully, and then I let that beauty point to Jesus. Letting people see the glory of Jesus through our lives — that is the true witness of a disciple.

Psychology has made a beautiful discovery here. In a 2015 study published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, Paul Piff, Dacher Keltner and colleagues at the University of California found that when people experience “awe” — for instance, standing among towering trees or before a vast natural landscape — they feel a sense of the “small self,” and that feeling significantly increases their altruism and generosity. In other words, when people see something greater than themselves, they don’t become depressed; they become better people and more willing to give.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly what worship does. The bigger Jesus becomes in our eyes, the smaller our “self” becomes; and the smaller the “self,” the freer, more generous and more able to love we become. Selflessness is not deprivation; selflessness is release.

Applying the 321 vision: this is where the 920 practice touches the ground. The 920 practice says that everyone we are in relationship with is our “2”; before them we practise living a selfless (0) life and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions. Galatians 5:22–23 says: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” You see, not one of these nine graces is for showing off; every one of them is for others to enjoy. A fruit tree never eats its own fruit. And the 235 relationships remind us: become a “2” — a spiritual companion — with someone who is selfless; build “3,” spiritual parents and spiritual children; become “5,” a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. In relationships like these, the glory will naturally not settle on any one person.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: From the Self-Centred Life to Selflessness — Let Jesus Receive All the Glory
sections.html:
Let’s set what we have learned today back into the overall framework of the 321 vision.

The Three Foundations. Jesus is my role model: he said, “I don’t seek my own glory” (John 8:50); on the cross he gave himself away completely, becoming our pattern for glorifying God. The Bible is my standard: we don’t rely on feelings to judge whether something “counts as stealing glory”; we go back to the text — Romans 11:36, Isaiah 42:8, Matthew 6:2 all point in the same direction. The Holy Spirit is my guide: only the Holy Spirit can shine a light on the hidden motives of our hearts and let us see when we have quietly turned the spotlight onto ourselves.

The Two Core Values. Last lesson was “let Jesus be King”; this lesson is “let Jesus receive all the glory.” The two cannot be separated. You cannot let Jesus reign as King while collecting the glory for yourself; nor can you give the glory to God with your lips while refusing to let him be Lord of your daily life. Kingship is about sovereignty; glory is about the goal. One concerns “who has the final say”; the other concerns “who I live for.”

The Goal: establish God’s system. The greatest difference between God’s system and the human system lies in which way the glory flows. In the human system, glory flows upwards to the one person at the top; in God’s system, glory passes through every person and flows upwards to Jesus. In God’s system, everyone is a channel; no one is a reservoir.

The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of the problem. The temptation our first parents faced in Eden was “you will be like God, knowing good and evil” (Genesis 3:5) — the desire to take God’s place. Christ Jesus took the exact opposite road. Philippians 2:6–8 says he, “existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” He went down, and God raised him up; and the end point of Philippians 2:11 is “to the glory of God the Father.” This is the road of selflessness, and it is also the road of glory.

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. 1 Peter 5:5–6 says: “‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’ Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time.” Note this: exalting is God’s work; humbling ourselves is our work. The moment we scramble to exalt ourselves, we snatch away God’s work and lose God’s grace as well. Humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

Life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. What makes the scramble for glory so terrible is that it puts the “task” ahead of “people”: to make the job look good, to make my event look like a success, I will run over people, use people, go around people. When the glory goes to Jesus, people are set free, because no one has to be sacrificed to build my stage.

The priority of relationships: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and finally with things. If my relationship with God is right, I don’t need to extract affirmation from people; if my relationship with myself is right, I can face honestly my old habit of craving face without despairing; if my relationship with others is right, I can cheer wholeheartedly for someone else’s success; and finally, things will be put in their proper place — as a tool God uses, not as proof of who I am.

A shift in perspective. From man’s perspective to God’s: man asks, “Who got the limelight this time?” God asks, “Who was built up this time?” From the earthly perspective to the heavenly: earth looks at rankings; heaven looks at faithfulness. From the temporary perspective to the eternal: temporary applause lasts three seconds; eternal commendation lasts forever. From the worldly perspective to the godly: the logic of the world is “strive and grab”; the logic of God is “receive.”

The 920 practice and the 235 relationships. The 920 practice has us live out the selfless “0” before every “2,” bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions — glory is not given to God with our mouths but with our fruit. The 235 relationships have us remind one another — among spiritual companions, spiritual parents and spiritual children, and a fivefold-ministry team: today, has the glory been flowing in the wrong direction?

The Path of Serving: Spirit → Understanding → Life → Service → God. The Holy Spirit is my guide, shining light on my hidden motives; the Bible is my standard, correcting my mistaken mindset; Jesus is my role model, leading me onto the road he walked when he emptied himself; let Jesus be King, handing sovereignty back to him; and finally, let Jesus receive all the glory. The end of this road is not my achievement; it is his name.

sections.heading: Practice for Daily Living: Giving the Glory to Jesus Every Day
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three very practical exercises. The 321 vision says there are eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Let’s use these eight stages to take the three exercises deeper.

Exercise 1: After everything you do, ask: “Was this to glorify Jesus, or to glorify me?”

Every day, after finishing a task, a piece of service or an interaction, stop and ask yourself: “Did this give Jesus the glory, or did it give me satisfaction?” This reflection helps us keep adjusting our attitude and turn the spotlight back onto Jesus.

Information: first put the truth into your mind. Memorise Romans 11:36 today: “For of him, and through him, and to him are all things. To him be the glory for ever! Amen.”

Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light. Pray: “Lord, let me see who I am really doing this for today.” Revelation is not new knowledge; it is a truth you’ve long known suddenly becoming your own.

Conviction: acknowledge from the heart that “the glory was never mine in the first place.” It isn’t that you grudgingly give it up; it simply never belonged to you.

Implementation: ask this question at three fixed times each day — midday, early evening and before bed. Set three reminders on your phone, each titled “For whom?”

Evaluation: write one line each evening. Was there a moment today when, deep down, I secretly wanted people to see me? Write it down honestly, without dressing it up.

Correction: confess that moment, and immediately do something in the opposite direction — send a message giving the credit to someone else.

Repetition: keep practising for twenty-one days in a row. A mindset is not changed by a single flash of insight, but by repetition.

Multiplication: bring someone along to do it with you. The person you bring along is your “2.”

Exercise 2: Once a week, choose one act of “deliberate hiddenness”

For example: when you succeed or perform well, don’t talk about it; simply offer thanks in prayer. Give the glory to the team and to God, not to yourself. Quietly help someone else succeed without asking to be noticed. Exercises like these help us honour Jesus as great from the heart, instead of letting the glory settle on ourselves.

Information: memorise Matthew 6:3–4: “But when you do merciful deeds, don’t let your left hand know what your right hand does, so that your merciful deeds may be in secret, then your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly.”

Revelation: let the Holy Spirit point out the area you are least willing to hide — your expertise? your giving? your spiritual maturity? That area is very often the very thing God wants you to hand over.

Conviction: believe that the Father “who sees in secret” is real. When no one sees, it doesn’t mean no one sees.

Implementation: pick one specific thing this week. For example: an anonymous gift; an act of service you don’t post about; letting someone else present your good idea in a meeting.

Evaluation: afterwards, does your heart feel light or resentful? The places where we feel resentful are the places where we are still competing with God for the glory.

Correction: bring that resentment into prayer; don’t suppress it and don’t indulge it — hand it to the Lord.

Repetition: once a week, for three months. Let hiddenness turn from a “painful assignment” into a “habit of freedom.”

Multiplication: at the right time, share your experience of hiddenness — not to show off how humble you are, but so that your brothers and sisters know this road can be walked.

Exercise 3: With your spiritual companion, ask each other one question: “Did you let Jesus receive the glory this week?”

Each week, share three questions with your spiritual companion: Where this week did I choose to step back so that the Lord could be lifted up? Where did I carelessly steal the Lord’s glory and need to repent? In what situation next week am I willing to choose to hide myself, so that people see only Jesus? Reminders like these help us keep bringing the focus of glory back to where it belongs.

Information: memorise Proverbs 27:17: “Iron sharpens iron; so a man sharpens his friend’s countenance.”

Revelation: understand that we cannot see our own blind spots — which is exactly why God gives us spiritual companions.

Conviction: accepting that “I need to be reminded” is itself the starting point of humility.

Implementation: this week, arrange with one “2” — a selfless spiritual companion — a fixed time and the same three questions.

Evaluation: when you share, state the facts and don’t justify yourself. Self-justification is protecting the “self” that hasn’t yet died.

Correction: pray for each other, and give each other concrete suggestions.

Repetition: keep it weekly, and don’t let busyness interrupt it.

Multiplication: once the two of you are walking steadily, each bring along one more person, becoming the “3” of the 235 relationships — spiritual parents and spiritual children — and finally establishing the “5,” a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: All the Glory to Jesus
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, we’ve come to the end of today’s lesson.

What we are is his creation; what we can do is his gift; what we accomplish is his using us; the fruit we bear is his provision.

Paul put it most honestly: “But by the grace of God I am what I am. His grace which was given to me was not futile, but I worked more than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.” (1 Corinthians 15:10) You see, he did not dare to put even his “working more than all of them” down to his own account.

We have nothing to boast about; even our faithfulness, our passion, our abilities and our service were first made possible by him. That being so, let us not seize the glory, not share the glory, not hoard the glory, but give all the glory, wholly, to Jesus.

Only when the glory returns to him will revival come to the church; only when we are willing to be hidden will the beauty of Jesus be seen; only when we let Jesus receive all the glory will our lives not be in vain.

Psalm 115:1 has been the prayer of the saints in every generation: “Not to us, Yahweh, not to us, but to your name give glory, for your loving kindness, and for your truth’s sake.” Notice that “not to us” is repeated twice. The first time is the mind’s acknowledgement; the second is the heart’s surrender. We need to say it twice, because our “self” really is that stubborn.

Let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory. These are the Two Core Values of 321, and the direction of our whole lives. When no one in the church is fighting for glory any more, the Holy Spirit has room to move freely; and when the Holy Spirit has room to move freely, revival begins.

Will you resolve today and say: “Lord, not me but you be seen; not for me but for you; all the glory, wholly to you!”

keyVerses: “For of him, and through him, and to him are all things. To him be the glory for ever! Amen.” (Romans 11:36)
practices: After everything you do, ask: “Was this to glorify Jesus, or to glorify me?”
Once a week, choose one act of “deliberate hiddenness”
Ask your spiritual companion one question: “Did you let Jesus receive the glory this week?”
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we worship you.
We acknowledge that all things are of you, through you and to you; to you be the glory for ever.

Lord, forgive us. So often we give you the glory with our lips while secretly keeping a little for ourselves in our hearts. We long to be seen when we serve, we forget to give thanks when we succeed, and we grow bitter when we are overlooked. Wash us with your precious blood, and with your cross deal with the “self” within us that has not yet died.

Holy Spirit, shine your light on our hidden motives, and let us see when we have turned the spotlight onto ourselves. Give us the courage to be gladly hidden, a heart big enough to cheer for others, and the freedom to give the credit away.
Lord, we are willing to let you be King, and willing to let you receive all the glory. Make our lives a clean window, so that when people look through us, what they see is not us, but you.
Lord, not me but you be seen; not for me but for you; all the glory, wholly to you.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Discussion 1: “For of him, and through him, and to him are all things. To him be the glory for ever! Amen.” (Romans 11:36) Share something you’ve recently been deeply invested in — your service, your work or your family. If you examine it honestly, how much of that thing’s “source, channel and goal” points to Jesus, and how much points to yourself?

Discussion 2: “Most certainly I tell you, they have received their reward.” (Matthew 6:2) In what situations are you most likely to “collect your reward in full here on earth”? What act of “deliberate hiddenness” are you willing to take this week, to give the glory to Jesus alone?

sections.heading: 1. Introduction: Two Cities, Two Ways of Life
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. This early morning, I’d like to ask you first to be still for one minute and recall every little decision you made yesterday.

Yesterday at the office, when someone claimed the credit for themselves, what was your first reaction inside? Last night, when someone in your family said something cutting, did you choose to answer back, or did you choose to stay quiet?

Each of these things is small — so small that we would never write them down in our prayer journal. But brothers and sisters, here is a spiritual secret: you don’t decide which kingdom you belong to in one great battle. You hand yourself over to one kingdom or the other, bit by bit, through a thousand small choices.

In AD 410 the city of Rome was captured, and the whole Mediterranean world was thrown into terror. In that shaken era Augustine wrote The City of God, and in Book 14, chapter 28, he wrote words that would shape Europe for fifteen hundred years: two loves have made two cities; love of self, even to the contempt of God, made the earthly city; love of God, even to the contempt of self, made the heavenly city.

Two loves, two cities. This is the single thread that runs through the Bible from Genesis to Revelation: throughout human history two systems have always run side by side — one is the Babylonian system, the other is God’s system.

We have already walked through six lessons together: from the end-times call to “come out of Babylon,” to how to overcome the Babylonian system, and then laying the Three Foundations one stone at a time — Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide — and then gripping the Two Core Values firmly: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory.

Today we come to the final link of the 321 vision, the destination to which all the foundations and core values are ultimately pointing — the Goal: establish God’s system.

Brothers and sisters, the Three Foundations are not three pieces of knowledge, and the Two Core Values are not two slogans; they are building materials — the steel and the concrete — and they are meant to be built into something. If you have learned the Three Foundations and memorised the Two Core Values but have no Goal, all you have in your hands is a pile of materials scattered on the ground, and no house.

God has never been only about tearing down; God is about building up. He calls us out of Babylon, not to leave us standing in the wilderness in the wind, but to establish a system that belongs to him — in us, in our families and in our fellowship.

Today we are going to see seven things together: why we must establish God’s system; that even in Babylon we can live out the pattern of God’s kingdom; that the key lies in every single choice; that the pattern of action is know — do — receive; that falling down doesn’t matter, because when you get up you can move forward; and the point that sets us most free of all — living out 321 is not by effort but by grace; and finally, how habits become a system, and the system becomes life. Let’s build our house on the rock together.

sections.heading: 2. Scripture Background: What Is Babylon? And What Is God’s System?
sections.html:
To understand the call to “come out of Babylon,” we first have to get to know Babylon.

1. Babylon in history

Historically, Babylon lay on the banks of the Euphrates, about eighty kilometres south of present-day Baghdad in Iraq. Nebuchadnezzar II, who reigned from 605 to 562 BC, built it into the most magnificent city of the ancient world: the empire’s wealth, military power, religion and culture were all concentrated in this one city.

For the people of the Bible, Babylon was an agonising memory. In 605 BC Nebuchadnezzar first took Jerusalem and carried off a group of young nobles, among them Daniel and his three friends; in 586 BC Jerusalem fell, the temple was burned, and the kingdom of Judah came to an end.

But brothers and sisters, the Bible’s concern with Babylon has never been merely political history.

2. Babylon in the spiritual sense

The name Babylon first appears as Babel in Genesis 11. “They said, ‘Come, let’s build ourselves a city, and a tower whose top reaches to the sky, and let’s make a name for ourselves, lest we be scattered abroad on the surface of the whole earth.’” (Genesis 11:4)

Look at the three key phrases in this verse: “let’s build ourselves,” “let’s make a name for ourselves,” “lest we be scattered” — people want to build by themselves, people want to make their own name great, people seek security in themselves. This is the DNA of the Babylonian system; in the language of 321, it is the self-centred life: making self the centre, self the glory and self the safeguard. The lesson puts it very precisely: “Babylon means every system that is worldly, centred on man and set against God.”

Today’s Babylon has no gates of glazed brick, but it takes more refined forms: the set of values that tells you to “fight your way to the top for yourself,” the scoring system that measures a person’s worth by performance, looks and the number of likes, the rhythm of life that, without your noticing, puts God in the very last slot of your diary.

3. Three calls to “come out”

Three times the Bible calls God’s people to “come out,” each time going deeper than the last.

The first is a geographical coming out. Isaiah 48:20: “Leave Babylon! Flee from the Chaldeans! With a voice of singing announce this, tell it even to the end of the earth: say, ‘Yahweh has redeemed his servant Jacob!’” In 538 BC Cyrus king of Persia issued his decree, fulfilling this call.

The second is a moral and spiritual coming out. 2 Corinthians 6:17: “Therefore ‘Come out from among them, and be separate,’ says the Lord. ‘Touch no unclean thing. I will receive you.’” People may already be in grace, and yet their hearts may still be lingering in Babylon.

The third is the final, end-times coming out. Revelation 18:4: “Come out of her, my people, that you have no participation in her sins, and that you don’t receive of her plagues.” The apostle John wrote Revelation on the island of Patmos in the 90s AD. At that time it was the Roman Empire that was oppressing the church, yet the Holy Spirit did not use the name “Rome”; he used “Babylon” — because Babylon is not a place name in the past tense; it is a system that exists in every generation.

Pay special attention to two words in Revelation 18:4: “my people.” Those God calls out are his own people. A person can already be saved and still be living inside the Babylonian system; can already be a child of God and still think in the patterns of Babel. That is why we need this lesson.

4. God’s system: God has always been building

So what is it that God wants us to establish?

Ephesians 2:20–22: “being built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the chief cornerstone; in whom the whole building, fitted together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord; in whom you also are built together for a habitation of God in the Spirit.”

“Built together” in the original is συνοικοδομεῖσθε, formed from “together” plus “to build a house,” and it is in the passive voice — it is not that we build ourselves; we are “being” built together. This grammatical detail is the key to this lesson: God’s system is not something people build for God; it is what God builds in us by the Holy Spirit. Our part is to obey — every day to place this living stone that is ourselves into his hands. 1 Peter 2:5 also says: “You also, as living stones, are built up as a spiritual house, to be a holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.”

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? Babylon says, “Let’s build ourselves a city”; God says, “You also are built together.” Babylon’s verb is the active “I build”; the kingdom’s verb is the passive “being built.” One is the self-centred life; the other is selflessness. One wants to make our own name great; the other wants Jesus to receive all the glory.

And Psalm 127:1 wrote the conclusion out plainly long ago: “Unless Yahweh builds the house, they who build it labor in vain. Unless Yahweh watches over the city, the watchman guards it in vain.”

sections.heading: 3. Key Point 1: The Only Way Out of Babylon Is to Establish God’s System
sections.html:
The lesson opens by saying that God’s call to his people — “come out of Babylon” — is not a geographical relocation but a change of spiritual system.

Brothers and sisters, that sentence is worth a lifetime of meditation. Because our most common mistake is to understand “coming out” as “leaving a certain place.”

The Israelites are the best example. It took God one night, through Moses, to bring them out of Egypt; but it took forty years to bring Egypt out of them. Numbers 11:5 records their complaint: “We remember the fish, which we ate in Egypt for nothing; the cucumbers, and the melons, and the leeks, and the onions, and the garlic.” The people came out; the system did not.

In the same way, we may have been baptised for years, we may already be serving in the fellowship, and yet still be living our days the Babylonian way: measuring our worth by comparison, protecting our position by manoeuvring, numbing the emptiness inside with busyness.

Why isn’t “leaving” enough? Why must we “establish”?

The Lord Jesus told a sobering parable. Matthew 12:43–44: “When an unclean spirit has gone out of a man, he passes through waterless places, seeking rest, and doesn’t find it. Then he says, ‘I will return into my house from which I came out,’ and when he has come back, he finds it empty, swept, and put in order.”

Notice the word “empty.” The house had been swept clean, but it was empty; and an empty house cannot be held. As a result, verse 45 says, the last state of that man became worse than the first.

So “coming out” alone is not enough. You can’t just clear out; you must move in. You can’t just tear down; you must build.

The lesson says it clearly: “To truly escape Babylon, the only way out is to establish God’s system, with Christ at its centre.”

When do we slide back into Babylon?

The lesson gives an extremely precise diagnosis: “When people leave the Three Foundations and the Two Core Values, they naturally fall into the Worldly system and use their own methods to build a human kingdom.”

Notice the word “naturally.” Falling into Babylon takes no effort, just as a house gathers dust without any effort and a garden grows weeds without any effort. Spiritual desolation is not a sudden event; it is a stretch of time when no one is keeping watch.

Conversely, the lesson also gives the remedy: “As long as we return every day to the Three Foundations — letting Jesus be our role model, letting the Bible be our standard, letting the Holy Spirit be our guide — together with the Two Core Values — letting Jesus be King and letting Jesus receive the glory — we are establishing God’s system.”

Listen carefully to the tense of that verb: “we are establishing.” Not “we will establish one day,” but “we are establishing right now.” The moment you opened your Bible this morning, you were establishing it; the moment at noon today when you swallow a retort you wanted to fire back, you are establishing it.

An everyday illustration: two builders

At the end of the Sermon on the Mount the Lord Jesus said (Matthew 7:24–25): “Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine, and does them, I will liken him to a wise man, who built his house on a rock. The rain came down, the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat on that house; and it didn’t fall, for it was founded on the rock.”

Both men built houses. On a sunny day they may have looked exactly the same; the one on the sand may even have gone up faster and looked better. The difference lay below ground, where no one could see.

Brothers and sisters, your spiritual system is that “below ground”: it’s your fifteen minutes alone with God early in the morning, your honesty when no one is watching, your obedience in the small things. On a sunny day you can’t see the difference; when the storm comes, the difference is everything.

Applying 321: from man’s perspective to God’s perspective

The 321 vision says we must go through a fourfold shift of perspective: from man’s to God’s, from earthly to heavenly, from temporary to eternal, from worldly to godly. The Babylonian system is man’s, earthly, temporary and worldly; God’s system is God’s, heavenly, eternal and godly. 2 Corinthians 4:18 says: “while we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.”

So the first step in establishing God’s system is not changing behaviour but changing the mindset. Romans 12:2 says: “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” The root of the original word for “conformed” carries the sense of “a mould, a pattern,” while “transformed” is μεταμορφοῦσθε — the “metamorphosis” by which a caterpillar becomes a butterfly. God does not want us to touch up the mould of Babylon; he wants us to exchange our whole life from the inside out — and that is exactly 321’s fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry.

sections.heading: 4. Key Point 2: Even in Babylon, We Can Live Out the Pattern of God’s Kingdom
sections.html:
At this point some of you may be thinking: “Pastor, I understand the teaching, but my office is Babylon, my extended family is Babylon — I simply can’t get out.”

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly what the second part of the lesson answers: “Although Daniel and his three friends lived in Babylon, they chose not to be defiled and not to compromise, and they held fast to their reverence for God and their loyalty to him.”

Daniel: holding to the first choice in the king’s palace

In 605 BC, when Daniel was taken captive, he was probably only in his teens. He was brought into Nebuchadnezzar’s palace. His name was changed — Daniel (meaning “God is my judge”) became Belteshazzar. He was taught the language and learning of the Chaldeans for three years. He was assigned the king’s food and the king’s wine. New surroundings, new name, new education, new diet: a complete programme of system re-engineering.

Daniel could not choose his surroundings, could not refuse the new name, could not skip the classes. But the Bible records the one thing he could choose — Daniel 1:8: “But Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the king’s dainties, nor with the wine which he drank. Therefore he requested of the prince of the eunuchs that he might not defile himself.”

The Hebrew behind “purposed” literally means “to set it upon the heart” (sim al-lev). Brothers and sisters, God’s system is established starting from the heart, not from the environment. Daniel could not change Babylon, but inside Babylon he could draw a line and say: this step I will not take.

And the result? A man who held on to God’s system inside Babylon went on to stand firm through three successive regimes.

The three friends: holding to “but if not” before the furnace

In Daniel 3, Nebuchadnezzar set up a golden image and ordered the whole nation to fall down and worship it. Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego stayed standing and would not kneel. The king was furious and ordered them to be thrown into the burning fiery furnace.

Their reply is one of the most courageous declarations of faith in the Old Testament. Daniel 3:17–18: “If it happens, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace; and he will deliver us out of your hand, O king. But if not, let it be known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods or worship the golden image which you have set up.”

“But if not” — those three words are the touchstone of God’s system. Many people believe in God because of what God will do for them; that kind of faith is still Babylonian, because the centre is still “me.” “But if not” faith says: even if God doesn’t do what I want, I will still serve him. That is selflessness; that is letting Jesus be King.

In the end God did not rescue them out of the fire; he was with them in the fire. In Daniel 3:25 the king said in astonishment: “Look, I see four men loose, walking in the middle of the fire, and they are unharmed. The appearance of the fourth is like a son of the gods.”

The lesson says: “Though they were in a foreign land, they lived out the light of God’s system, so that everyone saw the glory of God.” Exactly so — Nebuchadnezzar, a pagan king, finally said in Daniel 4:37: “Now I, Nebuchadnezzar, praise and extol and honor the King of heaven.”

Daniel’s secret: habit

Daniel 6:10 records a hugely important detail: “When Daniel knew that the writing was signed, he went into his house (now his windows were open in his room toward Jerusalem) and he kneeled on his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did before.”

Notice the last words: “as he did before.”

Brothers and sisters, what Daniel did in the crisis of the lions’ den was not a burst of last-minute heroics but a habit kept unchanged for decades. When the crisis came, he didn’t need to decide whether to pray, because he had decided long before; he simply had to do what he always did. That is the power of a system: when pressure comes, you don’t make your choice on the strength of willpower in the moment; you respond naturally out of a structure built up over a long time.

In his Principles of Psychology, published in 1890, the psychologist William James wrote that habit is the enormous flywheel of society. It takes a great deal of force to get a flywheel turning, but once it is turning, it is hard to stop. God’s system is that flywheel in our lives.

Applying 321: life first, then relationships, then ministry

Daniel didn’t launch a religious reformation the moment he entered the palace. First he guarded his own relationship with God (life); then he won the trust of the chief of the eunuchs (relationships); only last was he promoted to govern the affairs of the kingdom (ministry).

321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry; and the priority of relationships is first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and finally with things. We often reverse the order: rushing to do things without life, rushing to change others without first being changed by God — and so the bigger the ministry, the drier the life. Daniel’s example is this: first settle your heart, and leave the rest to God.

sections.heading: 5. Key Point 3: The Key to Establishing God’s System Lies in Every Single Choice
sections.html:
The lesson says something very striking: “A system is not a one-off decision but the accumulation of countless choices.”

Then the lesson lists three pairs of questions, and I’d like you to take them to heart:

Will I choose to indulge myself, or choose to let Jesus be King?

Will I choose to act on my feelings, or obey the principles of the Bible?

Will I choose to put myself on display, or let Jesus receive the glory?

And then the lesson draws a conclusion that is one of the golden sayings of this lesson: “Choose once, and it has an effect; choose countless times, and it forms a system; let the system run long enough, and it becomes life.”

The witness of the Bible: choosing is the Bible’s repeated call

The Bible never treats people as machines; it is always calling people to choose.

Moses said on the plains of Moab (Deuteronomy 30:19): “I have set before you life and death, the blessing and the curse. Therefore choose life, that you may live, you and your descendants.” Joshua said at Shechem (Joshua 24:15): “but as for me and my house, we will serve Yahweh.” Elijah asked on Mount Carmel (1 Kings 18:21): “How long will you waver between the two sides? If Yahweh is God, follow him; but if Baal, then follow him.”

Brothers and sisters, God never forces you into his system. He respects your choice, because love must be free.

Choices in small things are the real choices

The Lord Jesus said in Luke 16:10: “He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much. He who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much.”

We often imagine that the decisive spiritual moments are the big scenes: whether to change jobs, whether to give ourselves to full-time ministry, whether to forgive the person who hurt us deeply. But the truth is, by the time the big scene arrives, your response has long since been decided by your choices in a thousand small scenes.

In a study published in 2010 in the European Journal of Social Psychology, the University College London psychologist Phillippa Lally and her colleagues followed ninety-six participants as they formed new habits and found that it took an average of sixty-six days for a behaviour to become automatic, with individual differences ranging from eighteen to two hundred and fifty-four days; and missing an occasional day along the way did not significantly damage the formation of the habit.

Brothers and sisters, did you hear that? A spiritual system takes time; one slip will not destroy your system — only giving up will.

An everyday illustration: how a riverbed is formed

Have you ever seen muddy ground after a heavy rain? Where the water has flowed, it leaves a shallow trace, and the next time water comes it flows that way more easily; the more it flows, the deeper the channel, until finally a riverbed is formed. Neuroscience tells us the brain works the same way: when a group of neurons fire together repeatedly, the axons connecting them are wrapped layer upon layer in myelin, and signals travel dramatically faster.

Brothers and sisters, every time you choose to let Jesus be King, you are digging one channel deeper in your life; every time you choose to indulge yourself, you are digging another one deeper. The question is not whether you are digging, but which channel you’re digging.

Applying 321: Jesus is the focal point

321 says: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. Why does every choice matter so much? Because every choice is an adjustment of our focus. When Peter was walking on the water, the Bible says (Matthew 14:30): “But when he saw that the wind was strong, he was afraid, and beginning to sink.” He didn’t begin to sink because the waves got bigger; he began to sink because he looked at the waves and not at the Lord. May every choice we make be a movement of turning our eyes back to Jesus.

sections.heading: 6. Key Point 4: The 321 Pattern of Action — Know, Do, Receive
sections.html:
The lesson says: “To establish God’s system, it isn’t enough just to know; you have to do it in order to receive it.”

Then the lesson lays out these three levels very clearly: knowing the principles of 321 is only the beginning; truly living out the 321 life is the key; and as you keep making these choices again and again, the 321 system becomes internalised as part of your life — and you have received God’s system.

Knowing: information is not life

James 1:22 says: “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.”

“Deluding your own selves” in the original carries the sense of “deceiving by false reasoning.” What is the false reasoning? Treating “I understand it” as if it meant “I’ve done it.”

Believers in our generation have heard more sermons than any generation in church history, but hearing much is not the same as growing well. Knowledge that doesn’t turn into obedience turns into pride. 1 Corinthians 8:1 says: “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.”

Doing: the Lord Jesus’ own standard

In Matthew 7:24 the Lord Jesus spoke of “everyone … who hears these words of mine, and does them.” He didn’t say “and nods,” nor “and takes notes.” In John 13:17, after washing his disciples’ feet, the Lord Jesus said: “If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.” Notice the structure of the verse: know — do — be blessed. The blessing doesn’t lie between knowing and doing; the blessing comes after doing. Too many Christians stop on the empty ground in the middle and then ask in bewilderment: “Why don’t I experience God?”

Receiving: internalised into life

Hebrews 5:14: “But solid food is for those who are full grown, who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern good and evil.” The root of the original word for “exercised” is the word from which we get “gymnasium,” and it is in the perfect tense, describing an ongoing state produced by long training. Spiritual discernment doesn’t drop out of the sky; it is trained. 1 Timothy 4:7–8: “Exercise yourself toward godliness. For bodily exercise has some value, but godliness has value in all things, having the promise of the life which is now, and of that which is to come.”

When you’re wrong, change

The lesson closes this section with a sentence full of a shepherd’s heart: “Don’t be afraid of mistakes; what is most to be feared is refusing to repent. Wherever in life you go off course, as long as you change when you’re wrong, you are still on God’s road.”

Brothers and sisters, memorise these three words: wrong? then change.

1 John 1:9: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” “Confess” in the original is ὁμολογῶμεν, meaning “to say the same thing” — to say the same thing as God. Repentance is not self-reproach, not stewing in regret at yourself; it is coming over to God’s side and admitting that he sees rightly.

“Repentance” in the New Testament is μετάνοια, which literally means “a change of mind.” This is exactly what 321 calls the first of the fivefold changes: a change of mindset.

Applying 321: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves

321 says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the brain and you fret, rely on the heart and you’re glad. If “know — do — receive” stays only in the head, it becomes a self-improvement programme — the most exhausting religion there is. Proverbs 4:23 says: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” What we need is not to try harder, but to draw nearer.

sections.heading: 7. Key Point 5: Falling Down Doesn’t Matter — Get Up and You Can Move Forward
sections.html:
The lesson says: “In spiritual training we will certainly have times when we drift off course and fall, but this is nothing to be afraid of; the key is whether we are willing to choose again to return to 321.”

Then the lesson uses a very good comparison: “It is like learning to walk: losing your balance and falling is exactly the process of learning to be steady and move forward.”

A surprising statistic

In a study published in 2012 in the journal Psychological Science, the New York University psychologist Karen Adolph and her colleagues video-recorded more than a hundred infants who had just learned to walk, and found that a toddler takes on average about 2,368 steps an hour — and falls about seventeen times.

Brothers and sisters, let me ask you: has any baby ever fallen seventeen times and decided, “That’s it, I’m never walking again”? Never. For a baby, falling is not evidence of failure; falling is part of learning. And that study found that the children who walked more and fell more were actually the ones who improved fastest. Accumulated experience matters more than being careful.

How the Bible sees falling

Proverbs 24:16: “for a righteous man falls seven times and rises up again; but the wicked are overthrown by calamity.”

The Bible doesn’t say the righteous never fall; it says that when the righteous fall, they “rise up again.” The difference between the righteous and the wicked is not whether they fall, but whether they get up.

Psalm 37:23–24: “A man’s steps are established by Yahweh. He delights in his way. Though he stumble, he shall not fall, for Yahweh holds him up with his hand.” The beauty of these verses is that they don’t deny we will stumble; they simply tell us there is a hand that is always holding us up. Micah 7:8 is even the declaration of a captive people among the ruins: “When I fall, I will arise. When I sit in darkness, Yahweh will be a light to me.”

Peter’s story

One of the disciples who fell hardest in the Bible was Peter: in the high priest’s courtyard he denied the Lord three times, and he went out and wept bitterly. If the story had stopped there, Peter would have been a failure. But after his resurrection the Lord Jesus lit a charcoal fire on the shore of the Sea of Tiberias — a charcoal fire just like the one in the courtyard on the night Peter fell — and three times asked him, “Do you love me more than these?” (John 21:15) Three falls, three restorations. The Lord was not humiliating Peter; he was restoring him. Not long afterwards, the man who had fallen stood up at Pentecost and preached, and three thousand people believed.

The lesson puts it superbly: “True failure is not falling down, but refusing to get up again.”

Applying 321: “Evaluation, Correction, Repetition” in the eight stages of changing our mindset

321’s eight stages of changing our mindset are: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Notice that “Evaluation” and “Correction” are written right into the process — in God’s design, falling and correcting are not accidents but a stop that has been planned for.

A system that does not allow failure is the Babylonian system, because it depends on human performance; a system that allows failure but does not allow giving up is God’s system, because it depends on God’s grace. Lamentations 3:22–23: “It is because of Yahweh’s loving kindnesses that we are not consumed, because his compassion doesn’t fail. They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness.” This is why we hold our morning devotion every morning — because his mercies are new every morning.

sections.heading: 8. Key Point 6: Living Out 321 Is Not by Effort, but by Grace
sections.html:
In this section the lesson says something almost counter-intuitive: “Many people say, ‘It sounds simple, but it’s hard to do.’ But in the practice of 321 it’s the other way round — it sounds simple, and it’s even simpler to do.”

Why? The lesson says: “Because it doesn’t depend on human willpower, but on God’s grace.”

Grace is not slackness; grace is power

First let me clear up a common misunderstanding: relying on grace does not mean doing nothing; relying on grace is about where the power to do it comes from.

Philippians 2:12–13 puts both sides in one sentence: “work out your own salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure.” Look at that word “for.” “Works” in the original is ἐνεργῶν, the source of the English word “energy,” meaning “to set energy in motion, to make effective.” God is not standing on the shore shouting encouragement; God is the engine running inside us.

1 Corinthians 15:10: “But by the grace of God I am what I am. … I worked more than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.” Paul was the hardest-working man in the New Testament, and also the one who insisted most firmly, “not I, but the grace of God.” Hard work and grace are not in conflict; we simply need to be clear about the source.

The warning of Galatians

In Galatians 3:3 Paul rebukes the Galatians: “Are you so foolish? Having begun in the Spirit, are you now completed in the flesh?” What a precisely aimed jab: we were all saved by grace, yet we often try to become holy by our own strength, building God’s temple by Babylon’s methods. This is exactly the lesson’s warning: “If we are proud and self-righteous and try to establish a spiritual system by our own strength, we will in the end surely fail.”

An iron law of the spiritual life

The lesson says: “The humble receive grace; the proud are resisted. This is an iron law of the spiritual life.”

This comes from James 4:6, which reads: “But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’” 1 Peter 5:5 says the same.

“Resists” in the original is ἀντιτάσσεται, a military term meaning “to draw up in battle array against, to set the ranks in opposition.” Brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: God does not merely dislike pride; God draws up his battle lines against pride.

Why? 321 puts it well: pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take the place of God; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. What’s more, pride provokes pride and both sides lose; humility inspires humility and both sides win.

Why is it “even simpler to do” for the humble?

Because the humble don’t have to carry the burden of “I have to prove myself.”

The Lord Jesus said in Matthew 11:28–30: “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.”

In the ancient world a yoke was often a double yoke: on one side a strong, mature ox, on the other a young ox still learning, and the one really pulling the plough was the strong one. When the Lord says, “Take my yoke,” he means: come, get in the harness beside me, and I’ll do the pulling.

The English writer C. S. Lewis, in Mere Christianity, describes the truly humble person: when you meet him, all you will think is that he seemed to take a real interest in what you said to him; he will not be thinking about humility, because he will not be thinking about himself at all.

Brothers and sisters, this is what 321 calls “selflessness”: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living it out; “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me.

Galatians 2:20: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.”

Applying 321: humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan
