The core message of 321 says: humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.

Satan’s fall was pride. Isaiah 14:13–14: “You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! … I will make myself like the Most High!’” Did you notice that string of “I will”s? That is the manifesto of the self-centred life.

The Lord Jesus is the opposite. Philippians 2:6–8: “who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” “Emptied himself” in the original is ἐκένωσεν, “he poured himself out” — the most perfect definition of selflessness.

Brothers and sisters, we cannot become humble by trying harder, because “striving to be humble” can itself very easily become another form of pride. All we can do is come to Jesus and let his life be lived out in us.

sections.heading: 9. Integrating the 321 Vision: Everything Is for This One Goal
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, having come this far, let’s spread out the whole map of 321 and look at it once more.

The Three Foundations, the Two Core Values, the Goal

The Three Foundations are: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. The Two Core Values are: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. The Goal is: establish God’s system.

Notice the logic of this structure: the Three Foundations are the groundwork, the Two Core Values are the beams and pillars, and the Goal is the building itself. So if someone memorises 321 as three slogans, they have misunderstood it: 321 is a set of building plans, and plans are meant to produce a house.

The fivefold change

321 says the fivefold change is in mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. A change of mindset — Babylon is not a place but a system; coming out is not moving house but switching to a different set of operating principles. A change of life — the person inside who says “I will build, I will make my name great” is gradually exchanged for the one who says “‘I’ no longer live, but Christ lives in me.” A change of daily living — this new life shows up in your mornings, your diary, your wallet. A change of relationships — you no longer fight to win in conflicts with your co-workers in ministry; you begin to be able to bow your head first. A change of ministry — God places his commission into the hands of a vessel that has already been built.

Brothers and sisters, remember the order: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

The 920 practice

321 says: everyone we are in relationship with is our “2”; before them we practise living a selfless (0) life and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions.

Galatians 5:22–23: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” Notice that the Bible says “fruit,” singular; these nine are not nine elective courses but nine facets of one life. And fruit is not manufactured; it grows.

Brothers and sisters, this is how God’s system is established: not by my straining to look patient at the office, but by letting Christ live in me, so that patience flows out naturally.

The ultimate direction of the Goal

321 says that we establish God’s system in order to fulfil the Lord’s Prayer, to press on into the end time revival, and to walk alongside every person until they become an overcomer.

The heart of the Lord’s Prayer is Matthew 6:10: “Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.” God’s system is the shape God’s will takes when it is done on earth: a family living by 321 is a small piece of the territory of God’s kingdom; a fellowship living by 321 is an outpost of the kingdom of heaven. And the final outcome has already been proclaimed in Revelation 11:15: “The kingdom of the world has become the Kingdom of our Lord, and of his Christ. He will reign forever and ever!”

sections.heading: 10. Putting It into Practice: How to Establish God’s System in Everyday Life
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three very concrete exercises. Brothers and sisters, please take out a pen and write them down.

Exercise 1: Every morning, first settle on one “321 choice”

The lesson says to begin each morning by asking yourself three questions:

Today, am I willing to let Jesus be King, rather than deciding by myself?

Today, am I willing to let Jesus receive the glory, rather than seeking to make myself conspicuous?

Today, will I take the Bible as my standard, Jesus as my role model and the Holy Spirit as my guide?

The lesson says: “A declaration and resolution like this is the beginning of establishing God’s system.” Note the timing — you settle it “first”: before you look at your phone, before you open your email, before your children’s crying sweeps you into the rush of the day.

The Lord Jesus himself did exactly this. Mark 1:35: “Early in the morning, while it was still dark, he rose up and went out, and departed into a deserted place, and prayed there.” Psalm 5:3 also says: “Yahweh, in the morning you will hear my voice. In the morning I will lay my requests before you, and will watch expectantly.”

The first choice of the day sets the direction for all the other choices of the day. That is what our 321 Morning Devotion is about.

Exercise 2: In every small decision, choose 321 principles

The lesson lists three situations: when emotions rise, let the Holy Spirit guide me rather than letting my own will explode; when facing conflict with co-workers, let Jesus be King rather than fighting to win; when facing pressure and temptation, let the principles of the Bible decide how I respond, rather than acting on my feelings.

When emotions rise, James 1:19–20 says: “let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger; for the anger of man doesn’t produce the righteousness of God.” Be quick to listen, slow to speak, and slower still to anger.

In conflict with co-workers, Philippians 2:3 says: “doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself.” Letting Jesus be King means this: the outcome of this matter is not for me to decide, nor for the other person to decide; it is for the Lord to decide.

Under pressure and temptation, the Lord Jesus gave us the model when he was tempted in the wilderness. Matthew 4:4: “It is written, ‘Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds out of God’s mouth.’” Three temptations, and three times the answer was “It is written.”

Exercise 3: Before each day ends, look back in your devotional time

The lesson says to ask three questions before each day ends:

At what moment did I not let Jesus be King?

Where did I seek my own glory?

In what matter did I depart from the Bible or ignore the prompting of the Holy Spirit?

And then the lesson adds this precious reminder: “Reflection is not condemnation, but repentance and renewal. To turn back is to build again.”

Psalm 139:23–24 is the best evening prayer: “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way.” Notice that this prayer does not end with “Condemn me,” but with “lead me in the everlasting way.” The purpose of self-examination is guidance, not accusation.

Deepening the exercises with the eight stages of changing our mindset

321’s eight stages of changing our mindset are: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Let’s place today’s exercises into these eight stages one by one.

1. Information: today you have already received it — Babylon is a system, and God’s system has to be established through every single choice.

2. Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to turn information into revelation. Ephesians 1:17: “that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give to you a spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him.” Stop and pray today: Lord, let me see which part of me is still living in Babylon.

3. Conviction: revelation that doesn’t lead to conviction is only being moved. Conviction says: I believe this is true, and I am willing to adjust my life accordingly.

4. Implementation: starting tomorrow morning, do Exercise 1 — the first thing after you get up is not your phone but those three questions.

5. Evaluation: every evening, do Exercise 3, and ask yourself at what moment today you made yourself king.

6. Correction: as soon as you find you’ve gone off course, turn back at once. Wrong? Then change — don’t put it off till next week.

7. Repetition: this is the most crucial step and the most unglamorous. The 2010 study by Lally’s team at University College London reminds us that it takes an average of sixty-six days for a behaviour to become automatic. Give yourself sixty-six days, not six.

8. Multiplication: when you begin to receive, go and find a “2” and pass on to them what you have received. 2 Timothy 2:2: “The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.” There are four generations in this verse: Paul, Timothy, faithful men, and others. That is multiplication; that is a system.

sections.heading: 11. Key Point 7: Habit Becomes a System, and the System Becomes Life
sections.html:
The lesson says: “The 321 life begins as training, then becomes habit, and finally becomes the natural overflow of life. As we choose again and again and practise again and again, 321 is no longer a framework but the very substance of our life.”

Brothers and sisters, look at these three stages: in the training stage it takes effort, and you have to remind yourself; in the habit stage it is natural, and you don’t need reminding; in the life stage it is joyful, and you wouldn’t want to do otherwise. A child learning the piano spends the first year counting beats and practising scales — that is training; by the third year the fingers move without thinking — that is habit; by the tenth year he sits down at the piano not to practise but because he loves it — that is life.

The lesson goes on: “God’s system is established bit by bit in our daily living. A life like this draws God’s presence and glory, and also draws people to Christ.” Matthew 5:16: “Even so, let your light shine before men; that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven.” What people see is the good works, but the one who receives the glory is the Father — and that is exactly the Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory.

Psalm 1:2–3 describes this kind of life: “but his delight is in Yahweh’s law. On his law he meditates day and night. He will be like a tree planted by the streams of water, that produces its fruit in its season, whose leaf also does not wither. Whatever he does shall prosper.”

A tree doesn’t strain to bear fruit; a tree only has to be planted by the streams of water. Brothers and sisters, where your roots go down determines what fruit you will bear.

sections.heading: 12. Closing and Call: Revival Begins with Each Day’s 321 Choice
sections.html:
The lesson’s closing words say: “The key to revival is not waiting for the right moment or a special conference, but beginning with each person’s 321 choices, every day.”

Brothers and sisters, we all long for revival, and we often think: when will it be our turn? Today the lesson gives an answer that pierces the heart: revival is not far away; revival is in the choice you made this morning.

The truly great revivals of history almost never began in a great auditorium. In August 1727 the Moravian Brethren at Herrnhut experienced an outpouring of the Holy Spirit, and soon afterwards began a round-the-clock prayer watch in shifts, day and night without ceasing, which lasted more than a hundred years. A hundred years of revival began with a group of people deciding to kneel down, every day, according to a rota.

Revival is not a firework; revival is a furnace. A firework needs lighting once; a furnace needs fuel added every day.

The lesson finally gives us a declaration, and I invite you, brothers and sisters, to say it with me from your heart:

“I will come out of Babylon; I will establish God’s system. I will let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive the glory, and let my life reflect the pattern of the kingdom of heaven!”

Brothers and sisters, will you begin to make this choice today? May we no longer use our own methods to build human kingdoms; may we return every day to the Three Foundations, hold fast to the Two Core Values and face towards that one Goal.

Because on that day, the Bible says (Revelation 21:3): “Behold, God’s dwelling is with people, and he will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God.” Babylon will fall; God’s system will endure forever. And today that everlasting building is being built, beginning with every tiny choice of yours and mine.

May all the glory be to him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb, forever and ever. Amen.

keyVerses: “I heard another voice from heaven, saying, ‘Come out of her, my people, that you have no participation in her sins, and that you don’t receive of her plagues.’” (Revelation 18:4)
“Leave Babylon! Flee from the Chaldeans! With a voice of singing announce this, tell it even to the end of the earth: say, ‘Yahweh has redeemed his servant Jacob!’” (Isaiah 48:20)
“in whom you also are built together for a habitation of God in the Spirit.” (Ephesians 2:22)
practices: In every small decision, choose 321 principles
Before each day ends, look back in your devotional time
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, we thank you. You did not leave us in Babylon; you called us out. Nor did you abandon us in the wilderness; you want to build your own system in us.

Lord, shine your light on us and let us see which corners within us are still running the Babylonian way — the thoughts that want to make our own name great, the choices in small things where we indulge ourselves again and again.

Lord Jesus, we are willing to let you be King, and willing to let you receive all the glory. Be our role model all our lives; may your word be our standard day by day, and may the Holy Spirit be our guide moment by moment.

Give us grace to choose you in every small decision. When we fall, hold us up with your hand and help us stand and walk on; make our training become habit, our habit become a system, and our system become life, so that people may see your glory in us.
Let your Kingdom come; let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Revelation 18:4: “I heard another voice from heaven, saying, ‘Come out of her, my people, that you have no participation in her sins, and that you don’t receive of her plagues.’” Be specific: in your life right now (at work, at home, at school or online), which area is the place where you are most easily assimilated into the “Babylonian system”? This week, what “321 choice” are you willing to settle on for that area?

Daniel 1:8: “But Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the king’s dainties, nor with the wine which he drank. Therefore he requested of the prince of the eunuchs that he might not defile himself.” Daniel couldn’t change his environment, but he could set a boundary in his heart. Share a time when you held your ground in your faith under pressure, or a time you wish you could do over. What did you learn from it about how God’s system is established through “falling, getting up and choosing again”?
l007.title: Establish God’s System
l007.subtitle: The Goal · Come Out of Babylon and Establish God’s System
l007.partTitle: Unit 1 · 3-2-1 — Towards the End Time Revival

sections.heading: Introduction: A Heart That Has Stopped, and the People Who Kneel
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. I’d like you to begin by picturing a scene.

A man suddenly collapses in the street. His heart has stopped. A ring of people gathers round. Some take out their phones and film. Some talk loudly about what’s happening. Some hurry to call an ambulance. But no one crouches down, lays one hand over the other, and presses down on that man’s chest.

The American Heart Association points out that when cardiac arrest happens outside a hospital, if a bystander begins CPR straight away, the person’s chance of survival can double or even triple. Double or triple, brothers and sisters. The difference doesn’t lie with the man who fell. The difference lies with the people standing beside him — whether or not they are willing to kneel down.

Today’s lesson is titled “Pressing On towards the End Time Revival”. Let me begin with something that may make us a little uncomfortable: this world is not about to fall ill — this world has already collapsed. The heart of humanity stopped on that day in Eden. And God has been searching ever since for people who are willing to kneel down.

We often picture “revival” as a conference, a gathering, a speaker, a song that moves us to tears. The meeting ends, the lights go out, the next day life carries on as before, and we say, “Ah, that was a wonderful weekend.” Brothers and sisters, that isn’t revival — that’s being moved. Being moved is precious, but it passes. Revival doesn’t pass, because revival is the dead coming back to life.

I want to ask you three questions. Please answer them honestly in your heart.

First: if God brought down the fire of revival on you today, what one thing in your life would have to change immediately?

Second: when was the last time you truly said, “Lord, you be in charge of this”?

Third: are you waiting for revival, or are you standing in its way?

In this lesson we’re going to walk five stretches of road together: the definition of revival, the core of revival, the hope of revival, the path of revival and the cost of revival. And at the end we’ll put it all into four practices you can begin tomorrow morning. Because revival has never been a topic. Revival is a decision.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: From the Blessing of Genesis to the Throne of Revelation
sections.html: To understand “revival”, we first have to know what exactly humanity lost. The Bible is a book that begins in a garden and ends in a city; the great stretch in between is the story of God, step by step, redeeming what humanity had lost.

sections.heading: 1. The Background to Genesis 1:28
sections.html:
Genesis came from the hand of Moses. In the general view of evangelical scholars, the Pentateuch was written sometime between the fifteenth and thirteenth centuries BC, and its first readers were the people of Israel in the wilderness, newly out of Egypt. This people had a serious identity problem: they had been slaves for four hundred years. Slaves don’t rule; slaves are only ruled. The very word “reign” had no place in a slave’s mindset.

So when God, through Moses, set the first chapter of Genesis before them, it was as if he were saying: remember, you were never meant to be slaves — you are kings entrusted with the stewardship of the whole earth.

Two Hebrew words matter a great deal here. The word for “subdue” in “subdue it” is כָּבַשׁ (kabash), which originally means “to bring under foot, to bring into order”. The word for “have dominion” in “have dominion over the fish of the sea” is רָדָה (radah), meaning “to reign, to rule, to govern”. The first identity God gave humanity was not labourer but steward; not slave but king.

But notice one thing: this kingship is an entrusted kingship. Genesis 1:26 says, “God said, ‘Let’s make man in our image, after our likeness. Let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the sky, and over the livestock, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creeps on the earth.’” Humanity reigns as the image of God. In other words, human beings are truly kings only when they reflect God and represent God. A mirror turned away from the light reflects nothing at all.

That is exactly where the human tragedy lies. In Genesis 3:5 Satan says, “for God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.” He didn’t urge them to break a moral rule; he urged them to change places — not to be the king God had appointed, but to be their own god. The moment humanity left its originally intended position, its kingship collapsed.

The result showed itself at once. Genesis 4:8 records: “Cain said to Abel, his brother, ‘Let’s go into the field.’ While they were in the field, Cain rose up against Abel, his brother, and killed him.” God had meant humanity to “be fruitful and multiply”, yet people began to kill one another; God had meant them to “subdue the earth”, yet they were subdued by their own lusts. By Genesis 6:5, Scripture sums it up: “Yahweh saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of man’s heart was continually only evil.”

This is just what the lesson says: humanity not only lost the blessing of multiplying and ruling, but fell into a vicious cycle of strife and destruction against one another.

sections.heading: 2. The Background to Revelation 3:21
sections.html:
The author of Revelation is the apostle John. According to the consistent witness of church history, it was written around AD 95, during the reign of the Roman emperor Domitian, a time when the church was being persecuted. John had been exiled to the island of Patmos because of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus. He wrote to seven churches in Asia Minor.

Our theme verse comes from the letter to the church in Laodicea. Laodicea was an extremely wealthy city, famous for its banking, its black wool textiles and its eye salve. Yet the Lord’s words to this church are very severe: “Because you say, ‘I am rich, and have gotten riches, and have need of nothing;’ and don’t know that you are the wretched one, miserable, poor, blind, and naked” (Revelation 3:17).

Brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: the church in Laodicea was not short of money; it was short of life. They had everything except the Lord. And that is a portrait of many churches and many Christians today — plenty of programmes, ministries filled to the brim, calendars packed solid, and hearts that are cold.

And yet the Lord did not cast them off. He says, “As many as I love, I reprove and chasten. Be zealous therefore, and repent” (Revelation 3:19). Then he speaks the words that have shaken the church in every age: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, then I will come in to him, and will dine with him, and he with me” (Revelation 3:20).

Only then comes 3:21: “He who overcomes, I will give to him to sit down with me on my throne, as I also overcame, and sat down with my Father on his throne.”

Do you see it? From “subdue it” in Genesis 1:28 to “sit down with me” in Revelation 3:21, God’s purpose has never changed. In the beginning he wanted humanity to reign, and at the end he still wants humanity to reign. Every story in between is called redemption — and the moment redemption actually takes hold in you and me is called revival.

sections.heading: 3. The Background to Habakkuk 3:2
sections.html:
The prophet Habakkuk served around the end of the seventh century BC, on the eve of the kingdom of Judah’s fall to Babylon. He saw the land full of violence, the law paralysed and justice plainly perverted, and he cried out to God. But God’s answer made him tremble all the more: God was going to raise up the Chaldeans (the Babylonians) to punish Judah.

In an age like that, when no way out could be seen, Habakkuk prayed: “Yahweh … renew your work in the middle of the years” — where the Chinese Union Version reads, “revive your work”. Notice that he didn’t say, “Revive my ministry.” He said, “Revive your work.” This is the most mature prayer for revival in the Bible — the main character in revival is not me; it is God.

The Hebrew word behind “revive” here is חָיָה (chayah) in its Piel stem (the intensive, factitive form), which literally means “to make alive”. The same word appears in Psalm 85:6: “Won’t you revive us again, that your people may rejoice in you?”

So the lesson is exactly right: the original meaning of revival is “to make alive again”. Revival is not warming up; it is coming back to life. It is not repair; it is resurrection.

sections.heading: Key Point 1: The Definition of Revival — Life Restored out of Death
sections.html:
Right at the start the lesson sets the tone for us: the original meaning of revival is “to make alive again”. It isn’t just that the church grows lively and attendance goes up. Its deeper meaning is this: humanity’s relationship with God is restored, life is renewed, and the world is turned upside down by the truth.

The scriptural basis

The apostle Paul says to the church in Ephesus, “You were made alive when you were dead in transgressions and sins” (Ephesians 2:1). And again: “But God, being rich in mercy, for his great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead through our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ—by grace you have been saved” (Ephesians 2:4–5).

The Greek for “made alive together” is συζωοποιέω (syzōopoieō), built from three parts — “together”, “life” and “to make” — and it means, literally, “to make alive together with Christ”. It is a word Paul coined himself, because the words that already existed weren’t enough. That is how far revival reaches beyond language.

Look, too, at a parable the Lord Jesus himself told. When the prodigal son came home, his father said, “for this, my son, was dead, and is alive again” (Luke 15:24). The Greek for “is alive again” is ἀναζάω (anazaō) — “to live once more”. The son’s body had been alive the whole time, yet his father said he had been dead. So in God’s eyes, leaving the Father’s house and living inside yourself is death.

The clearest picture of all is in Ezekiel. God brought the prophet to a valley full of dry bones and asked him, “Son of man, can these bones live?” (Ezekiel 37:3). The prophet didn’t dare give an answer; he only said, “Lord Yahweh, you know.” Then God said, “Behold, I will cause breath to enter into you, and you will live” (Ezekiel 37:5). And what happened? “So I prophesied as he commanded me, and the breath came into them, and they lived, and stood up on their feet, an exceedingly great army” (Ezekiel 37:10).

Brothers and sisters, notice the order: first they lived, then they stood up, and only last of all did they become an army. Life comes first, action follows, and ministry comes last. That is exactly what 321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry.

Scripture interpreting Scripture: revival is not warming up but coming back to life

Some people say, “But our church is full of energy! Full every week, growing every year.” Ezekiel shows us, though, that dry bones can be arranged very neatly. Neat is not the same as alive. In Revelation 3:1 the Lord says to the church in Sardis, “I know your works, that you have a reputation of being alive, but you are dead.” A reputation of being alive — what a sobering diagnosis.

So we have to tell three things apart: liveliness is not revival, growth is not revival, being moved is not revival. Revival has only one test: what was dead is now alive; what had turned its back on God now turns its face to him.

An illustration from life: from CPR to the renewal of cells

Go back to the scene in the introduction. The principle of CPR is actually very simple: hands on the outside take the place of the heart that has stopped, pushing the blood out so that oxygen keeps reaching the brain. The rescuer cannot create life. He only keeps the channel open and waits for that heart to start beating again on its own.

Brothers and sisters, that is our place in revival. We cannot manufacture revival; revival is the work of the Holy Spirit. But we can kneel down. We can put our hands there. We can pray. We can refuse to give up. And the God who raises the dead — he will make the heart beat again.

Here’s another scientific fact. A research team led by Jonas Frisén at the Karolinska Institute in Sweden published a study in the journal Cell in 2005. Using the carbon-14 left in the atmosphere by Cold War nuclear tests, they measured the “birth date” of cells in the human body, and confirmed that the cells of many of the body’s tissues are continually being renewed and replaced. In other words, many of the cells in your body today are not the same batch you had ten years ago.

If God built a mechanism of “constant renewal” even into our flesh, how much more into our souls? Paul says, “Therefore we don’t faint, but though our outward man is decaying, yet our inward man is renewed day by day” (2 Corinthians 4:16). Revival is not a one-off event; it is a state of life that is continually being renewed.

Applying the 321 Vision

In the language of 321, revival is moving from the old self and the self-centred life into the new self and selflessness. The self-centred life is death; selflessness is life. Paul says, “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me” (Galatians 2:20).

Please hear this clearly: selflessness does not mean wiping yourself out and becoming someone with no feelings and no thoughts. Selflessness is stepping out of that small, cramped “self” and entering into the boundlessness of Christ. For the self-centred person, the biggest world there is is himself; for the selfless person, his world is as big as Christ is.

So the first step of revival is not taken on the church platform. It is taken inside you. This morning, are you willing to let the Lord come alive in you once again?

sections.heading: Key Point 2: The Core of Revival — Restoring the Glory and the Calling We Lost
sections.html:
The lesson puts it very plainly: revival is not swapping one activity for another or holding a few more conferences. It is people being restored to their original glory and identity. Where we fell, there we must get back up. Eve’s failure lay in “wanting to be God herself”. If we want to enter revival today, the key is this — give sovereignty back to God, and let Jesus be King.

The scriptural basis

What did humanity lose? Paul says it all in one sentence: “for all have sinned, and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23).

The Greek for “fall short” is ὑστερέω (hystereō), meaning “to fail to reach, to lack, to lag behind”. God didn’t cancel humanity’s glory; humanity can no longer reach the glory of God. It’s like a prince wandering homeless in the streets: his royal blood hasn’t changed, but his life looks nothing like a prince’s.

How did humanity fall? Genesis 3:5 records the serpent’s words: “for God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.” The heart of the problem isn’t the fruit; it’s “like God”. That is pride: leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place.

So the road to restoration has to be the same road walked in reverse. James 4:6 says, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” However pride came in, humility has to walk back out that same way. That is what 321 means when it says: humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan.

Scripture interpreting Scripture: how the second Adam walked the way back

The first Adam said in the garden, “I want to be like God.” The second Adam said in the garden of Gethsemane, “nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire” (Matthew 26:39).

Paul lays out this road as clearly as it could be: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross” (Philippians 2:5–8).

The Greek for “emptied himself” is κενόω (kenoō), “to empty oneself out”. Notice that Jesus didn’t lose his divinity; he laid down his right to use it. He was God all along, yet he willingly returned to the servant’s place.

And then? “Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name” (Philippians 2:9).

Brothers and sisters, this is the most important law in the universe: the way down is the way up. Humanity tried to raise itself up and fell from glory; the Son of God willingly lowered himself and was exalted to the highest place.

An illustration from life: two goats that wouldn’t give way

There’s an old story about two goats meeting on a single-log bridge. The bridge was narrow — only wide enough for one goat to cross. They glared at each other, and neither would back down. In the end they locked horns, and both of them fell into the river.

There’s a line in 321 that cuts me to the heart every time I think of it: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. Those two goats are the perfect footnote to “both sides lose”. If just one of them had been willing to lie down and let the other step over, both would have lived.

That’s how quarrels between husband and wife go, that’s how church splits go, and that’s how wars between nations go. Human history is the history of two goats butting heads on a bridge. And revival is when someone is willing to lie down first.

Confirmation from psychology

The American psychologist Carol Dweck of Stanford University has spent many years researching “mindset”. She points out that people have two basic mindsets. One is a “fixed mindset”, which treats every challenge as a verdict on one’s own worth, and so cannot admit mistakes or accept criticism. The other is a “growth mindset”, which treats challenges as opportunities to learn, and so is willing to be corrected and willing to change.

Dweck’s research is not meant to replace the Bible, but from one angle it confirms a biblical insight: a person who must constantly prove himself and protect his image cannot learn, and cannot grow up.

That is precisely the predicament of the self-centred life. For the self-centred person, everything revolves around “me”: my face, my rights, my opinions, my achievements. So what God deals with has never been our ability. It’s our “self”.

Applying the 321 Vision: the Two Core Values

The Two Core Values of 321 are the core of revival: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory.

Letting Jesus be King settles the question of who has the final say; letting Jesus receive the glory settles the question of who we are doing it for. If these two things aren’t settled, then the more zealous we are, the more likely it is that we’re simply establishing our own system.

So the lesson says: revival is not about making people famous but about Jesus receiving the glory; revival is not about making the church bigger but about the kingdom of God coming; revival is not passing enthusiasm but the re-establishing of God’s system, for ever.

Brothers and sisters, let me ask a very practical question: if you did a good deed and no one ever knew it was you, would you still be willing to do it? If you would, revival has already begun in you.

sections.heading: Key Point 3: The Hope of Revival — Overcomers Will Reign with Christ
sections.html:
The lesson says that Revelation promises the overcoming people of God that they will sit with Christ on his throne and rule with him. This isn’t a blessing only for the future. It begins today, as in our daily living we keep practising letting Jesus reign, and slowly recover our spiritual authority and influence.

The scriptural basis

Let’s read the theme verse once more: “He who overcomes, I will give to him to sit down with me on my throne, as I also overcame, and sat down with my Father on his throne” (Revelation 3:21).

Notice the word “as”. The way we reign must be just “as” the way Jesus reigns. How did Jesus overcome? He didn’t overcome with the sword; he overcame on the cross. So our road to sitting with him on his throne must also pass through obedience and the denying of self.

Revelation 5:10 says, “and made us kings and priests to our God, and we will reign on the earth.” Notice: we reign “on the earth” — not starting only once we get to heaven.

And the final outcome is already written: “The seventh angel sounded, and great voices in heaven followed, saying, ‘The kingdom of the world has become the Kingdom of our Lord, and of his Christ. He will reign forever and ever!’” (Revelation 11:15).

Scripture interpreting Scripture: what “overcoming” means

The Greek for “overcome” in Revelation is νικάω (nikaō). Its content is spelled out most clearly in Revelation 12:11: “They overcame him because of the Lamb’s blood, and because of the word of their testimony. They didn’t love their life, even to death.”

Three things: the blood of the Lamb — not my goodness; the word of their testimony — not my eloquence; not loving their life — not my holding back.

So overcomers are not spiritual supermen. Overcomers are ordinary people who have handed over their sovereignty, given away the glory and laid down their lives.

What the lesson calls becoming “fishers for men”

The lesson reminds us: when we learn to be “fishers for men”, no longer promoting ourselves but proclaiming Jesus, we are already entering revival.

“He said to them, ‘Come after me, and I will make you fishers for men’” (Matthew 4:19).

Notice the Lord’s order: first “come after me”, and only then “fishers for men”. Life first, then relationships, then ministry. When someone who isn’t following the Lord goes out to win people, all he brings back are followers of himself, not disciples of Christ.

Confirmation from history: the revival of the early church

The lesson says that the revival of the early church swept across the entire Roman Empire. That’s no exaggeration. Acts 17:6 records that the people of Thessalonica dragged Jason off, crying out, “These who have turned the world upside down have come here also.” A group of people with no status, no resources and no army was regarded by a whole empire as a force turning the world upside down.

In The Rise of Christianity, published in 1996, the American sociologist Rodney Stark used a model of population growth to calculate that if the number of Christians grew at about forty per cent per decade, that alone would be enough to take them from a tiny minority in the first century to a quite considerable share of the Roman Empire’s population by the early fourth century. He particularly points out that this growth didn’t come from large gatherings. It came household by household, relationship by relationship, through act after act of self-denial as believers cared for the sick during plagues.

Brothers and sisters, did you hear that? Revival spreads through relationships, not through venues. That is exactly what 321 calls the 235 relationships — becoming a “2”, a spiritual companion, with someone who is selfless; establishing the “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children; and becoming the “5”, a team of spiritual comrades in a fivefold-ministry team.

Applying the 321 Vision: begin reigning today

Many people push “reigning with Christ” far off into the future. But the lesson reminds us: this is a practice that begins today.

How do we practise it? The moment you’re about to lose your temper, let Jesus reign — and in that matter, you are reigning. The moment you’ve been misunderstood and long to explain yourself, let Jesus reign — and in that matter, you are reigning. The moment you’ve achieved something and long to be noticed, let Jesus receive the glory — and in that matter, you are reigning.

Reigning isn’t controlling other people; reigning is governing yourself. It isn’t subduing your circumstances; it’s refusing to be subdued by yourself in the middle of them.

The 920 practice of 321 puts it well: everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”. When, before each “2”, we practise living out a selfless (0) life, we will bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions — “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law” (Galatians 5:22–23).

Brothers and sisters, the end time revival will shake the nations, and every nation and people will confess that Jesus is Lord: “that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, those on earth, and those under the earth, and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father” (Philippians 2:10–11). This is a revival unlike any before or after it, the summit of all the ages, the glorious plan God ordained in his heart long ago. And its starting point is the choice you make at home this morning.

sections.heading: Key Point 4: The Path of Revival — From the Inside Out, to the Ends of the Earth
sections.html:
The lesson says that revival is first of all an inner transformation — the human heart wakes up, repents and is renewed, begins to make Jesus its centre, and no longer lives for itself. Then revival goes on to affect families, churches, workplaces, society and culture, and can even change the direction of a nation.

The scriptural basis: the road map the Lord himself drew

Before the Lord Jesus ascended, he left us one sentence, the clearest road map of revival there is: “But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you. You will be witnesses to me in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the uttermost parts of the earth” (Acts 1:8).

Jerusalem, all Judea, Samaria, the uttermost parts of the earth — these are concentric circles spreading outward ring by ring. But notice the clause at the very front: “when the Holy Spirit has come upon you”. First the inside, then the outside; first power, then witness.

Turn that order upside down and you get a very weary kind of Christian: charging outwards with all his might while being empty inside. God has never changed the circumstances first. God changes the person first.

Scripture interpreting Scripture: the heart is the source of everything

Proverbs 4:23 says, “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.”

Paul says, “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God” (Romans 12:2).

The Greek for “transformed” in “be transformed by the renewing of your mind” is μεταμορφόω (metamorphoō) — “to change form”, the very change by which a caterpillar becomes a butterfly. It isn’t painting the caterpillar a new colour; it’s remaking it entirely from the inside. It is also the same word used when the Lord Jesus was transfigured on the mountain (Matthew 17:2).

So the path of revival is this: the mindset changes first, and then the life changes; once the life changes, daily living changes; once daily living changes, relationships change; and once relationships change, ministry bears fruit. This is the fivefold change of 321: mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry.

Many people want to start from step five and go straight to doing great ministry. The result is ministry built on a life that hasn’t been renewed — like putting up a tower block on sand.

An analogy from science: how deep a tree’s roots go

When we look at a great tree, we always look at its branches and leaves. But botany tells us that the root systems of many trees spread far beyond the crown we can see with our eyes, and that most of the fine roots that take in water lie in relatively shallow soil just below the surface, stretching out very widely in every direction. How tall a tree can grow, and whether it can stand in the wind, depends not on what’s above but on what’s below.

Brothers and sisters, we often envy other people’s branches and leaves, yet we won’t put in the work of putting down roots. Revival isn’t gluing on more leaves. Revival is letting the roots grow deeper.

Confirmation from history: how revival shakes society

The lesson says that true revival has never been quiet; it shakes history and turns an era upside down. Church history confirms this again and again.

The great Welsh Revival of 1904–1905 was led by a young preacher, Evan Roberts. According to records from the time and the accounts of later historians, those who came to the Lord during that revival numbered in the tens of thousands. Even more striking were the changes in society — the pubs lost their trade, court cases dropped, and there are even accounts that the miners stopped swearing in the pits, so that for a while the pit ponies hauling the coal couldn’t understand their new commands.

That is “from the inside out”. Nobody launched a social reform movement. People’s hearts changed, and society changed.

The great Pyongyang Revival in Korea in 1907 was the same. It began with public confession of sin and reconciliation with one another, and went on to shape profoundly the prayer tradition of the whole Korean church. The fire of revival always burns first in the human conscience, and only then spreads into the culture.

Applying the 321 Vision: first God, then ourselves, then others, and last of all things

321 teaches the priority of relationships: first our relationship with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things. That is simply another way of saying “from the inside out, to the ends of the earth”.

For many people the order is exactly reversed: first they get busy with things; when the things never get finished, they blame people; when they can’t get on with people, they write themselves off; and in the end they don’t even want to see God. Get the order wrong, and people fall apart.

321 also teaches a shift in perspective: from the human perspective to God’s perspective, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. Paul says, “If then you were raised together with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated on the right hand of God. Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth” (Colossians 3:1–2).

Brothers and sisters, when you woke up this morning, was your first thought an earthly one or a heavenly one? A temporary one or an eternal one? Revival begins in that smallest of places.

The lesson says: a revival like this is not a brief excitement but lasting change; not a chance event but the full coming of the kingdom of God. Lasting — that is the true mark of revival.

sections.heading: Key Point 5: The Cost of Revival — Not a Slogan, but a Life
sections.html:
The lesson says it with absolute certainty: revival has never been free. The fire of revival is lit with “life” as its firewood.

The scriptural basis

The Lord Jesus said, “Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24).

Keep a grain of wheat and it’s safe — but it will always be just one grain. The arithmetic of revival is exactly the reverse of the world’s: hold on and you lose; let go and you gain.

Paul says, “Therefore I urge you, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service” (Romans 12:1).

The phrase “living sacrifice” carries a tension within it: a sacrifice is supposed to be dead, but a living sacrifice has to go on being offered while it lives. As someone has well said, the biggest problem with a living sacrifice is that it keeps crawling off the altar. So offering ourselves isn’t a one-time thing; it’s every day.

Three testimonies the lesson gives

First, Stephen. Acts 7:59–60 records: “They stoned Stephen as he called out, saying, ‘Lord Jesus, receive my spirit!’ He kneeled down, and cried with a loud voice, ‘Lord, don’t hold this sin against them!’ When he had said this, he fell asleep.”

He died, and the church came alive. Acts 8:1 says, “A great persecution arose against the assembly which was in Jerusalem in that day. They were all scattered abroad throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except for the apostles.” Then 8:4 says, “Therefore those who were scattered abroad went around preaching the word.” One grain of wheat fell into the ground, and the gospel walked out of Jerusalem. That is just what the lesson says: Stephen’s death opened the way to the explosive growth of the early church.

Second, Paul. The lesson quotes Paul’s words from Acts 20:24: “But these things don’t count; nor do I hold my life dear to myself, so that I may finish my race with joy, and the ministry which I received from the Lord Jesus, to fully testify to the Good News of the grace of God.” To finish that race, Paul did not even hold his own life dear.

Third, the apostles as a whole. According to the consistent tradition of church history, apart from John, most of the Lord’s disciples were martyred for him. They left behind no magnificent buildings, yet with their blood they opened the history of revival.

An analogy from science: the cone that needs fire to open

In the Rocky Mountains of North America there is a tree called the lodgepole pine. Its cones are sealed with a coating of resin and normally stay tightly shut, so the seeds can’t get out. Only when a forest fire sweeps through and the heat melts the resin do the cones split open; then the seeds fall onto ground the fire has cleared and filled with nutrients, and a new forest grows.

Ecologists call this trait serotiny. Brothers and sisters, what a fitting picture: some seeds cannot be released except through fire.

So when God allows the fire to reach you, don’t think only of escape. Perhaps that is the very moment he means to open you up and release the seed inside you. The lesson is right: be willing to enter the process of being broken and refined, so that your life can carry a greater glory.

Confirmation from a famous saying and from psychology

The nineteenth-century evangelist D. L. Moody heard a sentence as a young man — generally believed to have been spoken to him by the English preacher Henry Varley: “The world has yet to see what God can do with a man fully consecrated to him.” Moody later said that he decided then and there: I will be that man. And God truly used this shoe-shop salesman, who had no formal theological training, to shake both Britain and America.

From the standpoint of psychology this is no accident either. The American psychologist Angela Duckworth of the University of Pennsylvania, in a study published in 2007 in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, put forward the concept of “grit”, showing that for long-term achievement, sustained passion and perseverance often predict success or failure better than talent does.

Let me stress again: psychology is only a helper; it can never override the Bible. But at the very least it reminds us of one thing — the fruit of God’s kingdom has never gone to the cleverest people. It goes to the people who never give up.

Applying the 321 Vision: a trust that stakes your life

The lesson uses a very powerful phrase: if we want to experience the end time revival, we can’t just “play at faith”; we have to “stake our lives on our trust”.

What is playing at faith? It’s treating faith as an ornament on our daily living: come when you’re free, pray when you need something, take time off when it’s inconvenient. What is staking your life on your trust? It’s handing over your sovereignty entirely, without even keeping a way back.

321 says: selflessness overcomes Satan. What Satan fears most is not the gifted Christian; it’s the Christian who has no “self” left. Because with someone who has no “self”, he has nothing to get hold of — you can’t take anything from a person who has already given up everything.

The lesson ends by saying: if anyone is willing to offer himself as a living sacrifice, the fire of revival will fall. Brothers and sisters, are we willing to lay down everything for the kingdom of God, holding nothing back?

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: Revival Is Returning to Our Originally Intended Position
sections.html:
Having come this far, let’s set this lesson within the framework of 321 and look at it once more. You’ll find the whole picture is very clear.

The Three Foundations

Jesus is my role model: the pattern of revival is the road of Philippians 2 — “emptying himself, humbling himself, obeying, being exalted”. As he overcame, so we overcome.

The Bible is my standard: revival isn’t judged by feelings. Being moved can deceive us, numbers can deceive us, atmosphere can deceive us — the Bible will not. What Habakkuk asked for was the revival of “your work”, not the revival of my imagination.

The Holy Spirit is my guide: revival is the work of the Holy Spirit. Acts 1:8 makes it very clear — first the Holy Spirit comes, then there is power, then there is witness. Our responsibility is not to make the fire but to prepare the firewood.

The Two Core Values

Let Jesus be King: this settles the question of who is in charge. Eve’s failure was wanting to be God herself; our revival is giving sovereignty back to God. Let man be man and let God be God — that is humility; that is returning to our originally intended position.

Let Jesus receive all the glory: this settles the question of who we are doing it for. Revival is not about making people famous; it’s about Jesus receiving the glory. Any service that makes people look up at you will sooner or later go wrong.

The Goal

Establish God’s system. The lesson says: revival is not passing enthusiasm but the re-establishing of God’s system, for ever. That is precisely the Goal of 321.

Where does the difference between the two systems lie? The Worldly system has humanity, “self” and self-interest at its centre, and is driven by pride and comparison; God’s system has Jesus at its centre, and is driven by humility and the denying of self. Revival is the change from one system to the other.

The fivefold change and the shift in perspective

Change the mindset, and the life changes; change the life, and daily living changes; change daily living, and relationships change; change relationships, and only then does ministry bear real fruit. The mindset this lesson sets out to change is very clear: revival is not an event; revival is life. Revival doesn’t start with someone else; revival starts with me.

At the same time we must shift four perspectives: from the human perspective to God’s perspective, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. When what you see is eternity, the loss in front of you grows smaller; when what you see is the glory of God, your own face matters far less.

The 920 practice and the 235 relationships

The 920 practice: from today, treat everyone you have a relationship with as the “2” God has given you. Before each of them, practise selflessness (0), and ask the Holy Spirit to produce the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions. Your family, your colleagues, your neighbours — they are your harvest field for revival.

The 235 relationships: don’t go it alone. Find a selfless companion to be your “2”; establish spiritual parents and spiritual children as your “3”; and finally serve alongside spiritual comrades in a fivefold-ministry team as your “5”. The revival of the early church didn’t depend on one hero; it depended on a web of relationships.

The Path of Serving is walked the same way: Spirit (the Holy Spirit is my guide), Understanding (the Bible is my standard), Life (Jesus is my role model), Service (let Jesus be King), God (let Jesus receive all the glory). May every one of us walk this road to the end.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: How to Press On towards the End Time Revival
sections.html:
The lesson gives us four ways to put this into practice. We’ll keep the lesson’s practices as they are, and deepen each one in turn using 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition and Multiplication.

Practice 1: Resolve each day to let Jesus be King (sovereignty belongs to him)

What the lesson says: the first thing when you get up, pray and hand over your sovereignty for the day — not relying on your own will, not following your own plans. When you face difficulties, choose to obey God’s word rather than handling things in the flesh.

Information: first know one fact — sovereignty was never mine to begin with. “For of him, and through him, and to him are all things” (Romans 11:36).

Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to let you truly see, in one specific matter, that “I have been keeping this in my own hands all along”. Without seeing it, there is no real handing over.

Conviction: admit from your heart that God being in charge is better than me being in charge. Not forced into it — persuaded.

Implementation: tomorrow morning, when you open your eyes, before you scroll through your phone, say first, “Lord, this day is yours. My time, my emotions, my decisions — I hand them all to you.”

Evaluation: before bed, spend three minutes asking yourself: at what moment today did I snatch my sovereignty back?

Correction: confess that moment, and then think concretely: the next time the same situation comes up, how am I going to respond?

Repetition: a team led by Phillippa Lally at University College London published a study in 2010 in the European Journal of Social Psychology showing that it takes on average about sixty-six days for a new habit to become automatic — with very wide individual differences. So don’t give up after three days just because you don’t feel anything. Repetition is the unavoidable road of spiritual discipline.

Multiplication: find someone, invite them to make this morning surrender with you, and check in with each other once a week.

Practice 2: Let Jesus receive the glory each day (he is the aim)

What the lesson says: each time you finish something, thank the Lord and say, “All the glory to you”; don’t promote yourself or compete for people’s applause; learn to step back out of sight, so that Jesus is seen.

Information: “Whether therefore you eat, or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God” (1 Corinthians 10:31). Glorifying God isn’t something for a few spiritual moments; it’s for small things like eating and drinking.

Revelation: ask the Lord to show you the situation where you’re most likely to “steal glory”. Is it when you’re speaking? When you’re posting online? Or when someone else is being praised?

Conviction: believe this — when the glory goes to God, you lose nothing. John the Baptist said, “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30). He didn’t become smaller for it; on the contrary, the Lord said, “among those who are born of women there has not arisen anyone greater than John the Baptizer” (Matthew 11:11).

Implementation: each time you finish something, great or small, say out loud, “All the glory to you!”

Evaluation: this week, was there a time when I did something in order to be seen?

Correction: next time, deliberately do a good deed that no one will know about.

Repetition: the American psychologists Robert Emmons and Michael McCullough published a study in 2003 in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology which found that participants who regularly recorded things they were grateful for scored markedly higher on well-being and life satisfaction than the control group. Thanksgiving needs repetition, and so does giving glory.

Multiplication: in your small group, take the lead in making “Thank you, Lord” something everyone says without thinking.

Practice 3: Practise the 321 actions at a set time each week

What the lesson says: examine yourself on whether you are living out the Three Foundations (Jesus my role model, the Bible my standard, the Holy Spirit my guide); review whether you are practising the Two Core Values (let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive the glory); and if you have drifted, repent at once, stand up, and choose the right direction again.

Information: the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal — this is the standard we share.

Revelation: each week, find a quiet time and let the Holy Spirit shine his light. “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way” (Psalm 139:23–24).

Conviction: self-examination is not self-accusation; we examine ourselves so that we can go further.

Implementation: take a sheet of paper and write down six questions — This week, did I take Jesus as my role model? Did I take the Bible as my standard? Did I follow the guidance of the Holy Spirit? Did I let Jesus be King? Did I let Jesus receive the glory? Am I establishing God’s system, or my own?

Evaluation: which one is weakest? Why?

Correction: pick only the weakest one and set one small step you can manage next week. Don’t try to change five things at once; change one thing at a time.

Repetition: the same time, the same place, the same slot every week.

Multiplication: do it with one other person, and that’s the “2” of 321; bring someone along to do it, and that’s the “3”.

Practice 4: Offer yourself to become a vessel of revival

What the lesson says: pray every day, “Lord, I want to be a vessel of revival — please begin with me”; answer God’s call with courage, not running away, willing to be torn down and built up; be willing to enter the process of being broken and refined, so that your life can carry a greater glory.

Information: the worth of a vessel lies not in itself but in who it holds. “But we have this treasure in clay vessels, that the exceeding greatness of the power may be of God, and not from ourselves” (2 Corinthians 4:7).

Revelation: ask God to show you which part of you has not yet been handed over.

Conviction: being torn down is not being thrown away. In the potter’s hands, being remade is grace: “When the vessel that he made of the clay was marred in the hand of the potter, he made it again another vessel, as seemed good to the potter to make it” (Jeremiah 18:4).

Implementation: pray aloud every day, “Lord, I want to be a vessel of revival — please begin with me.”

Evaluation: this month, has God touched a sore spot in me over some matter? Was my response resistance, or surrender?

Correction: take that point of resistance and hand it over, concretely.

Repetition: keep on until this prayer is no longer a slogan but your real longing.

Multiplication: when God really does begin with you, the people around you will see it. Then you won’t need to say much; your life will be the most powerful message.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: It Begins with Me
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, the lesson’s conclusion puts it beautifully: revival is not an unreachable dream, nor a movement waiting for someone else to start it. Revival begins with the 321 choices you and I make every day.

Let’s go back to the scene from the introduction. A man has collapsed in the street, and a ring of people stands watching. The one God is looking for is the person willing to crouch down.

Through all the ages, God’s revivals have never started with the majority. One Habakkuk, as his nation was about to fall, praying, “Renew your work in the middle of the years.” One Stephen, kneeling down to ask forgiveness for the people stoning him. One Moody, hearing a single sentence and saying, “I will be that man.”

God is still asking the same question today: whom can I begin with?

We don’t wait until we have power before God uses us; it’s when God uses us that we discover the power. We don’t wait until the church is revived before we change; the moment we change, the church begins to be revived.

So let Jesus be King. Let him reign over your schedule, reign in your wallet, reign in your marriage, reign over your temper, reign over your ambitions.

So let Jesus receive all the glory. Take one step back, and he shows a little more; become a little smaller, and he becomes a little greater.

“Arise, shine; for your light has come, and Yahweh’s glory has risen on you” (Isaiah 60:1).

“For the earth will be filled with the knowledge of Yahweh’s glory, as the waters cover the sea” (Habakkuk 2:14).

Brothers and sisters, are you willing to be one of those in this end time revival? Not a spectator, but firewood. Not waiting for revival, but becoming revival.

keyVerses: “God blessed them. God said to them, ‘Be fruitful, multiply, fill the earth, and subdue it. Have dominion over the fish of the sea, over the birds of the sky, and over every living thing that moves on the earth’” (Genesis 1:28).
“He who overcomes, I will give to him to sit down with me on my throne, as I also overcame, and sat down with my Father on his throne” (Revelation 3:21).

“Yahweh, I have heard of your fame. I stand in awe of your deeds, Yahweh. Renew your work in the middle of the years. In the middle of the years make it known. In wrath, you remember mercy” (Habakkuk 3:2).
practices: Resolve each day to let Jesus be King (sovereignty belongs to him)
Let Jesus receive the glory each day (he is the aim)
Practise the 321 actions at a set time each week
Offer yourself to become a vessel of revival
prayer: Lord Jesus, we worship you. You are the God who gives life to the dead and calls into being what did not exist.

Lord, we confess that we often treat revival as an event, yet refuse to pay the price with our lives; we envy other people’s branches and leaves, yet won’t let you put down roots in us. Please forgive us.
Lord, today we hand our sovereignty back to you. Our time, our families, our work, our emotions, our plans — we place them all in your hands. From today, reign as King within us.
Lord, we hand the glory back to you as well. Take away our longing to be seen, and make us willing to step back out of sight, so that people see only Jesus.

Lord, I want to be a vessel of revival — please begin with me. I am willing to be torn down, willing to be refined, willing to be like that grain of wheat that falls into the ground. Kindle the fire of revival, and let me live out a life that is different.
Your Kingdom come, your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Question 1: “He who overcomes, I will give to him to sit down with me on my throne, as I also overcame, and sat down with my Father on his throne” (Revelation 3:21). The Lord says the way we overcome must be just “as” he overcame. Share: this week, what is one specific situation you need to face by letting Jesus be King, rather than in the flesh?

Question 2: “Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24). The fire of revival is lit with life as its firewood. Share honestly: what is one thing you’re still gripping tightly in your hand, not yet willing to let fall into the ground? How can we pray for one another?
l008.title: Towards the End Time Revival
l008.subtitle: Entering God’s Original Intention and Glory
l008.partTitle: Unit 1 · 3-2-1 — Towards the End Time Revival

sections.heading: Introduction: One Well, Three Rings
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. May the peace of the Lord come upon you this early morning.

Let me begin with a question: if God were to start working in you today, where would you want him to begin?

Most of us would answer — with my circumstances. Lord, change my job, change my family, change our church. But the order the Bible shows us is exactly the reverse. God never begins by changing circumstances; he begins by changing people. And he doesn’t begin by changing a crowd; he begins by changing one person.

Let me tell you a true story.

In 1727, in a little place in eastern Germany called Herrnhut, there lived a band of believers who had come there as refugees. They came from different countries, different denominations, different languages, and persecution for their faith had gathered them onto the estate of Count Nikolaus Ludwig von Zinzendorf (1700–1760). Put enough people together and trouble comes. They criticised one another, condemned one another, argued endlessly over whose theology was orthodox, and the whole village was on the verge of splitting apart.

On 12 May that year, Zinzendorf went from house to house and led the whole village to sign a “Brotherly Agreement”, a covenant with one another: to lay down their rivalry, to love one another, and to serve with one heart. On 13 August they took Communion together. And on that very day, the Holy Spirit was poured out. No one could describe what happened in that moment. All they knew was that the walls between them were gone and their hearts had melted.

What followed changed the whole history of modern missions. That village of fewer than three hundred people began a round-the-clock relay of prayer, one shift handing on to the next, that continued for more than a hundred years. Out of that furnace of prayer went missionaries, wave after wave of them, to the West Indies, Greenland, Africa and South America. Years later an English clergyman named John Wesley (1703–1791) was caught in a storm at sea. He watched the Moravian believers on board singing hymns calmly while the waves crashed around them, and his heart was shaken. Not long afterwards, in Aldersgate Street in London, he felt his heart “strangely warmed”, and from there he set the whole Methodist movement in England ablaze.

Brothers and sisters, do you see it?

One man’s humbling brought a community into unity; one community’s unity brought a prayer meeting that lasted a hundred years; and one prayer meeting changed the destiny of several continents.

That is what today’s lesson is about: the three tiers of revival. Personal revival, revival of the church, revival of the Kingdom.

These three are not three parallel lines, nor three options from which you may pick one. They are three stretches of a single road, three rings rippling outward from one well of living water. Personal revival is for the sake of the church’s revival; the church’s revival is for the sake of the Kingdom’s revival; and the revival of the Kingdom is the very heart of Jesus Christ.

Let me put today’s conclusion up front: revival waits for no one, and it does not run on feelings. What it waits for is a people who are willing, day by day, to choose obedience, unity and wholehearted giving. And all of it begins with the choice you and I make right now.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: The Moment the Trumpet Sounds
sections.html: Before we open the three key points, let’s first stand where our theme verse originally stood. A verse gives off its own true light only when we return it to its context.

sections.heading: 1. Author, Date and Readers
sections.html:
The author of Revelation is the apostle John. Three times in the book he calls himself John (Revelation 1:1, 1:4, 22:8); he is the disciple whom the Lord Jesus loved. According to the consistent witness of church history, the book was written around AD 95, towards the end of the reign of the Roman emperor Domitian (who ruled AD 81–96). At the time John had been banished to the island of Patmos for preaching.

He puts it like this himself: “I John, your brother and partner with you in the oppression, Kingdom, and perseverance in Christ Jesus, was on the isle that is called Patmos because of God’s Word and the testimony of Jesus Christ.” (Revelation 1:9)

Notice the three words in that sentence: oppression, Kingdom, perseverance. Put those three together and you have the skeleton of Revelation. Believers are in tribulation now, they will enter the Kingdom in the future, and what they need in the meantime is perseverance.

The letter was addressed to seven churches in Asia Minor. These were not prosperous, triumphant churches. The church in Ephesus had left its first love; the church in Smyrna was in tribulation and poverty; the church in Pergamum lived where Satan’s throne is; the church in Thyatira had been infiltrated by false teaching; the church in Sardis had a name for being alive but was dead; the church in Laodicea was lukewarm. Only the church in Philadelphia received no rebuke from the Lord.

In other words, Revelation is not a victory song written for winners; it is a shot of courage for the weary.

sections.heading: 2. The Seventh Trumpet: From Contest to Belonging
sections.html:
Revelation 11:15 stands in the middle of the three series of visions — the seven seals, the seven trumpets and the seven bowls. The seventh angel’s trumpet is the last of the seven trumpets and the turning point of the whole book. As soon as it sounds, loud voices in heaven proclaim that the kingdom of the world has become the Kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ.

One word here is worth stopping for. “The kingdom of the world” is, in the original Greek, the singular form of βασιλεία (basileia), meaning “kingship, royal rule”. It is not talking about territory on a map; it is talking about to whom sovereignty belongs. So what this verse really proclaims is this: the rule over this world has now changed hands.

Notice the tense of the verb. “Has become” is an aorist in the original, carrying the tone of something already settled. John is not saying “one day it will become”; he is saying that in God’s eternal plan this is already decided. Heaven proclaims it first; then it comes to pass on earth.

Brothers and sisters, this is the foundation for all our talk of revival. Revival is not us straining to snatch the world back. Revival is our response to the proclamation heaven has already made — letting that kingship, already accomplished, be acknowledged and displayed step by step in my life, in our church and in this land.

sections.heading: 3. What the Word “Revival” Originally Means
sections.html:
When the Bible speaks of revival, the Hebrew verb it often uses is חָיָה (chayah), whose basic meaning is “to live”. Its causative form means “to make alive again”. So the psalmist prays:

“Won’t you revive us again, that your people may rejoice in you?” (Psalm 85:6)

“Revive” is chayah. The essence of revival is not dressing up something dead so it looks a little nicer; it is putting breath back into what was dead.

The prophet Habakkuk asked the same thing: “Yahweh, I have heard of your fame. I stand in awe of your deeds, Yahweh. Renew your work in the middle of the years. In the middle of the years make it known. In wrath, you remember mercy.” (Habakkuk 3:2)

In the New Testament, Peter, preaching in Solomon’s Porch, used another word. He said: “whom heaven must receive until the times of restoration of all things, which God spoke long ago by the mouth of his holy prophets.” (Acts 3:21) The Greek for “restoration of all things” is ἀποκατάστασις (apokatastasis), meaning “restoration to the state something was always meant to be in”.

Put those two words together and revival becomes clear: revival is making the dead live again, setting the crooked straight, bringing everything back to God’s original intention in creation.

So revival is not an emotional high, nor the stirring of a single special conference. Revival is God’s life moving again; it is God’s order being established again.

And the order in which God does this is: first one person, then a group of people, and then the whole earth.

Brothers and sisters, let’s now look at it step by step.

sections.heading: 1. Personal Revival: Change That Begins with a Choice
sections.html:
1. Revival Starts with a Heart Set Alight Again

The lesson puts it plainly: personal revival is the starting point and the foundation of the end time revival.

The first thing God wants to do is not to hand us a plan or give us a set of methods, but to set alight again our love and zeal for Jesus, to awaken the heart that once burned for the Lord.

What the Lord Jesus said to the church in Ephesus is worth each of us hearing quietly once more this morning:

“But I have this against you, that you left your first love. Remember therefore from where you have fallen, and repent and do the first works.” (Revelation 2:4-5)

Notice the Lord’s diagnosis. He did not say the church in Ephesus wasn’t doing enough. In fact the Lord praised them first: “I know your works, and your toil and perseverance” (Revelation 2:2). They had works, they had toil, they had perseverance, and they had the discernment to expose false teaching. And yet the Lord said: there is one thing.

One thing. Not ten — one.

You left your first love.

Brothers and sisters, what a sobering warning this is. A person can serve without a break while their love grows cold; a person can never miss a meeting while their heart is elsewhere; a person can expound a great deal of teaching and yet not have shed a single tear for the Lord in a very long time.

The Lord’s prescription has three parts: remember, repent, do the first works. Remembering is the reawakening of memory; repenting is the turning around of direction; doing the first works is the restarting of action.

All three parts of the prescription point to the same thing — coming back to Jesus.

The disciples of the early church were ordinary people. Peter was a fisherman, Matthew a tax collector, Simon a Zealot. They had no learning and no standing. When the council “saw the boldness of Peter and John, and had perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marveled. They recognized that they had been with Jesus” (Acts 4:13).

Look at that line: they recognised that they had been with Jesus.

Their lives were turned completely upside down — no longer living for themselves, but willing to give themselves to the Lord without holding anything back — and there is only one explanation: they had met Jesus.

2. The Key to Personal Revival Is Choice

The lesson says: the key to personal revival lies in choice.

That sentence deserves a whole morning of reflection.

We often think of revival as something that “happens” — one day the Holy Spirit suddenly pours out, and suddenly I’m on fire. We would never deny the sovereignty of the Holy Spirit; the wind blows where it wills. But the Bible tells us just as clearly that God never forces anyone. He puts the choice in our hands.

At the end of his life Joshua gathered all Israel at Shechem and said to them:

“If it seems evil to you to serve Yahweh, choose today whom you will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were beyond the River, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land you dwell; but as for me and my house, we will serve Yahweh.” (Joshua 24:15)

“Choose today.”

Revival isn’t tomorrow’s business; it’s today’s. It isn’t “let’s wait until things get better”; it’s making the decision now.

And what is the content of that choice? The lesson says: leaving the self-centred system and returning to God’s system.
