This is the very heart of the 321 vision. The problem of the old self can be summed up in one word — “self”. “Self” is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of every problem. Satan’s “I will” long ago was nothing other than putting himself in God’s place. From that moment on there have been two systems in the universe: one centred on self and one centred on God.

So personal revival, in the end, is a transfer of sovereignty. The lesson puts it beautifully: this is not merely a change of outward behaviour; it is a transfer of sovereignty that begins in the heart — no longer being king myself, but letting Jesus reign in my life.

Paul sums it up in one sentence:

“I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20)

“No longer I, but Christ.” That is selflessness.

Brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: selflessness is not having nothing. It is not wiping yourself out, not becoming a person with no thoughts and no feelings. Selflessness is “zero” — setting yourself back to zero so that God’s infinity can flow out through you. A zero on its own is nothing; but put it after a one and it becomes ten; add another zero and it becomes a hundred.

Selflessness is not becoming smaller; selflessness is entering into the infinite.

3. A Confirmation from Psychology: Habits and “If–Then Plans”

Psychology offers a fascinating piece of supporting evidence here.

In a study published in 2002 in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, the University of Southern California psychologist Wendy Wood and her colleagues found that around 43 per cent of what people do each day is habitual behaviour, repeated in the same settings.

In other words, we think we are “deciding” all day long, but nearly half the time we are simply “replaying”.

That is why so many people pray year after year, “Lord, revive me,” and never change. We are asking for a feeling, but the track of a life is laid by choices; without new choices, there is only the old replay.

So how do we break the replay?

In a paper published in 1999 in American Psychologist, the New York University psychologist Peter Gollwitzer put forward a concept called “implementation intentions” — that is, “if … then …” plans. He found that a vague goal (“I’m going to exercise more”) often comes to nothing; but write it as a specific trigger (“If my alarm goes off at seven in the morning, then I put on my shoes and go out”), and the rate of success rises markedly.

Brothers and sisters, spiritual training works the same way.

Don’t just say, “I want to love the Lord more.” Say: “If I wake up in the morning, then my first words will be: Lord, today it is not about what I want; may your will be done.”

Don’t just say, “I want to obey the Holy Spirit.” Say: “If I feel a prick of conviction in my heart, then I will stop at once and go no further.”

Only specific choices become a new track.

Of course, psychology is only a helper. What truly changes people is not technique; it is the Holy Spirit. Zechariah said it long ago: “‘Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit,’ says Yahweh of Armies.” (Zechariah 4:6) Methods help us set our hearts in the right place; the Holy Spirit is the one who lights the fire.

4. Applying the 321 Vision: Fivefold Change Begins with Mindset

The 321 vision says that human change is fivefold: mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry.

Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living; change daily living and you change relationships; change relationships and you change ministry.

Notice that the starting point is mindset, not ministry. Many people are in a hurry to “do something” without first letting their mindset be turned around. The result is new ministry done with an old mindset, God’s work done in the way of “self” — and the more we do, the more tired and empty we become.

Paul says: “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” (Romans 12:2)

“Transformed by the renewing of your mind”: the Greek for “renewing” is ἀνακαίνωσις (anakainōsis), a renewal of the very nature of a thing, not a surface renovation. And “conformed” and “transformed” are two quite different words in the original: the first speaks of imitating an outward shape; the second speaks of a change of substance from the inside out — and it is the very word used when the Lord Jesus was transfigured on the mountain (Matthew 17:2).

Brothers and sisters, what God wants is not for us to look like Christians on the outside; what God wants is for us to be truly changed inside into the likeness of Christ.

And the shift in perspective runs in four directions: from man’s perspective to God’s perspective, from an earthly perspective to a heavenly one, from a temporary perspective to an eternal one, and from a worldly perspective to a godly one.

Look at something from far enough away and its weight changes. The person who made you angry this morning, seen in the light of eternity, is your “2”; the thing that is making you anxious today, seen from heaven, is no more than a tool in the Lord’s hand.

5. The Lesson’s Practices for Daily Living (Personal)

The lesson has prepared three practices for us. Let’s take them one at a time.

First, every morning, hand over your sovereignty again in prayer: “Lord, today it is not about what I want; may your will be done.”

This is the road the Lord Jesus himself walked. In Gethsemane he said: “nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire.” (Matthew 26:39) Revival never begins with getting; it begins with handing over.

Second, pay deliberate attention to the promptings of the Holy Spirit and learn to obey in small things. A little more patience with your family; choosing honesty at work.

Why small things? Because the Lord said: “He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much” (Luke 16:10). The voice of the Holy Spirit is usually quiet, and it shows up in small things. A person who ignores the Holy Spirit in small things will not hear him in big things either.

Third, examine yourself once a week: “Where did I indulge myself this week? In what things did I let Jesus be King?”

This is what 321 calls Evaluation. Without evaluation, practice is only motion; with evaluation, practice becomes life.

The lesson ends by saying: as more and more believers begin to make choices like these, personal revival will spread step by step and prepare the way for the revival of the church.

One candle lights another and grows no dimmer for it. That is the arithmetic of revival.

sections.heading: 2. Revival of the Church: The Power of Multiplication in Unity
sections.html:
1. Revival Is Not Numbers; It Is a Body Joined Together

The lesson says: the end time revival is not the revival of a few individuals; it is the renewal and transformation of the whole church.

Notice this sentence in the lesson: if a church truly experiences revival, it is not merely an increase in numbers; it is relationships full of love and sincerity, full of the Lord’s presence and the power of witness.

That sentence puts the centre of gravity of revival back where it belongs. Numbers will grow — that is the fruit; relationships are renewed — that is the root.

Acts chapter 2 gives us a complete picture. On the day of Pentecost Peter stood up and preached, and Scripture records:

“Then those who gladly received his word were baptized. There were added that day about three thousand souls.” (Acts 2:41)

This is how the biblical record puts it: on the day of Pentecost about three thousand were added (Acts 2:41); later “many of those who heard the word believed, and the number of the men came to be about five thousand” (Acts 4:4); and “the Lord added to the assembly day by day those who were being saved” (Acts 2:47).

Added day by day — that is God’s work, not human ability. On that point the lesson is entirely right.

But notice that before the growth in numbers, Scripture first records the way they lived:

“They continued steadfastly in the apostles’ teaching and fellowship, in the breaking of bread, and prayer.” (Acts 2:42)

“Day by day, continuing steadfastly with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread at home, they took their food with gladness and singleness of heart, praising God, and having favor with all the people. The Lord added to the assembly day by day those who were being saved.” (Acts 2:46-47)

First came “with one accord”; then came “added day by day”. First relationships, then growth.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly the order 321 speaks of: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

2. What the Lord Prayed for the Church Is Unity

On the night before he went to the cross, the Lord Jesus prayed for believers of every generation:

“that they may all be one; even as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be one in us; that the world may believe that you sent me.” (John 17:21)

Look at the structure of this prayer. The standard of unity is the unity of the Father and the Son; the purpose of unity is that the world may believe.

In other words, unity itself is the most powerful witness to the gospel. The world may not be able to read our theology, but it can read our relationships.

Paul describes it with the picture of a body:

“but speaking truth in love, we may grow up in all things into him who is the head, Christ, from whom all the body, being fitted and knit together through that which every joint supplies, according to the working in measure of each individual part, makes the body increase to the building up of itself in love.” (Ephesians 4:15-16)

“Fitted and knit together”, “every joint supplies”, “the working … of each individual part”, and then — “makes the body increase”.

Brothers and sisters, do you see the cause and effect? Growth is the result of being joined together. If a body has dislocated joints and torn ligaments, however much you feed it, it will not grow well.

The psalm says: “See how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to live together in unity!” (Psalm 133:1) And the psalm ends: “for there Yahweh gives the blessing, even life forever more.” (Psalm 133:3)

The blessing God has ordained is found “there” — in the place where brothers live together in unity. The place of unity is the channel of blessing.

3. The Mark of Revival Is Multiplication, Not Division

The lesson makes a vital statement: one important mark of the church’s revival is “multiplication”, but this multiplication is not division; it is increase within unity.

What is the difference between the two?

Division is splitting apart because relationships have broken; multiplication is expanding because life is overflowing. After a division, both sides are wounded; after a multiplication, both sides grow.

The root of division, as 321 makes clear, is pride. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place. Pride provokes pride and both sides lose; humility draws out humility and both sides win.

And what does Paul say?

“doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself; each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others. Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus.” (Philippians 2:3-5)

“Each counting others better than himself” — that is the secret of unity, and it is the practice of humility.

And true multiplication looks like this:

“The word of God increased and the number of the disciples greatly multiplied in Jerusalem. A great company of the priests were obedient to the faith.” (Acts 6:7)

What’s striking is that the verses just before this one record the church handling a conflict — the Greek-speaking Jews complained against the Hebrews because their widows were being overlooked in the daily distribution. The apostles neither suppressed the matter nor let it tear the church apart. Instead they appointed seven deacons, and the problem became the occasion for a new office to be born.

A conflict handled rightly becomes a doorway to multiplication.

Paul handed Timothy the method of multiplication: “The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.” (2 Timothy 2:2)

There are four generations in that one verse: Paul, Timothy, faithful men, and others. The multiplication of life depends not on events but on people bringing people along.

4. Supporting Evidence from Science and Research: The Power of Relationships

The Harvard Study of Adult Development began in 1938 and has followed the same group of people for more than eighty years, making it one of the longest-running longitudinal studies ever conducted. Its current director, Robert Waldinger, has explained its clearest conclusion many times in public: good relationships do more than wealth or fame to keep people healthy and happy, and help them live longer.

When God made man he said: “It is not good for the man to be alone” (Genesis 2:18). Eighty years of scientific research have simply written a footnote to that ancient sentence.

Another example comes from the workplace. Between 2012 and 2015 Google ran “Project Aristotle”, studying well over a hundred teams within the company to discover what makes a team effective. It found that the most important factor was not how clever the members were or how many degrees they held, but the team’s “psychological safety” — a concept put forward in 1999 by Amy Edmondson of Harvard Business School, meaning that members dare to admit mistakes and voice disagreement without fear of being humiliated.

Brothers and sisters, if everyone in a church has to keep up appearances and no one dares to admit weakness, that is not holiness; that is fear. A truly revived church is a place where people dare to speak the truth and dare to shed tears.

5. Applying the 321 Vision: 235 Relationships and the 920 Practice

The lesson’s three practices fit neatly with two of 321’s frameworks for practice.

The first practice: build a culture of spiritual family — not just coming to meetings, but building genuine relationships with brothers and sisters, loving and supporting one another.

This is the first step of “235 relationships”. Find someone who will pursue selflessness together with you, to be your “2” — your spiritual companion. Two people, not for the sake of pouring out complaints, but to remind one another, pray for one another and build one another up.

The second practice: learn to be a disciple and to make disciples — take the initiative to care for and walk alongside a spiritual companion, building one another up and growing together.

This is the second step of “235” — establishing your “3”: spiritual parents and spiritual children. With spiritual parents we won’t go astray; with spiritual children we won’t stagnate. Go further still and you come to the “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades, “for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving, to the building up of the body of Christ” (Ephesians 4:12).

The third practice: be of one heart with the church’s leaders — not criticising or judging, but praying for them, supporting them, and taking up together God’s vision for the church.

This one is the hardest, yet the most crucial. Because criticism is pride’s most convenient outlet. A word of criticism costs nothing, yet it can make us look clever.

This is where the 920 practice comes in: everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”. Facing that person, we practise living out the selfless life (0) and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions —

“But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22-23)

Brothers and sisters, next time you feel like criticising someone, put that person in the place of your “2”, and ask yourself: which fruit do I need to bring out right now?

The lesson’s conclusion is beautifully put: the church’s revival is not a flurry of activities; it is the joining together of a body. When all the members are joined with one heart, serving one another and building one another up, the tide of revival will pour out and nothing will be able to hold it back.

sections.heading: 3. Revival of the Kingdom: Churches Joined Together, Jesus Reigning as King
sections.html:
1. The Highest Goal of God’s End-Time Work

The lesson says: the revival of the Kingdom is the highest goal of God’s work in the last days.

We must be careful not to set the goal of revival too low. If our goal is only “more people in our church”, our eyes are still fixed on the earth. God’s heart has always been bigger than our plans.

When the Lord Jesus taught us to pray, the first three requests were not for ourselves at all:

“Pray like this: ‘Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy. Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.’” (Matthew 6:9-10)

May your name be kept holy, may your Kingdom come, may your will be done.

Brothers and sisters, these three longings come in order. First God’s name, then God’s Kingdom, then God’s will. His name is who God is; his Kingdom is God’s rule; his will is God’s plan. When we truly treat God as God, his Kingdom comes; and when his Kingdom comes, his will is done on earth.

The lesson asks a wonderful question in its closing: aren’t the three longings at the start of the Lord’s Prayer the very order of revival?

2. The Army Joel Saw

The lesson says: according to the prophecy of Joel, in the last days God himself will lead a vast army.

Let’s supply the text of that prophecy. The prophet Joel describes the scene on that day:

“Yahweh thunders his voice before his army; for his forces are very great; for he is strong who obeys his command; for the day of Yahweh is great and very awesome, and who can endure it?” (Joel 2:11)

Notice two things. First, this army has a commander — “Yahweh thunders his voice before his army”. Second, this army’s strength does not lie in itself — “he is strong who obeys his command”.

Joel goes on to speak the words quoted in every revival:

“It will happen afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your old men will dream dreams. Your young men will see visions.” (Joel 2:28)

When Peter stood up on the day of Pentecost, the first thing he did to explain what was happening was to quote this passage (Acts 2:16-17). In other words, Pentecost was the first instalment of this prophecy’s fulfilment, and the end time revival will be its full realisation.

What does that “exceedingly great army” look like? Ezekiel shows us:

“He said to me, ‘Son of man, can these bones live?’ I answered, ‘Lord Yahweh, you know.’” (Ezekiel 37:3)

“So I prophesied as he commanded me, and the breath came into them, and they lived, and stood up on their feet, an exceedingly great army.” (Ezekiel 37:10)

Brothers and sisters, see the order clearly: first the bones, then bone joining to bone, then the breath entering, then standing up, and only at the end “an exceedingly great army”.

A heap of scattered bones, however many, is still just a heap of bones. The bones must be joined to one another, and there must be breath, before they become an army.

The lesson says: this is not one church, but all the churches united, a single army under the command of Christ, bringing shock and victory wherever it goes. That is exactly the vision Ezekiel saw.

3. The Mark of This Army: No More Judging One Another

The lesson is very honest here: the mark of this army is that there is no more grabbing and competing, no more judging one another, but joining together and becoming one, letting Jesus reign as King among us.

Why single out “no more grabbing and competing”? Because this is exactly where revivals in history have most often been cut short.

The church’s enemy has never been the church next door. Our “wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against the principalities, against the powers, against the world’s rulers of the darkness of this age, and against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 6:12).

When two churches compete with each other, Satan doesn’t need to do anything; he only has to stand by and watch. Pride provokes pride and both sides lose; humility draws out humility and both sides win.

Here an example from the natural world helps. In 2014, Steven Portugal and his colleagues published a study in the journal Nature. Using northern bald ibises fitted with satellite positioning devices, they showed directly for the first time that birds flying in a V formation precisely adjust their position and the timing of their wingbeats to make use of the upwash from the wings of the bird ahead, and so save energy. Earlier still, in 1970, Lissaman & Shollenberger calculated aerodynamically in the journal Science that a flock of birds flying in a V could extend its range by about 70 per cent compared with flying alone.

A bird flying alone can only fly as far as its own limit; a flock flying together can reach places no single bird could reach on its own.

Brothers and sisters, there is a key to the V formation: the bird in front works hardest, and they take turns. Only a flock willing to take turns can fly far.

Isn’t that what “let Jesus be King” means? When Jesus reigns as King in our midst, no one needs to fight for the front position; and when no one fights for position, the formation can hold.

4. The Proclamation from Heaven

In this section the lesson quotes today’s theme verse. Let’s read it through in full:

“The seventh angel sounded, and great voices in heaven followed, saying, ‘The kingdom of the world has become the Kingdom of our Lord, and of his Christ. He will reign forever and ever!’” (Revelation 11:15)

Brothers and sisters, notice that these words are spoken first “in heaven”. On earth the battle is still raging; in heaven victory has already been proclaimed.

This is exactly the shift in perspective 321 speaks of: from an earthly perspective to a heavenly one; from a temporary perspective to an eternal one.

When you look only at the earth, what you see is the weakness of the church, the corruption of society, the hardness of your family; when you lift your eyes to heaven, what you hear is that the trumpet has already sounded and the kingship is already settled.

This is not escapism; it is recalibration. For “we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal” (2 Corinthians 4:18).

And God’s promise to the overcomers is: “and made us kings and priests to our God, and we will reign on the earth.” (Revelation 5:10)

Reign on the earth — not waiting until heaven, but on the earth.

5. Applying the 321 Vision: Restoring the System of God’s Rule

Each item in the lesson’s third set of practices lifts our eyes higher:

First, change your perspective: don’t only see the needs of your own church, but pray for and bless the churches of your whole city and nation.

A very practical exercise: this week, pray for a church that is not your own, and ask God to bless it — and mean it. You’ll find that the first thing this prayer changes is you.

Second, take the initiative to cooperate with other churches and organisations rather than compete with them. Take part in united prayer, united mission and city transformation efforts.

Cooperation costs something, because cooperation means I can’t have it all. But the Lord said: “unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.” (John 12:24)

Third, live out the values of God’s Kingdom in the workplace, the family and the community, so that God’s glory does not stay inside the church but spreads over the whole earth.

The Lord said: “God’s Kingdom is within you” (the Chinese Union Version notes that “within you” may also be read “among you”) (Luke 17:21). The Kingdom of God is not a building; it is a reign. When you choose honesty in the office, God’s Kingdom is there; when you choose to apologise first at home, God’s Kingdom is there.

The lesson concludes: the revival of the Kingdom is not one denomination flourishing; it is the system of God’s rule being restored in every sphere. When God’s will is done on earth as it is in heaven, God’s Kingdom is established on earth.

This is exactly 321’s “the Goal” — to establish God’s system.

sections.heading: 4. Integrating the 321 Vision: One Road, Five Stations
sections.html:
Let’s take today’s three tiers of revival and look at them again within the 321 framework. You’ll find that they are really one and the same road.

1. The Three Foundations, the Two Core Values, the Goal

The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide.

Personal revival is these Three Foundations being established in one person. Jesus is my role model — so I no longer live by my own ideas; the Bible is my standard — so I no longer make decisions by feeling; the Holy Spirit is my guide — so I no longer charge ahead on my own cleverness.

The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory.

The church’s revival is these Two Core Values being realised among a group of people. Let Jesus be King — so it is not me who is king, and not you either; let Jesus receive all the glory — and so unity becomes possible, because if the glory doesn’t come to me, I have no need to compete with you.

The Goal: establish God’s system.

The revival of the Kingdom is this one Goal being accomplished across the whole earth. The system of God’s rule is restored in every sphere.

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? The three tiers of revival are the three levels of 321. The individual takes hold of the Three Foundations, the church lives out the Two Core Values, and the Kingdom accomplishes the Goal.

2. The Path of Serving: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God

321 also maps this road as five stations: Spirit (the Holy Spirit is my guide), Understanding (the Bible is my standard), Life (Jesus is my role model), Service (let Jesus be King), God (let Jesus receive all the glory).

First comes the prompting of the Holy Spirit, and then understanding of Scripture; with understanding, life is shaped into the Lord’s likeness; when life is right, service doesn’t lose its shape; and when service keeps its shape, the glory goes to God.

Many people walk this road backwards. They rush into service first, then discover that their life can’t keep up; and only when they can’t hold on any longer do they turn back to look for the Holy Spirit.

321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. Get the order right and the road goes far.

3. Rely on the Heart and the Holy Spirit, Not on the Brain and Ourselves

On the road to revival, the greatest temptation is to use our own methods to “manufacture” revival.

321 has a very simple reminder: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the brain and you’ll fret, rely on the heart and you’ll rejoice.

Solomon said: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23)

The wellspring of life flows out of the heart, not out of the head.

Brothers and sisters, this doesn’t mean we stop thinking. It means our thinking must be led by a heart that is open to God. The brain calculates gains and losses; the heart longs for God. Revival comes from longing, not from calculating.

4. Jesus Is the Focal Point

Finally, 321 reminds us: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances.

Focus on yourself and you’ll become proud or insecure; focus on others and you’ll compare or judge; focus on your circumstances and you’ll be afraid or complain.

Only when Jesus is the focal point are we changed. For “we all, with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, even as from the Lord, the Spirit” (2 Corinthians 3:18).

Seeing is becoming. That is the simplest formula of revival.

sections.heading: 5. Putting It into Practice: Walking Through the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset
sections.html:
The lesson gives us nine practices, spread across three levels: personal, church and Kingdom. Now let’s walk through them using 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — so that the practices really touch the ground.

Stage One: Information

First, commit the content of the lesson to memory: revival has three tiers — personal, church and Kingdom; and their order is the individual as the starting point, the church as the vessel, and the Kingdom as the goal.

Today, please copy the theme verse onto a piece of paper and stick it where you can see it: “The kingdom of the world has become the Kingdom of our Lord, and of his Christ. He will reign forever and ever!” (Revelation 11:15)

Information doesn’t automatically become life, but without information nothing ever begins.

Stage Two: Revelation

Information goes into the head; revelation goes into the heart.

Please be still and pray to the Lord: “Lord, please show me — what do these three tiers of revival have to do with me?”

Then listen. Revelation is often a very short sentence, a very specific name, a matter you’ve been avoiding all along.

Stage Three: Conviction

Conviction is your heart saying, “Yes, Lord, you’re right.”

This step is the hardest, because it requires us to admit we were wrong. The church in Ephesus had to admit, “I have left my first love”; we too need to admit: I really do often make myself king.

Without conviction there is no real repentance; without repentance there is no revival.

Stage Four: Implementation

Turn the lesson’s nine practices into specific “if … then …” actions.

At the personal level: if I wake up in the morning, then my first prayer will be, “Lord, today it is not about what I want; may your will be done.” If I sense the prompting of the Holy Spirit in my heart, then I will obey at once in that one small thing.

At the church level: if I’m going to a meeting this week, then I will take the initiative to really care for at least one brother or sister, not just say hello. If I feel like criticising a church leader, then I will stop and pray for them for three minutes instead.

At the Kingdom level: if I pray for my own church, then I will also pray for another church. If I face a choice at work, then I will ask: does this choice let Jesus be King here?

Stage Five: Evaluation

The lesson itself gives us the questions for evaluation: “Where did I indulge myself this week? In what things did I let Jesus be King?”

Please set aside a regular time each week, be still for ten minutes, and answer those two questions honestly. Don’t beat yourself up, and don’t let yourself off the hook.

David said: “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way.” (Psalm 139:23-24)

Stage Six: Correction

After evaluation must come correction; otherwise evaluation only turns into self-reproach.

Correction is specific: if you said something wrong, go and apologise; if a habit is holding you back, replace it; if a relationship is broken, take the first step to mend it.

“If therefore you are offering your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has anything against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go your way. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.” (Matthew 5:23-24)

The Lord puts reconciliation before sacrifice. That is “relationships first, then ministry”.

Stage Seven: Repetition

Once is not enough; it has to be repeated.

Wood’s research reminds us that habits are formed through repetition. Spiritual practice is the same: one prayer is an event; praying every day is a life.

“Day by day, continuing steadfastly with one accord in the temple” (Acts 2:46) — “day by day”, “continuing steadfastly”: that is repetition.

Stage Eight: Multiplication

The last stage, and the key stage of revival: multiplication.

“The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.” (2 Timothy 2:2)

Brothers and sisters, don’t let what you have received today stop with you. Find someone and pass it on.

If one person’s revival does not multiply, it ends with that one person; if one person’s revival multiplies, it becomes the revival of the church; and if the church’s revival multiplies, it becomes the revival of the Kingdom.

That is why the lesson says: one important mark of the church’s revival is “multiplication”.

sections.heading: 6. Closing and Call: The Journey of Revival Begins with You and Me
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s come back to the lesson’s closing words:

Personal revival is for the sake of the church’s revival; the church’s revival is for the sake of the Kingdom’s revival; and the revival of the Kingdom is the very heart of Jesus.

The core vision of this book comes down to three sentences: begin to change as an individual, choosing to let Jesus be King; live out unity in the church and enter into spiritual multiplication; and then bear witness to God’s Kingdom in society and the nation, with all the glory going to Jesus Christ.

It is generally said that the nineteenth-century evangelist Dwight L. Moody (1837–1899) heard a sentence as a young man that changed his life. The sentence was: “The world has yet to see what God can do through a man who is fully consecrated to him.” When Moody heard it, he said to himself: I will be that man. And God really did use this shoe-shop clerk, who had never had any formal theological training, to shake both Britain and America.

Brothers and sisters, this morning that same sentence is set before you.

The world has yet to see what God can do through one person who is fully consecrated to him.

Will you be that person?

Revival waits for no one, and it does not run on feelings. What it waits for is a people who are willing, day by day, to choose obedience, unity and wholehearted giving.

What it is waiting for is you.

The trumpet has already sounded. Heaven’s proclamation has already gone out: the kingdom of the world has become the Kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ; he will reign forever and ever.

Now let us answer that proclamation here on earth.

Let Jesus reign as King in your heart — that is personal revival.

Let Jesus reign as King among us — that is the revival of the church.

Let Jesus reign as King over this land — that is the revival of the Kingdom.

And all the glory goes to our Lord Jesus Christ alone.

keyVerses: “The seventh angel sounded, and great voices in heaven followed, saying, ‘The kingdom of the world has become the Kingdom of our Lord, and of his Christ. He will reign forever and ever!’” (Revelation 11:15)
“Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.” (Matthew 6:10)
practices: Every morning, hand over your sovereignty again in prayer: “Lord, today it is not about what I want; may your will be done.”
Pay deliberate attention to the promptings of the Holy Spirit, and learn to obey in small things.
Examine yourself once a week: “Where did I indulge myself this week? In what things did I let Jesus be King?”
Build a culture of spiritual family — not just coming to meetings, but building genuine relationships with brothers and sisters, loving and supporting one another.
Learn to be a disciple and to make disciples — take the initiative to care for and walk alongside a spiritual companion, building one another up and growing together.
Be of one heart with the church’s leaders — not criticising or judging, but praying for them, supporting them, and taking up together God’s vision for the church.
Change your perspective: don’t only see the needs of your own church, but pray for and bless the churches of your whole city and nation.
Take the initiative to cooperate with other churches and organisations rather than compete with them. Take part in united prayer, united mission and city transformation efforts.
Live out the values of God’s Kingdom in the workplace, the family and the community, so that God’s glory does not stay inside the church but spreads over the whole earth.
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,
We worship you, for you are the Lord who will reign as King forever and ever. The trumpet has already sounded; your Kingdom will surely come.

Lord, forgive us. So often we ask you to change our circumstances but will not let you change us; so often we are busy serving but have left our first love; so often we speak of unity with our lips while in our hearts we compare and judge.
This morning we place our sovereignty back in your hands. Set alight our love for you, and make our hearts burn again.

Lord, make us willing people. Willing to obey in small things, willing to be humble in our relationships, willing to be members that join the body together in the church, willing to pray for and bless our city, our nation and all the churches.
Send your Spirit, and pour him out on all flesh. Make the dry bones stand up and become an exceedingly great army.
May your name be kept holy, may your Kingdom come, may your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: The lesson says: “The key to personal revival lies in choice.” Joshua said: “choose today whom you will serve … as for me and my house, we will serve Yahweh.” (Joshua 24:15) Please share: this week, what specific matter do you need to make a fresh choice about, so that Jesus reigns as King in it? How do you plan to go about it?

The Lord Jesus prayed: “that they may all be one … that the world may believe that you sent me.” (John 17:21) Please share: in your small group, your church or your relationships with other churches, is there a relationship that needs mending or connecting? If unity is the most powerful witness, what first step are you willing to take?
