sections.heading: Introduction: Are You Standing on the Right Platform?
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning I’d like to begin by asking you to look at a picture with me.

A man is standing on a railway platform, gripping his ticket tightly, his eyes fixed on the tracks stretching away into the distance. He waits an hour, and no train comes. He waits two hours, and still no train. By the third hour he begins to wonder whether something has happened to it. Just then a station attendant walks past, glances at his ticket and says flatly, “Sir, this train doesn’t leave from this platform. It’s on the other side.”

It wasn’t that he had no ticket. It wasn’t that he didn’t want to get on. He was simply standing in the wrong place.

Brothers and sisters, I want to ask you very honestly: how many of us approach revival just like that? We hold the promises in our hands, we carry a longing in our hearts, and we pray it often enough with our lips: “Lord, please revive us.” Yet one year waits out the next, one conference waits out the next, one stirring of the heart waits out the next, and revival always seems to be somewhere far off. We always feel the train still hasn’t pulled into the station.

The text of this lesson opens with a sentence of real weight: we are no longer waiting passively. We believe that God will bring revival; it is something he has promised with his own lips. If we have not yet seen it fully realised, it is not because God is unwilling, but because on our side we have not yet fully aligned ourselves with his heart.

That sentence is like a key that unlocks the whole lesson. The problem, it turns out, is not on God’s side; the problem is on ours. God’s fire has long been ready; it is only that the altar has not been repaired. God’s rain has long filled the sky; it is only that the field has not been broken up.

The prophet Hosea puts this order wonderfully: “Sow to yourselves in righteousness, reap according to kindness. Break up your fallow ground; for it is time to seek Yahweh, until he comes and rains righteousness on you” (Hosea 10:12). Brothers and sisters, notice the sequence here: first you sow, first you break up the ground, and only then does the rain come down. The rain is God’s gift; no human being can make a single drop of rain. But the fallow ground is ours to break up. God will not pick up the hoe for us.

So the lesson text is exactly right: revival has never been something we “wait for”; it is something we “walk out”. When we are willing to rise and respond, and to obey his word, revival will come upon us step by step.

And this is exactly where this lesson wants to lead us: to let revival be no longer just a vision, a slogan or a brief stirring, but a reality that can be lived out in the individual, in the church, and even in the whole Kingdom. This is not a spiritual dream. It is a moment in which God is truly preparing us to step into his heart.

Paul says, “Behold, now is the acceptable time. Behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians 6:2). In the original, that word “now” is used twice, as though someone were tapping twice on your ear: Now! Now! Not next year, not when the children are grown, not when I’m a little more spiritually mature — now.

Now is not the time to sit and look on. It is the time to rise and respond, to rise and act. This morning I want to invite you to take the word “wait” and exchange it for the word “walk”.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: A Thread of Hope among the Ruins
sections.html:
To grasp the weight of 2 Chronicles 7:14, we first need to know who this verse was spoken to, and in what situation.

In the Hebrew Bible, 1 and 2 Chronicles were originally a single book. Jewish tradition attributes it to Ezra the scribe, or to a group of priestly scribes of his time; scholars generally call its compiler “the Chronicler”. It was written after Israel’s return from exile, around the fifth century BC.

It was written for a remnant who had just come back from Babylon to Jerusalem. Their situation was anything but romantic. The city walls were broken, the temple was humble, the population was sparse, and enemies surrounded them on every side. The older people still remembered the splendour of Solomon’s temple, and when they saw the foundation of the second temple laid, they actually wept aloud (see Ezra 3:12).

In circumstances like these, the deepest question in their hearts was this: will God’s glory ever return? Is revival still possible? Do battered people like us still have a share in God’s plan?

The Chronicler sets out to answer exactly that question. He retells the scene of Solomon dedicating the temple. Chapter 6 of 2 Chronicles is Solomon’s long prayer of dedication; in chapter 7, verses 1 to 3, fire comes down from heaven and consumes the burnt offering and the sacrifices, the glory of Yahweh fills the house, and all Israel bow down on the pavement and worship. What a glorious day that was.

But the verses that follow are even more crucial. Chapter 7, verse 12 says, “Yahweh appeared to Solomon by night, and said to him, ‘I have heard your prayer, and have chosen this place for myself for a house of sacrifice.’” Then in verse 13 God first speaks the bad news: “If I shut up the sky so that there is no rain, or if I command the locust to devour the land, or if I send pestilence among my people”.

Brothers and sisters, see this clearly: verse 14 follows on from verse 13. God did not say these words when all was calm. He spoke verse 14 only after foretelling a shut-up sky, locusts and pestilence. In other words, 2 Chronicles 7:14 is not an abstract spiritual slogan. It is the road home that God left for his people in the darkest hour of their nation.

On this road there are four verbs, and every one of them deserves to be chewed on slowly.

The first is “humble themselves”. The Hebrew is kāna‘, meaning to bring oneself low, to submit, to bend down. It is not emotional self-deprecation, but surrender of the will — taking the self we have lifted high and setting it down.

The second is “pray”. The Hebrew pālal carries the sense of interceding, of laying a matter out before God. Prayer is not talking to yourself; it is speaking as one who stands between God and people.

The third is “seek my face”. The Hebrew word for “face” is pānîm, which stands for person, presence and relationship. Brothers and sisters, learn to tell the difference: to seek his “hand” is to want what is in his hand; to seek his “face” is to want him. So often our prayers keep seeking his hand — for healing, for a job, for children, for the fruits of revival — but God says, “First come and seek my face.”

The fourth is “turn from their wicked ways”. The Hebrew šûb means to turn around, to return, to repent. Repentance is not feeling sorry; it is turning around. You were walking that way, and now you turn a hundred and eighty degrees and walk this way.

After the four verbs come three promises: I will hear, I will forgive, I will heal. The Hebrew for “heal” is rāphā‘, the same root as in “Yahweh Rapha”, the Lord who heals. Pay special attention to the last phrase: “and will heal their land.” The healing of the land is bound up with the repentance of the people. This is what Scripture consistently shows us: once our relationship with God is restored, our relationships with one another, and with the land itself, also begin to be healed.

By the way, when the lesson text quotes this verse it reads “if they are humble”, whereas the Chinese Union Version actually reads “if they humble themselves”. The meaning is much the same, but we want to read Scripture accurately, so throughout this lesson we return to the wording of the Chinese Union Version, which matches the English we use here: “will humble themselves, pray, seek my face.”

sections.heading: 1. Revival Is God’s Work, and We Are Responsible to Prepare
sections.html:
Right at the start, the lesson text draws the most important line of all clearly: revival is not a human plan, nor something that human effort can force into being. Revival is God’s work, the work of the Holy Spirit. Only God can bring a true awakening and transformation of life.

We have to stand firmly on this point first; otherwise all our practices will become just another form of “relying on ourselves”.

The prophet Zechariah spoke a word to Zerubbabel that has become a boundary stone for all spiritual work through every generation: “Then he answered and spoke to me, saying, ‘This is Yahweh’s word to Zerubbabel, saying, “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit,” says Yahweh of Armies’” (Zechariah 4:6).

Habakkuk’s prayer is the same: “Yahweh, I have heard of your fame. I stand in awe of your deeds, Yahweh. Renew your work in the middle of the years. In the middle of the years make it known. In wrath, you remember mercy” (Habakkuk 3:2). Notice how he puts it — “renew your work”, which the Chinese Union Version renders “revive your work”. Revival has never been the reviving of our work; it is always the reviving of “his” work.

The psalmist prays in the same way: “Won’t you revive us again, that your people may rejoice in you?” (Psalm 85:6). That word “revive”, literally “make us live”, is the very picture of revival in the Old Testament: turning what is dead into what is alive. And turning the dead into the living has only ever been something God can do.

So what, then, is our responsibility?

God has not left us to stand by with folded arms. In 2 Chronicles 7:14 he sets out, plainly and clearly, the four things that are ours to do: humble ourselves, pray, seek his face, and turn from our wicked ways. And how true his promise is — “then I will hear from heaven, will forgive their sin, and will heal their land.”

In other words, revival is his work, but we must first be made ready to be vessels for his work.

Here is a helpful picture. The power station has electricity, but for that electricity to reach your home there must be wires, switches and sockets in between. The power comes from the power station; you cannot make electricity yourself. But if the wiring in your home is broken and the switch is off, you could stand right at the gate of the power station and still not have a light on. Humbling ourselves, praying, seeking and turning — that is reconnecting the wiring and turning the switch on.

Church history shows us so many examples of this.

In 1727, in a small village in eastern Germany called Herrnhut, a group of believers who had fled there from Moravia had been quarrelling and splitting into factions, and were on the verge of falling apart. Count Nikolaus Ludwig von Zinzendorf led them together in confessing their sins and being reconciled to one another. On 13 August that year, during a meeting, they experienced an outpouring of the Holy Spirit, and the whole community was renewed. Soon afterwards, on 27 August, twenty-four brothers and twenty-four sisters began to keep watch in prayer in shifts, each person for one hour a day, without stopping day or night. That relay of prayer went on for more than a hundred years. And from that little village of a few hundred people more missionaries were sent out than the whole Christian world had sent in the previous two hundred years combined.

Brothers and sisters, notice the order: first confession and reconciliation, then the outpouring of the Spirit; first the altar of prayer, then the fire of mission.

On 23 September 1857, an ordinary New York businessman named Jeremiah Lanphier held a lunchtime prayer meeting in an upstairs room of a church on Fulton Street. On the first day, when it began, he was the only one there; half an hour later, six people had trickled in. The second week there were twenty, the third week forty. Before long, rooms all over the business districts of New York were packed at midday with people on their knees in prayer, and this wave of prayer spread across the whole of America. Historians call it the great “Layman’s Prayer Revival” of 1857–58.

Six people. Brothers and sisters, God never despises how small your starting point is. He only asks whether you are willing to be the first to kneel down.

It is generally held that the British evangelist Henry Varley once said to the young D. L. Moody, “The world has yet to see what God will do with a man fully consecrated to him.” When Moody heard that, he said to himself, “I will be that man.” The rest of the story, the whole world knows.

From the perspective of the 321 vision, this is precisely the Three Foundations in practice. The Holy Spirit is my guide — revival is the work of the Holy Spirit, not my project proposal. The Bible is my standard — 2 Chronicles 7:14 sets out the conditions God himself wrote down, not a method we dreamed up ourselves. Jesus is my role model — though he existed in the form of God, he emptied himself, and the road he walked was precisely a road of humbling himself and obeying.

So we do not force God’s hand, but we prepare ourselves. We do not manufacture revival, but we dig open the mouth of the well.

sections.heading: 2. Only God’s System Can Enter into God’s Revival
sections.html:
The lesson text goes on to name the second key: true revival does not just happen in church meetings; it begins in the life of each individual. What this age needs is not more programmes and events, but more lives willing to let Jesus be King.

That sentence is worth stopping to think about.

We often assume that if only the meetings were a little bigger, the worship a little more fervent and the speakers a little more famous, revival would come. But the warmth of a good meeting often doesn’t survive the car park. True revival is not a few hours of excitement in the sanctuary; it is a different kind of life at your dinner table, at your desk in the office, in the conversations between husband and wife.

The lesson text puts it precisely: the heart of revival is to turn us from the Worldly system into God’s system — no longer being our own master, no longer exalting ourselves, but letting Jesus alone have the rule and the glory.

In Romans, Paul describes this change of system most clearly of all: “Therefore I urge you, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service. Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God” (Romans 12:1–2).

Here there are two Greek verbs that form a striking contrast.

The word for “be conformed” in “be conformed to this world” is syschēmatizesthe (συσχηματίζεσθε). Its root, schēma, means an outward pattern, a shell that can be swapped at any moment. It is like changing your clothes, your hairstyle or your phone case — the shape changes, but the substance does not.

The word for “be transformed” in “be transformed by the renewing of your mind” is metamorphousthe (μεταμορφοῦσθε). Its root, morphē, means essential form. This word later became the English word “metamorphosis”, which in biology describes a caterpillar turning into a butterfly.

Brothers and sisters, can you hear the difference? The world wants you to change your shell; God wants to change your life.

There is an astonishing scientific fact here. After a caterpillar forms its chrysalis, it does not simply grow wings bit by bit. Most of the tissue in its body is broken down by digestive enzymes into an almost liquid state, and then clusters of cells that had lain hidden in its body all along, called “imaginal discs”, rebuild it into a completely different creature, a butterfly. It is not a caterpillar with wings bolted on; it is a new creation.

Paul says, “Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new” (2 Corinthians 5:17). That is exactly what a change of system means.

The message of 321 fits here precisely. The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of every problem. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God. The Worldly system makes everyone want to be king, and the result is that pride provokes pride and both sides lose. God’s system has only one King, and the result is that humility inspires humility and both sides win.

That is why the Two Core Values of 321 are these: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. And the Goal is to establish God’s system.

Paul also gives us a new pair of glasses: “while we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal” (2 Corinthians 4:18). “If then you were raised together with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated on the right hand of God. Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth” (Colossians 3:1–2).

This is what 321 calls the four shifts of perspective: from man’s perspective to God’s perspective, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporal to the eternal, and from the worldly to the godly.

So how do we live this shift out? The lesson text gives a very practical answer: therefore we need to begin, from now on, to build the rhythms and habits of revival into our daily living. Not waiting until we feel moved before we act, but having concrete practices and disciplines even in the most ordinary days.

“Rhythms and habits” — these words fit beautifully with the way God made us. In a study published in 2002 in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, the Texas A&M University psychologist Wendy Wood and her colleagues found that a substantial proportion of what people do each day is repeated in the same settings and at the same times. In other words, our daily living is, in fact, made up of habits.

Brothers and sisters, this is an important reminder: if our spiritual life runs only on being moved, then most of our days will be empty. Because being moved is occasional, but habits are daily.

So next, the lesson text gives us three ways to put this into practice in our daily living. These three practices are the concrete steps that help us press on into revival: active obedience every day, fasting and prayer every week, and choosing to deny ourselves every week.

sections.heading: 3. Active Obedience Every Day: Let Jesus Be King
sections.html:
The lesson text describes the first practice like this: when you wake up in the morning, the first thing you do is not check your phone or plan your schedule, but close your eyes and say to the Lord, “Lord Jesus, today I am not the one in charge; you are King.”

Brothers and sisters, allow me to ask a very personal question: when you woke up this morning, what was the first thing you did?

For many people, the answer is: reach for the phone. Before our eyes are even fully open, the voices of the world have already come in — news, messages, to-do lists, comparison, anxiety. Our day has very often been set for us by other people before we have said a single word to God.

That is not how the people of the Bible began their day.

The psalmist says, “Yahweh, in the morning you will hear my voice. In the morning I will lay my requests before you, and will watch expectantly” (Psalm 5:3). “In the morning” comes twice here. Laying our hearts before the Lord in the morning is like going to God at first light each day to receive that day’s orders.

The Lord Jesus himself is our role model in this even more: “Early in the morning, while it was still dark, he rose up and went out, and departed into a deserted place, and prayed there” (Mark 1:35). Brothers and sisters, if even the Son of God rose before dawn to pray, what makes us think we can do without it?

The lesson text says that this kind of declaration is not merely piety in words; it is a reminder to ourselves that every choice, every emotion and every reaction today must be placed under the sovereignty of Jesus.

That word “sovereignty” is the key. Obedience is not the same as doing a great many spiritual things. Obedience is handing over the right to decide.

Samuel spoke an extremely sobering word to Saul: “Samuel said, ‘Has Yahweh as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying Yahweh’s voice? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams’” (1 Samuel 15:22). Saul offered many sacrifices, but he did not obey. Brothers and sisters, we can serve very busily and yet never let Jesus be King all day long.

The supreme role model of obedience is, of course, the Lord Jesus himself: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross” (Philippians 2:5–8).

The Greek for “emptied himself” is kenoō (κενόω), meaning to pour out, to empty. The Lord Jesus did not lose his divinity; he laid down the rights he could rightfully have used. This is exactly what 321 says: selflessness is not having nothing; it is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position, entering into the fullness of Jesus and living that fullness out.

The lesson text gives an example very close to everyday life: when you are misunderstood at work, do you immediately justify yourself? Or do you first take a step back and ask, “Lord, here, how do you want me to respond?”

Brothers and sisters, the difference of that one second decides between two completely different lives.

Immediately justifying yourself is the self-centred life speaking. Behind self-justification lies the fear of being misunderstood, the fear of losing face, the fear of being looked down on — that is a self sitting in the driver’s seat. Taking a step back to ask the Lord first is selflessness breathing. You hand over the steering wheel and move to the passenger seat yourself.

There is a very vivid picture of this: many Christians have invited Jesus into the car, but they only let him sit in the back seat. When a problem comes up they turn round and ask, “Lord, what do you think?” — and having asked, they go on driving themselves. Letting Jesus be King means this: he is in the driver’s seat and you are in the passenger seat. You can read the map, you can talk, you can sing hymns, but you don’t touch the steering wheel.

The lesson text says that as we learn to let Jesus reign at every moment, we will more and more live a selfless life — not following our own will, but following the Lord’s leading. This is exactly where personal revival begins.

Here I want to add an important note: why “every day”?

In a study published in 2010 in the European Journal of Social Psychology, Phillippa Lally of University College London and her colleagues followed ninety-six participants and found that it took on average about sixty-six days for a new behaviour to become an automatic habit, with very wide individual differences, anywhere from eighteen to two hundred and fifty-four days.

Brothers and sisters, these figures give us two lessons. First, don’t expect to feel something after three days. Second, don’t give up because you have missed a day — the same study found that missing an occasional day did not significantly undermine the forming of the habit.

Spiritual disciplines are just the same. Jesus said, “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Luke 9:23); the Chinese Union Version, like many English versions, reads “take up his cross daily”. Notice that word: daily. The cross is not a piece of luggage you carry once and are done with; it is a burden to be carried every day.

From the 321 perspective, this practice is “rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves”. When we rely on the brain and ourselves, we wake up each morning and start calculating, comparing and worrying, and the result is distress. When we rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, we wake up each morning and give up the throne, and the result is gladness. Proverbs says, “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23). The wellspring of life flows from the heart, not from the diary.

And the fivefold change 321 speaks of begins right here: change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change the daily living. This one declaration each morning looks like only thirty seconds, but it is changing your mindset — today I am not in charge; you are King.

How to practise (following the lesson text): each morning pray about sovereignty, and before every conflict or decision, first ask the Lord silently, “Jesus, what do you want me to do?”

sections.heading: 4. Fasting and Prayer Every Week: Fixing the Heart on God
sections.html:
The lesson text describes the second practice this way: amid our busyness, our hearts are easily taken captive by the world, so we need to stop with a regular rhythm and let our spirits be realigned with the Lord. Choose one day a week to fast (it may be one meal or the whole day, depending on your circumstances) and set that day apart as holy — not only stopping eating and drinking, but stopping the voices of the world, so that we can hear the voice of God.

“Stopping the voices of the world” — that phrase goes to the heart of fasting.

Fasting is most easily misunderstood in two ways. One is going hungry in exchange for God’s yes, as though it were a spiritual transaction. The other is harsh self-punishment, as though God liked watching us suffer. Scripture teaches neither.

The prophet Joel says, “‘Yet even now,’ says Yahweh, ‘turn to me with all your heart, and with fasting, and with weeping, and with mourning.’ Tear your heart, and not your garments, and turn to Yahweh, your God; for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness, and relents from sending calamity” (Joel 2:12–13).

“Tear your heart, and not your garments” — in the ancient Near East, tearing your clothes was the outward sign of grief. God says, “I don’t want that garment; I want your heart.” If fasting does not bring a broken heart and a turning back, it is nothing more than a diet.

Isaiah is even more direct: “Isn’t this the fast that I have chosen: to release the bonds of wickedness, to undo the straps of the yoke, to let the oppressed go free, and that you break every yoke?” (Isaiah 58:6). True fasting ultimately flows out into justice and mercy.

The Lord Jesus reminds us that fasting is to be done in secret: “Moreover when you fast, don’t be like the hypocrites, with sad faces. For they disfigure their faces, that they may be seen by men to be fasting. Most certainly I tell you, they have received their reward. But you, when you fast, anoint your head, and wash your face; so that you are not seen by men to be fasting, but by your Father who is in secret, and your Father, who sees in secret, will reward you” (Matthew 6:16–18).

Notice that the Lord says “when you fast”, not “if you fast”. He assumes his disciples will fast.

The revival and sending of the early church also came out of fasting and prayer: “As they served the Lord and fasted, the Holy Spirit said, ‘Separate Barnabas and Saul for me, for the work to which I have called them.’ Then, when they had fasted and prayed and laid their hands on them, they sent them away” (Acts 13:2–3). Brothers and sisters, the first commissioning for cross-cultural mission in human history was issued in the middle of a time of fasting and prayer.

Nehemiah was the same. When he heard that the walls of Jerusalem were broken down and its gates burned with fire, “When I heard these words, I sat down and wept, and mourned several days; and I fasted and prayed before the God of heaven” (Nehemiah 1:4). The wall was rebuilt in just fifty-two days, but before those fifty-two days there were months of fasting and prayer.

The lesson text tells us there are three things we can pray for while we fast.

First, repent of the coldness and pride in our own hearts. This is exactly the “humble themselves” and “turn from their wicked ways” of 2 Chronicles 7:14. The first stop of revival is always our own heart.

Second, pray for the unity and purity of the church. The Lord Jesus’ farewell prayer was this: “that they may all be one; even as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be one in us; that the world may believe that you sent me” (John 17:21).

Third, intercede for the expansion of the Kingdom and the preparation for the Lord’s return. The Lord taught us to pray, “Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven” (Matthew 6:10).

Brothers and sisters, have you noticed that the order of these three is exactly what 321 calls the priority of relationships — first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things? First deal with your own heart, then with the unity of the church, and only then with the ministry of the Kingdom. Life first, then relationships, then ministry.

The lesson text puts it beautifully: fasting like this is not only training in self-control; it is training in longing, so that the fire for God within us is kindled again.

There is a scientific discovery worth mentioning here, which can serve as an apt illustration. The Japanese scientist Yoshinori Ohsumi was awarded the 2016 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discovering the mechanisms of cellular “autophagy”. When cells are short of nutrients, they switch on autophagy, breaking down and recycling old, damaged and surplus components in order to sustain more important functions.

Please note, I am not saying fasting can save anyone; salvation is by grace alone, through faith. What I am saying is that the body God made is itself speaking a language to us: when the supply from outside is paused, the clean-up inside begins.

It is the same spiritually. When we set aside a meal, half a day, the notifications on our phone, the things normally drowned out by the noise rise to the surface — unresolved bitterness, hidden pride, greed that has been quietly growing. Fasting does not create problems; fasting simply turns the volume down so that you can hear the voice that was there all along.

From the 321 perspective, this practice corresponds most directly to one of the Three Foundations: the Holy Spirit is my guide. We stop, not in order to do nothing, but in order to be able to hear. On Mount Horeb Elijah experienced a great wind, an earthquake and a fire, but Yahweh was not in them; at last there was “a still small voice” (1 Kings 19:12). A still small voice can only be heard in quietness.

How to practise (following the lesson text): choose one day each week to fast (at least one meal), set aside time for quiet solitude, focus on prayer, and write down the key things the Holy Spirit brings to mind.

One more practical word: brothers and sisters with particular health conditions — for example, pregnancy, diabetes, those on medication or currently undergoing treatment — please consult your doctor first. You can set the time apart as holy by “fasting one meal”, “fasting from your phone” or “fasting from entertainment”. What God looks at is the heart, not the stomach.

sections.heading: 5. Choosing to Deny Ourselves Every Week, Living Out Selflessness: Letting Love Flow in Our Relationships
sections.html:
The lesson text describes the third practice this way: revival is not only in the prayer meeting; even more, it is lived out in our relationships with one another.

That sentence is enormously important. Because the mistake we most easily make is to lock revival up inside our meetings. A person can weep buckets in a prayer meeting and then go home and be unable to say a simple “I’m sorry”.

The lesson text says: choose one person each week (it may be your spouse, your child, a co-worker or an acquaintance) and express the love of Christ to them in a concrete way: an apology, a word of encouragement, a meal, a hug. When you take the initiative to step out of your “self” in order to honour, perfect and accompany the other person, you are choosing to deny yourself and living out a selfless life.

“Denying of self” is the most basic thing the Lord Jesus asks of his disciples: “He said to all, ‘If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me’” (Luke 9:23).

The Greek for “deny himself” is aparneomai heauton (ἀπαρνέομαι ἑαυτόν), literally “to disown oneself”. Interestingly, this word shares its root with the word used when Peter three times “denied the Lord”. Brothers and sisters, what a striking contrast: Peter denied the Lord, yet disciples are called to deny themselves. Here the two roads of life part ways.

Paul turned this into his own life confession: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me” (Galatians 2:20).

This is exactly what 321 says: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness of Jesus and living it out; “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me.

Notice the words the lesson text uses: step out of your “self” to honour, perfect and accompany the other person. These three verbs are very precise. To honour is to regard the other person as better than yourself; to perfect is to help them become better than yourself; to accompany is to give away your own time. All three require you first to give up a little of your own place.

The Lord himself gave us a new commandment: “A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another. Just as I have loved you, you also love one another. By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:34–35).

And 1 John reminds us that love must touch the ground: “My little children, let’s not love in word only, or with the tongue only, but in deed and truth” (1 John 3:18). An apology, a meal, a hug — that is exactly “in deed and truth”.

The lesson text then offers a spiritual insight: these simple acts may look ordinary, but they are the most powerful tools for tearing down the enemy’s strongholds — because love makes us one, oneness brings the Lord glory, and glory naturally draws the work of the Holy Spirit.

This logic is entirely in line with Scripture. The psalm says, “See how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to live together in unity!” (Psalm 133:1). And the psalm ends, “for there Yahweh gives the blessing, even life forever more” (Psalm 133:3). Look at that one word: “there”. The blessing God has ordained comes down on the place where people live together in unity.

Brothers and sisters, we often ask God to send his blessing down upon us, but God says, “The blessing was ordained long ago; it is just that it comes down ‘there’ — on the place where people live together in unity.” If you are not there, it is not that there is no blessing; it is that you are not at the delivery address.

Psychological research confirms this direction too. In a study published in 2008 in the journal Science, Elizabeth Dunn and Lara Aknin of the University of British Columbia in Canada, together with Michael Norton of Harvard Business School, found that people who spent money on others reported greater happiness than those who spent the same amount on themselves.

In addition, the Harvard Study of Adult Development, which began in 1938 and is still going today, is one of the longest-running studies of adult life in human history. Its current director, Robert Waldinger, has pointed out many times that the study’s clearest conclusion is not about wealth or fame: it is that good relationships make people happier and healthier.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly what 321 has been saying all along: people matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

This practice is also the 920 practice in action. Every person we are in relationship with is our “2”. As we practise living a selfless (0) life in that relationship, we bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law” (Galatians 5:22–23).

And as we keep walking this way, we enter into 235 relationships: with selfless people we become a “2”, spiritual companions to one another; we establish a “3”, becoming spiritual parents and spiritual children; and finally we become a “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades — “He gave some to be apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, shepherds and teachers; for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving, to the building up of the body of Christ” (Ephesians 4:11–12).

Notice the wording here in Ephesians: “the perfecting of the saints”. Perfecting is exactly what the lesson text is talking about.

How to practise (following the lesson text): each week take the initiative to care for one person, help or bless others with practical action, and name them before God in prayer, asking him to bless them.

sections.heading: 6. Integrating the 321 Vision: A Road Map for Revival
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s set the three practices of this lesson back into the whole picture of the 321 vision and take a look. You will find they are not three scattered good deeds, but one clear road.

The Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal

The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model — he emptied himself and took the form of obedience. The Bible is my standard — 2 Chronicles 7:14 is not our invention, but conditions laid down by God’s own lips. The Holy Spirit is my guide — revival is the work of the Holy Spirit, not our project.

The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King — this is exactly the morning declaration of the first practice. Let Jesus receive all the glory — this is exactly what the third practice says: love makes us one, and oneness brings the Lord glory.

The Goal: establish God’s system — this is exactly the theme of the second part of the lesson text: turning from the Worldly system into God’s system.

The Old Self Is Self-Centred; the New Self Is Selfless

The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of every problem. In the Garden of Eden, the words “you will be like God” (Genesis 3:5) marked the first time humanity wanted to leave its originally intended position, seize rights and take God’s place.

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God.

James says, “But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble’” (James 4:6). And again, “Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he will exalt you” (James 4:10). Notice that phrase “humble yourselves”: it is the very same road as 2 Chronicles 7:14.

Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. It is so in a family, so in a church, and so in a nation. Very often revival is slow in coming, not because God is unwilling, but because in our relationships with one another each of us is still sitting on our own throne and refusing to come down.

The Fivefold Change

321 says change is fivefold: mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change the daily living.

Put this lesson into that framework, and the thread becomes very clear.

A change of mindset: revival is not something we wait for, but something we walk out. This is the first mindset this lesson wants to replace.

A change of life: from the self-centred life to selflessness, from me being in charge to letting Jesus be King.

A change of daily living: active obedience every day and fasting and prayer every week — revival now has a rhythm and habits.

A change of relationships: choosing to deny ourselves every week and letting love flow in our relationships.

A change of ministry: when life, daily living and relationships have all been renewed, the expansion of the Kingdom is the natural result, not a performance squeezed out by sheer effort.

So the order is: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. And the priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things.

The Shifts of Perspective

From man’s perspective to God’s perspective: no longer asking, “What’s in this for me?” but asking, “Lord, what do you want me to do?”

From the earthly to the heavenly: no longer seeing only the difficulties in front of us, but seeing the One who sits on the throne.

From the temporal to the eternal: “For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal” (2 Corinthians 4:18).

From the worldly to the godly: no longer conformed to this world, but transformed by the renewing of our minds.

The Path of Serving and the Ultimate Goal

The Path of Serving in 321 is: Spirit (the Holy Spirit is my guide), Understanding (the Bible is my standard), Life (Jesus is my role model), Service (let Jesus be King), God (let Jesus receive all the glory).

And our goal is to establish God’s system, fulfilling what the Lord’s Prayer says, “Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven” (Matthew 6:10), pressing on into the end time revival and walking alongside every person until they become an overcomer.

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? The three practices of this lesson are not just three good habits. They are three doors into God’s system: active obedience every day is the door with God; fasting and prayer every week is the door with ourselves; choosing to deny ourselves every week is the door with others. When all three doors are open, revival begins to flow out from you.

sections.heading: 7. Putting It into Practice: Walking into Revival through the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset
sections.html:
The lesson text gives us three very concrete practices. Now let’s use the eight stages of changing our mindset from 321 — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to plant these three practices firmly into our daily living.

Stage 1: Information

First let the truth get into your head. Copy the three practices of this lesson onto a card and stick it somewhere you are sure to see it every day:

1. Each morning pray about sovereignty, and before every conflict or decision, first ask the Lord silently, “Jesus, what do you want me to do?”

2. Choose one day each week to fast (at least one meal), set aside time for quiet solitude, focus on prayer, and write down the key things the Holy Spirit brings to mind.

3. Each week take the initiative to care for one person, help or bless others with practical action, and name them before God in prayer, asking him to bless them.

At the same time, memorise 2 Chronicles 7:14. Information is not the same as life, but without information the Holy Spirit has no material to work with.

Stage 2: Revelation

Ask the Holy Spirit to turn information into revelation. Pray, “Lord, please show me where, on my side, I am still not aligned with your heart.”

Then be still for three minutes and write down the first thing the Holy Spirit brings to mind. That one thing is very often where your personal revival begins.

Stage 3: Conviction

Conviction is when your heart truly believes this is right and willingly accepts it.

Face the resistance in your heart honestly: “Where would I find the time in the morning?” “Fasting makes me dizzy.” “That person wronged me first.” Write these objections down one by one, and beside each one write a verse of Scripture as your answer. For example, if the objection is “I don’t have time”, write the verse “In the morning I will lay my requests before you” (Psalm 5:3).

Stage 4: Implementation

Start today. Don’t wait until next Monday.

Tomorrow morning, don’t touch your phone first. Close your eyes and say that one sentence: “Lord Jesus, today I am not the one in charge; you are King.” Thirty seconds is enough.

Within this week, choose a day and a meal to fast, and use that time to be still.

Within this week, settle on that one person, and decide what concrete way you will use — an apology, a word of encouragement, a meal, a hug.

Stage 5: Evaluation

Set a fixed time each week (Sunday evening is a good choice), take out your notebook, and honestly ask yourself three questions:

This week, on how many days did I really give up the throne in the morning?

Did my fasting tear my heart, or only my garments?

What I did for that one person — did it come from love, or from duty?

Stage 6: Correction

Evaluation is not for condemnation; it is for correction.

If you can’t manage the mornings, set your alarm ten minutes earlier, or charge your phone in the living room. If fasting a whole day is too much, start with one meal. If the relationship with that person is too strained, start with a single text message.

The principle of correction is: lower the threshold, not the standard. Better small and lasting than big and abandoned.

Stage 7: Repetition

Remember those sixty-six days? Lally’s research reminds us that new habits take time.

Give yourself one season — three months. Over those three months, allow yourself to miss a few days, but don’t allow yourself to stop. If you miss a day, pick it up again the next day. Don’t let the enemy pin you down with the words, “Look, you’ve failed again.”

“Let’s not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season, if we don’t give up” (Galatians 6:9).

Stage 8: Multiplication

Revival will always multiply in the end; otherwise it isn’t revival.

Find a brother or sister, share these three practices with them, and invite them to walk with you for three months, checking in with each other once a week. This is what 321 calls a “2” — becoming spiritual companions with someone who is selfless.

Then, once they too are standing firm, encourage them to take someone else along. That is a “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children.

The Moravian prayer began with twenty-four plus twenty-four; the New York revival began with six people. Brothers and sisters, God never looks at the size of the starting point. He only looks at whether you are willing to multiply.

sections.heading: 8. Closing and Call: Step by Step, Revival Begins with You
sections.html:
As for the lesson text’s closing words, I want to read them to you almost word for word, because they already say it well enough.

Dear brothers and sisters, revival will not suddenly drop out of the sky; it begins little by little in your life and mine. Today, if we are willing to begin to obey, to fast and seek, to choose to deny ourselves and live out selflessness, the Spirit of God will move among us, bringing renewal and transformation.

This is God’s moment — not some time in the future, and not waiting for someone else. It is now, and it is you.

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully to those two words: it’s you.

Not waiting for the pastor to warm up first, not waiting for the small-group leader to change first, not waiting for your spouse to apologise first, not waiting for the church to have a vision first. It’s you.

Because revival has never been the name of an event. Revival is what happens when one person kneels down before God first.

When Moses saw the bush burning and yet not consumed, he said, “I will go now, and see this great sight” (Exodus 3:3). If he had not turned aside, God would not have called to him from the bush. Brothers and sisters, God’s fire is already there. The question is whether you will turn aside.

“Do this, knowing the time, that it is already time for you to awaken out of sleep, for salvation is now nearer to us than when we first believed” (Romans 13:11).

“Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the Lord’s work, because you know that your labor is not in vain in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 15:58).

May we rise up, no longer looking on, no longer putting it off, but with one choice, one prayer and one action, press on into the great revival God has already prepared for us.

One choice — today I am not in charge; you are King.

One prayer — Lord, revive your work in the middle of the years.

One action — today I will go and love that one person.

Let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. This is revival, and it is the direction of our whole lives.

keyVerses: “If my people, who are called by my name, will humble themselves, pray, seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then I will hear from heaven, will forgive their sin, and will heal their land” (2 Chronicles 7:14).
practices: Each morning pray about sovereignty; before every conflict or decision, first ask the Lord silently, “Jesus, what do you want me to do?”
Choose one day each week to fast (at least one meal); set aside quiet time alone to focus on prayer, and write down the key things the Holy Spirit brings to mind.
Each week take the initiative to care for one person; help or bless them with practical action, and name them in prayer for blessing.
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you.

You have said that if your people, who are called by your name, will humble themselves, pray, seek your face, and turn from their wicked ways, you will hear from heaven, forgive our sin and heal our land. Lord, today we stand on this promise.
Forgive us for our passivity. We have waited too long without breaking up the fallow ground; we have sought your hand far too much, and sought your face far too little.
Lord, I humble myself before you. I hand my throne back to you. From this morning on, I am not the one in charge; you are King.
Holy Spirit, help me, before every conflict and every decision, first to be still and ask you, “Jesus, what do you want me to do?”
Give me a heart that longs for you, willing to stop each week and set apart time to seek you alone. Speak to me in the stillness, and let me hear your still small voice.
Pour your love into my heart, so that this week I can step out towards that one person — to say that apology, to give that word of encouragement, to give the time it takes to share that meal.
Lord, revive me, so that through me you can revive my family, my small group, my church and my city.
Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: 2 Chronicles 7:14 says, “If my people, who are called by my name, will humble themselves, pray, seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then I will hear from heaven, will forgive their sin, and will heal their land.” Of these four things — humbling yourself, praying, seeking his face and turning from wicked ways — which do you feel is currently your weakest? What, specifically, is the one thing the Holy Spirit has been reminding you these past few days to turn away from?

Luke 9:23 says, “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.” This week, which “2” will you choose, and what concrete action will you take to express Christ’s love to them? Please say that name and that action out loud in your small group, so that everyone can pray for you and also hold you accountable.
